### The Kronecker symbol matches primitive real characters with quadratic fields

**Remember:** Allow any integer below the bar, and characters become symbols.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11A15 (Power residues, reciprocity), 11R11, 11M06. arXiv math.NT. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** For integers D and n ≠ 0, (D/n) is the product of the Legendre symbols (D/p) over the odd primes p dividing \|n\|, with multiplicity. Each factor 2 gives 0 for even D, +1 for D ≡ ±1 modulo 8 and −1 otherwise, and the sign of n gives −1 when D and n are both negative. At n = 0, (D/0) is 1 if \|D\| = 1 and 0 otherwise (our own details).

**Problem.** For every nonzero D ≡ 0 or 1 modulo 4, n ↦ (D/n) is a real Dirichlet character modulo \|D\|, primitive exactly when D is a fundamental discriminant (1 included by convention). The nontrivial primitive ones correspond bijectively to quadratic fields, and for the field of discriminant D, (D/p) is 1, −1 or 0 as p splits, stays prime or ramifies.

**How the definition helps.** Because the symbol has a value at every integer, including negative and even ones, it can be a character on all of ℤ (our own). Quadratic reciprocity gives periodicity, the classification of quadratic characters gives primitivity, and the quadratic splitting law gives the prime behaviour (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Kronecker symbol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kronecker_symbol). It says: “In particular, primitive real Dirichlet characters χ are in a 1–1 correspondence with quadratic fields F=ℚ(√m), where m is a nonzero square-free integer”

**Sources:**

- [L. Kronecker, Zur Theorie der elliptischen Funktionen, Sitzungsberichte der Preussischen Akademie der Wissenschaften zu Berlin (1885) 761–784](https://archive.org/stream/sitzungsberichte1885deutsch#page/760) (link not checked)

### Counting cyclic generators gives the totient divisor sum

**Remember:** Each element generates exactly one subgroup, so each is counted once.

*True by definition.* MSC 11A25 (Arithmetic functions; related numbers; inversion formulas). arXiv math.NT. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** Define φ(d) as the number of generators of a cyclic group of order d, the elements whose powers fill the group. In a cyclic group of order n, the elements of order d are the generators of its subgroup of order d.

**Problem.** For n ≥ 1, the sum of φ(d) over the positive divisors d of n is n.

**How the definition helps.** Sorting the n elements by their order counts each once, and order d has φ(d) elements (our own argument). This works because a cyclic group of order n has exactly one subgroup of each order d dividing n.

**Wikipedia:** [Euler's totient function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euler%27s_totient_function). It says: “φ(d) is also equal to the number of possible generators of the cyclic group”

### Counting divisible integers makes the totient a Möbius sum

**Remember:** Weight common divisors by Möbius values to test coprimality.

*True by definition.* MSC 11A25 (Arithmetic functions; related numbers; inversion formulas). arXiv math.NT. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** Euler’s totient φ(n) counts the k from 1 to n with gcd(k, n) = 1. Test this condition with the sum of μ(d) over the common divisors d of k and n, which is 1 when gcd(k, n) = 1 and 0 otherwise.

**Problem.** For each positive integer n, φ(n) is the sum of μ(d)·(n/d) over positive divisors d of n.

**How the definition helps.** Swapping the order of the sums counts each divisor d of n once for each of its n/d multiples up to n, with weight μ(d) (our own argument). The test works because the common divisors of k and n are the divisors of gcd(k, n), and the Möbius divisor sum is 1 at 1 and 0 above 1.

**Paper or page:** [Euler Phi Function in terms of Möbius Function](https://proofwiki.org/wiki/Euler_Phi_Function_in_terms_of_Möbius_Function). It says: “∑ (d \| n) μ(d) n/d = φ(n)”

### Counting modular units makes Euler’s totient multiplicative

**Remember:** A pair is invertible exactly when both coordinates are invertible.

*True by definition.* MSC 11A25 (Arithmetic functions; related numbers; inversion formulas), 11A07. arXiv math.NT. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** Define φ(n) as the number of units in ℤ/nℤ, the residues modulo n that have a multiplicative inverse.

**How the definition helps.** Under the Chinese remainder isomorphism ℤ/mn ≅ ℤ/m × ℤ/n, a residue is a unit exactly when both coordinates are, so φ(mn) = φ(m)φ(n). Bézout’s identity shows that the units are the residues coprime to n, which matches the usual count (our own).

**nLab:** [multiplicative group of integers modulo n](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/multiplicative+group+of+integers+modulo+n). It says: “This is a corollary of the Chinese remainder theorem, which asserts that the canonical ring map ℤ/mn → ℤ/m × ℤ/n is an isomorphism if m, n are coprime.”

**Wikipedia:** [Euler's totient function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euler%27s_totient_function). It says: “the group of units of the ring ℤ/nℤ”

### Dirichlet convolution makes divisor power sums multiplicative

**Remember:** Divisor power sums are convolutions of two multiplicative functions.

*True by definition.* MSC 11A25 (Arithmetic functions; related numbers; inversion formulas). arXiv math.NT. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** The Dirichlet convolution f ∗ g sums f(d)g(n/d) over the positive divisors d of n. Define σₖ = 𝟙 ∗ gₖ, where 𝟙 is constantly 1 and gₖ(n) = nᵏ, so σₖ(n) sums the kth powers of the divisors of n.

**Problem.** If m and n are coprime positive integers, then σₖ(mn) = σₖ(m)σₖ(n). This includes the divisor count when k = 0.

**How the definition helps.** 𝟙 and gₖ are multiplicative, and convolution keeps this property, so σₖ is multiplicative. Convolution keeps it because each divisor of mn, for coprime m and n, is uniquely a divisor of m times a divisor of n.

**Wikipedia:** [Dirichlet convolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dirichlet_convolution), [Divisor function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Divisor_function). It says: “The Dirichlet convolution of two multiplicative functions is again multiplicative”

### Prime-power series turn convolution into ordinary multiplication

**Remember:** Split each exponent independently and multiply the resulting series.

*True by definition.* MSC 11A25 (Arithmetic functions; related numbers; inversion formulas). arXiv math.NT. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** A multiplicative function f has f(1) = 1 and f(ab) = f(a)f(b) whenever a and b share no prime; at each prime p, encode it by the series whose coefficient of Xᵏ is f(pᵏ). The Dirichlet convolution of f and g at n sums f(a)g(b) over ab = n. At pᵏ this sums f(pⁱ)g(pʲ) over i + j = k, the degree-k coefficient of the product series.

**Problem.** The Dirichlet convolution of two multiplicative functions is multiplicative. Its series at each prime is the product of the input series at that prime.

**How the definition helps.** Unique prime factorization makes the splits of the exponent at different primes independent, so the convolution at n is the product of its values at the prime powers of n (our own argument). At each prime, those values are the coefficients of the product series (our own argument).

**Paper or page:** [Dirichlet Convolution Preserves Multiplicativity](https://proofwiki.org/wiki/Dirichlet_Convolution_Preserves_Multiplicativity). It says: “Then their Dirichlet convolution f ∗ g is again multiplicative.”

### Prime-power sums multiply to give the Euler product

**Remember:** An Euler product chooses one exponent for each prime.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11A25 (Arithmetic functions; related numbers; inversion formulas), 11M41. arXiv math.NT. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** A complex function f on positive integers is multiplicative if f(1) = 1 and f(ab) = f(a)f(b) for coprime a and b. Its local factor at a prime p is ∑ₖ≥₀ f(pᵏ), and multiplying local factors picks one prime power from each.

**Problem.** Suppose f is multiplicative and the sum of \|f(n)\| over positive integers converges. The sum of f(n) then equals the product of its local factors over all primes.

**How the definition helps.** By unique factorization, the product of the local factors at primes up to x is the sum of f(n) over the n whose prime factors are all at most x (our own argument). Absolute convergence makes these sums tend to the full sum as x grows (our own argument).

**Wikipedia:** [Euler product](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euler_product). It says: “the existence of such a formal Euler product expansion is a necessary and sufficient condition that a(n) be multiplicative”

**Paper or page:** [Product Form of Sum on Completely Multiplicative Function](https://proofwiki.org/wiki/Product_Form_of_Sum_on_Completely_Multiplicative_Function). It says: “where the infinite product ranges over the primes.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Primitive root sums make the Möbius divisor sum vanish

**Remember:** Sum roots of exact order n to get μ(n).

*True by definition.* MSC 11A25 (Arithmetic functions; related numbers; inversion formulas), 11R18. arXiv math.NT. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** Define μ(n) as the sum of the primitive nth roots of unity, the roots for which n is the least positive power giving 1. Every nth root of unity is primitive for exactly one order d dividing n.

**Problem.** The sum of μ(d) over all positive divisors d of n is 1 if n = 1 and 0 otherwise.

**How the definition helps.** So the sum of μ(d) over the divisors d of n is the sum of all nth roots of unity. This is 1 for n = 1, and 0 for n &gt; 1 by the geometric series (our own). The usual formula has the same divisor sums, so Möbius inversion makes the two agree (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Möbius function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/M%C3%B6bius_function). It says: “each nth root of unity is a primitive dth root of unity for exactly one divisor d of n.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Square divisors give a count of squarefree integers

**Remember:** Use Möbius weights on square divisors to count numbers without them.

*True by definition.* MSC 11A25 (Arithmetic functions; related numbers; inversion formulas), 11N25. arXiv math.NT. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** A positive integer is squarefree when no prime square divides it. By the Möbius divisor sum, its indicator, 1 for squarefree and 0 otherwise, is the sum of μ(d) over the positive d with d² dividing it.

**Problem.** The fraction of squarefree integers among the first N positive integers tends to 6/π² as N grows.

**How the definition helps.** Summing the indicator up to N gives the sum of μ(d)⌊N/d²⌋ over d ≤ √N (our own argument). Removing the floors and extending the sum cost O(√N), so the fraction tends to ∑ μ(d)/d² = 1/ζ(2). The Euler product and the Basel sum ζ(2) = π²/6 give 6/π².

**Wikipedia:** [Square-free integer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Square-free_integer). It says: “Q(x) = 6x/π² + O(√x).”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### The unit group exponent gives Carmichael’s least universal power

**Remember:** The group exponent is the least power that sends every element to one.

*True by definition.* MSC 11A25 (Arithmetic functions; related numbers; inversion formulas), 11A07. arXiv math.NT. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** For n ≥ 2, λ(n) is the exponent of the group of units modulo n, the least positive power that sends every invertible residue to 1.

**Problem.** Every residue a coprime to n satisfies a<sup>λ</sup>(n) ≡ 1 modulo n, and no smaller positive power works for all such a. Also λ(n) divides φ(n), the number of invertible residues modulo n.

**How the definition helps.** The first two claims are the definition. The exponent is the least common multiple of the element orders, and each order divides φ(n) by Lagrange’s theorem (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Carmichael function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carmichael_function). It says: “if λ(n) is considered as defined by the recurrence of the previous section, then it satisfies the property stated in the introduction”

**Sources:**

- [R. D. Carmichael, Note on a new number theory function, Bulletin of the American Mathematical Society 16 (1910), 232–238](https://doi.org/10.1090/S0002-9904-1910-01892-9)

### The product definition of primes makes factorization unique

**Remember:** A prime that divides a product divides a factor, which you can cancel.

*True by definition.* MSC 11A51 (Factorization; primality), 13F15. arXiv math.NT, math.AC. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** Call an integer p prime if \|p\| &gt; 1 and, whenever p divides a product, it divides one of the factors.

**Problem.** If a nonzero integer factors into primes, the factorization is unique up to order and signs.

**How the definition helps.** In two prime factorizations of one integer, the first prime on one side divides one prime on the other side (our own). If one prime divides another, they differ only by a sign, so cancel the pair and repeat (our own). Euclid’s lemma, through Bézout’s identity, shows that this agrees with the usual definition by divisors.

**Wikipedia:** [Euclid's lemma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euclid%27s_lemma). It says: “It is used to define prime elements, a generalization of prime numbers to arbitrary commutative rings.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### A repeating block fixes a quadratic irrational

**Remember:** A repeating tail is a fixed point of its block map.

*True by definition.* MSC 11A55 (Continued fractions). arXiv math.NT. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** Read each continued fraction digit a as the map t ↦ a + 1/t, and a block of digits as the composite of its digit maps. The composite is a fraction t ↦ (At + B)/(Ct + D) with integer coefficients.

**Problem.** An irrational real number with an eventually periodic regular continued fraction satisfies a quadratic equation with integer coefficients.

**How the definition helps.** A repeating tail t is a fixed point of its block map, so Ct² + (D − A)t − B = 0 (our own argument). Positive digits give C &gt; 0, so the equation is truly quadratic. The initial digits apply a map with integer coefficients to t, which keeps the number in the same quadratic field.

**Wikipedia:** [Periodic continued fraction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Periodic_continued_fraction). It says: “if x is a regular periodic continued fraction, then x is a quadratic irrational number.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Matrix products give the determinant formula for continued fraction convergents

**Remember:** Multiply digit matrices in order to put consecutive convergents side by side.

*True by definition.* MSC 11A55 (Continued fractions). arXiv math.NT. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** For a continued fraction with integer a₀ and positive integer later digits aᵢ, let Mᵢ be the matrix with rows (aᵢ, 1) and (1, 0), which has determinant −1. Define hₙ and kₙ by the rows (hₙ, hₙ₋₁) and (kₙ, kₙ₋₁) of M₀⋯Mₙ, so hₙ/kₙ is the nth convergent.

**Problem.** For n ≥ 1, kₙhₙ₋₁ − kₙ₋₁hₙ = (−1)ⁿ. Thus hₙ and kₙ have no common divisor greater than one. Consecutive convergents differ by ±1/(kₙkₙ₋₁).

**How the definition helps.** The left side is minus the determinant of the product, and that determinant is (−1)ⁿ⁺¹. So a common divisor of hₙ and kₙ divides 1, and dividing by kₙkₙ₋₁ gives the difference of convergents. Each Mᵢ represents t ↦ aᵢ + 1/t, so the product builds the usual nested fraction (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Simple continued fraction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simple_continued_fraction). It says: “has determinant (−1)ⁿ⁺¹, and thus belongs to the group of 2 × 2 unimodular matrices GL(2, ℤ).”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Reduced quadratic surds are exactly those with purely periodic continued fractions

**Remember:** Above one, conjugate between minus one and zero: it repeats at once.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11A55 (Continued fractions), 11R11. arXiv math.NT. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** A quadratic surd ζ = (P + √D)/Q has integers P, Q and D, with D &gt; 0 not a square and Q dividing P² − D. It is reduced when ζ &gt; 1 and its conjugate η = (P − √D)/Q lies between −1 and 0.

**Problem.** The continued fraction of a quadratic surd repeats from its first term exactly when the surd is reduced. Then the expansion of −1/η repeats the same block in reverse order.

**How the definition helps.** These inequalities are exactly the hypotheses of Galois’s theorem on pure periodicity. On reduced surds, −1/η undoes one step of the continued fraction, so it runs the repeating block backwards (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Periodic continued fraction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Periodic_continued_fraction). It says: “Galois proved that the regular continued fraction which represents a quadratic surd ζ is purely periodic if and only if ζ is a reduced surd.”

**Sources:**

- [É. Galois, Démonstration d'un théorème sur les fractions continues périodiques, Annales de Mathématiques pures et appliquées 19 (1828–1829) 294–301](https://www.numdam.org/item/AMPA_1828-1829__19__294_0/)

### The coefficient definition of binomial coefficients gives Lucas’s theorem

**Remember:** Read binomial coefficients as polynomial coefficients, then factor by base-p digits.

*True by definition.* MSC 11B65 (Binomial coefficients; factorials; q-identities), 11A07. arXiv math.NT, math.CO. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** Define C(m, n) as the coefficient of Xⁿ in (1 + X)ᵐ, for nonnegative integers m and n. Modulo p, (1 + X)ᵐ splits by the base-p digits mᵢ of m into the product of the factors (1 + X<sup>(pⁱ)</sup>)<sup>(mᵢ)</sup>.

**Problem.** Let p be prime and let mᵢ and nᵢ be the base-p digits of m and n. Then C(m, n) is congruent modulo p to the product of C(mᵢ, nᵢ) over the digit positions.

**How the definition helps.** Repeating (1 + X)ᵖ ≡ 1 + Xᵖ gives (1 + X)<sup>(pⁱ)</sup> ≡ 1 + X<sup>(pⁱ)</sup> modulo p. Since base-p expansion is unique, Xⁿ in the product takes X<sup>(pⁱ)</sup> to the power nᵢ from the ith factor, contributing C(mᵢ, nᵢ). That coefficient is zero when nᵢ &gt; mᵢ (our own explanation).

**Wikipedia:** [Lucas's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lucas%27s_theorem). It says: “Comparing the coefficients of Xⁿ in the very first and last sum, we obtain Lucas's theorem.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Generating functions make Bernoulli polynomial differences telescope to power sums

**Remember:** Shifting x multiplies by exp(t), which cancels the denominator.

*True by definition.* MSC 11B68 (Bernoulli and Euler numbers and polynomials). arXiv math.NT, math.CO. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** Define Bₙ(x) as n! times the coefficient of tⁿ in t exp(xt)/(exp(t) − 1). Shifting x to x + 1 multiplies this series by exp(t), so the difference of the two series is t exp(xt), with no denominator (our own).

**Problem.** For n ≥ 1, Bₙ(x + 1) − Bₙ(x) = nxⁿ⁻¹. For positive integers p and m, the sum of kᵖ from k = 0 to m − 1 equals (Bₚ₊₁(m) − Bₚ₊₁(0))/(p + 1).

**How the definition helps.** The coefficient of tⁿ in t exp(xt) is xⁿ⁻¹/(n − 1)!, so Bₙ(x + 1) − Bₙ(x) = nxⁿ⁻¹. Summing this from x = 0 to m − 1 with n = p + 1 cancels all middle values. The integral definition agrees, since integrating the series from x to x + 1 gives exp(xt) (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Bernoulli polynomials](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bernoulli_polynomials). It says: “Using either the above integral representation of xⁿ or the identity Bₙ(x + 1) − Bₙ(x) = nxⁿ⁻¹, we have”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Taking B₁ = +1/2 removes a sign exception from two formulas

**Remember:** Plus one half is what ζ(0) = −1/2 asks for.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11B68 (Bernoulli and Euler numbers and polynomials), 11B57. arXiv math.NT. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** For n ≥ 0, define Bₙ as n! times the coefficient of tⁿ in t/(1 − exp(−t)), which gives B₁ = +1/2 (our own formulation). This series is t/(exp(t) − 1) + t, so it differs from the other convention only at B₁.

**Problem.** For integers n ≥ 1 and m ≥ 0, 1ᵐ + ⋯ + nᵐ = (1/(m + 1)) ∑ₖ₌₀ᵐ C(m + 1, k) Bₖ nᵐ⁺¹⁻ᵏ. Also Bₙ = −nζ(1 − n) for every integer n ≥ 1.

**How the definition helps.** The plus sign on B₁ makes the k = 1 term +nᵐ/2, as a sum that ends at n needs. The zeta formula needs the same sign, since ζ(0) = −1/2 (our own explanation).

**Wikipedia:** [Bernoulli number](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bernoulli_number). It says: “In the above Knuth meant B₁⁻; instead using B₁⁺ the formula avoids subtraction”

**Sources:**

- [D. E. Knuth, Johann Faulhaber and sums of powers, Mathematics of Computation (1993)](https://doi.org/10.1090/S0025-5718-1993-1197512-7)

### The generating function makes Bernoulli polynomial reflection one substitution

**Remember:** Swapping x for 1 − x just flips the sign of t.

*True by definition. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11B68 (Bernoulli and Euler numbers and polynomials). arXiv math.NT. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** Define the Bernoulli polynomial Bₙ(x) as n! times the coefficient of tⁿ in t·exp(tx)/(exp(t) − 1). In this series, replacing x by 1 − x has the same effect as replacing t by −t.

**Problem.** For every n ≥ 0, Bₙ(1 − x) = (−1)ⁿBₙ(x).

**How the definition helps.** In our own calculation, t·exp(t(1 − x))/(exp(t) − 1) equals (−t)·exp(−tx)/(exp(−t) − 1). Comparing coefficients of tⁿ gives the factor (−1)ⁿ.

**Paper or page:** [Generating Function for Bernoulli Polynomials](https://proofwiki.org/wiki/Generating_Function_for_Bernoulli_Polynomials). It says: “Then the generating function for Bₙ is:”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Change of polynomial basis makes the Stirling matrices inverse

**Remember:** Changing basis back undoes the first change.

*True by definition.* MSC 11B73 (Bell and Stirling numbers), 05A10. arXiv math.CO. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** The signed first-kind Stirling numbers express each falling factorial x(x − 1)⋯(x − n + 1), with the empty product 1 for n = 0, in powers of x. The second-kind numbers express each power xⁿ in falling factorials, so the two tables convert between the same two bases in opposite directions.

**Problem.** For any degree bound, the two square tables of Stirling coefficients, from degree zero to that bound, are inverse matrices.

**How the definition helps.** Converting to powers and back changes nothing, and polynomial coefficients are unique, so the product of the tables is the identity matrix (our own proof). Starting from counting definitions would first need the coefficients identified with signed counts of permutations by cycles and with counts of set partitions.

**Paper or page:** [Inverse of Stirling's Triangle expressed as Matrix](https://proofwiki.org/wiki/Inverse_of_Stirling's_Triangle_expressed_as_Matrix). It says: “Then: A = B⁻¹ that is: B = A⁻¹”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Missing labels give the explicit second Stirling formula

**Remember:** Subtract functions that miss labels, then forget the label names.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11B73 (Bell and Stirling numbers), 05A10, 05A18. arXiv math.CO. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** Define S(n,k) as the number of onto functions from n inputs to k labeled targets, functions that use every target, divided by k! for the labelings.

**Problem.** For positive integers n and k, k! S(n,k) equals the sum of (−1)ᵏ⁻ʲ (k choose j) jⁿ over j from 0 through k.

**How the definition helps.** Inclusion–exclusion counts onto functions by removing those that miss a target. Functions into a fixed set of j allowed targets number jⁿ, which gives the alternating sum (our own count). Forgetting target names turns each onto function into a partition into k blocks, and each partition has k! labelings.

**Wikipedia:** [Stirling numbers of the second kind](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stirling_numbers_of_the_second_kind). It says: “This can be derived by using inclusion-exclusion to count the surjections from n to k”

**Paper or page:** [Sum over k of m choose k by -1<sup>m-k</sup> by k to the n](https://proofwiki.org/wiki/Sum_over_k_of_m_choose_k_by_-1^m-k_by_k_to_the_n). It says: “∑ₖ (m choose k) (−1)ᵐ⁻ᵏ kⁿ = m! {n brace m}”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### An integer basis describes all solutions of a linear equation

**Remember:** One basis vector carries the value; the other leaves it unchanged.

*True by definition.* MSC 11D04 (Linear Diophantine equations), 11A05. arXiv math.NT. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** For integers a and b, not both zero, with greatest common divisor d, use the integer basis u = (r, s) and v = (b/d, −a/d) of ℤ², where ar + bs = d. In this basis the pair hu + tv has ax + by = hd, whatever t is.

**Problem.** The equation ax + by = c has integer solutions exactly when d divides c. If so, all solution pairs are (c/d)u + tv with t any integer.

**How the definition helps.** Since ax + by = hd, the equation ax + by = c says h = c/d and leaves t free (our own). Bézout’s identity supplies u. The matrix with columns u and v has determinant −1, so every integer pair has unique integer coordinates h and t.

**Paper or page:** [Solution of Linear Diophantine Equation](https://proofwiki.org/wiki/Solution_of_Linear_Diophantine_Equation). It says: “x = x₀ + (b/d)k, y = y₀ − (a/d)k”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Excluding square n gives Pell's equation infinitely many solutions

**Remember:** Exclude square parameters and choose the positive solution with least x.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11D09 (Quadratic and bilinear Diophantine equations), 11A55. arXiv math.NT. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** Pell's equation is x² − ny² = 1, with n a given positive integer that is not a perfect square. Its fundamental solution is the solution in positive integers with the smallest x.

**Problem.** For every nonsquare positive n, Pell's equation has a fundamental solution (x₁, y₁). All solutions in positive integers come from xₖ + yₖ√n = (x₁ + y₁√n)ᵏ.

**How the definition helps.** Excluding squares removes n = m², where (x − my)(x + my) = 1 forces y = 0 (our own). Lagrange’s theorem gives a positive solution for every nonsquare n, so a least one exists. Dividing any positive solution x + y√n repeatedly by x₁ + y₁√n lands in \[1, x₁ + y₁√n), and only 1 lies there, since a norm-one unit above 1 has positive coefficients (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Pell's equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pell%27s_equation). It says: “Joseph Louis Lagrange proved that, as long as n is not a perfect square, Pell's equation has infinitely many distinct integer solutions.”

**Sources:**

- [H. W. Lenstra Jr., Solving the Pell equation, Notices of the AMS 49 (2002) 182–192](https://www.ams.org/notices/200202/fea-lenstra.pdf) (link not checked)

### Pell solutions form a group as units of norm one

**Remember:** Norm-one elements multiply, and their conjugates give inverses.

*True by definition.* MSC 11D09 (Quadratic and bilinear Diophantine equations), 11R27. arXiv math.NT. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** For a positive nonsquare integer n, a Pell solution (x, y) is the number x + y√n in ℤ\[√n\] whose norm (x + y√n)(x − y√n) = x² − ny² equals 1. The norm is multiplicative, because replacing √n by −√n preserves products (our own).

**Problem.** The Pell solutions form a group under (x, y)(u, v) = (xu + nyv, xv + yu). The identity is (1, 0), and (x, −y) is the inverse of (x, y).

**How the definition helps.** Norms multiply, so a product of Pell solutions is a Pell solution, and x − y√n is the inverse because its product with x + y√n is 1 (our own). The rule on pairs is just multiplication in ℤ\[√n\], so associativity and the identity (1, 0) come for free (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Pell's equation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pell%27s_equation). It says: “a pair of integers (x, y) solves Pell's equation if and only if x + y√n is a unit with norm 1 in ℤ\[√n\].”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### The determinant of one period gives the Pell sign

**Remember:** Each digit flips the determinant, and the determinant is the Pell norm.

*True by definition.* MSC 11D09 (Quadratic and bilinear Diophantine equations), 11A55. arXiv math.NT. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** For a nonsquare integer D &gt; 1, let a be √D rounded down. The period matrix of √D is the product, in digit order, of one matrix \[\[b, 1\], \[1, 0\]\] of determinant −1 for each digit b in the repeating block of √D + a. Each matrix represents the digit map u ↦ b + 1/u.

**Problem.** Let x/y be the convergent formed from the first k digits of √D, where k is its shortest period length. Then x² − Dy² equals −1 for odd k and 1 for even k.

**How the definition helps.** Each digit contributes determinant −1, so the period matrix has determinant (−1)ᵏ (our own argument). Its first column is (x + ay, y), and since it fixes t = √D + a, a root of t² − 2at + a² − D = 0, its second column is ((D − a²)y, x − ay). So the determinant also equals x² − Dy².

**Paper or page:** [Solution to Pell's Equation](https://proofwiki.org/wiki/Solution_to_Pell's_Equation). It says: “and all solutions of: x² − ny² = ±1 are given in this way.”

**Sources:**

- [H. W. Lenstra Jr., Solving the Pell equation, Algorithmic Number Theory (2008), pp. 1–24](https://doi.org/10.1017/9781139049801.002)

### The quadratic norm makes Pell solutions close approximations

**Remember:** The conjugate of a Pell solution is small because the norm has magnitude one.

*True by definition.* MSC 11D09 (Quadratic and bilinear Diophantine equations), 11A55. arXiv math.NT. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** For a positive nonsquare integer D, the norm of x + y√D is its product with its conjugate x − y√D, which is x² − Dy². When the norm is ±1, the conjugate is the reciprocal in size: \|x − y√D\| = 1/(x + y√D).

**Problem.** For positive integer solutions of x² − Dy² = ±1, x/y is a convergent of √D, a fraction obtained by stopping its regular continued fraction.

**How the definition helps.** Norm ±1 makes \|x/y − √D\| = 1/\[y²(x/y + √D)\], which is less than 1/(2y²) since x ≥ y and D ≥ 2 (our own argument). Legendre’s approximation theorem says such close fractions in lowest terms are convergents. Here x and y are coprime, since the square of any common divisor divides 1.

**Paper or page:** [Solution of Pell's Equation is a Convergent](https://proofwiki.org/wiki/Solution_of_Pell's_Equation_is_a_Convergent). It says: “Then a/b is a convergent of √n.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Counting Gaussian factors gives the two-square divisor formula

**Remember:** Count Gaussian integers of norm n, one for each ordered pair of coordinates.

*True by definition.* MSC 11E25 (Sums of squares and representations by other particular quadratic forms), 11A25, 11D09. arXiv math.NT. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** Count the Gaussian integers a + bi of norm a² + b² = n, one for each ordered integer pair, signs and zeros included. Because Gaussian integers factor uniquely, this count is 4 for the units times a product of independent choices, one prime at a time.

**Problem.** Let d₁ and d₃ count positive divisors of n with remainders 1 and 3 modulo 4. For n &gt; 0, the number of pairs is 4(d₁ − d₃).

**How the definition helps.** Unique Gaussian factorization turns the count into 4 times a product of local choices (our own argument). Primes with remainder 1 modulo 4 split into conjugates and give e + 1 choices at exponent e, and 2 gives one choice. Primes with remainder 3 give one choice for even e and none otherwise, and d₁ − d₃ factors over primes in the same way.

**Wikipedia:** [Sum of squares function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sum_of_squares_function). It says: “r₂(n) = 4(d₁(n) − d₃(n))”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Counting representations with order and signs gives Jacobi's four-square formula

**Remember:** Count every sign and order; the count becomes a divisor sum.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11E25 (Sums of squares and representations by other particular quadratic forms), 11F27. arXiv math.NT. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** The number r₄(n) counts ordered integer 4-tuples with x₁² + x₂² + x₃² + x₄² = n, so order and signs both count and r₄(1) = 8. It is the coefficient of qⁿ in θ(q)⁴, where θ(q) sums q<sup>(m²)</sup> over all integers m.

**Problem.** For n ≥ 1, r₄(n) is 8 times the sum of the divisors of n that are not divisible by 4. In particular, r₄(p) = 8(p + 1) for a prime p.

**How the definition helps.** Counting ordered signed tuples makes r₄(n) a coefficient of the fourth power of a theta series (our own). Jacobi’s four-square identity evaluates this coefficient as eight times the stated divisor sum. For a prime p, the divisors 1 and p are both not divisible by 4 (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Jacobi's four-square theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacobi%27s_four-square_theorem). It says: “Two representations are considered different if their terms are in different order or if the integer being squared (not just the square) is different”

**Sources:**

- [M. D. Hirschhorn, A simple proof of Jacobi's four-square theorem, Proc. Amer. Math. Soc. 101 (1987) 436–438](https://doi.org/10.1090/S0002-9939-1987-0908644-9)

### Gaussian divisors give the two-square theorem for primes

**Remember:** Two squares make p a Gaussian norm, so p splits.

*True by definition.* MSC 11E25 (Sums of squares and representations by other particular quadratic forms), 11D09. arXiv math.NT. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** A Gaussian integer a + bi has norm (a + bi)(a − bi) = a² + b², and norms multiply. So a prime p is a sum of two squares exactly when p splits into two Gaussian nonunits, each then of norm p (our own argument).

**Problem.** A prime is a sum of two integer squares exactly when it is 2 or has remainder 1 upon division by 4.

**How the definition helps.** For p with remainder 1 modulo 4, the first supplement to quadratic reciprocity gives u with u² congruent to −1 modulo p. Then p divides (u + i)(u − i) but neither factor, so by unique factorization p is not a Gaussian prime and splits. Also 2 = 1² + 1², and squares modulo 4 rule out primes with remainder 3.

**Paper or page:** [Fermat's Two Squares Theorem](https://proofwiki.org/wiki/Fermat's_Two_Squares_Theorem). It says: “Then p can be expressed as the sum of two squares either: p = 2 or: p ≡ 1 (mod 4)”

**Sources:**

- [L. Euler, Demonstratio theorematis Fermatiani omnem numerum primum formae 4n+1 esse summam duorum quadratorum (1760), E241](https://scholarlycommons.pacific.edu/euler-works/241/)

### Gaussian factorization gives uniqueness for prime two-square sums

**Remember:** Switching Gaussian factors or rotating them does not change the squares.

*True by definition.* MSC 11E25 (Sums of squares and representations by other particular quadratic forms), 11D09. arXiv math.NT. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** Write p = a² + b² as the Gaussian factorization p = (a + bi)(a − bi), where Gaussian integers have integer coordinates. Two Gaussian factors are the same up to a unit when one is the other times 1, −1, i or −i, which only changes signs or swaps coordinates.

**Problem.** If a prime is the sum of two positive squares, the two squares are unique up to order.

**How the definition helps.** Each factor has prime norm p, so it is a Gaussian prime, and unique factorization fixes the pair up to order and units (our own argument). Units and conjugation only change signs or swap a and b, so the squares stay the same up to order.

**Paper or page:** [Fermat's Two Squares Theorem/Uniqueness Lemma](https://proofwiki.org/wiki/Fermat's_Two_Squares_Theorem/Uniqueness_Lemma). It says: “Then that expression would be unique except for the order of the two summands.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Gaussian norms force even exponents at primes that stay prime

**Remember:** A Gaussian prime equal to its conjugate appears twice in a norm.

*True by definition.* MSC 11E25 (Sums of squares and representations by other particular quadratic forms), 11D09. arXiv math.NT. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** View a² + b² as the norm of the Gaussian integer a + bi, its product with its conjugate a − bi, and recall that norms multiply. A prime with remainder 3 modulo 4 stays prime among Gaussian integers and equals its own conjugate, so it divides a + bi and a − bi equally often.

**Problem.** A positive integer is a sum of two integer squares exactly when every prime with remainder 3 modulo 4 has an even exponent.

**How the definition helps.** So each prime with remainder 3 modulo 4 appears in the norm to an even power (our own argument). Conversely, the square of such a prime is its norm, every other prime is a norm by the Gaussian prime classification, and norms multiply.

**Wikipedia:** [Sum of two squares theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sum_of_two_squares_theorem). It says: “its prime decomposition contains no factor pᵏ, where prime p ≡ 3 (mod 4) and k is odd.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Quaternion norms show that sums of four squares multiply

**Remember:** Quaternion norms multiply, so sums of four squares multiply.

*True by definition.* MSC 11E25 (Sums of squares and representations by other particular quadratic forms), 11R52. arXiv math.NT, math.RA. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** A quaternion α = a + bi + cj + dk with real coefficients has conjugate ᾱ = a − bi − cj − dk and squared norm N(α) = αᾱ = a² + b² + c² + d². This norm multiplies: N(αβ) = N(α)N(β).

**Problem.** A product of two sums of four real squares is again a sum of four squares. If both inputs use integers, the resulting squares also use integers.

**How the definition helps.** Conjugation reverses products, so N(αβ) = αββ̄ᾱ = αN(β)ᾱ = N(α)N(β), since N(β) is real (our own). The four coefficients of αβ give the required squares, and they are integers when the input coefficients are integers (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Euler's four-square identity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euler%27s_four-square_identity). It says: “the absolute value of the product of two quaternions is equal to the product of their absolute values”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### A half-open lattice cell turns Blichfeldt’s theorem into overlap

**Remember:** Fold the set into one cell and count overlaps.

*True by definition.* MSC 11H16 (Nonconvex bodies). arXiv math.NT. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** A full lattice is the set of integer combinations of a basis of Euclidean space, and its half-open cell is the set of combinations with coefficients in \[0, 1). The lattice translates of the cell tile space, so each point has exactly one translate inside the cell.

**Problem.** For a full lattice, every bounded measurable set of volume greater than the cell volume contains two distinct points differing by a lattice vector.

**How the definition helps.** Cut the set along the translated cells and move each piece back into the cell by a lattice vector, which preserves volume. Pieces of total volume above the cell volume must overlap. Two points that land together differ by a nonzero lattice vector (our own formulation).

**Wikipedia:** [Blichfeldt's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blichfeldt%27s_theorem). It says: “translate each of those pieces by an integer vector so that they all move into the same unit square.”

**Sources:**

- [H. F. Blichfeldt, A new principle in the geometry of numbers, with some applications, Transactions of the American Mathematical Society 15, 227–235 (1914).](https://doi.org/10.1090/S0002-9947-1914-1500976-6)

### Scaled errors make convergents optimal below the next denominator

**Remember:** Error times denominator becomes linear in the integer pair.

*True by definition.* MSC 11J70 (Continued fractions and generalizations), 11A55. arXiv math.NT. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** For an irrational x, the scaled error of an integer pair (a, b) is \|bx − a\|, the error of a/b multiplied by b. Inside the absolute value, bx − a is linear in (a, b), so signed errors add under integer combinations.

**Problem.** Let p/q and P/Q be successive convergents of an irrational x, fractions from stopping its continued fraction, with q &lt; Q. Among integer pairs (a, b) with 0 &lt; b &lt; Q, the pair (p, q) minimizes the scaled error.

**How the definition helps.** Since the determinant of (p, q) and (P, Q) is ±1, write (a, b) = m(p, q) + n(P, Q) with integers m and n (our own argument). If both are nonzero, 0 &lt; b &lt; Q gives them opposite signs, and the two signed errors also have opposite signs, so the magnitudes add. If n = 0, (a, b) is a positive multiple of (p, q).

**Paper or page:** [Convergents are Best Approximations](https://proofwiki.org/wiki/Convergents_are_Best_Approximations). It says: “\|qₙ x − pₙ\| ≤ \|b x − a\|”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### The next complete quotient gives the exact convergent error

**Remember:** Keep the whole tail, and subtraction leaves the determinant.

*True by definition.* MSC 11J70 (Continued fractions and generalizations), 11A55. arXiv math.NT. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** Stop the continued fraction of an irrational x at the convergent p/q, with previous convergent r/s, but keep the whole remaining tail as one number t, the next complete quotient. Then x = (pt + r)/(qt + s) exactly.

**Problem.** For irrational x, the error \|x − p/q\| equals 1/\[q(qt + s)\]. It is smaller than 1/(qQ), where Q is the next denominator.

**How the definition helps.** Subtracting p/q leaves the numerator rq − ps = ±1 by the convergent recurrences, so \|x − p/q\| = 1/\[q(qt + s)\] (our own argument). The next denominator is Q = q⌊t⌋ + s, which is less than qt + s because t is irrational.

**Paper or page:** [Bound for Difference of Irrational Number with Convergent](https://proofwiki.org/wiki/Bound_for_Difference_of_Irrational_Number_with_Convergent). It says: “\|x − Cₙ\| &lt; 1/(qₙ qₙ₊₁)”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Continuous averages reduce equidistribution to individual Fourier waves

**Remember:** Test each wave, then approximate every continuous test by sums of waves.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11K06 (General theory of distribution modulo 1), 42A10. arXiv math.CA. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** A real sequence is equidistributed modulo one if, for every continuous 1-periodic function f, the average of f over the first N terms tends to the integral of f over \[0, 1\] as N tends to infinity. Because averages are linear and bounded by the maximum of \|f\|, it is enough to test a uniformly dense family of functions.

**Problem.** A real sequence is equidistributed modulo one exactly when its sample averages of exp(2πikx) tend to zero for every nonzero integer k.

**How the definition helps.** Fejér’s theorem makes finite sums of waves exp(2πikx) uniformly dense, and the constant wave always passes, so only nonzero waves need checking (our own). Continuous upper and lower approximations to interval indicators recover the counting definition (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Theorem 1.2 (Weyl's criterion)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.06909v1). It says: “Then (xₙ) is uniformly distributed mod 1 if and only if for every non-zero v ∈ ℤᵏ, lim as N → ∞ of (1/N) ∑ₙ₌₁ᴺ e(v·xₙ) = 0,”

**Sources:**

- [Hermann Weyl, Über die Gleichverteilung von Zahlen mod. Eins (1916)](https://doi.org/10.1007/bf01475864)

### Primitive characters make every Gauss sum have absolute value √N

**Remember:** Primitive means no smaller modulus sees the character.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11L05 (Gauss and Kloosterman sums; generalizations), 11M06. arXiv math.NT. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** A Dirichlet character χ modulo N is primitive if it comes from no smaller modulus: for each proper divisor d of N, some two units congruent modulo d have different χ-values. Its Gauss sum is G(χ) = ∑ χ(a)exp(2πia/N) over residues a modulo N. Primitivity makes the sum ∑ χ(a)exp(2πiab/N) at every frequency b equal χ̄(b)G(χ), even for nonunit b (our own).

**Problem.** For every primitive Dirichlet character χ modulo N, \|G(χ)\| = √N. So G(χ) is never zero, and formulas may divide by it.

**How the definition helps.** By finite Parseval the squared sizes of the sums at all frequencies total Nφ(N), while the identity makes that total φ(N)\|G(χ)\|², so \|G(χ)\|² = N (our own). The principal character modulo 4 is not primitive, and its Gauss sum is i − i = 0 (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Gauss sum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gauss_sum), [Dirichlet character](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dirichlet_character). It says: “If χ is also primitive, then \|G(χ)\|=√N, in particular, it is nonzero.”

**Sources:**

- [H. Davenport, Multiplicative Number Theory, 2nd ed., Graduate Texts in Mathematics 74, Springer, 1980](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-1-4757-5927-3)
- [H. L. Montgomery and R. C. Vaughan, Multiplicative Number Theory I: Classical Theory, Cambridge University Press, 2006](https://doi.org/10.1017/CBO9780511618314)

### The character form makes conjugation of the Gauss sum a sign

**Remember:** Conjugate the exponential and the Legendre symbol supplies the sign.

*True by definition.* MSC 11L05 (Gauss and Kloosterman sums; generalizations), 11A15. arXiv math.NT. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** For an odd prime p and ζ = exp(2πi/p), the quadratic Gauss sum G is ∑ χ(a)ζᵃ over residues a, where χ is the Legendre symbol (0 at zero, 1 on nonzero squares, −1 elsewhere). Since χ(−a) = χ(−1)χ(a), conjugating G, which turns ζᵃ into ζ⁻ᵃ, multiplies it by χ(−1).

**Problem.** The quadratic Gauss sum satisfies G² = χ(−1)p.

**How the definition helps.** So G times its conjugate equals χ(−1)G², and hence G² = χ(−1)\|G\|² (our own argument). The magnitude theorem \|G\|² = p finishes the proof.

**nLab:** [quadratic reciprocity law](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/quadratic+reciprocity+law). It says: “S² = (−1/p) p.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Euler’s product shows zeta has no zeros where Re s &gt; 1

**Remember:** A product of nonzero factors with summable logarithms is not zero.

*True by definition. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11M06 (ζ (s) and L(s, χ)). arXiv math.NT. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** For Re s &gt; 1, write ζ(s) as the Euler product over primes p of 1/(1 − p⁻ˢ), which equals the usual sum of n⁻ˢ. Each factor is nonzero, and the logarithms of the factors are bounded in size by 2p<sup>(−Re s)</sup>, so they sum absolutely.

**Problem.** The Riemann zeta function has no zero in the half-plane Re s &gt; 1.

**How the definition helps.** A product of nonzero factors whose logarithms sum absolutely is the exponential of a finite number, so it cannot vanish (our own). The bound 2p<sup>(−Re s)</sup> comes from the power series for −log(1 − p⁻ˢ), and the sum converges by comparison with ∑ n<sup>(−Re s)</sup> (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Riemann zeta function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riemann_zeta_function). It says: “Both sides of the Euler product formula converge for Re(s) &gt; 1.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Dirichlet convolution gives the product formula for divisor series

**Remember:** Multiply the series to get the divisor sums as coefficients.

*True by definition. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11M41 (Other Dirichlet series and zeta functions), 11A25. arXiv math.NT. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** The Dirichlet convolution f ∗ g is the coefficient sequence of the product of the Dirichlet series ∑ f(n)n⁻ˢ and ∑ g(n)n⁻ˢ. Since m⁻ˢk⁻ˢ = (mk)⁻ˢ, its coefficient at n sums f(d)g(n/d) over the positive divisors d of n.

**Problem.** Let k ≥ 0 be an integer and σₖ(n) the sum of the kth powers of the positive divisors of n. For Re(s) &gt; k + 1, ∑ σₖ(n)n⁻ˢ = ζ(s)ζ(s − k), where ζ(s) is the sum of n⁻ˢ.

**How the definition helps.** σₖ is the convolution of the constant 1 with nᵏ, so its series is the product of ζ(s) and ζ(s − k). For Re(s) &gt; k + 1 both series converge absolutely, which justifies regrouping the product by n (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Dirichlet convolution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dirichlet_convolution). It says: “It describes the multiplication of two Dirichlet series in terms of their coefficients:”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Setting p(0) = 1 makes partition formulas work without special cases

**Remember:** Zero has exactly one partition: the empty one.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11P81 (Elementary theory of partitions), 05A17. arXiv math.NT, math.CO. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** For any integer n, p(n) counts finite multisets of positive integers with sum n. The empty multiset gives p(0) = 1, and no multiset has negative sum.

**Problem.** For n ≥ 1, p(n) = ∑ⱼ≥₁ (−1)ʲ⁺¹\[p(n − gⱼ) + p(n − hⱼ)\], with the pentagonal numbers gⱼ = j(3j − 1)/2 and hⱼ = j(3j + 1)/2. Also ∑ₙ≥₀ p(n)xⁿ equals the formal product of 1/(1 − xᵏ) over k ≥ 1.

**How the definition helps.** With these values the series has constant term 1 and terms with negative arguments vanish, so no formula needs a special case. Each factor 1/(1 − xᵏ) chooses how often the part k appears (our own). Multiplying by Euler’s pentagonal series gives the recurrence.

**Wikipedia:** [Partition function (number theory)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Partition_function_%28number_theory%29). It says: “As base cases, p(0) is taken to equal 1, and p(k) is taken to be zero for negative k.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### A quadratic quotient detects which odd primes stay Gaussian primes

**Remember:** Odd p stays prime when −1 is no square mod p.

*True by definition.* MSC 11R04 (Algebraic numbers; rings of algebraic integers), 13A15. arXiv math.NT, math.AC. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** View the Gaussian integers as ℤ\[x\]/(x² + 1), the polynomials with x² set equal to −1. Then the quotient by p is 𝔽ₚ\[x\]/(x² + 1), which has no zero divisors exactly when x² + 1 has no root modulo p (our own).

**Problem.** An odd prime number p stays prime in the Gaussian integers exactly when it leaves remainder 3 on division by 4.

**How the definition helps.** So p stays prime exactly when −1 is not a square modulo p (our own). For an odd prime p, −1 is a square exactly when p leaves remainder 1 modulo 4, by Euler’s criterion (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Gaussian integer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaussian_integer). It says: “A positive integer is a Gaussian prime if and only if it is a prime number that is congruent to 3 modulo 4”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Primitive roots give the cyclotomic factorization of xⁿ − 1

**Remember:** Group the roots by the first positive power that gives one.

*True by definition.* MSC 11R18 (Cyclotomic extensions), 11C08. arXiv math.NT. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** Define Φₙ as the product of x − ζ over the primitive nth roots of unity ζ, those for which n is the least positive power with ζⁿ = 1.

**Problem.** For every n ≥ 1, xⁿ − 1 is the product of Φₐ over all positive divisors a of n. The degree of Φₙ is φ(n), the number of integers from 1 to n coprime to n.

**How the definition helps.** Each root of xⁿ − 1 has a least power a with ζᵃ = 1, and a divides n, so sorting the roots by a gives the product. The primitive nth roots are exp(2πik/n) with k coprime to n, so Φₙ has degree φ(n).

**Wikipedia:** [Cyclotomic polynomial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cyclotomic_polynomial). It says: “Depending on the chosen definition, it is either the value of the degree or the irreducibility which is a nontrivial result.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### With p-adic integers as residue sequences, compatible residue roots give roots

**Remember:** A polynomial vanishes when it vanishes in every coordinate.

*True by definition.* MSC 11S05 (Polynomials), 12J25. arXiv math.NT. Level 2: later undergraduate.

**Definition.** Fix a prime p. A p-adic integer is a compatible sequence of residues aₙ modulo pⁿ, meaning aₙ₊₁ ≡ aₙ modulo pⁿ, added and multiplied one coordinate at a time.

**Problem.** Let f be a polynomial with p-adic integer coefficients. Then f has a p-adic root exactly when there are roots rₙ of f modulo pⁿ with rₙ₊₁ ≡ rₙ modulo pⁿ for every n.

**How the definition helps.** Because the ring operations act coordinate by coordinate, f at a compatible sequence (rₙ) is the sequence of values f(rₙ) modulo pⁿ, which are all zero (our own). Conversely, reducing a p-adic root modulo each pⁿ gives compatible roots (our own).

**nLab:** [p-adic integer](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/p-adic+integer). It says: “This is also a limit in the category of topological rings, taking the rings in the diagram to have discrete topologies.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Frobenius restriction gives quadratic reciprocity for Legendre symbols

**Remember:** Restrict cyclotomic Frobenius to the quadratic subfield; read its sign twice.

*True by definition.* MSC 11A15 (Power residues, reciprocity), 11R32, 11R18. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For distinct odd primes p and q, let L = ℚ(ζₚ) and let K = ℚ(√p\*) be its quadratic subfield, with p\* = ±p chosen congruent to 1 modulo 4. Frobenius at q is the automorphism of L with ζₚ ↦ ζₚ<sup>q</sup>, the one that induces the qth-power map on residue fields above q, and its sign on √p\* can be read from either description.

**Problem.** For distinct odd primes p and q, the Legendre symbols, which are 1 on nonzero squares and −1 on nonsquares, satisfy (q/p) = (p\*/q).

**How the definition helps.** Frobenius fixes K exactly when q lies in the subgroup of squares modulo p, so its sign on √p\* is (q/p) (our own explanation). As the qth-power map, it sends √p\* to (p\*)<sup>((q−1)/2)</sup>√p\*, which gives sign (p\*/q). A quadratic Gauss sum shows that K is the quadratic subfield of L (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Proofs of quadratic reciprocity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proofs_of_quadratic_reciprocity). It says: “The key fact about φ that we need is that for any subfield K of L, φ fixes K ⟺ q splits completely in K.”

**Paper or page:** [An Infinitely Large Napkin: Alg Nt: Frobenius](https://venhance.github.io/napkin/Napkin.pdf). It says: “For distinct odd primes p, q we have (p/q) = (q\*/p).”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Group transfer turns Gauss’s lemma into a power formula

**Remember:** Gauss’s sign is the transfer, and the transfer is a power.

*True by definition. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11A15 (Power residues, reciprocity), 20K01. arXiv math.NT, math.GR. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For an odd prime p and a residue a not divisible by p, pick one representative r from each pair {x, −x} of nonzero residues. Multiplication by a permutes the pairs, so ar ≡ εᵣs modulo p for a chosen s and a sign εᵣ = ±1, and the transfer of a is the product of these signs.

**Problem.** Let p be an odd prime not dividing a. Gauss’s lemma says the Legendre symbol (a/p), +1 for a square modulo p and −1 otherwise, equals (−1)ᵐ, where m counts the least positive residues of a, 2a, …, ((p − 1)/2)a above p/2.

**How the definition helps.** Multiplying all the equations ar ≡ εᵣs cancels the representatives, so the transfer is a<sup>((p−1)/2)</sup>, which is (a/p) by Euler’s criterion (our own). With representatives 1 through (p − 1)/2, the negative signs are exactly the residues above p/2.

**Wikipedia:** [Gauss's lemma (number theory)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gauss%27s_lemma_%28number_theory%29). It says: “Gauss's lemma may then be viewed as a computation that explicitly identifies this homomorphism as being the quadratic residue character.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Primary Eisenstein integers make cubic reciprocity plain symmetry

**Remember:** Choose the associate that is ±2 mod 3, then cubic symbols swap.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11A15 (Power residues, reciprocity), 11R18. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** An Eisenstein integer is a + bω with integers a, b and a primitive cube root of unity ω. It is primary when it is coprime to 3 and congruent to 2 or −2 modulo 3, a choice that fixes the associate up to a sign.

**Problem.** If α and β are primary and coprime, then the cubic residue symbols satisfy (α/β)₃ = (β/α)₃. Among λ, ωλ and ω²λ, one is primary whenever the norm of λ is coprime to 3.

**How the definition helps.** A primary numerator removes the possible cube-root-of-unity factor in Eisenstein’s cubic reciprocity law (our own explanation). The six units have distinct residues modulo 3, so exactly one rotation by 1, ω or ω² has residue ±2. The remaining sign has no effect because −1 is a cube (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Cubic reciprocity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cubic_reciprocity). It says: “A number is primary if it is coprime to 3 and congruent to an ordinary integer modulo (1−ω)², which is the same as saying it is congruent to ±2 modulo 3.”

**Sources:**

- [K. Ireland and M. Rosen, A Classical Introduction to Modern Number Theory, 2nd ed., Springer, 1990](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-1-4757-2103-4)
- [F. Lemmermeyer, Reciprocity Laws: From Euler to Eisenstein, Springer, 2000](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-662-12893-0)

### Primary Gaussian primes make quartic reciprocity statable

**Remember:** Among the four associates, take the one congruent to one modulo (1 + i)³.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11A15 (Power residues, reciprocity), 11R18. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A Gaussian integer is odd when 1 + i does not divide it, and an odd one is primary when it is congruent to 1 modulo (1 + i)³. Its four associates, its multiples by ±1 and ±i, cover the four invertible residues modulo (1 + i)³, so exactly one is primary (our own).

**Problem.** Every odd Gaussian integer has exactly one primary associate. For distinct primary primes π and θ, quartic reciprocity relates the quartic residue symbols \[π/θ\] and \[θ/π\] by an explicit sign.

**How the definition helps.** Fixing primary representatives removes the unit ambiguity in both quartic residue symbols when reciprocity swaps the primes (our own explanation). Gauss’s quartic reciprocity law then supplies the explicit sign (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Quartic reciprocity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quartic_reciprocity). It says: “In order to state the unique factorization theorem, it is necessary to have a way of distinguishing one of the associates of a number.”

**Sources:**

- [F. Lemmermeyer, Reciprocity Laws: From Euler to Eisenstein, Springer, 2000](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-662-12893-0)
- [G. Eisenstein, Lois de réciprocité, J. reine angew. Math. 28 (1844) 53–67](https://doi.org/10.1515/crll.1844.28.53)

### Weighting prime powers by log p makes prime counting match ζ′/ζ

**Remember:** Give every positive power of p the same weight log p, then sum.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11A25 (Arithmetic functions; related numbers; inversion formulas), 11N05, 11M06. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** The von Mangoldt function Λ(n) is log p when n = pᵏ for a prime p and some k ≥ 1, and 0 otherwise, and ψ(x) sums Λ(n) over n ≤ x. These weights are exactly what logarithmic differentiation of the Euler product produces.

**Problem.** For Re(s) &gt; 1, ∑ Λ(n)n⁻ˢ = −ζ′(s)/ζ(s), and for x &gt; 1 not a prime power, ψ(x) = x − ∑ρ x<sup>ρ</sup>/ρ − log(2π) − ½log(1 − x⁻²), summing nontrivial zeros with multiplicity symmetrically by height. Also ψ(x) \~ x is equivalent to the prime number theorem.

**How the definition helps.** Expanding −ζ′/ζ = ∑ₚ log p · p⁻ˢ/(1 − p⁻ˢ) gives log p at every power p⁻ᵏˢ, which is the series of Λ (our own). The von Mangoldt explicit formula then sums the pole contributions, counting each zero with multiplicity. Partial summation and the small share of higher prime powers give the equivalence with the prime number theorem (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Von Mangoldt function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Von_Mangoldt_function). It says: “Von Mangoldt provided a rigorous proof of an explicit formula for ψ(x) involving a sum over the non-trivial zeros of the Riemann zeta function. This was an important part of the first proof of the prime number theorem.”

**Sources:**

- [H. von Mangoldt, Zu Riemanns Abhandlung 'Ueber die Anzahl der Primzahlen unter einer gegebenen Grösse', J. reine angew. Math. 114 (1895) 255–305](https://doi.org/10.1515/crll.1895.114.255)
- [T. M. Apostol, Introduction to Analytic Number Theory, Springer, 1976](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-1-4757-5579-4)

### Large characters locate repeated differences

**Remember:** Make the large Fourier terms agree to get a positive count.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11B13 (Additive bases, including sumsets), 11B30. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For A of density α &gt; 0 in a finite vector space V over a prime field, the large spectrum is the set of characters χ whose Fourier coefficient, the mean of 1<sub>A</sub> χ̄ over V, has size at least √(α³/2). On the common kernel of these characters, each large term in the Fourier count of solutions to a + b − c − d = x is a nonnegative fourth power.

**Problem.** The common kernel lies in 2A − 2A, the set of sums a + b − c − d with all four terms from A. Its codimension is at most 2/α².

**How the definition helps.** The constant character alone gives α⁴, and Parseval bounds all small terms together by (α³/2)α = α⁴/2, so the count is positive (our own proof). Parseval also bounds the number of large characters by α/(α³/2) = 2/α², and each one costs at most one dimension.

**Paper or page:** [A bilinear Bogolyubov-Ruzsa lemma with poly-logarithmic bounds](https://arxiv.org/abs/1808.04965v2). It says: “there exists a subspace V of 𝔽ⁿ of codimension O(log⁴ α⁻¹) such that V ⊆ 2A−2A.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Minimal growth controls repeated sums

**Remember:** Use the least expensive subset at every addition.

*True by definition.* MSC 11B13 (Additive bases, including sumsets), 11P70. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For finite nonempty sets A and B in an abelian group, choose a nonempty X ⊆ A with the least growth ratio K = \|X + B\|/\|X\|, where X + B is the set of sums x + b. Minimality keeps the growth at most K after adding any finite set C: \|C + X + B\| ≤ K\|C + X\| (Petridis’s lemma).

**Problem.** For every positive integer j, \|X + jB\| ≤ Kʲ\|X\|, where jB is the set of sums of j elements of B.

**How the definition helps.** Minimality controls the overlaps between translates of X, which proves Petridis’s lemma. Take C = {0}, then B, 2B and so on, and induct on j (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Plünnecke–Ruzsa inequality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pl%C3%BCnnecke%E2%80%93Ruzsa_inequality). It says: “is a nonempty subset that minimizes the value of”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### The stabilizer of a sumset extends Cauchy–Davenport to all abelian groups

**Remember:** Measure sumsets against their stabilizer, and subgroups stop being counterexamples.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11B13 (Additive bases, including sumsets), 11P70. arXiv math.CO, math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For finite nonempty sets A and B in an abelian group, the stabilizer K of the sumset A + B = {a + b} is the subgroup of all g with (A + B) + g = A + B, the largest period of A + B.

**Problem.** Kneser's theorem bounds \|A + B\| from below for finite nonempty sets A and B in any abelian group. With K the stabilizer, it says \|A + B\| ≥ \|A + K\| + \|B + K\| − \|K\|.

**How the definition helps.** Using K, one bound covers periodic sumsets as well as aperiodic ones, where K = {0} gives \|A + B\| ≥ \|A\| + \|B\| − 1. For A = B = H a finite subgroup, K = H and equality holds (our own example).

**Wikipedia:** [https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kneser%27s<sub>theorem</sub>\_(combinatorics)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/https%3A//en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kneser%2527s_theorem_%28combinatorics%29). It says: “They may be regarded as extensions of the Cauchy–Davenport theorem, which also concerns sumsets in groups but is restricted to groups whose order is a prime number.”

**Paper or page:** [On Lev's periodicity conjecture](https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.15174). It says: “If A, B are two finite nonempty subsets of an abelian group G and K=Sym(A+B), then \|A+B\| ≥ \|A+K\|+\|B+K\|−\|K\|.”

**Sources:**

- [Christian Reiher, On Lev's periodicity conjecture, arXiv:2408.15174 (2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.15174)

### Balanced indicators expose missing progressions

**Remember:** Subtract the density before looking for missing patterns.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11B30 (Arithmetic combinatorics; higher degree uniformity). arXiv math.NT, math.CO. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** In a cyclic group of prime order N, let A have density α = \|A\|/N. Its balanced indicator is 1<sub>A</sub> − α, equal to 1 − α on A and −α elsewhere, so it measures how A differs from an evenly spread set.

**Problem.** Fix k≥3, with N≥k and Nαᵏ⁻¹≥2. If A contains no k-term progression with nonzero difference, its balanced indicator has Gowers norm of order k−1 at least αᵏ/(2k).

**How the definition helps.** With no nontrivial k-term progression, the normalized progression count is α/N, at most αᵏ/2, well below the αᵏ that the constant α gives (our own argument). Replacing each indicator in turn by α splits this discrepancy into k terms. The generalized von Neumann inequality bounds each term by the Gowers norm of the balanced indicator.

**Paper or page:** [An inverse theorem for the Gowers U³ norm](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0503014). It says: “Let k ≥ 3, let G be a finite additive group with (N,(k−1)!) = 1”

**Sources:**

- [Ben Green and Terence Tao, An inverse theorem for the Gowers U³ norm, arXiv:math/0503014v4](https://arxiv.org/abs/math/0503014)

### Centered Fourier uniformity counts three-term progressions

**Remember:** Remove the constant term so Fourier coefficients measure the counting error.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11B30 (Arithmetic combinatorics; higher degree uniformity). arXiv math.NT, math.CO. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Let A have density δ in a finite abelian group G of size n. A is Fourier ε-uniform if 1<sub>A</sub> − δ, its indicator minus the density, has every Fourier coefficient of modulus at most ε, a coefficient being its average against the conjugate of a character χ: G → unit circle.

**Problem.** Suppose n is odd and A is Fourier ε-uniform. The number of pairs (x,r) with x, x+r and x+2r in A differs from δ³n² by at most εn².

**How the definition helps.** Centering kills the constant coefficient, so the count minus δ³n² is a sum of terms with frequencies χ, χ and χ⁻² for nonconstant χ (our own explanation). Odd order makes χ⁻² nonconstant too, so uniformity bounds one factor by ε. Parseval’s identity bounds the sum of the other squared moduli by one.

**Paper or page:** [Quasirandomness in additive groups and hypergraphs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2107.01463). It says: “Let G be an additive group of odd order and suppose A ⊆ G is Fourier ε-uniform.”

**Sources:**

- [Davi Castro-Silva, Quasirandomness in additive groups and hypergraphs, arXiv:2107.01463v1](https://arxiv.org/abs/2107.01463)

### Coset averages absorb large Fourier coefficients

**Remember:** A character survives coset averaging exactly when it is trivial on the subspace.

*True by definition.* MSC 11B30 (Arithmetic combinatorics; higher degree uniformity). arXiv math.NT, math.CO. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For a subspace H of 𝔽ₚⁿ, the coset model g of f takes at x the mean of f over x + H, so it stays in \[0, 1\]. Coset averaging keeps each Fourier coefficient at a character trivial on H and kills every other one.

**Problem.** For every f from 𝔽ₚⁿ to \[0, 1\] and ε &gt; 0, there is a subspace H of codimension at most ε⁻². Every normalized Fourier coefficient of f minus its coset model has modulus at most ε.

**How the definition helps.** Take H to be the common kernel of the characters whose coefficients exceed ε in modulus; Parseval bounds their number, and so the codimension, by ε⁻² (our own explanation). Then f − g has zero coefficient at every character trivial on H. At every other character it has the coefficient of f, which is at most ε.

**Paper or page:** [Quasirandomness in additive groups and hypergraphs](https://arxiv.org/abs/2107.01463). It says: “being a linear combination of at most 1/ε² characters with coefficients bounded in magnitude by 1”

**Sources:**

- [Davi Castro-Silva, Quasirandomness in additive groups and hypergraphs, arXiv:2107.01463v1](https://arxiv.org/abs/2107.01463)
