### Ordered integrals split at junctions

**Remember:** A path junction cuts the sequence of integration times once.

*True by definition.* MSC 11G55 (Polylogarithms and relations with K-theory). arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** An iterated integral of forms f₁(t) dt, …, fₙ(t) dt along a piecewise smooth path integrates f₁(t₁) ⋯ fₙ(tₙ) over the ordered times 0 &lt; t₁ &lt; ⋯ &lt; tₙ &lt; 1. For polylogarithms the forms are dz/(z − a), with a a puncture.

**Problem.** Let paths γ and δ meet end to end and avoid the poles of the forms. The integral along the joined path equals ∑ₖ Iγ(ω₁,…,ωₖ) Iδ(ωₖ₊₁,…,ωₙ) for k = 0 to n, where empty integrals equal one.

**How the definition helps.** The ordered times cross the junction only once, so fixing the number k of times before it splits the simplex into a product of two ordered regions (our own). Summing over k gives the formula (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Duality on symmetric multiple polylogarithms](https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.08711). It says: “(Path composition formula) $\\displaystyle I<sub>\\gamma \\cdot \\gamma '</sub>(e\_{a<sub>1</sub>}\\cdots e\_{a<sub>k</sub>})=\\sum <sub>i=0</sub><sup>k</sup>I<sub>\\gamma </sub>(e\_{a<sub>1</sub>}\\cdots e\_{a<sub>i</sub>})I<sub>\\gamma '</sub>(e\_{a<sub>i+1</sub>}\\cdots e\_{a<sub>k</sub>})$.”

**Sources:**

- [Duality on symmetric multiple polylogarithms](https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.08711)

### Discriminant forms classify even overlattices

**Remember:** Even extensions correspond to subgroups on which the discriminant form vanishes.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11H06 (Lattices and convex bodies (number-theoretic aspects)), 11E81. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For a nonsingular even lattice L, its dual L\* is the set of rational vectors pairing integrally with L, and its discriminant form sends x + L in L\*/L to ⟨x,x⟩/2 modulo ℤ. A subgroup of L\*/L is isotropic if this form vanishes on it, which says exactly that the vectors over it have even norms.

**Problem.** Even lattices containing L with finite index in the same rational space correspond to isotropic subgroups of L\*/L. Up to isometries preserving L, they correspond to orbits of those subgroups under isometries of L.

**How the definition helps.** Every integral extension of L lies in L\*, so it is a subgroup of L\*/L (our own). That subgroup gives an even lattice exactly when the discriminant form vanishes on it, and polarization then makes all pairings integral (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Derived equivalence of elliptic K3 surfaces and Jacobians](https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.16638v3). It says: “the set of O(T)-orbits of isotropic subgroups of Aₜ”

**Sources:**

- [Viacheslav V. Nikulin, Integral symmetric bilinear forms and some of their applications](https://doi.org/10.1070/im1980v014n01abeh001060)

### Even positive definite unimodular lattices need dimension divisible by 8

**Remember:** Evenness gives translation symmetry, and unimodularity gives inversion symmetry.

*Rules out counterexamples. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11H06 (Lattices and convex bodies (number-theoretic aspects)), 11E12. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A lattice in ℝⁿ is unimodular when its Gram matrix, the matrix of dot products of a basis, has integer entries and determinant ±1, and even when every vector has even norm x·x. Evenness gives its theta series ∑ exp(πiz x·x) period one, and unimodularity makes it transform under z ↦ −1/z with factor (z/i) raised to n/2 (our own).

**Problem.** A positive definite even unimodular lattice exists only when n is divisible by 8, and E₈ and the Leech lattice are examples in dimensions 8 and 24. Odd unimodular lattices, such as ℤⁿ, exist in every dimension.

**How the definition helps.** The map z ↦ −1/(z+1) has order three, and applying the two rules three times gives the factor exp(−πin/4) (our own). The theta series is nonzero, so this factor is one and 8 divides n (our own). The odd lattice ℤⁿ lacks period one (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Unimodular lattice](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unimodular_lattice). It says: “If the lattice is even, the form has level 1, and if the lattice is odd the form has Γ₀(4) structure (i.e., it is a modular form of level 4).”

**Sources:**

- [J.-P. Serre, A Course in Arithmetic, Graduate Texts in Mathematics 7, Springer, 1973](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-1-4684-9884-4)
- [J. Milnor and D. Husemoller, Symmetric Bilinear Forms, Springer, 1973](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-642-88330-9)

### Unit covolume gives a Hermite maximum

**Remember:** Fix cell volume before maximizing the shortest length.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11H55 (Quadratic forms (reduction theory, extreme forms, etc.)), 11H31. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** The Hermite invariant of a Euclidean lattice is the squared length of its shortest nonzero vector after scaling the lattice so that a fundamental cell has volume one. Fixing the volume stops scaling alone from making the shortest length large.

**Problem.** In each dimension, some lattice attains the maximum Hermite invariant. Equivalently, some lattice attains the best lattice sphere-packing density in that dimension.

**How the definition helps.** Fixing volume puts the problem on unit-covolume lattices, where Mahler’s theorem makes the set with shortest length at least one compact (our own). Shortest length is continuous there, and the cubic lattice shows the maximum lies in that set (our own). Balls of radius half the shortest length give the matching packing density (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Mahler's compactness theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mahler%27s_compactness_theorem). It says: “The assertion of Mahler's theorem is equivalent to the compactness of the space of unit-covolume lattices in ℝⁿ whose systole is larger or equal than any fixed ε&gt;0.”

**Sources:**

- [Kurt Mahler, On lattice points in n-dimensional star bodies I. Existence theorems](https://doi.org/10.1098/rspa.1946.0072)

### Primitive counting explains the zeta factor

**Remember:** Every nonzero lattice vector has one primitive starting point.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11H60 (Mean value and transfer theorems). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A nonzero lattice vector is primitive if it is not k times a lattice vector for any integer k ≥ 2, so it is the first lattice point on its ray. The primitive Siegel transform of a bounded, compactly supported measurable function sums its values over the primitive vectors.

**Problem.** For n≥2, average the primitive transform over unit-covolume lattices using the SLₙ(ℝ)-invariant probability measure. The mean equals the integral of the function divided by ζ(n), the sum of reciprocal nth powers.

**How the definition helps.** Every nonzero lattice vector is k times exactly one primitive vector, so the full sum is a sum over k of primitive sums at dilation k, each with integral scaled by k⁻ⁿ (our own). Invariance makes the averaged primitive sum a constant c times the integral, and Siegel’s mean value theorem gives cζ(n) = 1 (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Inversion formulae for Siegel transforms](https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.11689v3), [Some measure-theoretical and dynamical properties of successive minima on the space of unimodular lattices](https://arxiv.org/abs/2212.14373v1). It says: “Then ∫ₓ f̂ dμₓ = (1/ζ(n)) ∫ℝⁿ f dm.”

**Sources:**

- [Carl Ludwig Siegel, A Mean Value Theorem in Geometry of Numbers](https://doi.org/10.2307/1969027)

### Character relations locate the orbit

**Remember:** Keep every integer relation satisfied by the step.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11J71 (Distribution modulo one). arXiv math.NT, math.DS. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For a step α on the torus ℝᵈ/ℤᵈ, let H be the closed subgroup of points x with k·x ∈ ℤ for every integer vector k with k·α ∈ ℤ. So H keeps exactly the integer relations that α satisfies.

**Problem.** The points nα become uniformly distributed on H. Their averages against every continuous function approach its integral under the translation-invariant probability on H.

**How the definition helps.** By Kronecker’s theorem these relations cut out the orbit closure, so H is the closure of the points nα. For each integer character, the orbit average tends to one when k·α is an integer and to zero otherwise, which matches its Haar integral on H (our own). Trigonometric approximation extends this to all continuous functions (our own).

**nLab:** [Haar integral](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Haar+integral). It says: “there exists a unique such integral, up to a scalar multiple.”

**Wikipedia:** [Kronecker's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kronecker%27s_theorem). It says: “the whole Kronecker theorem describes the closure of ⟨P⟩ as the intersection of the kernels”

**Paper or page:** [Metric uniform distribution on analytic curves](https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.06909v1). It says: “Then (xₙ) is uniformly distributed mod 1 if and only if for every non-zero v ∈ ℤᵏ,”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Uniformly separated frequencies give metric equidistribution

**Remember:** For almost every multiplier, separated frequencies spread uniformly.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11J71 (Distribution modulo one). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Call a real sequence uniformly separated if some g &gt; 0 satisfies \|aₙ − aₘ\| ≥ g whenever n ≠ m, so no two terms lie closer than a fixed gap.

**Problem.** If a real sequence (aₙ) is uniformly separated, then for almost every real x the sequence aₙx is uniformly distributed modulo one. That is, the fraction of terms landing in each interval approaches its length.

**How the definition helps.** The gap keeps exponential averages of aₙx over n ≤ N small, with mean square O(log N/N) on any bounded interval of x at each nonzero integer frequency (our own). The Davenport–Erdős–LeVeque criterion turns this into uniform distribution for almost every x (our own). Separation excludes aₙ = 1/n, whose multiples tend to zero modulo one (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Metric uniform distribution on analytic curves](https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.06909v1). It says: “Then for almost every x ∈ ℝ the sequence (aₙx) is uniformly distributed modulo 1.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Powered intervals give approximation dimension

**Remember:** Keep the rational centers and shrink each interval by a power.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11J83 (Metric theory). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For a &gt; 1, W(a) is the set of real x within q⁻²ᵃ of p/q for infinitely many reduced fractions p/q with q &gt; 0. These are the Dirichlet intervals around each p/q, of radius q⁻², with each radius raised to the power a (our own).

**Problem.** Let a be greater than one. The real numbers approximable infinitely often within the inverse 2a-th power of the denominator have Hausdorff dimension 1/a. Hausdorff dimension measures size by covers at small scales.

**How the definition helps.** Dirichlet’s theorem gives full measure before shrinking, so the mass transference principle gives dimension at least 1/a after raising radii to the power a (our own). For the upper bound, each bounded interval has O(q) fractions with denominator q, and their covering sums converge in every dimension above 1/a (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Diophantine approximation in metric space](https://arxiv.org/abs/2105.06776v1). It says: “Let a &gt; 1 and for a ball B, denote by Bᵃ a ball of the same centre as B and of diameter (diam B)ᵃ.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Independent bases prevent power cancellation

**Remember:** With no multiplicative relation among bases, irrational exponents cannot cancel out.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11J86 (Linear forms in logarithms; Baker's method), 11J81. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Positive numbers are multiplicatively independent if no product of integer powers of them equals one except with all exponents zero, so their real logarithms are linearly independent over ℚ. Powers of the positive bases use these real logarithms.

**Problem.** Take multiplicatively independent positive algebraic bases and algebraic exponents. If at least one exponent is irrational, the product of those powers is transcendental.

**How the definition helps.** Independence makes the logarithms rationally independent, so Baker’s theorem makes them linearly independent over the algebraic numbers (our own). If the product were algebraic, Baker’s theorem would force its logarithm ∑ βᵢ log αᵢ to be a rational combination of the log αᵢ, and independence would make every βᵢ rational (our own). Dependent bases fail: 2<sup>(2√2)</sup> · 4<sup>(−√2)</sup> = 1 (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Baker's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baker%27s_theorem). It says: “In particular this number is nonzero, so 1 and λᵢ are linearly independent over the algebraic numbers.”

**Sources:**

- [Alan Baker, Linear forms in the logarithms of algebraic numbers](https://doi.org/10.1112/s0025579300003971)

### Local ratios make approximation projective

**Remember:** Divide out the size of the coordinates at every place.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11J87 (Schmidt Subspace Theorem and applications). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Represent a point of projective space over a number field K by a nonzero vector x, and measure its size at each place by Mᵥ = maxᵢ \|xᵢ\|ᵥ, with absolute values normalized so the product formula holds. Its height is H(x) = ∏ᵥ Mᵥ, and each ratio \|L(x)\|ᵥ/Mᵥ does not change when x is scaled (our own).

**Problem.** Choose d independent K-linear forms in d variables at each of finitely many places, and fix ε &gt; 0. The points where the product of all ratios \|L(x)\|ᵥ/Mᵥ is below 1/Hᵈ⁺ᵋ lie in finitely many proper projective linear subspaces.

**How the definition helps.** Scaling x multiplies each numerator and denominator by the same absolute value, and the product formula keeps H fixed, so the inequality is a condition on projective points (our own). The subspace theorem supplies the finite union, and its affine and projective versions are equivalent.

**Paper or page:** [Diophantine approximation and the subspace theorem](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.00731v1), [Diophantine approximation and the subspace theorem](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.00731v1). It says: “The projective subspace theorem is equivalent to the affine subspace theorem.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### No zero subsums makes unit solutions finite

**Remember:** Remove cancelling groups before counting solutions.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11J87 (Schmidt Subspace Theorem and applications), 11D61. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** An S-unit is a nonzero element of a number field whose principal ideal has prime factors only in a fixed finite set S. A solution of a linear equation in S-units is nondegenerate if no nonempty group of terms on the left sums to zero.

**Problem.** Over a number field, a fixed linear equation in S-units with nonzero coefficients and right side one has finitely many nondegenerate solutions.

**How the definition helps.** A vanishing subsum can be scaled by any S-unit without changing the equation, which gives infinite families (our own). For example, over ℚ with 2 in S, x + y + z = 1 has the solutions (2ᵏ, −2ᵏ, 1) for every k (our own). The S-unit theorem, proved with the subspace theorem, gives finiteness otherwise (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Sum of terms of recurrence sequences and S-units in the solution sets of norm form equations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.01688v1). It says: “has no vanishing subsums.”

**Sources:**

- [Jan-Hendrik Evertse, Hans Peter Schlickewei and Wolfgang M. Schmidt, Linear Equations in Variables which Lie in a Multiplicative Group](https://doi.org/10.2307/3062133)

### Fourier tests reveal polynomial equidistribution

**Remember:** Fractional parts spread evenly when every nonzero Fourier average dies.

*True by definition.* MSC 11K06 (General theory of distribution modulo 1), 11K31. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A sequence is uniformly distributed modulo 1 when its fractional parts land in each interval with frequency equal to the interval’s length. By Weyl’s criterion, this holds exactly when for every nonzero integer h the average of exp(2πihxₙ) over the first N terms tends to zero.

**Problem.** The values of a real polynomial at the positive integers are uniformly distributed modulo 1 if some nonconstant coefficient is irrational.

**How the definition helps.** Weyl’s criterion reduces the claim to cancellation in exponential sums of the polynomial (our own). After splitting into residue classes to make the rational coefficients constant modulo one, van der Corput differencing lowers the degree while keeping an irrational leading coefficient (our own). A linear phase with irrational coefficient gives a bounded geometric sum (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Equidistributed sequence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Equidistributed_sequence). It says: “the sequence p(n) is uniformly distributed modulo 1.”

**Sources:**

- [Hermann Weyl, Über die Gleichverteilung von Zahlen mod. Eins](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF01475864)

### Equidistribution makes normal numbers a consequence of ergodicity

**Remember:** A normal number’s orbit under times-b visits intervals at their lengths.

*True by definition.* MSC 11K16 (Normal numbers, radix expansions, Pisot numbers, Salem numbers, good lattice points, etc.), 37A44. arXiv math.NT, math.DS. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A real x is normal in base b ≥ 2 if every block of k digits occurs with frequency b⁻ᵏ. Equivalently, the orbit of x under multiplication by b modulo 1 visits each interval of \[0, 1) with frequency equal to its length.

**Problem.** For each integer base b ≥ 2, Lebesgue-almost every real number is normal in base b.

**How the definition helps.** So normality says that time averages of interval indicators equal space averages for the map x ↦ bx mod 1. This map preserves Lebesgue measure and is ergodic, so Birkhoff’s theorem gives the right frequencies for almost every x, for the countably many rational intervals at once (our own). Approximation by these intervals gives every interval (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Normal number](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Normal_number). It says: “A number x is normal in base b if and only if the sequence {\\left( b<sup>k</sup> x \\right) }<sub>k=0</sub><sup>\\infty</sup> is equidistributed modulo 1”

**Sources:**

- [É. Borel, Les probabilités dénombrables et leurs applications arithmétiques, Rend. Circ. Mat. Palermo 27 (1909) 247–271](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF03019651)

### Block tests expose hidden dependence

**Remember:** Counting blocks catches dependencies that counting single points misses.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11K36 (Well-distributed sequences and other variations), 11K06. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A sequence is completely uniformly distributed modulo 1 if, for every length k, the points of the unit cube formed by k consecutive fractional parts fill each box with frequency equal to its volume. Ordinary uniform distribution is the case k = 1.

**Problem.** For almost every α &gt; 1, the sequence of positive integer powers of α is completely uniformly distributed modulo 1. For irrational α, its positive integer multiples are uniformly distributed but fail the block test at length two.

**How the definition helps.** Blocks of length two see the relation between neighbors, which single terms cannot see. For powers of α, Koksma’s metric theorem applies to each nonzero integer combination of shifted powers (our own). For multiples of irrational α, adjacent pairs lie on the line y = x + α modulo one, so a box off that line gets no pairs (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Equidistributed sequence](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Equidistributed_sequence). It says: “is completely uniformly distributed for almost all α &gt; 1”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Continued fraction blocks bound rotation discrepancy

**Remember:** Cut the orbit into return-time blocks, each spread almost evenly.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11K38 (Irregularities of distribution, discrepancy). arXiv math.NT, math.DS. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Write N greedily as a sum of continued fraction denominators q<sub>k</sub> of the irrational α, each used at most a<sub>k+1</sub> times, where a<sub>k+1</sub> is the next continued fraction entry. Split the first N rotation points into consecutive blocks of these lengths. Each block of length q<sub>k</sub> puts within two of the expected number of points into every arc (our own).

**Problem.** If the continued fraction entries of α are bounded, the points x+jα modulo one have discrepancy O(log N/N), uniformly in x. The discrepancy is the largest gap between the fraction of points in an arc and the arc length.

**How the definition helps.** Each block adds at most two to the count error in any arc, by the Denjoy–Koksma inequality, so the error is at most twice the number of blocks (our own). Bounded entries bound each multiplicity, and the denominators at least double every two steps, so O(log N) blocks suffice (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Dynamics of multicritical circle maps](https://arxiv.org/abs/2103.01153v1), [Limit laws of maximal Birkhoff sums for circle rotations via quantum modular forms](https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.07796v1). It says: “Let {qₙ}ₙ∈ℕ be the sequence of return times given by ρ.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Fourier cutoffs bound arc discrepancy

**Remember:** Sandwich the arc between two short Fourier sums.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11K38 (Irregularities of distribution, discrepancy). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For an arc I of the circle ℝ/ℤ and an integer M ≥ 1, Selberg's polynomials are trigonometric polynomials P₋ ≤ 1<sub>I</sub> ≤ P₊ of degree at most M that sandwich the arc's indicator at every point. Their constant terms are \|I\| ± 1/(M+1), and the coefficient at each frequency k ≠ 0 is at most C/\|k\|, with C absolute (our own).

**Problem.** Let μ be a probability measure on the circle with Fourier coefficients μ̂(k) = ∫exp(−2πikx) dμ(x). The largest value of \|μ(I) − \|I\|\| over arcs I is at most C(1/M + ∑ₖ₌₁ᴹ \|μ̂(k)\|/k), with C absolute.

**How the definition helps.** Integrating P₋ ≤ 1<sub>I</sub> ≤ P₊ against μ traps μ(I) between two finite Fourier sums (our own). The constant terms give \|I\| with error 1/(M+1), and each other frequency k adds at most C\|μ̂(k)\|/k (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Erdős–Turán inequality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Erd%C5%91s%E2%80%93Tur%C3%A1n_inequality). It says: “where the supremum is over all arcs A ⊂ ℝ/ℤ of the unit circle”

**Sources:**

### Square-summed frequencies bound worst arc error

**Remember:** One square-sum number controls the whole weighted Fourier sum.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11K38 (Irregularities of distribution, discrepancy). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For a probability measure μ on the circle with Fourier coefficients μ̂(k) = ∫exp(−2πikx) dμ(x), let A ≥ 0 satisfy A² = ∑ₖ₌₁∞ \|μ̂(k)\|²/k². By Cauchy–Schwarz, A controls every partial weighted sum: ∑ₖ₌₁ᴹ \|μ̂(k)\|/k ≤ √M·A (our own).

**Problem.** Every arc I satisfies \|μ(I) − \|I\|\| ≤ C·A<sup>(2/3)</sup>, with a universal constant C.

**How the definition helps.** Erdős–Turán bounds the error by C(1/M + ∑ₖ₌₁ᴹ \|μ̂(k)\|/k), which is at most C(1/M + √M·A) (our own). For 0 &lt; A ≤ 1, taking M near A<sup>(−2/3)</sup> makes both terms of size A<sup>(2/3)</sup> (our own). If A = 0 let M grow, and if A &gt; 1 the trivial bound one suffices (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Erdős–Turán inequality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Erd%C5%91s%E2%80%93Tur%C3%A1n_inequality). It says: “This inequality holds for arbitrary natural numbers m,n”

### Gauss averages give denominator growth

**Remember:** The denominator is the reciprocal of the orbit's product.

*True by definition.* MSC 11K50 (Metric theory of continued fractions). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** The Gauss map T sends an irrational x in (0,1) to the fractional part of 1/x and preserves the probability density 1/((1+x) log 2). The product x·Tx⋯Tⁿ⁻¹x equals 1/qₙ up to a factor at most 2, so log qₙ is a sum of −log Tʲx up to log 2 (our own).

**Problem.** Let qₙ be the denominator of the nth continued fraction convergent of x. For almost every x in (0,1), (log qₙ)/n tends to π²/(12 log 2).

**How the definition helps.** Exactly, 1/(x·Tx⋯Tⁿ⁻¹x) = qₙ + qₙ₋₁Tⁿx, which lies between qₙ and 2qₙ (our own). So (log qₙ)/n is a time average of −log x up to O(1/n). Ergodicity of T makes it converge almost everywhere to the integral of −log x against the invariant density, which is π²/(12 log 2) (our own).

**nLab:** [continued fraction](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/continued+fraction). It says: “then τ is an ergodic transformation with respect to μ”

**Wikipedia:** [Lévy's constant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/L%C3%A9vy%27s_constant). It says: “The term “Lévy's constant” is sometimes used to refer to π²/(12 ln 2)”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### The Gauss map turns continued fraction digits into ergodic averages

**Remember:** The Gauss map shifts the digits one place left.

*True by definition.* MSC 11K50 (Metric theory of continued fractions), 37A44. arXiv math.NT, math.DS. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** The Gauss map T sends an irrational x in (0,1) to the fractional part of 1/x. It shifts the continued fraction digits: the nth digit aₙ of x is the first digit a₁ of Tⁿ⁻¹x, the integer part of 1/Tⁿ⁻¹x.

**Problem.** Khinchin’s theorem: for Lebesgue-almost every x in (0,1), the geometric mean of its first n continued fraction digits tends to one constant, about 2.685.

**How the definition helps.** The logarithm of the geometric mean is the time average of log a₁ along the orbit of x (our own). The map is ergodic for the Gauss measure, which has the same null sets as Lebesgue measure. Since digit j has Gauss measure O(j⁻²), log a₁ is integrable, and Birkhoff’s theorem gives the limit (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Khinchin's constant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Khinchin%27s_constant). It says: “Moreover, it can be proved that T is an ergodic transformation of the measurable space I endowed with the probability measure μ (this is the hard part of the proof).”

**Sources:**

- [C. Ryll-Nardzewski, On the ergodic theorems (II) (Ergodic theory of continued fractions), Studia Math. 12 (1951) 74–79](https://doi.org/10.4064/sm-12-1-74-79)

### Completion transfers the Weil bound

**Remember:** Complete the short sum with Fourier modes, then apply Weil.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11L05 (Gauss and Kloosterman sums; generalizations). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For a prime p and b ≢ 0 modulo p, let T(x) = exp(2πibx⁻¹/p) for units x, with the inverse modulo p, and T(0) = 0. Completion writes the indicator of an interval of at most p integers as a Fourier sum over residues modulo p. This turns a sum of T over the interval into a weighted sum of complete Kloosterman sums.

**Problem.** For every integer a and every interval I of at most p consecutive integers, the sum of T(x)exp(2πiax/p) over x in I has absolute value at most C√p log(2p), with C absolute.

**How the definition helps.** Each Fourier mode only shifts the linear coefficient of a complete Kloosterman sum, which is at most 2√p by Weil, or −1 when that coefficient is zero (our own). A geometric sum bounds the total size of the interval's normalized Fourier coefficients by O(log(2p)) (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Kloosterman sum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kloosterman_sum). It says: “Short Kloosterman sums are defined as trigonometric sums of the form”

**Sources:**

- [André Weil, On Some Exponential Sums (1948)](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.34.5.204)

### Grouping modulo pʳ isolates stationary residues

**Remember:** Inside a class modulo pʳ, the phase is a straight line.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11L05 (Gauss and Kloosterman sums; generalizations). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For an odd prime p, r ≥ 1 and a, b prime to p, the Kloosterman sum S(a,b;p²ʳ) sums exp(2πi(ax+bx⁻¹)/p²ʳ) over units x modulo p²ʳ. Group its terms by the class u of x modulo pʳ. Writing x = u + pʳt gives x⁻¹ ≡ u⁻¹ − pʳtu⁻² modulo p²ʳ, so the phase is linear in t (our own).

**Problem.** Let p be odd and let a,b be integers prime to p. The class of u contributes zero unless au²≡b modulo pʳ. When the congruence holds, it contributes pʳ times the term at any member.

**How the definition helps.** On each class the sum is a complete geometric sum in t of exp(2πit(a − bu⁻²)/pʳ) (our own). It vanishes unless a ≡ bu⁻² modulo pʳ, that is au² ≡ b, and then all pʳ terms are equal (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Subconvexity for GL₂ × GL₂ L-functions in the depth aspect](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.18727v1). It says: “Then, S(a,b;pⁿ) = 0 if ab ∉ (ℤₚˣ)².”

**Sources:**

- [Tengyou Zhu, Subconvexity for GL₂ × GL₂ L-functions in the depth aspect](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.18727v1)

### Hyper-Kloosterman transforms are Gauss powers

**Remember:** A character splits the product constraint into one Gauss sum per variable.

*True by definition. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11L05 (Gauss and Kloosterman sums; generalizations). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For a prime p and r ≥ 1, the hyper-Kloosterman sum Kᵣ(a) sums exp(2πi(x₁+⋯+xᵣ)/p) over nonzero residues x₁,…,xᵣ with product a modulo p. For a multiplicative character χ modulo p, the Gauss sum G(χ) sums χ(x)exp(2πix/p) over nonzero residues x (our own).

**Problem.** For every multiplicative character χ, summing χ(a)Kᵣ(a) over nonzero residues a gives G(χ)ʳ.

**How the definition helps.** Summing over a leaves each unrestricted r-tuple of nonzero residues exactly once (our own). Multiplicativity gives χ(a)=χ(x₁)⋯χ(xᵣ), so the sum factors into r copies of G(χ) (our own).

**Paper or page:** [The sixth moment of Dirichlet L-functions at the central point](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.01457v1). It says: “where the hyper-Kloosterman sum”

### Joint primitivity prevents oversized sums

**Remember:** No common factor, so the modulus is the true period.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11L05 (Gauss and Kloosterman sums; generalizations). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** The Kloosterman sum K(a,b;q), for q ≥ 2, sums exp(2πi(ax+bx⁻¹)/q) over invertible residues x modulo q, with x⁻¹ the inverse modulo q. The pair (a,b) is jointly primitive when gcd(a,b,q) = 1, so no common factor lets the phases repeat with a smaller period (our own).

**Problem.** On jointly primitive pairs, \|K(a,b;q)\| ≤ τ(q)√q, where τ counts positive divisors. Without the condition the bound fails, for example when q = 25 and a = b = 0.

**How the definition helps.** The general estimate \|K(a,b;q)\| ≤ τ(q)√gcd(a,b,q)·√q has gcd factor one exactly under this condition. For q = 25 and a = b = 0, all 20 terms equal one, but τ(25)√25 = 15 (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Kloosterman sum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kloosterman_sum). It says: “\|K(a,b;m)\| ≤ τ(m) √gcd(a,b,m) √m.”

**Sources:**

- [André Weil, On Some Exponential Sums (1948)](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.34.5.204)

### Smooth weights suppress distant frequencies

**Remember:** Smooth weights make far frequencies die fast.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11L05 (Gauss and Kloosterman sums; generalizations). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For a prime p and b prime to p, let K(n) = exp(2πibn⁻¹/p) for n prime to p and K(n) = 0 otherwise, and write K̂(h) = ∑ₓ K(x)exp(2πihx/p) over residues x modulo p. Weight n by W(n/N), with W smooth and compactly supported on ℝ. Its transform Ŵ(t) = ∫W(x)exp(−2πitx) dx then decays faster than any power of t (our own).

**Problem.** Summing K(n)W(n/N) over all integers gives (N/p)∑ₕ K̂(h)Ŵ(Nh/p), with h over all integers. For each A &gt; 0 and H ≥ max(1,p/N), the terms with \|h\| &gt; H contribute at most C√p(p/(NH))ᴬ, with C depending only on A and W.

**How the definition helps.** Smoothness makes Ŵ(Nh/p) tiny once \|h\| is well beyond p/N, by repeated integration by parts (our own). Poisson summation on each residue class gives the identity, and Weil’s bound \|K̂(h)\| ≤ 2√p controls each tail term (our own).

**Paper or page:** [On a Finite Field Analogue of van der Corput Differencing](https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.02525v1). It says: “any even smooth function V compactly supported on ℝ”

### Exponent pairs interpolate

**Remember:** Exponent pairs are powers, so mixing bounds mixes the powers.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11L07 (Estimates on exponential sums). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** An exponent pair (k,l), with 0 ≤ k ≤ ½ ≤ l ≤ 1, gives the bound C(T/Nˢ)ᵏNˡ for every sum of exp(2πif(n)) over integers n in a subinterval of \[N,2N\]. For each s &gt; 0 there must be R ≥ 1, δ ∈ (0,1) and C &gt; 0 that make this hold whenever N ≥ 1, T ≥ Nˢ and f′ is close to g(x) = T/xˢ. Close means \|(f′)⁽ʲ⁾ − g⁽ʲ⁾\| ≤ δ\|g⁽ʲ⁾\| on \[N,2N\] for 0 ≤ j &lt; R (our own).

**Problem.** Every convex combination of two exponent pairs is an exponent pair.

**How the definition helps.** The bound is a product of powers, so a weighted geometric mean of two such bounds has the interpolated powers (our own). Take the larger R and the smaller δ so that both bounds apply, then use min(X,Y) ≤ X<sup>θY^</sup>(1−θ) for 0 ≤ θ ≤ 1 (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Van der Corput's method](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Van_der_Corput%27s_method). It says: “The set of exponents pairs is convex.”

### Monotone slopes prevent coherent repetition

**Remember:** Slopes that drift one way and avoid integers cannot resonate.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11L07 (Estimates on exponential sums). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Let f be continuously differentiable on a bounded interval I, with f′ monotone and at least λ &gt; 0 away from every integer throughout I. Then the phase steps f(n+1) − f(n) move steadily in one direction inside a single gap between consecutive integers (our own).

**Problem.** The sum of exp(2πif(n)) over integers n in a bounded I is O(1/λ), with an absolute constant. Without monotonicity this bound can fail even with λ = 3/8.

**How the definition helps.** Summation by parts with these monotone steps bounds the sum by the variation of 1/(exp(2πiu) − 1) over u in that gap, at least λ from its ends, which is O(1/λ) (our own). For f(t) = t/2 + cos(πt)/(8π), f′ stays in \[3/8, 5/8\], but each even–odd pair of terms adds 2i sin(1/4), so the sums grow without bound (our own).

**Paper or page:** [On Sárközy's theorem for shifted primes](https://arxiv.org/abs/2206.08001v3). It says: “Let f : I → ℝ be continuously differentiable such that f′ is monotonic and ∥f′(t)∥ ≥ λ on I.”

**Sources:**

- [Hugh L. Montgomery and Robert C. Vaughan, Multiplicative Number Theory II, Theorem 16.5](https://personal.science.psu.edu/rcv4/571s25/montgomery-vaughanII.pdf)

### Separated phases factor major arcs

**Remember:** Residues carry the rational phase; the integral carries the slow drift.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11L07 (Estimates on exponential sums). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Split the phase into a rational part A(x)/q and a slowly varying real part B(x), with A(x) = ∑ aⱼxʲ for integers a₁,…,aₖ jointly coprime to q and B(x) = ∑ βⱼxʲ for real βⱼ, 1 ≤ j ≤ k. The rational part depends only on x modulo q and has residue mean C, the mean of exp(2πiA(x)/q) over x modulo q. The slow part is approximated by the integral I of exp(2πiB(x)) over \[0,N\].

**Problem.** The sum of exp(2πi∑ (aⱼ/q+βⱼ)nʲ) over 1 ≤ n ≤ N equals CI plus an error. The error is O(q(1+∑ \|βⱼ\|Nʲ)), with a constant depending only on k.

**How the definition helps.** On each residue class the rational phase is constant, so only exp(2πiB) needs summing (our own). Partial summation shows each class sum differs from I/q by O(1 + ∫₀ᴺ \|B′(x)\| dx), and summing over the q classes gives CI with the stated error (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Lᵖ maximal estimates for Weyl sums with k ≥ 3 on 𝕋](https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.15527v1). It says: “S<sub>k</sub>(\\bm {u},N) = q<sup>-1</sup>S<sub>k</sub>(q<sup>-1</sup>\\bm {r};q)I(\\bm {\\xi }) + \\Delta .”

**Sources:**

- [Xuezhi Chen, Changxing Miao, Jiye Yuan, Tengfei Zhao, Lᵖ maximal estimates for Weyl sums with k ≥ 3 on 𝕋](https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.15527v1)

### Vinogradov moments count power sums

**Remember:** Integrating over the cube keeps only tuples with matching power sums.

*True by definition.* MSC 11L07 (Estimates on exponential sums). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For positive integers k, N and s, let F(α) = ∑ₙ₌₁ᴺ exp(2πi(α₁n + α₂n² + ⋯ + αₖnᵏ)) for α in \[0,1\]ᵏ. The mean value is the integral of \|F(α)\|²ˢ over this cube. Each coordinate integral of exp(2πimα) over \[0,1\] is one if the integer m is zero and zero otherwise.

**Problem.** The mean value counts ordered pairs of lists, each containing s integers from 1 through N. The lists must have equal sums of jth powers for every j from 1 through k.

**How the definition helps.** Expanding \|F\|²ˢ = FˢF̄ˢ gives one term for each ordered pair of lists of s integers from 1 through N (our own). Each term integrates to one when the two lists have equal jth power sums for every j ≤ k, and to zero otherwise (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Decoupling estimates in Fourier analysis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2207.00652v1). It says: “For any finite set A ⊂ ℤᵈ, ∫<sub>\[0,1\]<sup>d</sub></sup> \|f<sub>A</sub>(x)\|<sup>2s</sup> dx = E<sub>s</sub>(A).”

### Reciprocal roots bound polynomial prime sums

**Remember:** Weight each prime power by the degree of its prime.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11L20 (Sums over primes), 11T23. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Let χ be a nonprincipal Dirichlet character on 𝔽𝓆\[T\], extended by zero off the units, and let L(u,χ) = ∑ χ(f)u<sup>(deg f)</sup> over monic polynomials f. The weight Λ(f) is deg P if f = Pʲ for a monic irreducible P and j ≥ 1, and zero otherwise. It is chosen so that uL′/L = ∑ Λ(f)χ(f)u<sup>(deg f)</sup> (our own).

**Problem.** Let d be the degree of L(u,χ). For n ≥ 1, the sum of Λ(f)χ(f) over degree-n monic polynomials has modulus at most d√(qⁿ).

**How the definition helps.** L(u,χ) is a polynomial ∏(1 − γᵢu) of degree d, so the degree-n coefficient of uL′/L is −∑ γᵢⁿ (our own). Weil’s theorem gives \|γᵢ\| ≤ √q, so the sum is at most d√(qⁿ).

**Paper or page:** [Equidistribution of high traces of random matrices over finite fields and cancellation in character sums of high conductor](https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.01344). It says: “we have \|γᵢ\| ∈ {1, √q} for all 1 ≤ i ≤ d(χ).”

### Conductors isolate primitive correlations

**Remember:** Each character belongs to the one modulus where it first appears.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11L40 (Estimates on character sums). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Every Dirichlet character χ modulo q comes from exactly one primitive character, modulo its conductor d, the least divisor of q through which χ factors on units; χ is primitive when d = q. For n and m prime to q, C(q) sums χ(n) times the conjugate of χ(m) over primitive χ modulo q.

**Problem.** C(q) equals the sum of μ(q/d)φ(d) over divisors d \| q satisfying n ≡ m modulo d. Here μ is the Möbius function and φ is Euler’s totient function.

**How the definition helps.** Grouping all characters modulo q by conductor gives ∑<sub>d\|q</sub> C(d), and orthogonality makes this φ(q) if n ≡ m modulo q and zero otherwise (our own). Möbius inversion over the divisors of q then isolates C(q) (our own).

### Balanced cutoffs shorten sums

**Remember:** Cut both sums at one point so their terms pair up.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11M06 (ζ (s) and L(s, χ)). arXiv math.NT, math.CV. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Approximate ζ(½ + it) by two reflected Dirichlet sums cut off at the same point m = ⌊√(t/(2π))⌋. Multiplying by exp(iθ(t)), where θ(t) = Im log Γ(¼ + it/2) − (t/2)log π with the continuous logarithm real at t = 0, makes the two terms with each index n complex conjugates (our own).

**Problem.** Let C(t) sum cos(θ(t) − t log n)/√n for 1 ≤ n ≤ m. Then exp(iθ(t))ζ(½ + it) = 2C(t) + O(t⁻¹⁄⁴) as t tends to infinity.

**How the definition helps.** Each conjugate pair adds to 2cos(θ(t) − t log n)/√n, so the pairs give 2C(t) (our own). The approximate functional equation with equal cutoffs gives the error O(t⁻¹⁄⁴) (our own).

**Remember:** Integrate once and each zero gets a second denominator.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11M06 (ζ (s) and L(s, χ)), 11N05. arXiv math.NT, math.CV. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Integrate the prime-power count once: A(x) = ∫₁ˣ ψ(u) du, where ψ(x) sums log p over prime powers pᵏ ≤ x. This gives each nontrivial zero ρ of ζ the extra denominator ρ + 1, so the sum over zeros converges absolutely (our own).

**Problem.** For x &gt; 1, A(x) equals x²/2 − x log(2π) + ζ′(−1)/ζ(−1) − ∑ρ exp((ρ+1) log x)/(ρ(ρ+1)) − ∑ₖ exp((1−2k) log x)/(2k(2k−1)). The first sum runs over nontrivial zeros with multiplicity, the second over integers k ≥ 1, and both converge absolutely.

**How the definition helps.** For fixed x each zero term is O(1/\|ρ\|²), and there are O(T log T) zeros up to height T, so the sum converges absolutely (our own). Moving the integration path past the poles gives the formula and needs bounds for ζ′/ζ on that path (our own).

### Logarithmic time enables Wiener–Ikehara

**Remember:** Logarithmic time places each prime power at its logarithm.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11M06 (ζ (s) and L(s, χ)), 11N05. arXiv math.NT, math.CV. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Put the prime count on a logarithmic time axis: A(y) = ψ(exp y) for y ≥ 0, where ψ(x) sums log p over prime powers pᵏ ≤ x. Then A is nondecreasing with Laplace transform −ζ′(s)/(sζ(s)) for Re s &gt; 1, the form that the Wiener–Ikehara theorem needs (our own).

**Problem.** If the Riemann zeta function ζ has no zeros on Re s = 1, then ψ(x)/x tends to 1. Consequently π(x), the number of primes up to x, is asymptotic to x/log x.

**How the definition helps.** Under the hypothesis, the transform minus 1/(s − 1) is analytic near each point of Re s = 1, so Wiener–Ikehara gives A(y)/exp(y) → 1. Removing higher prime powers and applying partial summation gives the assertion for π.

### Mellin weights remove jump terms

**Remember:** A smooth cutoff makes the far zeros fade out.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11M06 (ζ (s) and L(s, χ)), 11N05. arXiv math.NT, math.CV. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Replace the sharp cutoff in a sum of Λ(n) by a smooth weight w with compact support in (1,∞), where Λ(n) = log p if n is a power of a prime p and zero otherwise. Its Mellin transform W(s) = ∫₁∞ w(u) exp((s−1) log u) du then decays faster than any power of the height on vertical lines, so the sum over zeros converges absolutely (our own).

**Problem.** The sum of Λ(n)w(n) over integers n ≥ 1 equals W(1) − ∑ρ W(ρ) − ∑ₖ W(−2k), with ρ over nontrivial zeros counted with multiplicity and k over integers k ≥ 1. Both sums converge absolutely.

**How the definition helps.** Repeated integration by parts gives the fast decay of W (our own). Inverting the transform writes the sum as an integral of −(ζ′/ζ)(s)W(s), and bounds between zeros let the path move left, where the pole at one, the zeros and the trivial zeros give the three terms (our own).

**nLab:** [Mellin transform](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Mellin+transform). It says: “its Mellin transform is the function given by the integral expression”

**Wikipedia:** [Explicit formulae for L-functions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Explicit_formulae_for_L-functions). It says: “F is a smooth function all of whose derivatives are rapidly decreasing”

### Primitive characters give Dirichlet L-functions a clean functional equation

**Remember:** Strip a character to its true period before reflecting.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11M06 (ζ (s) and L(s, χ)), 11L05. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** The conductor of a Dirichlet character χ modulo q is the least divisor d of q such that χ on units comes from a character modulo d. Call χ primitive if d = q, so that its L-function L(s,χ) = ∑ χ(n)n⁻ˢ (Re s &gt; 1) has no extra Euler factors at primes dividing q but not d (our own).

**Problem.** Let χ be primitive modulo q &gt; 1, with δ = 0 if χ(−1) = 1 and δ = 1 otherwise, and put Λ(s,χ) = (q/π)<sup>((s+δ)/2)</sup> Γ((s+δ)/2) L(s,χ). Then Λ is entire and Λ(s,χ) = W(χ)Λ(1−s, χ̄) with \|W(χ)\| = 1.

**How the definition helps.** Primitivity removes the extra finite factors that break reflection symmetry (our own). For example, inducing the character modulo 3 to modulus 6 multiplies L by 1 + 2⁻ˢ, which has zeros on Re s = 0 but none on Re s = 1 (our own). For primitive χ, Poisson summation gives the functional equation, and the normalized Gauss sum has modulus one.

**Wikipedia:** [Dirichlet character](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dirichlet_character), [Dirichlet L-function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dirichlet_L-function), [Selberg class](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Selberg_class). It says: “Primitive characters often simplify (or make possible) formulas in the theories of L-functions and modular forms.”

**Sources:**

- [H. Davenport, Multiplicative Number Theory, 2nd ed., Graduate Texts in Mathematics 74, Springer, 1980](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-1-4757-5927-3)
- [H. L. Montgomery and R. C. Vaughan, Multiplicative Number Theory I: Classical Theory, Cambridge University Press, 2006](https://doi.org/10.1017/CBO9780511618314)

### Riemann’s Hankel integral extends zeta to the whole plane

**Remember:** A loop around zero keeps the formula alive where the series dies.

*True by definition. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11M06 (ζ (s) and L(s, χ)), 30B40. arXiv math.NT, math.CV. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For nonintegral s, Riemann's expression is iΓ(1−s)/(2π) times the integral of (−x)<sup>(s−1)</sup>/(exp x − 1) along a Hankel contour, with the principal branch of log(−x). The contour approaches zero above the positive axis, circles zero counterclockwise within \|x\| &lt; 2π, and returns below the axis. It stays away from zero and from the poles 2πik, so the integral is entire in s and only Γ(1−s) can create poles (our own).

**Problem.** The zeta function extends to the whole complex plane with only a simple pole at s = 1.

**How the definition helps.** Collapsing the contour onto the axis for nonintegral s with Re s &gt; 1 recovers the series, so the expression continues ζ. The finite series values remove the apparent poles at integers above one, and integral comparison gives ζ(s) ∼ 1/(s−1) as real s decreases to one.

**Wikipedia:** [Riemann zeta function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riemann_zeta_function). It says: “2\\sin(\\pi s)\\Gamma(s)\\zeta(s) =i\\oint<sub>H</sub> \\frac{(-x)<sup>s-1</sup>}{e<sup>x-1}\\</sup>,\\mathrm{d}x”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Shifted kernels cancel opposite poles

**Remember:** Add the shifted terms first, so their opposite poles cancel.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11M06 (ζ (s) and L(s, χ)). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Let X(s) = π<sup>(s−½)</sup>Γ((1−s)/2)/Γ(s/2), so that ζ(s) = X(s)ζ(1−s), and let s = ½ + it with t real. The combined shifted kernel is K(z,t) = ζ(1+z) + X(s+z)X(1−s)ζ(1−z). Its two terms have poles 1/z and −1/z at z = 0, so their sum stays finite (our own).

**Problem.** For real t, the kernel K(z,t) has a removable singularity at z = 0, with value 2γ − X′(s)/X(s), where γ is Euler's constant.

**How the definition helps.** Use X(s)X(1−s) = 1, ζ(1+z) = 1/z + γ + O(z) and ζ(1−z) = −1/z + γ + O(z) (our own). Expanding X(s+z) = X(s) + zX′(s) + O(z²), the 1/z terms cancel and the constant is 2γ − X′(s)/X(s) (our own). This kernel is the main term in a shifted second moment of ζ.

**Paper or page:** [Shifted second moment of the Riemann zeta function and a Fourier type kernel](https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.04247). It says: “ζ(1+a−b) + ψ(a,b,t)ζ(1+b−a)”

**Sources:**

- [Parikshit Dutta, Debashis Ghoshal, Krishnan Rajkumar, Shifted second moment of the Riemann zeta function and a Fourier type kernel](https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.04247)

### Subtraction isolates prime zeta singularities

**Remember:** Prime zeta equals log zeta up to a tail of higher powers.

*True by definition.* MSC 11M06 (ζ (s) and L(s, χ)). arXiv math.NT, math.CV. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** The prime zeta function is P(s) = ∑ p⁻ˢ over primes p, for Re s &gt; 1. The Euler product gives log ζ(s) = ∑ₚ∑ₖ p<sup>(−ks)</sup>/k, whose k = 1 terms are exactly P(s), so the remainder R(s) = P(s) − log ζ(s) keeps only the terms with k ≥ 2 (our own).

**Problem.** The remainder R extends holomorphically to Re s &gt; ½. So in that half-plane P continues along paths that avoid the zeros and the pole of ζ, with the same logarithmic singularities as log ζ.

**How the definition helps.** Every term of R has exponent at least two, so its series converges absolutely and locally uniformly for Re s &gt; ½ (our own). So P = log ζ + R continues wherever log ζ does, with the same logarithmic singularities (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Prime zeta function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prime_zeta_function). It says: “with an infinite number of logarithmic singularities”

**Sources:**

- [C.-E. Fröberg, On the prime zeta function (1968)](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF01933420)

### The Riemann xi function is built to be entire and symmetric

**Remember:** Multiply zeta by its missing factors, and it becomes symmetric and entire.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11M06 (ζ (s) and L(s, χ)), 11M26. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** The Riemann xi function ξ(s) = ½s(s−1)π<sup>(−s/2)</sup>Γ(s/2)ζ(s) multiplies ζ by exactly the factors that cancel its pole and trivial zeros and make its functional equation symmetric. Take limits at removable singularities.

**Problem.** The function ξ is entire, real on the real line, satisfies ξ(1−s) = ξ(s), and has as zeros exactly the nontrivial zeros ρ of ζ. It has the product ξ(s) = ½ ∏ (1 − s/ρ), pairing conjugate zeros and counting multiplicities.

**How the definition helps.** The factor π<sup>(−s/2)</sup>Γ(s/2) turns the zeta functional equation into ξ(1−s) = ξ(s) (our own). The trivial zeros cancel the gamma poles at negative even integers, and s(s−1) removes the poles at zero and one. Hadamard factorization for ξ of order one, with the symmetry and ξ(0) = ½, gives the paired product.

**Wikipedia:** [Riemann xi function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riemann_xi_function). It says: “In mathematics, the Riemann xi function is a variant of the Riemann zeta function, and is defined so as to have a particularly simple functional equation.”

**Sources:**

- [B. Riemann, Ueber die Anzahl der Primzahlen unter einer gegebenen Grösse, Monatsberichte der Berliner Akademie, 1859](https://www.maths.tcd.ie/pub/HistMath/People/Riemann/Zeta/)

### A product with nonnegative coefficients rules out a zero at one

**Remember:** Multiply by zeta to turn character values into nonnegative divisor sums.

*True by definition. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11M20 (Real zeros of L(s, χ); results on L(1, χ)). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For a real nonprincipal Dirichlet character χ, multiply L(s,χ) by ζ(s). For Re s &gt; 1 the product has coefficient a(n) = ∑<sub>d\|n</sub> χ(d) at n, and these are nonnegative and at least one when n is a square (our own).

**Problem.** For every such character, L(1,χ) is nonzero.

**How the definition helps.** The coefficients are multiplicative, and at a prime power they sum successive powers of 0, 1 or −1, which gives the sign facts (our own). So the series diverges at s = ½. A zero of L at one would cancel the pole of ζ and make the product entire, contradicting Landau’s singularity theorem for nonnegative Dirichlet series.

**Wikipedia:** [Dirichlet L-function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dirichlet_L-function). It says: “In his proof, Dirichlet showed that L(s,χ) is non-zero at s = 1.”

**Paper or page:** [A note on prime number races and zero free regions for L functions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2001.00764v3). It says: “and has a singularity at σ𝒸.”

### A zeta quotient isolates quadratic zeros

**Remember:** Dividing out zeta, which is negative on (0,1), leaves the character.

*True by definition.* MSC 11M20 (Real zeros of L(s, χ); results on L(1, χ)), 11R11. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For a quadratic field K of discriminant D, the Dedekind zeta function factors as ζᴷ(s) = ζ(s)L(s,χᴰ), so the quotient ζᴷ/ζ is the L-function of the quadratic character χᴰ. On 0 &lt; s &lt; 1 the factor ζ(s) is negative, so it is never zero there (our own).

**Problem.** On the real interval 0 &lt; s &lt; 1, ζᴷ and L(s,χᴰ) have exactly the same zeros with the same multiplicities. Here χᴰ denotes the primitive quadratic character attached to D.

**How the definition helps.** The alternating series (1 − 2<sup>(1−s)</sup>)ζ(s) = ∑ (−1)<sup>(n−1)</sup> n⁻ˢ is positive while 1 − 2<sup>(1−s)</sup> is negative, so ζ(s) &lt; 0 on that interval (our own). Multiplication by this nonzero factor preserves every zero and its multiplicity.

**Wikipedia:** [Siegel zero](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siegel_zero). It says: “ζℚ(√D)(s) = ζ(s) L(s,χᴰ)”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Euler factors preserve Siegel bounds

**Remember:** Bound the primitive value first, then put back the missing factors.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11M20 (Real zeros of L(s, χ); results on L(1, χ)), 11M06. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Every character χ modulo q comes from a primitive character χ∗ modulo some d dividing q, the least modulus that determines χ on units. Then L(s,χ) is L(s,χ∗) times the finite product of 1 − χ∗(p)p⁻ˢ over primes p dividing q (our own).

**Problem.** For every ε &gt; 0 there exists c(ε) &gt; 0 such that every real nonprincipal character χ modulo q satisfies L(1,χ) ≥ c(ε)q<sup>(−ε)</sup>.

**How the definition helps.** At s = 1 each correction factor is at least 1 − 1/p, so their product is at least φ(q)/q, which exceeds a constant depending on ε times q<sup>(−ε/2)</sup> (our own). Siegel’s theorem at exponent ε/2 bounds L(1,χ∗) below by a constant times d<sup>(−ε/2)</sup> ≥ q<sup>(−ε/2)</sup>.

**Wikipedia:** [Dirichlet L-function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dirichlet_L-function). It says: “multiplied by only a finite number of factors.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Harmonic subtraction computes L-values

**Remember:** Subtract the same harmonic tail from each residue class.

*True by definition.* MSC 11M20 (Real zeros of L(s, χ); results on L(1, χ)), 11M35. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Define H(u) = ∑ₘ₌₀∞ (1/(m+u) − 1/(m+1)) for 0 &lt; u ≤ 1. Each residue class alone gives a divergent harmonic sum, and H subtracts the same reference term 1/(m+1) from every class so that each converges.

**Problem.** Let χ be a Dirichlet character modulo q whose values on invertible residues are not all one. Then L(1,χ) = (1/q) ∑ χ(a)H(a/q) over 1 ≤ a ≤ q, and H(u) = −Γ′(u)/Γ(u) − γ, with Γ Euler’s gamma function and γ Euler’s constant.

**How the definition helps.** The character values sum to zero, so the common reference terms cancel, and summing complete blocks of q terms recovers the original series (our own). Differentiating the logarithm of Euler’s product for Γ gives the formula for H.

**Wikipedia:** [Dirichlet L-function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dirichlet_L-function). It says: “linear combinations of the Hurwitz zeta function at rational values.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Logarithmic gaps simplify zero repulsion

**Remember:** Measure each zero's gap from one in units of 1/log(qT).

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11M20 (Real zeros of L(s, χ); results on L(1, χ)), 11M26. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For an integer q ≥ 3 and a height T ≥ 2, measure the distance of a zero σ + it of a Dirichlet L-function modulo q from the line Re s = 1 in units of 1/log(qT). Its scaled distance is (1 − σ)log(qT).

**Problem.** There exist computable absolute constants 0 &lt; c &lt; 1 and c′ &gt; 0 with the following property. Suppose a quadratic character modulo q has a real zero β with scaled distance δ &lt; c. Every other zero of any Dirichlet L-function modulo q at height \|t\| ≤ T has scaled distance at least c′ log(1/δ).

**How the definition helps.** Measured in the same units, the Deuring–Heilbronn theorem becomes this single-logarithm bound (our own). It says that an exceptional zero very close to one pushes every other zero further from the line.

**Paper or page:** [Condtional Bounds on Siegel Zeros](https://arxiv.org/abs/2010.01308). It says: “the product over all characters of modulus q including the exceptional one, has no other zero in the domain”

**Sources:**

- [D. R. Heath-Brown, Zero-free regions for Dirichlet L-functions, and the least prime in an arithmetic progression (1992)](https://doi.org/10.1112/plms/s3-64.2.265)

### Odd parity gives class numbers

**Remember:** For an odd quadratic character, the first moment counts classes.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11M20 (Real zeros of L(s, χ); results on L(1, χ)), 11R29. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Fix a prime q &gt; 3 with q ≡ 3 modulo 4, and let χ be the Legendre symbol modulo q: zero on multiples of q, one on nonzero squares, minus one otherwise. Then χ is odd, χ(−1) = −1, so its first moment ∑ aχ(a) over 1 ≤ a &lt; q equals −qL(0,χ) and is nonzero (our own).

**Problem.** The number of ideal classes of ℚ(√(−q)) equals −1/q times this first moment.

**How the definition helps.** The functional equation gives L(1,χ) = πL(0,χ)/√q, and the class number formula gives L(1,χ) = πh/√q, so h = L(0,χ) (our own). For an even character, such as the quadratic character modulo 5, pairing a with q − a makes the moment zero, although L(1,χ) is positive.

**Wikipedia:** [Class number formula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Class_number_formula). It says: “Dirichlet also showed that the L-series can be written in a finite form”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### One quadratic factor controls abelian exceptions

**Remember:** One quadratic factor can recur in many fields.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11M20 (Real zeros of L(s, χ); results on L(1, χ)), 11R42. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** The zeta function of an abelian number field K is the product of the L-functions of the primitive Dirichlet characters attached to its Galois group, primitive meaning of least modulus agreeing on units. One primitive character gives the same L-factor in every field that uses it, so its zeros appear in all those fields at once (our own). The family is all such fields of absolute discriminant at most Q, for a fixed Q ≥ 10.

**Problem.** For some absolute c &gt; 0, if a field in this family has a real zeta zero β with 1 − c/log Q &lt; β &lt; 1, then exactly one quadratic field F supplies this zero. The fields in the family whose zeta functions vanish at β are precisely those containing F.

**How the definition helps.** The conductor–discriminant formula bounds each character's modulus by Q, and the cited result allows at most one exceptional primitive character, which is quadratic. A field's zeta function contains that character's factor exactly when the field contains its quadratic field F.

**Paper or page:** [An explicit version of Bombieri's log-free density estimate and Sárközy's theorem for shifted primes](https://arxiv.org/abs/2208.11123). It says: “there exists a unique primitive quadratic character χ∗ (mod q∗) with q∗ ≤ Q”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Regulators normalize Siegel’s class bounds

**Remember:** The residue at one is one L-value for every quadratic field.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11M20 (Real zeros of L(s, χ); results on L(1, χ)), 11R29. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For a quadratic field K of discriminant D, let A(K) be the residue at s = 1 of its Dedekind zeta function, which treats real and imaginary fields alike. Since ζᴷ(s) = ζ(s)L(s,χ) for the quadratic character χ of K and ζ has residue one, A(K) = L(1,χ) (our own).

**Problem.** For every ε &gt; 0 some c(ε) &gt; 0 satisfies A(K) ≥ c(ε) exp(−ε log ∣D∣) for all quadratic fields K.

**How the definition helps.** The residue turns both kinds of field into the single value L(1,χ). Siegel's theorem bounds that value below by c(ε)\|D\|<sup>(−ε)</sup>, since χ has modulus \|D\|.

**nLab:** [class number formula](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/class+number+formula). It says: “is proportional the product of the regulator with the class number of K”

**Sources:**

- [C. L. Siegel, Über die Classenzahl quadratischer Zahlkörper (1935)](https://doi.org/10.4064/aa-1-1-83-86)

### Removing the exceptional factor bounds derivatives

**Remember:** Remove the exceptional zero before taking the logarithmic derivative.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11M20 (Real zeros of L(s, χ); results on L(1, χ)). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Fix a real primitive nonprincipal character χ of conductor q and a small enough absolute constant c &gt; 0. If L(s,χ) has a real zero β &gt; 1 − c/log q, put F(s) = L(s,χ)/(s − β), extended by continuity, and otherwise F = L(s,χ). Then F′/F = L′/L − 1/(s − β), so the exceptional zero's term is gone (our own).

**Problem.** There is an absolute constant C such that \|F′(1)/F(1)\| ≤ C log q. When β exists, L′(1,χ)/L(1,χ) equals 1/(1−β) plus F′(1)/F(1).

**How the definition helps.** Evaluating F′/F = L′/L − 1/(s − β) at s = 1 gives the stated relation (our own). The explicit formula, the classical zero-free region and the Euler product at 1 + 1/log q bound the remaining zero terms by O(log q).

**Wikipedia:** [Siegel zero](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siegel_zero). It says: “classical estimates for the number of non-trivial zeros”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Two quadratic zeros share one pole

**Remember:** Two zeros, one pole: positivity forbids both near one.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11M20 (Real zeros of L(s, χ); results on L(1, χ)), 11R11. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For distinct primitive quadratic characters χ₁ and χ₂, form F(s) = ζ(s)L(s,χ₁)L(s,χ₂)L(s,χ₁χ₂), where χ₁χ₂(n) = χ₁(n)χ₂(n). It contains both candidate zeros but has only one pole, at s = 1. Its −F′/F has the nonnegative coefficients Λ(n)(1+χ₁(n))(1+χ₂(n)) (our own).

**Problem.** Let β₁ and β₂ be real zeros in (0,1) of the respective L-functions, with moduli q₁ and q₂. Then max(1−β₁,1−β₂) ≥ c/log(q₁q₂) for an absolute c &gt; 0.

**How the definition helps.** The product has one pole because χ₁χ₂ is nonprincipal (our own). The Landau–Page argument applies the explicit formula to this nonnegative sum just right of one, where the single pole term cannot outweigh two zero terms that are both close to one.

**Paper or page:** [Condtional Bounds on Siegel Zeros](https://arxiv.org/abs/2010.01308). It says: “then it is real and associated to a unique, quadratic χ mod q.”

### Continuous angles count zeros

**Remember:** Follow the turn instead of resetting the angle.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11M26 (Nonreal zeros of ζ (s) and L(s, χ); Riemann and other hypotheses). arXiv math.NT, math.CV. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Let T &gt; 0 avoid the heights of nontrivial zeta zeros. S(T) is the argument of ζ(½+iT) divided by π, followed continuously from argument zero at ζ(2) along the segments from 2 to 2+iT to ½+iT, so that it keeps every full turn (our own).

**Problem.** The number of zeta zeros with imaginary part strictly between zero and T, counted with multiplicity, equals 1 + θ(T)/π + S(T). Here θ(T) = Im log Γ(¼ + iT/2) − (T/2)log π, using the continuous logarithm real at T = 0.

**How the definition helps.** The argument principle counts zeros by the total turn of ζ around a closed rectangle (our own). The symmetry of the completed zeta function reduces that turn to the stated path, and the gamma factor gives θ(T)/π (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Riemann–Siegel theta function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riemann%E2%80%93Siegel_theta_function). It says: “the argument is chosen in such a way that a continuous function is obtained”

### Cosine gaps exclude zeros

**Remember:** The first cosine must outweigh the constant term.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11M26 (Nonreal zeros of ζ (s) and L(s, χ); Riemann and other hypotheses). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Use a cosine polynomial P(u) = ∑ⱼ₌₀ᵐ aⱼcos(ju) that is nonnegative on ℝ, with all aⱼ ≥ 0 and a₁ &gt; a₀ &gt; 0, for example (1 + cos u)² with a₀ = 3/2 and a₁ = 2. Then ∑ aⱼ Re(−ζ′/ζ)(σ + ijt) is a sum over prime powers n of Λ(n)n<sup>(−σ)</sup>P(t log n) ≥ 0 (our own).

**Problem.** For each such P there is a constant c &gt; 0. If \|t\| ≥ 2 and σ ≥ 1 − c/log \|t\|, then ζ(σ + it) is nonzero.

**How the definition helps.** For a zero β + it and σ &gt; 1, nonnegativity and the explicit formula give a₁/(σ − β) ≤ a₀/(σ − 1) + O(log \|t\|), after discarding the other zeros (our own). Taking σ − 1 a small multiple of 1/log \|t\| then gives the bound, since a₁ &gt; a₀.

**Paper or page:** [Optimal Cosine Polynomials for Riemann Zeta Zero-Free Region](https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.01385). It says: “Historically, E. Landau used a particular type of non-negative cosine polynomial to construct this region.”

### Fourth powers exclude boundary zeros

**Remember:** Fourth-power weights make every prime count nonnegatively.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11M26 (Nonreal zeros of ζ (s) and L(s, χ); Riemann and other hypotheses). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For Re s &gt; 1, let Φ(s) = ∑ₚ (log p)p⁻ˢ over primes. For real t ≠ 0, combine Φ(s+irt) for r = −2,…,2 with weights 1, 4, 6, 4, 1, the coefficients of a fourth power. Then each prime gets the nonnegative factor (2cos(t log(p)/2))⁴ for real s &gt; 1 (our own).

**Problem.** The Riemann zeta function has no zero on Re s = 1.

**How the definition helps.** Comparison with −ζ′/ζ shows that the combination times s − 1 tends to 6 − 8μ − 2ν as s decreases to one, where μ and ν are the orders of zero of ζ at 1 + it and 1 + 2it. Nonnegativity forces 6 − 8μ − 2ν ≥ 0, so μ = 0 for every nonzero t.

**nLab:** [proof of the prime number theorem](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/proof+of+the+prime+number+theorem). It says: “from which, in conjunction with 1., 2., 3. above, we deduce 0 ≤ 6 − 8μ − 2ν, so that μ = 0.”

### Gram signs certify zeros

**Remember:** Positive zeta at both Gram points means Z changed sign.

*True by definition.* MSC 11M26 (Nonreal zeros of ζ (s) and L(s, χ); Riemann and other hypotheses). arXiv math.NT, math.CV. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Successive Gram points g &lt; h are heights where θ(t) = Im log Γ(¼ + it/2) − (t/2)log π, with the continuous logarithm real at t = 0, increases through nπ and (n+1)π. Retain (g,h) if ζ(½+ig) and ζ(½+ih) are both positive. Since exp(iθ) is +1 at one point and −1 at the other, the real function Z(t) = exp(iθ(t))ζ(½+it) then has opposite signs at g and h (our own).

**Problem.** Every retained interval has a zero ½ + it with g &lt; t &lt; h. The test gives no guarantee about a rejected interval or uniqueness in a retained interval.

**How the definition helps.** The functional equation makes Z real for every real t (our own), so continuity forces a zero of Z, and hence of ζ(½+it), strictly between g and h.

**Wikipedia:** [Riemann–Siegel theta function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riemann%E2%80%93Siegel_theta_function). It says: “and if this is positive at two successive Gram points, Z(t) must have a zero in the interval.”

### Integrated gaps certify completeness

**Remember:** A missed zero leaves a gap throughout the later count.

*True by definition.* MSC 11M26 (Nonreal zeros of ζ (s) and L(s, χ); Riemann and other hypotheses). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Let N(t) count zeta zeros with heights in (0,t\], with multiplicity, and let M(t) count the zeros found so far, a fixed subset of those occurrences, up to height t. Write S(t) = N(t) − 1 − θ(t)/π, with θ(t) = Im log Γ(¼+it/2) − (t/2)log π for the continuous logarithm real at t = 0. A zero missed below A makes N − M at least one at every height in \[A, B\] (our own).

**Problem.** Let 0 &lt; A &lt; B, and let U bound the integral of S over \[A, B\] from above. Let V be the integral of 1 + θ(t)/π − M(t) over that interval. If U + V &lt; B − A, then M(A) = N(A).

**How the definition helps.** Since N − M = S + (1 + θ/π − M), its integral over \[A, B\] is at most U + V (our own). If M(A) &lt; N(A), that integral is at least B − A, which contradicts U + V &lt; B − A (our own). Turing’s method supplies the difficult bound U (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Turing's method](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Turing%27s_method). It says: “It was discovered by Alan Turing and published in 1953”

**Sources:**

- [A. M. Turing, Some Calculations of the Riemann Zeta-Function (1953)](https://doi.org/10.1112/plms/s3-3.1.99)
- [R. S. Lehman, On the Distribution of Zeros of the Riemann Zeta-Function (1970)](https://doi.org/10.1112/plms/s3-20.2.303)

### Paired zeros cancel exponentials

**Remember:** Center xi so it is even, then pair opposite zeros.

*True by definition.* MSC 11M26 (Nonreal zeros of ζ (s) and L(s, χ); Riemann and other hypotheses). arXiv math.NT, math.CV. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Center the xi function: Ξ(z) = ξ(½ + z), where ξ(s) = ½s(s−1)π<sup>(−s/2)</sup>Γ(s/2)ζ(s), taken by continuity at removable singularities. The functional equation makes Ξ even, so its zeros come in pairs ±a, and each pair gives a factor 1 − (z/a)² with no exponential (our own).

**Problem.** For every z, Ξ(z)/Ξ(0) equals the product of 1 − (z/a)² over one zero from each pair, with multiplicity. This product converges locally uniformly with absolutely summable deviations from 1.

**How the definition helps.** Hadamard’s theorem for order one gives Ξ(z) = Ξ(0)exp(bz)∏(1 − z/a)exp(z/a) (our own). Evenness forces b = 0, pairing cancels the exponentials, and the convergence of ∑ 1/\|a\|² gives the locally uniform convergence (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Completed Riemann Zeta Function has Order One](https://proofwiki.org/wiki/Completed_Riemann_Zeta_Function_has_Order_One). It says: “The completed Riemann zeta function ξ has order at most 1.”

**Sources:**

- [B. Riemann, On the Number of Prime Numbers less than a Given Quantity (1859), translated by D. R. Wilkins](https://www.claymath.org/wp-content/uploads/2023/04/Wilkins-translation.pdf)

### Phase choices strengthen gap bounds

**Remember:** Remove a constant phase speed without moving the zeros.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11M26 (Nonreal zeros of ζ (s) and L(s, χ); Riemann and other hypotheses), 11M06. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Let F(t) = ζ(½+it)A(½+it), where A is a nonzero Dirichlet polynomial. Twisting by a constant phase speed, exp(ict)F(t), keeps the zeros and changes the derivative's modulus to \|F′ + icF\|, so on \[a,b\] choose the real c that minimizes the integral of \|F′ + icF\|² (our own).

**Problem.** Let a &lt; b be heights of critical-line zeta zeros. On \[a,b\], let R be the integral of \|F\|² divided by the minimized integral of \|F′ + icF\|². Some successive critical-line zero heights in \[a,b\] differ by at least π√R.

**How the definition helps.** On each gap between successive zeros, Wirtinger’s inequality bounds the integral of \|F\|² by the squared gap divided by π², times the integral of \|F′ + icF\|². If every gap were shorter than π√R, summing over the gaps would contradict the definition of R (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Amplified Fourth Moment of the Riemann Zeta-Function and Applications](https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.14415). It says: “3\\lambda \_0(v)\\int <sub>a</sub><sup>b</sup>\|f(t)\|<sup>4dt\\leq</sup> \\Big(\\frac{b-a}{\\pi }\\Big)<sup>4\\int</sup> <sub>a</sub><sup>b</sup>\|f’(t)\|<sup>4dt</sup> +6v\\Big(\\frac{b-a}{\\pi }\\Big)<sup>2\\int</sup> <sub>a</sub><sup>b</sup>\|f(t)f’(t)\|<sup>2dt</sup>,”

**Sources:**

- [Hung M. Bui, Richard R. Hall, Martin Subira Jorge, Amplified Fourth Moment of the Riemann Zeta-Function and Applications](https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.14415)

### Phase correction reveals critical zeros

**Remember:** Remove the phase so that a sign change detects a zero.

*True by definition.* MSC 11M26 (Nonreal zeros of ζ (s) and L(s, χ); Riemann and other hypotheses). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Hardy’s function Z(t) = exp(iθ(t))ζ(½+it) rotates ζ on the critical line by the phase θ(t) = Im log Γ(¼+it/2) − (t/2)log π, with the continuous logarithm real at zero. The phase is chosen so that Z is real, and the factor exp(iθ(t)) has modulus one, so it never vanishes (our own).

**Problem.** On the critical line Re s=1/2, Hardy’s Z takes real values and has the same zeros, with multiplicity, as the Riemann zeta function ζ. Opposite signs at two heights guarantee a zero between them.

**How the definition helps.** With this phase, the functional equation says that Z(t) equals its complex conjugate (our own). Since exp(iθ) never vanishes, Z and ζ have the same zeros with multiplicity, and the intermediate value theorem gives a zero between heights of opposite sign (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Z function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Z_function). It says: “It follows from the functional equation of the Riemann zeta function that the Z function is real for real values of t.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Separated heights avoid poles

**Remember:** Leave a small gap between the contour and every zero.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11M26 (Nonreal zeros of ζ (s) and L(s, χ); Riemann and other hypotheses). arXiv math.NT, math.CV. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Fix a small enough absolute constant c &gt; 0. Call a height U separated at scale T if \|U − Im ρ\| ≥ c/log T for every zero ρ of ζ with 0 &lt; Re ρ &lt; 1. Then every term 1/(σ + iU − ρ) in the expansion of ζ′/ζ has size at most (log T)/c (our own).

**Problem.** For each sufficiently large T there is a separated U in \[T, T + 1\]. At this height (ζ′/ζ)(σ + iU) = O((log T)²) uniformly for −1 ≤ σ ≤ 2.

**How the definition helps.** Only O(log T) zeros have heights between T − 1 and T + 2, so removing an interval of radius c/log T around each leaves room in \[T, T + 1\] when c is small (our own). At such U, the O(log T) nearby terms are each O(log T), and the distant terms together contribute O(log T) (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Explicit estimates for the Goldbach summatory function](https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.00323). It says: “If χ is a principal character, then ∑ (T &lt; \|γᵪ\| ≤ T + 1) 1 &lt; (1/π + 0.68) log(T + 1) + 7.407 + 25/(12πT).”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Subtracting the main term reveals a region without zeros

**Remember:** Remove the pole at one to test for other poles.

*True by definition.* MSC 11M26 (Nonreal zeros of ζ (s) and L(s, χ); Riemann and other hypotheses), 11N05. arXiv math.NT, math.CV. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Subtract the main term: E(x) = ψ(x) − x, where ψ(x) sums log p over prime powers pᵏ ≤ x. Its transform F(s) = ∫₁∞ E(x) exp(−(s + 1) log x) dx satisfies sF(s) = −(ζ′/ζ)(s) − s/(s − 1), so the pole at one is removed and any other pole must come from a zero of ζ (our own).

**Problem.** If E(x) = O(exp(θ log x)) for some ½ ≤ θ &lt; 1, then ζ has no zeros in Re s &gt; θ. In Re s &gt; 1, sF(s) = −(ζ′/ζ)(s) − s/(s − 1).

**How the definition helps.** Partial summation from the series for −ζ′/ζ gives the identity (our own). The power bound makes the integral converge locally uniformly for Re s &gt; θ, so F is holomorphic there (our own). A zeta zero in that half-plane would give a pole in the continued identity (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Logarithmic Derivative of Riemann Zeta Function](https://proofwiki.org/wiki/Logarithmic_Derivative_of_Riemann_Zeta_Function). It says: “−ζ′(s)/ζ(s) = ∑ₙ≥₁ Λ(n)n⁻ˢ”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Subtraction isolates nearby zeros

**Remember:** Subtract at the same height to damp distant zeros.

*True by definition. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11M26 (Nonreal zeros of ζ (s) and L(s, χ); Riemann and other hypotheses). arXiv math.NT, math.CV. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Subtract the value at the same height: D(s) = (ζ′/ζ)(σ + it) − (ζ′/ζ)(2 + it). In the Hadamard expansion, each zero ρ then contributes 1/(s − ρ) − 1/(2 + it − ρ), which is O(1/\|t − Im ρ\|²) for distant zeros (our own).

**Problem.** Let s = σ + it, with −1 ≤ σ ≤ 2 and \|t\| ≥ 2. Away from zeros, (ζ′/ζ)(s) equals the sum of 1/(s − ρ) over \|Im ρ − t\| ≤ 1, plus O(log \|t\|). Count zeros with multiplicity.

**How the definition helps.** The count O(log(2+\|u\|)) of zeros per unit height at u bounds the distant terms by O(log \|t\|) in total, and the nearby terms 1/(2 + it − ρ) obey the same bound. The Euler product at 2 + it and Stirling’s estimate control the remaining terms.

**Paper or page:** [Product Equation for Riemann Zeta Function](https://proofwiki.org/wiki/Product_Equation_for_Riemann_Zeta_Function). It says: “∑ρ (1/(s − ρ) + 1/ρ)”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### The stuffle product makes multiple zeta values an algebra

**Remember:** Interleave the indices and add exponents when summation variables coincide.

*True by definition.* MSC 11M32 (Multiple Dirichlet series and zeta functions and multizeta values), 16T30. arXiv math.NT, math.QA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For positive integers k₁,…,kᵣ with k₁ ≥ 2, ζ(k₁,…,kᵣ) sums ∏ nᵢ<sup>(−kᵢ)</sup> over integers n₁ &gt; ⋯ &gt; nᵣ ≥ 1. The stuffle of two index lists lists every way to merge their summation variables into one decreasing order. It sums all order-preserving interleavings, where one entry from each list may share a place and then the entries add, counting each interleaving separately.
