**Problem.** The product of two multiple zeta values is a sum of multiple zeta values. So their ℚ-span 𝒵 is a ring.

**How the definition helps.** Ordering all the variables in the product of two such sums gives exactly the stuffles, with equal variables adding their exponents (our own). Every resulting index starts with an exponent of at least two, so each sum converges, and bilinearity gives closure of the ℚ-span under multiplication.

**Paper or page:** [Generalized quasi-shuffle products](https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.12386). It says: “For v,w ∈ ℌ⁰ we have ζ(v)ζ(w)=ζ(v∗w). In particular, the space 𝒵 is a ℚ-algebra.”

**Sources:**

- [Masataka Satoh, Generalized quasi-shuffle products, arXiv:2303.12386 (2023)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.12386)
- [Michael E. Hoffman, The Algebra of Multiple Harmonic Series, Journal of Algebra (1997)](https://doi.org/10.1006/jabr.1997.7127)

### Word integrals make shuffles multiplicative

**Remember:** Multiplying ordered integrals interleaves their variables.

*True by definition.* MSC 11M32 (Multiple Dirichlet series and zeta functions and multizeta values). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Write a multiple zeta value as an iterated integral over 1 &gt; t₁ &gt; ⋯ &gt; tₖ &gt; 0: encode each index s as s−1 zeros followed by a one, and read zero as dt/t and one as dt/(1−t). The shuffle of two words sums all interleavings that keep each word’s order, counted separately, which are the ways to merge two ordered lists of variables (our own).

**Problem.** For two words starting with zero and ending with one, the product of their multiple zeta values equals the sum of their shuffled integrals.

**How the definition helps.** The product of two integrals over ordered domains splits into one ordered region per shuffle, after discarding diagonals of measure zero (our own). Each region gives the integral of the shuffled word. The work lies in proving the integral represents the original nested sum.

**Wikipedia:** [Multiple zeta function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multiple_zeta_function). It says: “This result is extremely useful due to a well-known result regarding products of iterated integrals”

**Paper or page:** [Discrete iterated integrals and cyclic sum formulas](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.16161v2). It says: “(Shuffle product formula) Iγ(xγ; w ⧢ w′; yγ) = Iγ(xγ; w; yγ)Iγ(xγ; w′; yγ).”

**Sources:**

- [Discrete iterated integrals and cyclic sum formulas](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.16161v2)

### Word reflection gives zeta duality

**Remember:** Reverse the word and swap its letters without changing the value.

*True by definition.* MSC 11M32 (Multiple Dirichlet series and zeta functions and multizeta values). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Write a multiple zeta value with first index s₁ ≥ 2 as an integral over 1 &gt; t₁ &gt; ⋯ &gt; tₖ &gt; 0 of a word: each index s becomes s−1 zeros followed by a one, with zero read as dt/t and one as dt/(1−t). The dual word reverses the order and swaps zeros and ones, which is what the substitution t ↦ 1 − t does to the integral (our own).

**Problem.** Every multiple zeta value equals the multiple zeta value of its dual word.

**How the definition helps.** Replacing every t by 1 − t swaps the two forms and reverses the variable order, so it keeps the ordered domain (our own). The integral representation of the nested series then transfers this equality to the zeta values.

**Wikipedia:** [Multiple zeta function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Multiple_zeta_function). It says: “it is possible to express colored multiple zeta values (and thus their special cases) as certain multivariable integrals.”

**Paper or page:** [Proving dualities for qMZVs with connected sums](https://arxiv.org/abs/2111.00058v1). It says: “For every admissible index k, we have ζ(k) = ζ(k∨).”

**Sources:**

- [Discrete iterated integrals and cyclic sum formulas](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.16161v2)

### Hurwitz zeta cancels character poles

**Remember:** Every residue class shares one pole; the character sum cancels it.

*True by definition.* MSC 11M35 (Hurwitz and Lerch zeta functions). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** The Hurwitz zeta function ζ(s,a), for a &gt; 0, sums (n+a)⁻ˢ over integers n ≥ 0 and continues to the plane with one simple pole, at s = 1, of residue 1. Grouping n by its residue r modulo q writes a Dirichlet L-function as q⁻ˢ ∑ χ(r)ζ(s,r/q), over 1 ≤ r ≤ q (our own).

**Problem.** If the Dirichlet character χ is not 1 on every invertible residue, its L-function extends holomorphically to the whole complex plane.

**How the definition helps.** Each ζ(s,r/q) has the same pole at s = 1 with residue 1, so the pole of the sum has residue ∑ χ(r)/q (our own). This character sum is zero when χ is not identically 1 on the invertible residues, so the pole cancels (our own). The real work is the continuation of each Hurwitz zeta function.

**Wikipedia:** [Hurwitz zeta function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurwitz_zeta_function). It says: “At s = 1, it has a simple pole with residue 1.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Selberg factors weight repeats

**Remember:** Shifting s by every k builds one geometric series per geodesic.

*True by definition.* MSC 11M36 (Selberg zeta functions and regularized determinants; applications to spectral theory, Dirichlet series, Eisenstein series, etc. (explicit formulas)), 11F72. arXiv math.SP, math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** On a closed oriented surface of curvature −1, a primitive closed geodesic is one that does not trace a shorter closed geodesic several times. For Re s &gt; 1, the Selberg zeta function Z(s) is the product of 1−exp(−(s+k)ℓ) over primitive oriented geodesics of length ℓ and over all integers k ≥ 0.

**Problem.** For Re(s) &gt; 1, Z′(s)/Z(s) equals the sum of ℓ exp(−smℓ)/(1 − exp(−mℓ)) over the primitive geodesics and all positive integers m.

**How the definition helps.** Logarithmic differentiation gives the terms ℓ exp(−(s+k)mℓ) for m ≥ 1, and summing the geometric series over k gives the factor 1/(1−exp(−mℓ)) (our own). The geodesic counting estimate justifies differentiating and rearranging.

**Wikipedia:** [Selberg zeta function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Selberg_zeta_function). It says: “where p runs over conjugacy classes of prime geodesics (equivalently, conjugacy classes of primitive hyperbolic elements of Γ)”

**Sources:**

- [Dennis A. Hejhal, The Selberg Trace Formula for PSL(2,ℝ), volume I (1976).](https://doi.org/10.1007/BFb0079608)

### Degree bounds primitive factor counts

**Remember:** Every proper factor costs at least one unit of degree.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11M41 (Other Dirichlet series and zeta functions). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A Selberg-class function F ≠ 1 is primitive if every factorization F = GH inside the class has G = 1 or H = 1. Its degree d(F), twice the sum of the slopes λ of its gamma factors Γ(λs+μ), adds under products and is at least 1 when F ≠ 1.

**Problem.** Every member F other than 1 is a product of at most ⌊d(F)⌋ primitive factors.

**How the definition helps.** Each split adds one factor and each factor costs at least one unit of degree, so splitting stops after at most ⌊d(F)⌋ factors. Additivity follows from the definition, and the lower bound 1 is the degree gap theorem. No unique factorization is needed.

**Wikipedia:** [Selberg class](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Selberg_class). It says: “every function F ≠ 1 can be written as a product of primitive functions”

**Sources:**

- [Kaczorowski and Perelli, On the structure of the Selberg class, I: 0≤d≤1](https://doi.org/10.1007/bf02392574)

### Deleted Euler factors break reflection

**Remember:** Deleting a prime adds zeros that have no mirror partners.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11M41 (Other Dirichlet series and zeta functions). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A Selberg functional equation says that the completion Φ(s) = QˢF(s)∏ⱼΓ(λⱼs+μⱼ), with finitely many factors, Q &gt; 0, λⱼ &gt; 0 and Re μⱼ ≥ 0, equals ε times the conjugate of Φ(1−s̄) for some \|ε\| = 1. So every zero ρ of Φ has a mirror zero at 1−ρ̄ (our own).

**Problem.** The series over odd integers, F(s) = (1−2⁻ˢ)ζ(s), satisfies the other Selberg axioms but has no such functional equation.

**How the definition helps.** The factor 1−2⁻ˢ gives infinitely many zeros on Re s = 0, and the finitely many gamma factors can cancel at most finitely many of them (our own). Their mirrors would lie on Re s = 1. Away from s = 1, ζ, 1−2⁻ˢ and every completing factor are finite and nonzero there, so those mirrors cannot exist.

**Wikipedia:** [Selberg class](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Selberg_class). It says: “Without this functional equation, the class would have Dirichlet L-functions for any imprimitive character.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Exponential Euler factors cannot vanish

**Remember:** An exponential never vanishes, so the Euler product axiom forbids zeros.

*Rules out counterexamples. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11M41 (Other Dirichlet series and zeta functions). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** The Selberg Euler product axiom says that F is an exponential: F(s) = exp(∑ₙ b(n)n⁻ˢ) for Re s &gt; 1, with b(n) zero outside prime powers. Some constants C &gt; 0 and θ &lt; ½ must satisfy \|b(pʳ)\| ≤ Cp<sup>(rθ)</sup> for every prime p and integer r ≥ 1.

**Problem.** Every Selberg-class function is nonzero for Re s &gt; 1. The Davenport–Heilbronn function satisfies the other axioms and has zeros in this half-plane.

**How the definition helps.** The exponential of a convergent series never vanishes, so F has no zeros for Re s &gt; 1 (our own). The series converges because b(p) is the Dirichlet coefficient of F at primes, and higher powers converge since 2(Re s−θ) &gt; 1. The Davenport–Heilbronn theorem supplies zeros with Re s &gt; 1 for the counterexample.

**Wikipedia:** [Selberg class](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Selberg_class). It says: “Despite having an analytic continuation, having periodic coefficients (thus satisfying the Ramanujan conjecture), and satisfying the functional equation, it has zeros lying off the critical line.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Gamma slopes govern zero counts

**Remember:** Each gamma slope adds its own share to the density of zeros.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11M41 (Other Dirichlet series and zeta functions). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** The degree d of a Selberg-class function F is twice the sum of the slopes λ of the gamma factors Γ(λs+μ) in its completion. Each slope sets how fast its gamma factor turns the argument of the completion as Im s grows (our own).

**Problem.** For fixed F, let N(T) count the zeros of its completion with 0 &lt; Im s ≤ T, with multiplicity. Then N(T) = dT log T/(2π) + O(T), with the implied constant depending on F.

**How the definition helps.** By the argument principle, N(T) is a change of argument of the completion around a rectangle (our own). Stirling's formula makes each factor Γ(λs+μ) contribute about λT log T/π, so the slopes add up to dT log T/(2π). Contour estimates bound the rest by O(T).

**Wikipedia:** [Selberg class](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Selberg_class). It says: “Denoting the number of non-trivial zeros of F with 0 ≤ Im(s) ≤ T”

**Sources:**

- [Iwaniec and Kowalski, Analytic Number Theory, Chapter 5](https://doi.org/10.1090/coll/053)

### Gamma slopes make degrees additive

**Remember:** Multiply the series, join the slope lists, add the degrees.

*True by definition.* MSC 11M41 (Other Dirichlet series and zeta functions). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** The degree of a Selberg-class function is twice the sum of the slopes λ, counted with repetition, of the gamma factors Γ(λs+μ) in its functional equation. This sum does not depend on which functional equation is chosen.

**Problem.** If F and G are in the Selberg class, then the degree of FG is the sum of their degrees.

**How the definition helps.** Multiplying F by G joins the two lists of gamma factors, so the slope sums add. Counting factors instead would fail, because the gamma multiplication formula can split one factor into several (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Selberg class](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Selberg_class). It says: “Since this sum is independent of the choice of functional equation, it is well-defined for any function F.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Nonnegative coefficients prevent cancellation in Dirichlet sums

**Remember:** Partial sums that never decrease cannot hide a jump.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11M45 (Tauberian theorems). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A Dirichlet series F(s) = ∑ a(n)n⁻ˢ has nonnegative coefficients a(n), so its partial sums never decrease.

**Problem.** Suppose the series converges for Re s&gt;1. For some c&gt;0, suppose F(s)−c/(s−1) extends holomorphically across every point of Re s=1. Then the partial sum up to x, divided by x, tends to c.

**How the definition helps.** The Wiener–Ikehara theorem turns the pole data into the limit when partial sums never decrease, since then no later drop can cancel a jump. Without this the claim fails: start from coefficients one, add 2ᵏ at 2ᵏ and subtract 2ᵏ at 2ᵏ+1 for each k ≥ 1 (our own). These corrections are holomorphic for Re s &gt; 0, yet the partial sum divided by x is two at 2ᵏ and one at 2ᵏ+1 (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Wiener–Ikehara theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wiener%E2%80%93Ikehara_theorem). It says: “where a(n) is non-negative.”

**Sources:**

- [Norbert Wiener, Tauberian Theorems (1932)](https://doi.org/10.2307/1968102)

### Repeated integration gives counting sums a faster decaying kernel

**Remember:** Each integration adds one denominator factor and speeds the kernel's decay.

*True by definition. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11M45 (Tauberian theorems). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For a positive integer k, the k-fold smoothed sum integrates the counting sum A(X) = ∑<sub>n≤X</sub> a(n) k times from zero. Equivalently, it weights each a(n) with n ≤ X by (X−n)ᵏ/k!, whose Mellin kernel is 1/\[s(s+1)⋯(s+k)\] instead of the 1/s of the plain count (our own).

**Problem.** Suppose F(s) = ∑ a(n)n⁻ˢ converges absolutely on Re s = c &gt; 0. Then for X &gt; 0 the smoothed sum equals 1/(2πi) times the integral of F(s)Xˢ⁺ᵏ/\[s(s+1)⋯(s+k)\] up the line Re s = c.

**How the definition helps.** Mellin inversion of the kernel 1/\[s(s+1)⋯(s+k)\] gives the weight (X−n)ᵏ/k! term by term, and absolute convergence lets the sum and the integral swap (our own). Each extra factor in the denominator makes the kernel decay by one more power of the height (our own).

**Paper or page:** [An Explicit Tauberian Theorem taking Averaged Inputs with an Application to Counting Abelian Number Fields](https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.20814v1). It says: “\\frac{\\Gamma (s)}{\\Gamma (s+k+1)} X<sup>s+k</sup>”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Logarithmic integrals sharpen prime estimates

**Remember:** Integrate the changing prime density instead of freezing it at x.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11N05 (Distribution of primes), 11M26. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Li(x) = ∫₂ˣ dt/log t adds up the prime density 1/log t at each point up to x, so it follows the density as it changes. The simpler main term x/log x uses the density at the right endpoint for the whole range.

**Problem.** If the Riemann hypothesis holds, then π(x) − Li(x) = O(√x log x). In contrast, π(x) − x/log x is asymptotic to x/(log x)², even without that hypothesis.

**How the definition helps.** Integration by parts gives Li(x) = x/log x + x/(log x)² + O(x/(log x)³), so x/log x drops a term far larger than √x log x (our own). Under the Riemann hypothesis, von Koch's theorem gives the square-root error for Li(x) (our own). The prime number theorem with the classical error term then gives the second claim (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Prime number theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prime_number_theorem). It says: “it turned out that Dirichlet's approximation is considerably better if one considers the differences instead of quotients.”

**Sources:**

- [H. von Koch, Sur la distribution des nombres premiers (1901)](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF02403071)

### Taking the halfway value at jumps makes Riemann's explicit formula exact

**Remember:** At a jump, the inverse transform lands halfway, so count half.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11N05 (Distribution of primes), 11M26. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Riemann's prime-power count Π₀(x), for x &gt; 1, adds 1/n for each prime power pⁿ &lt; x and adds 1/(2n) when pⁿ = x. So at each jump it takes the average of its left and right limits; π₀ uses the same rule for primes alone (n = 1).

**Problem.** For x &gt; 1, Π₀(x) = li(x) − lim(T→∞) ∑<sub>\|Im ρ\|≤T</sub> Ei(ρ log x) − log 2 + I(x), with ρ over nontrivial zeta zeros with multiplicity and Ei on its principal branch. Here li(x) = Ei(log x), I(x) is the integral of 1/\[t(t²−1) log t\] from x to infinity, and Möbius inversion gives π₀(x).

**How the definition helps.** The formula is an inverse Mellin transform of log ζ(s), and such a transform takes the average value at a jump (our own). So with a right-continuous count the formula would fail at every prime power (our own). The hard part is the convergence of the sum over zeros, which von Mangoldt proved in 1895.

**Wikipedia:** [Prime-counting function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prime-counting_function). It says: “it takes a value halfway between the two sides at the discontinuities of π(x). That added detail is used because the function may then be defined by an inverse Mellin transform.”

**Sources:**

- [B. Riemann, Ueber die Anzahl der Primzahlen unter einer gegebenen Grösse, Monatsberichte der Berliner Akademie, 1859](https://www.maths.tcd.ie/pub/HistMath/People/Riemann/Zeta/)
- [H. von Mangoldt, Zu Riemanns Abhandlung 'Ueber die Anzahl der Primzahlen unter einer gegebenen Grösse', J. reine angew. Math. 114 (1895) 255–305](https://doi.org/10.1515/crll.1895.114.255)

### Vaughan’s cutoffs split prime sums

**Remember:** Cut μ and Λ into short and long parts, then expand.

*True by definition.* MSC 11N05 (Distribution of primes). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For cutoffs U,V ≥ 1, split the Möbius function μ into its part μₛ on n ≤ V and the rest μℓ = μ−μₛ, and split the von Mangoldt function Λ into Λₛ on n ≤ U and the rest Λℓ = Λ−Λₛ. Products are Dirichlet convolutions, f∗g(n) = ∑<sub>d∣n</sub> f(d)g(n/d).

**Problem.** With 1 the constant function one, Vaughan's identity reads Λ = μₛ∗log + Λₛ − μₛ∗1∗Λₛ + μℓ∗1∗Λℓ.

**How the definition helps.** Write Λ = μ∗log = μₛ∗log + μℓ∗log, and in the second term expand log = 1∗Λₛ + 1∗Λℓ (our own). Since μ∗1 is the convolution identity, μℓ∗1∗Λₛ equals Λₛ − μₛ∗1∗Λₛ. The term μℓ∗1∗Λℓ is what remains.

**Wikipedia:** [Vaughan's identity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vaughan%27s_identity). It says: “four distinct sums based on the expansion of the logarithmic derivative of the Riemann zeta function”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Dirichlet density makes primes in progressions easy to measure

**Remember:** A prime set's share of ∑ p⁻ˢ as s falls to one.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11N13 (Primes in congruence classes), 11R45. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** The Dirichlet density of a set A of primes is the share of the divergent sum ∑ p⁻ˢ that comes from A as s decreases to 1: lim(s↓1) (∑<sub>p∈A</sub> p⁻ˢ)/(∑<sub>p</sub> p⁻ˢ), if the limit exists.

**Problem.** For coprime a and q, the primes p ≡ a mod q have Dirichlet density 1/φ(q), where φ is Euler's totient function.

**How the definition helps.** By character orthogonality, ∑<sub>p≡a</sub> p⁻ˢ is (1/φ(q)) ∑\_χ χ̄(a) log L(s,χ) up to a bounded error from prime powers (our own). The principal character gives (1/φ(q)) times the whole divergent term, and the others stay bounded because L(1,χ) ≠ 0. Dividing by ∑ p⁻ˢ gives 1/φ(q).

**Wikipedia:** [Dirichlet density](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dirichlet_density). It says: “the Dirichlet density (or analytic density) of a set of primes, named after Peter Gustav Lejeune Dirichlet, is a measure of the size of the set that is easier to use than the natural density.”

**Sources:**

- [P. G. L. Dirichlet, Beweis des Satzes, dass jede unbegrenzte arithmetische Progression ... unendlich viele Primzahlen enthält (1837), reprinted by Cambridge University Press](https://doi.org/10.1017/CBO9781139237321.012)

### Log weights linearize Siegel–Walfisz

**Remember:** With log weights, each reduced class expects exactly x/φ(q).

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11N13 (Primes in congruence classes). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** ψ(x;q,a) counts the prime powers n ≤ x with n ≡ a mod q, each with the von Mangoldt weight Λ(n) = log p when n is a power of the prime p. The weight log p cancels the prime density 1/log p, so the expected count is x/φ(q), where φ(q) counts the classes coprime to q (our own).

**Problem.** For fixed A &gt; 0 there is c &gt; 0 such that ψ(x;q,a) = x/φ(q) + O(x exp(−c√log x)). The estimate is uniform for x ≥ 3, gcd(a,q) = 1 and q ≤ (log x)ᴬ.

**How the definition helps.** The weights are the coefficients of −L′/L, and the pole of the principal character's L-function gives the linear main term (our own). Character orthogonality gives each reduced class the same share 1/φ(q). The Siegel–Walfisz theorem supplies the uniform error in this range of moduli.

**Wikipedia:** [Siegel–Walfisz theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siegel%E2%80%93Walfisz_theorem). It says: “whenever (a, q) = 1 and q ≤ (log x)ᴺ”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Matching signs cancel prime bias

**Remember:** Pair classes where the exceptional character agrees, and its bias cancels.

*True by definition.* MSC 11N13 (Primes in congruence classes), 11M20. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Let θ(x;q,a) sum log p over primes p &lt; x with p ≡ a mod q. Pair two units a and b modulo q when the possible exceptional real character modulo q, the one that the classical zero-free region allows a zero near 1, takes the same value at a and b. If there is no exceptional character, every pair of units is allowed.

**Problem.** For some absolute c,d,C &gt; 0 and all x ≥ 3, take q ≤ exp(c√(log x)). Every such pair satisfies \|θ(x;q,a)−θ(x;q,b)\| ≤ Cx exp(−d√(log x)).

**How the definition helps.** Each θ(x;q,a) is a main term x/φ(q), plus an exceptional term weighted by the character's value at a, plus a small error (our own). Paired units have equal values, so the main and exceptional terms cancel in the difference. The prime ideal theorem specialized to ℚ bounds the two remaining errors uniformly.

**Paper or page:** [Notes on Mitsui's Prime Number Theorem with Siegel zeros](https://arxiv.org/abs/2209.11816). It says: “where β is the potential Siegel zero mod 𝔮.”

**Sources:**

- [Wataru Kai, Notes on Mitsui's Prime Number Theorem with Siegel zeros](https://arxiv.org/abs/2209.11816)

### Maximal errors control shorter intervals

**Remember:** Control every endpoint, and any interval is a difference of two.

*True by definition.* MSC 11N13 (Primes in congruence classes). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For gcd(a,q) = 1, the error E(t;q,a) is the sum of log p over prime powers pᵏ ≤ t in the class of a, minus t/φ(q). The maximal error D(x;q) is the largest \|E(t;q,a)\| over reduced a and all endpoints 0 ≤ t ≤ x, so it controls every interval \[u,v\] and not only \[0,x\].

**Problem.** Fix A &gt; 0 and set Q = √x/(log x)ᴮ, with B large enough in terms of A. Then the sum over q ≤ Q of the largest \|E(v;q,a) − E(u;q,a)\|, over reduced a and 0 ≤ u ≤ v ≤ x, is O(x/(log x)ᴬ).

**How the definition helps.** By the triangle inequality each interval error is at most 2D(x;q), because D controls both endpoints (our own explanation). An estimate at t = x alone says nothing about earlier endpoints. The maximal Bombieri–Vinogradov theorem bounds the sum of D(x;q) over q ≤ Q.

**Wikipedia:** [Bombieri–Vinogradov theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bombieri%E2%80%93Vinogradov_theorem). It says: “averaged over the moduli q up to Q.”

**Sources:**

- [Enrico Bombieri, On the large sieve (1965)](https://doi.org/10.1112/S0025579300005313)

### Reduced classes exclude the even progression

**Remember:** Primes spread evenly only over classes coprime to the modulus.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11N13 (Primes in congruence classes). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A reduced class a modulo q is one with gcd(a,q) = 1; φ(q) counts these classes and π(x;q,a) counts the primes up to x in the class. Any other class contains at most one prime, because all its members share a factor with q (our own).

**Problem.** For every fixed A &gt; 0, π(x;q,a) ∼ (∫₂ˣ dt/log t)/φ(q) as x tends to infinity, uniformly over reduced classes with q ≤ (log x)ᴬ.

**How the definition helps.** A class with gcd(a,q) &gt; 1, such as the even class modulo 2, holds at most one prime, so it cannot carry the main term (our own). For reduced classes the Siegel–Walfisz theorem gives the uniform estimate, with error smaller than the main term in this range (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Primes of the form $ax+by$ in certain intervals with small solutions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2510.01781v1). It says: “Let A be a positive real number and m, l two coprime integers with 1 ≤ m ≤ (log x)ᴬ.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Square roots measure prime power corrections

**Remember:** Square roots of a decide which primes square into the class.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11N13 (Primes in congruence classes), 11N05. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Let ψ(x;q,a) weight each prime power pᵏ ≤ x with pᵏ ≡ a mod q by log p, and let θ(x;q,a) keep only the primes. Let r(q,a) count the square roots of a, the classes b with b² ≡ a mod q. A prime square p² lies in the class of a exactly when p lies in one of these root classes.

**Problem.** For fixed q ≥ 2 and reduced a, ψ(x;q,a) − θ(x;q,a) = r(q,a)√x/φ(q) + o(√x) as x tends to infinity.

**How the definition helps.** The gap ψ − θ is mainly the sum of log p over primes p ≤ √x in the root classes (our own explanation). The prime number theorem for each fixed invertible class makes each root class contribute about √x/φ(q). Cubes and higher powers add only o(√x) in total (our own derivation).

**nLab:** [proof of the prime number theorem](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/proof+of+the+prime+number+theorem). It says: “Proving the asymptotic result θ(x) ∼ x will involve complex analysis applied to the Riemann zeta function.”

**Wikipedia:** [Chebyshev function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chebyshev_function). It says: “with the sum extending over all prime powers not exceeding x”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Buchstab’s function unifies rough counts

**Remember:** The delay function records what remains after the least prime is removed.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11N25 (Distribution of integers with specified multiplicative constraints). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** An integer is y-rough if it has no prime factor below y. Buchstab's function ω(u) is 1/u on \[1,2\] and continues continuously for u &gt; 2 by (uω(u))′ = ω(u−1), the shift by one that removing the least prime causes (our own).

**Problem.** Fix u&gt;1 and set y=exp((log x)/u). As x tends to infinity, the count of y-rough positive integers at most x is asymptotic to xω(u)/log y.

**How the definition helps.** The rough count obeys Buchstab's identity, which groups rough integers by their least prime, and the delay equation is the limit form of that identity (our own). For 1 &lt; u ≤ 2 only primes affect the main term, giving 1/u by the prime number theorem. The analytic step passes from the prime sum to the integral form of the delay equation.

**Wikipedia:** [Buchstab function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buchstab_function). It says: “The Buchstab function is used to count rough numbers.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Dickman’s delay bounds smooth densities

**Remember:** u times ρ(u) is ρ's average over the previous unit interval.

*True by definition.* MSC 11N25 (Distribution of integers with specified multiplicative constraints). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** The Dickman function ρ(u) is the limiting proportion of integers up to x whose prime factors are all at most x<sup>(1/u)</sup>. It equals 1 on \[0,1\] and for u &gt; 1 satisfies uρ′(u) = −ρ(u−1), which integrates to uρ(u) = ∫<sub>u−1</sub>ᵘ ρ(v) dv (our own).

**Problem.** For u ≥ 1, ρ(u) ≤ 1/⌊u⌋!, where ⌊u⌋ is the integer part of u.

**How the definition helps.** Since ρ is positive and decreasing, the integral is at most ρ(u−1), so uρ(u) ≤ ρ(u−1), and iterating gives 1/⌊u⌋! (our own). Positivity holds because at a first zero the integral of a positive function would be zero. Dickman's density theorem identifies this solution with the limiting proportion.

**Wikipedia:** [Dickman function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dickman_function). It says: “The Dickman–de Bruijn function ρ(u) is a continuous function that satisfies the delay differential equation”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Squarefree smooth counts separate densities

**Remember:** Sieve out squares by Möbius and keep the same Dickman profile.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11N25 (Distribution of integers with specified multiplicative constraints). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Ψ(x,y) counts positive integers up to x with all prime factors at most y. Writing the squarefree indicator as ∑<sub>d²∣n</sub> μ(d), with μ the Möbius function, turns the squarefree count into ∑ μ(d)Ψ(x/d², y) over y-smooth d (our own).

**Problem.** Fix u ≥ 1, set y = exp((log x)/u), and let ρ(u) be the limit of Ψ(x,y)/x as x tends to infinity. The count with the additional squarefree restriction is asymptotic to xρ(u)/ζ(2), where ζ(2) = ∑ 1/n².

**How the definition helps.** Each term μ(d)Ψ(x/d², y)/x tends to μ(d)ρ(u)/d², because x/d² and y have nearly the same Dickman parameter and ρ is continuous (our own). The terms are bounded by 1/d², so dominated convergence gives the factor ∑ μ(d)/d² = 1/ζ(2).

**Wikipedia:** [Dickman function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dickman_function). It says: “Dickman proved that, when a is fixed, we have Ψ(x, x⁽¹⁄ᵃ⁾) ∼ xρ(a)”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Adjoints transpose the large sieve

**Remember:** Take the conjugate transpose to exchange samples and coefficients.

*True by definition.* MSC 11N35 (Sieves). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Let A be the matrix with entry exp(2πinαᵣ) in row r and column n, for N ≥ 1 consecutive integers n and points αᵣ on ℝ/ℤ; the large sieve bounds its operator norm. A matrix and its conjugate transpose have the same operator norm, the largest ratio of output length to nonzero input length.

**Problem.** Suppose distinct sample indices give points at circle distance at least δ, where 0 &lt; δ ≤ 1/2. Then ∑ₙ \|∑ᵣ bᵣ exp(−2πinαᵣ)\|² ≤ (N − 1 + 1/δ) ∑ᵣ \|bᵣ\|² for all complex bᵣ.

**How the definition helps.** The sum in the problem is the squared length of the conjugate transpose of A applied to (bᵣ), so the large sieve's norm bound applies to it directly. In our own formulation, this replaces a second estimate of exponential sums.

**Wikipedia:** [Large sieve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Large_sieve). It says: “equals the norm of its adjoint”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Liouville signs expose sieve parity

**Remember:** Even and odd factor counts look the same to every divisibility test.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11N35 (Sieves). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** The Liouville sign λ(n) = (−1)<sup>Ω</sup>(n), where Ω(n) counts prime factors with multiplicity, splits 1 ≤ n ≤ x into the even weight (1+λ(n))/2 and the odd weight (1−λ(n))/2. Both weights put mass x/(2d) + r(d) on the multiples of each d, with the same main term.

**Problem.** Fix 0 &lt; θ &lt; 1 and A &gt; 0, and sum \|r(d)\| over d up to x raised to θ. For either weight this sum is O(x/(log x)ᴬ). After removing multiples of primes at most √x, the even weight totals one and the odd weight totals asymptotically x/log x.

**How the definition helps.** After removing multiples of primes up to √x, only 1 and the primes in (√x,x\] remain, so the even weight keeps 1 and the odd weight keeps about x/log x. Each r(d) is half a Liouville sum up to x/d plus rounding, since λ(dm) = λ(d)λ(m), and the prime number theorem with an error term makes these small (our own). So divisibility estimates alone cannot give a lower bound of order x/log x.

**Wikipedia:** [Parity problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Parity_problem). It says: “The set with an odd number of factors is just the primes between x¹⁄² and x”

**Sources:**

- [J. Friedlander and H. Iwaniec, Asymptotic sieve for primes, Annals of Mathematics 148 (1998), 1041–1065.](https://doi.org/10.2307/121035)

### Local density handles crowded samples

**Remember:** Bound the occupancy of short arcs, even when points coincide.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11N35 (Sieves). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** On the circle ℝ/ℤ, let K be the largest number of samples, counted with multiplicity, in any half-open arc of length δ. Unlike the smallest gap, K stays useful when samples coincide.

**Problem.** Take 0 &lt; δ ≤ 1/2 and a polynomial T(α) = ∑ₙ aₙ exp(2πinα) with N consecutive integer frequencies. Then ∑ \|T(α)\|² ≤ 2K(N − 1 + 1/δ) ∑ₙ \|aₙ\|², where the left sum runs over all samples.

**How the definition helps.** The samples split into at most 2K lists of δ-spaced points, and the separated large sieve bounds each list (our own). Split the circle into two half-open semicircles, sort each, and deal its samples cyclically into K lists (our own). Consecutive entries of a list are K places apart, so their gap is at least δ, or K + 1 samples would lie in one arc (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Infinitude of palindromic almost-prime numbers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.16637v3). It says: “For any set of δ-spaced points”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Local occupancy bounds clustered samples

**Remember:** Charge for the size of a cluster, not its smallest gap.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11N35 (Sieves), 42A05. arXiv math.NT, math.CA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For sample points on ℝ/ℤ and an integer N ≥ 2, let K be the largest number of samples, counted with repetition, in any closed arc of length 1/N. It replaces the smallest distance between two samples, which is zero when samples repeat.

**Problem.** Let S be a trigonometric polynomial on N consecutive integer frequencies. Put M = ∫₀¹ \|S(x)\|² dx. Summing \|S(x)\|² over all samples gives at most 4KNM.

**How the definition helps.** Each sample has at most 2K−2 other samples within distance 1/N, so greedy colouring splits the samples into at most 2K−1 groups with spacing at least 1/N (our own). The additive large sieve bounds each group by 2NM, and (2K−1)·2NM ≤ 4KNM.

**Paper or page:** [On large sieve inequalities involving pth powers of trigonometric polynomials](https://arxiv.org/abs/2209.12294). It says: “\\sum <sub>j=1</sub><sup>r\|s</sup>(x<sub>j</sub>)\|<sup>p\\le</sup> \\frac{pN\\sigma (\\delta ; N)}{2\\sqrt{\\pi }}\\cdot \\frac{ \\Gamma \\Bigl(p/2\\Bigr)}{\\Gamma \\Bigl(p/2+1/2\\Bigr)}\\\| s\\\| ^p<sub>L<sup>p</sup>(\\mathbb T)</sub>”

**Sources:**

- [H. L. Montgomery and R. C. Vaughan, The large sieve, Mathematika 20 (1973), 119–134](https://doi.org/10.1112/S0025579300004708)
- [Saulius Norvidas, On large sieve inequalities involving pth powers of trigonometric polynomials](https://arxiv.org/abs/2209.12294)

### Local odds multiply across primes

**Remember:** Center each class indicator so its Fourier energy multiplies.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11N35 (Sieves). arXiv math.NT, math.CO. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For each prime p ≤ Q, choose classes modulo p that A avoids, a fraction ω(p) &lt; 1 of all classes, and let Iₚ indicate the other classes. Centre it as hₚ = Iₚ/(1−ω(p)) − 1, which has mean zero, and for squarefree q ≤ Q multiply hₚ over the primes p dividing q (one for q = 1).

**Problem.** Let A lie in N consecutive integers, let Q ≥ 2 be an integer, and let G be the sum over squarefree q ≤ Q of the product of ω(p)/(1−ω(p)) over primes p dividing q (one for q = 1). Then \|A\| ≤ (N − 1 + Q²)/G.

**How the definition helps.** Centring removes the constant frequency at each prime, so by the Chinese remainder theorem the product for q sees only reduced fractions with denominator q (our own). On A this product equals the product of the local odds ω(p)/(1−ω(p)), and so does its mean square. Parseval, Cauchy–Schwarz and the additive large sieve, summed over q, give the bound.

**Paper or page:** [Diophantine stability and second order terms](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.12144v1). It says: “ω(ℓ)/(1−ω(ℓ))”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Logarithmic collisions give Gallagher’s sieve

**Remember:** Each pair's log-weighted collisions add up to at most log N.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11N35 (Sieves). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Let A be a subset of {1,…,N} and Q a finite set of prime powers. A collision is a pair of distinct members of A that agree modulo some q in Q, weighted by Λ(q) = log p when q is a power of the prime p. The total weight of one pair is at most log N, since the weights of all prime powers dividing its difference m sum to log m &lt; log N (our own).

**Problem.** Suppose A occupies at most g(q) classes modulo each q in Q, with g(q) ≥ 1. Put U = ∑ Λ(q) and V = ∑ Λ(q)/g(q), summing over Q. If V &gt; log N, then \|A\| ≤ (U − log N)/(V − log N).

**How the definition helps.** Each pair carries at most log N, while Cauchy–Schwarz gives at least \|A\|²/g(q) − \|A\| ordered collisions modulo q. Summing with weights Λ(q) gives \|A\|²V − \|A\|U ≤ \|A\|(\|A\|−1) log N, which rearranges to the bound for nonempty A. For empty A the bound follows from U ≥ V &gt; log N.

**Wikipedia:** [Larger sieve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Larger_sieve). It says: “there are at most g(q) residue classes modulo q, which contain elements of A.”

**Sources:**

- [P. X. Gallagher, A larger sieve, Acta Arithmetica 18 (1971), 77–81.](https://doi.org/10.4064/aa-18-1-77-81)

### New coordinates minimize Selberg’s sieve

**Remember:** In the new coordinates the form is diagonal, and Cauchy–Schwarz finishes.

*True by definition.* MSC 11N35 (Sieves). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Selberg's quadratic form sums λ(d)λ(e)/f(lcm(d,e)) over d,e in a nonempty finite divisor-closed set D of squarefree integers, with real weights λ and multiplicative f,g satisfying g(p) = f(p)−1 &gt; 0 at primes. In the new coordinates y(r), the sum of λ(d)/f(d) over multiples d of r in D, the form is the diagonal sum ∑ g(r)y(r)² (our own).

**Problem.** Under the condition λ(1) = 1, the minimum of Selberg's quadratic form is the reciprocal of the sum of 1/g(r) over r in D.

**How the definition helps.** The constraint becomes λ(1) = ∑ μ(r)y(r) = 1, so Cauchy–Schwarz gives the minimum 1/∑ 1/g(r), attained when y(r) is proportional to μ(r)/g(r). The diagonal form comes from f(gcd(d,e)) = ∑<sub>r∣gcd(d,e)</sub> g(r), and Möbius inversion makes the change of coordinates invertible (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Selberg sieve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Selberg_sieve). It says: “Let the function g be obtained from f by Möbius inversion”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Primitive characters prevent sieve repetitions

**Remember:** Count each primitive character only at its own modulus.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11N35 (Sieves), 11L40. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A Dirichlet character modulo q, a multiplicative character of the invertible residues extended by zero, is primitive if it does not come from a character modulo a proper divisor of q. So each character is counted at one modulus only, and its Gauss sum has squared modulus q.

**Problem.** For complex a(n) on N consecutive integers, put D(χ) = ∑ a(n)χ(n), and let φ(q) count the invertible residues. Then the sum of q\|D(χ)\|²/φ(q) over positive q ≤ Q and primitive χ modulo q is at most (N − 1 + Q²)∑ \|a(n)\|².

**How the definition helps.** Because the Gauss sum has squared modulus q, orthogonality turns each character sum into exponential sums at reduced fractions, which the additive large sieve bounds. Without primitivity, the principal character would count again at every prime modulus (our own). With coefficients one on \[1,N\], each copy contributes at least N²/4, which violates the bound for large Q and N much larger than Q² (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Gauss sum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gauss_sum). It says: “If χ is also primitive, then \|G(χ)\| = √N, in particular, it is nonzero.”

**Sources:**

- [H. L. Montgomery and R. C. Vaughan, The large sieve, Mathematika 20 (1973), 119–134](https://doi.org/10.1112/S0025579300004708)

### Primitivity removes repeated character rows

**Remember:** Count each character once, at the modulus where it is primitive.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11N35 (Sieves). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A Dirichlet character modulo q, a homomorphism from the invertible classes to the nonzero complex numbers extended by zero, is primitive if it does not come from a character modulo a proper divisor of q. So each character is counted at one modulus only.

**Problem.** Take complex aₙ on N consecutive integers and Q ≥ 1, and let φ(q) count invertible classes. Summing (q/φ(q))\|∑ₙ aₙχ(n)\|² over positive q ≤ Q and primitive characters χ modulo q gives at most (Q² + N)∑ₙ \|aₙ\|².

**How the definition helps.** Primitivity stops the principal character from appearing again at every prime modulus (our own). With aₙ = 1 on \[1,N\] and N ≥ Q², each copy contributes at least N²/4, and their number grows without bound while the bound stays at most 2N². The multiplicative large sieve gives the stated bound for primitive characters.

**Paper or page:** [The second moment of Dirichlet twists of a GL₄ automorphic L-function](https://arxiv.org/abs/2110.01783v2). It says: “For any complex numbers aₙ (M ≤ n &lt; M + N), we have”

**Sources:**

- [H. L. Montgomery and R. C. Vaughan, The large sieve, Mathematika 20 (1973), 119–134.](https://doi.org/10.1112/s0025579300004708)

### Reduced fractions separate sieve samples

**Remember:** Reduced fractions prevent several denominators from charging for the same sample.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11N35 (Sieves). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For each positive q ≤ Q, take the fractions a/q with 0 ≤ a &lt; q and gcd(a,q) = 1, as points on ℝ/ℤ with circle distance to the nearest integer. Two distinct reduced fractions differ by a fraction with denominator at most Q², so they are at least 1/Q² apart (our own).

**Problem.** For any N consecutive integer indices, put S(x) = ∑ a(n) exp(2πinx) over those indices. Then the sum of \|S(a/q)\|² over the reduced fractions is at most (N − 1 + Q²)∑ \|a(n)\|².

**How the definition helps.** The additive large sieve at spacing 1/Q² gives the bound (our own spacing argument). Without reduction, the point zero occurs once for every denominator. With all coefficients one these copies contribute QN², which violates the bound for Q ≥ 2 and large N.

**Wikipedia:** [Large sieve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Large_sieve). It says: “for all x near rational numbers of the form a/p.”

**Sources:**

- [H. L. Montgomery and R. C. Vaughan, The large sieve, Mathematika 20 (1973), 119–134](https://doi.org/10.1112/S0025579300004708)

### Selberg majorants prove sieve bounds

**Remember:** Dominate the interval while cutting off every cross term.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11N35 (Sieves), 42A38. arXiv math.NT, math.CA. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For a closed interval I of length L and 0 &lt; δ &lt; 1, Selberg's majorant B is an integrable function that lies above the indicator of I. Its Fourier transform, taken with exp(−2πixξ), vanishes outside \[−δ,δ\], and its integral is L + 1/δ.

**Problem.** Take points xⱼ whose pairwise distances modulo one exceed δ. Put S(x) = ∑ a(n) exp(2πinx), summing over integers in I. Then ∑ \|S(xⱼ)\|² ≤ (L + 1/δ)∑ \|a(n)\|².

**How the definition helps.** Use B as a weight on the frequencies in the dual form of the inequality, which has the same norm (our own). Poisson summation then keeps only the diagonal terms, because the transform vanishes at every sample distance, each larger than δ modulo one. Each diagonal term has weight L + 1/δ by the integral condition.

**Wikipedia:** [Large sieve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Large_sieve). It says: “It is also possible to derive the large sieve from majorants in the style of Selberg”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Spacing rules out repeated samples

**Remember:** Distinct samples must sit at least δ apart around the circle.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11N35 (Sieves). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Points on the circle ℝ/ℤ are δ-spaced if any two with distinct indices are at circle distance at least δ, the distance from their difference to the nearest integer. In particular, no point is listed twice.

**Problem.** Take complex coefficients aₙ on N consecutive integers, with N ≥ 1, and put T(α) = ∑ₙ aₙ exp(2πinα). For 0 &lt; δ ≤ 1/2, the sum of \|T(α)\|² over δ-spaced points is at most (N − 1 + 1/δ) ∑ₙ \|aₙ\|².

**How the definition helps.** Spacing forbids repeated samples, which could make the left side arbitrarily large (our own). For example, with a single coefficient equal to one and the rest zero, each copy of a repeated point adds one (our own). The large sieve inequality bounds the sum for δ-spaced points.

**Paper or page:** [Infinitude of palindromic almost-prime numbers](https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.16637v3). It says: “For any set of δ-spaced points”

**Sources:**

- [H. L. Montgomery and R. C. Vaughan, The large sieve, Mathematika 20 (1973), 119–134.](https://doi.org/10.1112/s0025579300004708)

### Squares bound the Selberg sieve

**Remember:** The square is one on survivors and never negative elsewhere.

*True by definition.* MSC 11N35 (Sieves). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Choose finitely many primes and call an integer sifted if none of them divides it. Give each divisor of their product a real weight, with weight 1 at divisor 1, and for each integer square the sum of the weights of the divisors it has; this square is 1 on sifted integers and never negative (our own).

**Problem.** In any finite sample of positive integers, the sum of these squares bounds the number of sifted integers from above.

**How the definition helps.** Each sifted integer contributes exactly one and every other integer at least zero, so the sum of squares bounds the count (our own). Unlike inclusion–exclusion, which is exact but has alternating signs, the weights are free, and Selberg chooses them to make the bound small.

**Wikipedia:** [Selberg sieve](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Selberg_sieve). It says: “Selberg replaced the values of the Möbius function which arise in this by a system of weights which are then optimised to fit the given problem.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Buchstab’s function counts rough numbers

**Remember:** Subtract one from the logarithmic ratio when peeling off a prime.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11N36 (Applications of sieve methods). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A positive integer is y-rough if it has no prime factor below y. Buchstab's function ω(u) is 1/u on 1 ≤ u ≤ 2 and continues continuously for u &gt; 2 by requiring the derivative of uω(u) to equal ω(u−1).

**Problem.** Fix u &gt; 1 and let y be x raised to 1/u. As x tends to infinity, the number of y-rough integers up to x is asymptotic to xω(u)/log y.

**How the definition helps.** Removing the least prime p from a rough integer lowers the ratio log x/log p by one, which is the shift in the delay equation (our own). For 1 &lt; u ≤ 2 only primes contribute to the main term, giving 1/u. For larger u, Buchstab's identity groups composites by their least prime, and the prime number theorem turns it into the integral form of the delay equation.

**Wikipedia:** [Buchstab function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buchstab_function). It says: “The Buchstab function is used to count rough numbers.”

**Paper or page:** [The Schinzel-Szekeres function](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.13038v2). It says: “ω(v) is Buchstab’s function.”

**Sources:**

- [A. Buchstab, Asymptotische Abschätzung einer allgemeinen zahlentheoretischen Funktion, Matematicheskii Sbornik 2 (1937), 1239–1246.](https://m.mathnet.ru/php/archive.phtml?jrnid=sm&option_lang=eng&paperid=5649&wshow=paper)

### Least factors partition sieve losses

**Remember:** Assign each discarded number to its first prime divisor.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11N36 (Applications of sieve methods). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For a finite set A of positive integers, S(A,z) counts its members with no prime factor below z, and Aₚ = {n/p ∣ n ∈ A and p divides n}. Assign each discarded member to its least prime factor p; then n/p has no prime factor below p.

**Problem.** For 2≤z≤y, S(A,y)=S(A,z)−∑ S(Aₚ,p), with the sum over primes z≤p&lt;y. In an interval contained in (√x,x\], taking y&gt;√x makes the surviving numbers exactly the primes at least y.

**How the definition helps.** Each member with a prime factor in \[z,y) but none below z is counted once, by its least prime p, in S(Aₚ,p) (our own). Counting by every prime divisor would charge 15 to both 3 and 5. Every composite up to x has a prime factor at most √x, which gives the interval claim.

**Wikipedia:** [Rough number](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rough_number). It says: “whose prime factors are all greater than or equal to”

**Sources:**

- [A. Buchstab, Asymptotische Abschätzung einer allgemeinen zahlentheoretischen Funktion, Matematicheskii Sbornik 2 (1937), 1239–1246](https://www.mathnet.ru/php/archive.phtml?jrnid=sm&option_lang=eng&paperid=5649&wshow=paper)
- [Runbo Li, The number of primes in short intervals and numerical calculations for Harman's sieve](https://arxiv.org/abs/2308.04458)

### Nearest powers control means

**Remember:** A multiplicative function has a large mean only near some nⁱᵗ.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11N37 (Asymptotic results on arithmetic functions). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For multiplicative f with \|f(n)\| ≤ 1, its distance from the power nⁱᵗ is the sum of (1−Re(f(p)exp(−it log p)))/p over primes p ≤ x. Let M be the smallest such distance over \|t\| ≤ T, the distance to the nearest power.

**Problem.** For x ≥ 3, divide the sum of f(n) over n ≤ x by x. For T ≥ 1, the modulus of this average is at most C((1+M)exp(−M)+1/T) with an absolute constant C.

**How the definition helps.** Halász's mean value theorem bounds the mean of f by its distance to the nearest power. Our own reading is that one minimum M replaces a separate comparison with each frequency.

**Paper or page:** [Gap problems for integer-valued multiplicative functions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.11636). It says: “Let x ≥ 3 and T ≥ 1. Let g ∶ ℕ → 𝕌 be a multiplicative function.”

**Sources:**

- [Gap problems for integer-valued multiplicative functions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.11636)
- [Andrew Granville and K. Soundararajan, Decay of Mean Values of Multiplicative Functions (2003)](https://doi.org/10.4153/CJM-2003-047-0)

### The factor at two can erase means

**Remember:** One vanishing local factor can erase the entire mean.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11N37 (Asymptotic results on arithmetic functions). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For multiplicative f with \|f(n)\| ≤ 1 and real t, put h(n) = f(n)exp(−it log n); f has finite distance at t if ∑ₚ(1−Re h(p))/p converges over primes. The local factor at two is B = (1+∑ⱼ≥₁ h(2ʲ)/2ʲ)/2, which is zero only when h(2ʲ) = −1 for every j ≥ 1.

**Problem.** Assume f has finite distance from the power at t. The modulus of the average of f(1),…,f(N) tends to a positive limit exactly when B ≠ 0.

**How the definition helps.** Halász's theorem shows that the mean has a positive limiting modulus except when this local factor vanishes (our own local-factor formulation). The factor can vanish only if h(2ʲ) = −1 for all j, since the weights 1/2ʲ add to one.

**Paper or page:** [Furstenberg systems of pretentious and MRT multiplicative functions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.03121). It says: “then there exist a non-zero L ∈ ℂ and a slowly varying sequence”

**Sources:**

- [Furstenberg systems of pretentious and MRT multiplicative functions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.03121)

### Wirsing’s factors isolate prime bias

**Remember:** Remove the average prime weight before multiplying local factors.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11N37 (Asymptotic results on arithmetic functions). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Let f be nonnegative and multiplicative with f(1) = 1 and f(pʲ) ≤ Cjᴬ for fixed C,A &gt; 0, every prime p and every j ≥ 1. For ξ &gt; 0 the local factor is L(p) = (1−1/p)<sup>ξ</sup> ∑ⱼ≥₀ f(pʲ)/pʲ, where (1−1/p)<sup>ξ</sup> removes the average prime contribution ξ/p (our own).

**Problem.** Suppose ∑ₚ≤ₓ f(p) = ξx/log x + O(x/(log x)ʳ) for some 1 &lt; r &lt; 2. Then ∑ₙ≤ₓ f(n) divided by x(log x)<sup>(ξ−1)</sup> tends to ∏ₚ L(p)/Γ(ξ). The prime product converges to a positive number.

**How the definition helps.** In our own calculation, log L(p) = (f(p)−ξ)/p + O(1/p²), and partial summation with the prime-sum hypothesis makes these terms converge. The Wirsing–Odoni theorem identifies the product as part of the leading constant.

**Paper or page:** [Multiplicative complements I](https://arxiv.org/abs/2204.00412). It says: “over the primes is convergent (and positive), and”

**Sources:**

- [Multiplicative complements I](https://arxiv.org/abs/2204.00412)
- [Eduard Wirsing, Das asymptotische Verhalten von Summen über multiplikative Funktionen (1961)](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/BF01351892)

### Zeta powers determine logarithmic growth

**Remember:** The zeta power carries the entire leading singularity.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11N37 (Asymptotic results on arithmetic functions). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For an integer k ≥ 1, let a(n) = k<sup>ω</sup>(n), where ω(n) counts the distinct prime divisors of n; its Dirichlet series has the same singularity at s = 1 as ζ(s)ᵏ. Dividing out leaves G(s) = ∑ a(n)n⁻ˢ/ζ(s)ᵏ, an Euler product that converges at s = 1 (our own).

**Problem.** The sum of a(n) over n ≤ x is asymptotic to G(1)x(log x)ᵏ⁻¹/(k−1)!. Here G(1) is the limit as s decreases to one.

**How the definition helps.** At s = 1 each prime factor of G is (1−1/p)ᵏ⁻¹(1+(k−1)/p), with no term in 1/p, so the product converges (our own). The Selberg–Delange theorem turns ζ(s)ᵏ times such a G into the coefficient sum G(1)x(log x)ᵏ⁻¹/(k−1)!.

**Paper or page:** [On divisor bounded multiplicative functions in short intervals](https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.08432). It says: “where cₖ is an explicit positive constant.”

**Sources:**

- [On divisor bounded multiplicative functions in short intervals](https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.08432)

### Diverging variance excludes single-prime limits

**Remember:** A bounded prime contribution cannot dominate an infinite total variance.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11N60 (Distribution functions associated with additive and positive multiplicative functions). arXiv math.NT, math.PR. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A strongly additive real function f has f(n) equal to the sum of f(p) over distinct primes p dividing n. Require \|f(p)\| ≤ 1 and that the variance B(x)² = ∑ f(p)²/p over primes p ≤ x tends to infinity. Then no single bounded prime term matters after dividing by B(x) (our own).

**Problem.** Write A(x)=∑ f(p)/p over primes p≤x. For uniform N from 1 to x, (f(N)−A(x))/B(x) converges in law to a standard normal.

**How the definition helps.** Divergence of B(x) makes every bounded prime term negligible after normalization, and the Erdős–Kac theorem then gives the normal limit (our own). Without it the claim fails: if f(2) = 1 is the only nonzero prime value, the normalized values are ±1/√2, each with limiting probability one half.

**Wikipedia:** [Erdős–Kac theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Erd%C5%91s%E2%80%93Kac_theorem). It says: “More generally, if f(n) is a strongly additive function”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Prime powers factor Erdős–Wintner

**Remember:** Independent prime contributions give one factor each in the limiting transform.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11N60 (Distribution functions associated with additive and positive multiplicative functions). arXiv math.NT, math.PR. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Let f be real and additive, so f(ab) = f(a)+f(b) for coprime a and b. Model f(N) by a sum of independent terms Xₚ = f(p<sup>V</sup>), one per prime p, where V = k with probability (1−1/p)/pᵏ, the chance that pᵏ exactly divides a random integer (our own).

**Problem.** Suppose ∑ 1/p converges over primes with \|f(p)\| &gt; 1, and ∑ f(p)/p and ∑ f(p)²/p converge over the other primes. For N uniform on {1,…,x}, f(N) then approaches the distribution with characteristic function ∏ E\[exp(itXₚ)\] as x tends to infinity.

**How the definition helps.** Independence turns the characteristic function of the sum into the product ∏ E\[exp(itXₚ)\] (our own explanation). Kolmogorov's three-series theorem makes the independent sum converge under the three conditions, since exponents above one occur at only finitely many primes almost surely. The Erdős–Wintner theorem identifies this law with the arithmetic limit.

**Wikipedia:** [Erdős–Wintner theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Erd%C5%91s%E2%80%93Wintner_theorem). It says: “It is an analogue of Kolmogorov's three-series theorem.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Prime values miss additive variance

**Remember:** A prime square can fluctuate even when every prime value vanishes.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11N60 (Distribution functions associated with additive and positive multiplicative functions). arXiv math.NT, math.PR. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For an additive f, meaning f(ab) = f(a)+f(b) for coprime a and b, measure the variance by B(x)² = ∑ \|f(q)\|²/q over all prime powers q = pᵏ ≤ x with k ≥ 1, not just primes. Centre at A(x) = ∑ f(q)(1−1/p)/q over the same prime powers.

**Problem.** The average of \|f(n)−A(x)\|² over n≤x is at most a constant times B(x)² for every x≥2. No constant works for all additive f if the sum defining B(x)² uses only primes.

**How the definition helps.** Values at higher prime powers can vary while every prime value is zero, so a variance over primes alone misses them (our own). With f(4) = 1 and every other prime-power value zero, f(n) indicates divisibility by four but not eight, and its mean-square error tends to 7/64. The Turán–Kubilius inequality gives the bound once all prime powers are included.

**Wikipedia:** [Turán–Kubilius inequality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tur%C3%A1n%E2%80%93Kubilius_inequality). It says: “It is useful for proving results about the normal order of an arithmetic function.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Truncation makes sieve moments Gaussian

**Remember:** Keep enough primes for the variance and few enough for every fixed moment.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11N60 (Distribution functions associated with additive and positive multiplicative functions). arXiv math.NT, math.PR. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For a large integer x, put L = log log x and y = exp((log x)/∜L), and choose N uniformly from {1,…,x}. Let T count only the small prime divisors of N, those at most y, and put μ = ∑ 1/p over primes p ≤ y.

**Problem.** For each fixed positive integer k, the kth moment of (T−μ)/√L tends to the kth standard normal moment. Also (ω(N)−L)/√L tends in law to the same normal law, where ω counts all distinct primes.

**How the definition helps.** The cutoff makes yᵏ/x tend to zero for each fixed k, so the kth moment differs from that of independent prime indicators by Oₖ(yᵏ/x) (our own). The independent model has variance asymptotic to L and Gaussian normalized moments. At most ∜L larger primes divide N, and Mertens' estimate gives μ = L + O(log L), so ω(N) has the same normal limit.

**Paper or page:** [On an Erdős--Kac-type conjecture of Elliott](https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.13585v3). It says: “Uniformly for 1 ≤ k ≤ (σℙ)⁽²⁄³⁾ we have”

**Sources:**

- [On an Erdős--Kac-type conjecture of Elliott](https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.13585v3)
- [Andrew Granville and K. Soundararajan, Sieving and the Erdős–Kac theorem](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-1-4020-5404-4_2)

### Zeta weights make primes independent

**Remember:** Weight by inverse powers and prime divisibility becomes independent.

*True by definition.* MSC 11N60 (Distribution functions associated with additive and positive multiplicative functions). arXiv math.NT, math.PR. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For s &gt; 1, draw a positive integer N with probability n⁻ˢ/ζ(s), where ζ(s) = ∑ n⁻ˢ, instead of uniformly from a bounded range. The multiples of d then have total probability d⁻ˢ, which multiplies over distinct primes (our own).

**Problem.** Let ω(N) count distinct prime divisors and put μ(s)=∑ 1/pˢ over all primes. Divisibility by distinct primes gives independent events. As s decreases to 1, (ω(N)−μ(s))/√μ(s) converges in distribution to a standard normal variable.

**How the definition helps.** Since the probability d⁻ˢ of divisibility by a squarefree d is the product over its primes, the prime divisibility events are independent (our own). The variance is μ(s) + O(1), which diverges as s decreases to one because ∑ 1/p diverges. The Lindeberg central limit theorem applies since every centred indicator is bounded by one.

**Paper or page:** [A Generalization of the Erdős-Kac Theorem](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.06860v1). It says: “Zeta(1+1/aⱼ)-distributed random variables”

**Sources:**

- [A Generalization of the Erdős-Kac Theorem](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.06860v1)

### Ignoring finitely many exceptions gives Waring's problem its true constant G(k)

**Remember:** Count every target for g and only sufficiently large targets for G.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11P05 (Waring's problem and variants). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For each positive integer k, g(k) is the least s such that every positive integer is a sum of at most s positive kth powers. G(k) is the least s that works for every sufficiently large integer, so finitely many small hard cases raise g(k) but not G(k).

**Problem.** G(k) ≤ k(3 log k + 11), by Vinogradov's refinements of the circle method. In contrast, a few small numbers force g(k) ≥ 2ᵏ + ⌊(3/2)ᵏ⌋ − 2.

**How the definition helps.** The number n = 2ᵏ⌊(3/2)ᵏ⌋ − 1 lies below 3ᵏ, so it uses only 1 and 2ᵏ, and the best choice is ⌊(3/2)ᵏ⌋ − 1 copies of 2ᵏ and 2ᵏ − 1 ones (our own). This one small number forces g(k) up but does not affect G(k). Vinogradov's circle method gives the estimate for large targets.

**Wikipedia:** [Waring's problem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Waring%27s_problem). It says: “G(k) is defined to be the least positive integer s such that every sufficiently large integer (i.e. every integer greater than some constant) can be represented as a sum of at most s positive integers to the power of k.”

**Sources:**

- [G. H. Hardy and J. E. Littlewood, Some problems of 'Partitio Numerorum' IV: The singular series in Waring's problem and the value of the number G(k), Math. Z. 12 (1922) 161–188](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF01482074)

### Log weights simplify Vinogradov’s asymptotic

**Remember:** Log weights remove the prime density from the main term.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11P32 (Goldbach-type theorems; other additive questions involving primes), 11P55. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Weight each prime power m = pᵏ by Λ(m) = log p and every other integer by zero, which cancels the prime density 1/log m (our own). Let r(N) be the weighted count of ordered triples of positive integers with a+b+c = N.

**Problem.** For odd N tending to infinity and fixed A &gt; 0, r(N) = ½G(N)N² + O(N²/(log N)ᴬ). Here G(N) is the product over primes p of 1 − 1/(p−1)² when p divides N and of 1 + 1/(p−1)³ otherwise.

**How the definition helps.** With log weights each term has average size one, so the main term is ½N², the number of triples, times local factors (our own). The prime number theorem in arithmetic progressions estimates the weighted sum near fractions with small denominators. Bounding the sum at the remaining frequencies takes a separate estimate.

**Wikipedia:** [Vinogradov's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vinogradov%27s_theorem). It says: “r(N) = ½G(N)N² + O(N² log⁻ᴬ N)”

**Sources:**

- [I. Vinogradow, Some theorems concerning the theory of primes (1937), Theorem 2](https://www.mathnet.ru/php/archive.phtml?jrnid=sm&option_lang=eng&paperid=5565&wshow=paper)

### Major arcs expose Vaughan’s saving

**Remember:** Keep small denominators out of the minor arcs.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11P32 (Goldbach-type theorems; other additive questions involving primes), 11P55, 11L07. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For large N and B &gt; 0, put L = (log N)ᴮ and S(α) = ∑ₙ≤ᴺ Λ(n)exp(2πiαn), with von Mangoldt weights Λ(n). The minor arcs are the frequencies modulo one farther than 2L/(qN) from every reduced a/q with 1 ≤ q ≤ L, so every good rational approximation to them has denominator above L (our own).

**Problem.** For each A &gt; 0, take B &gt; 2A + 8. On the minor arcs \|S(α)\| = O(N/(log N)ᴬ), uniformly in α as N grows.

**How the definition helps.** Dirichlet's theorem gives a reduced a/q with q ≤ ⌊N/L⌋ and error at most 1/(q⌊N/L⌋), and on the minor arcs this forces q &gt; L (our own). Vaughan's estimate bounds \|S(α)\| by O((N/√q + N⁴⁄⁵ + √(Nq))(log N)⁴). Both terms with q are at most N/√L, which gives the saving since B &gt; 2A + 8.

**Wikipedia:** [Vinogradov's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vinogradov%27s_theorem). It says: “The set of real numbers close to such rational points is usually referred to as the major arcs, the complement forms the minor arcs.”

**Paper or page:** [Almost all primes are not needed in Ternary Goldbach](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.08968v1). It says: “Let u ≥ 1, α ∈ ℝ and consider a reduced fraction a/q such that \|α − a/q\| ≤ 1/q².”

**Sources:**

- [R. C. Vaughan, Sommes trigonométriques sur les nombres premiers (1977), pp. 981–983](https://personal.science.psu.edu/rcv4/pubswww.pdf)

### Modulo twenty-four selects five prime squares

**Remember:** Each prime above three has square one modulo twenty-four.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11P32 (Goldbach-type theorems; other additive questions involving primes), 11P55, 11P05. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Call an integer admissible if it is 5 modulo 24, because every prime greater than 3 has square 1 modulo 24 (our own).

**Problem.** Every sufficiently large admissible integer is the sum of five squares of primes greater than 3. No integer outside the class can be such a sum with all five primes greater than 3.

**How the definition helps.** A prime above three is odd and not a multiple of three, so its square is one modulo eight and modulo three, hence modulo 24 (our own). Five such squares therefore sum to five modulo 24. Liu and Zhan's near-equal-prime form of the five-square theorem represents every sufficiently large admissible integer with primes above three.

**Paper or page:** [On the density version of quadratic Waring's problem and the quadratic Waring--Goldbach problem](https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.14939v3). It says: “for all sufficiently large integers y that are congruent to s mod 24”

**Sources:**

- [Jianya Liu and Tao Zhan, Hua’s Theorem on Prime Squares in Short Intervals (2000)](https://doi.org/10.1007/s101140000077)

### Unit classes isolate Goldbach parity

**Remember:** Count nonzero classes to see the parity obstruction.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11P32 (Goldbach-type theorems; other additive questions involving primes), 11P55. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For each prime p, let σ(p,N) be p times the number of triples of nonzero residues with sum N modulo p, divided by (p−1)³, and let G(N) be the product of these factors over all primes. At p = 2 the only nonzero residue is 1, and 1+1+1 is odd.

**Problem.** For even N the product G(N) vanishes. For odd N it has a positive lower bound that does not depend on N.

**How the definition helps.** So σ(2,N) is zero for even N and two for odd N (our own). For odd p, counting gives 1 − 1/(p−1)² when p divides N and 1 + 1/(p−1)³ otherwise. Both are at least 1 − 1/(p−1)², and the product of these lower bounds over p &gt; 2 is positive since ∑ 1/(p−1)² converges.

**Wikipedia:** [Vinogradov's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vinogradov%27s_theorem). It says: “If N is odd, then G(N) is roughly 1”

**Sources:**

- [I. Vinogradow, Some theorems concerning the theory of primes (1937), Theorem 2](https://www.mathnet.ru/php/archive.phtml?jrnid=sm&option_lang=eng&paperid=5565&wshow=paper)

### Dual forms reveal Kloosterman phases

**Remember:** Completing the square leaves minus the dual form over 4a.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11P55 (Applications of the Hardy-Littlewood method), 11L05. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Modulo an odd prime p, the dual form of Q(x) = xᵀMx, with M symmetric and invertible, is D(c) = cᵀM⁻¹c. It is the constant that completing the square leaves: aQ(x) + c·x is a times Q at a shifted point, minus D(c)/(4a) (our own). The Kloosterman sum K(m,n) sums e(ma+na⁻¹) over nonzero residues a, with e(t) = exp(2πit/p).

**Problem.** Let Q have even dimension s, and fix an integer N and a vector c modulo p. The sum of e(a(Q(x)−N)+c·x) over all vectors x and nonzero residues a has absolute value pˢ⁄² times \|K(−N,−D(c)/4)\|, with division modulo p.

**How the definition helps.** After completing the square, the phase that depends on a is e(−aN − D(c)/(4a)), which is the Kloosterman phase (our own). The shifted sum over x is a Gauss sum of modulus pˢ⁄², and its phase does not depend on a because s is even.

**Wikipedia:** [Kloosterman sum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kloosterman_sum). It says: “If a = 0 or b = 0 then the Kloosterman sum reduces to the Ramanujan sum.”

**Paper or page:** [Counting solutions to quadratic polynomials](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.04328v1). It says: “S(m,n;q) = \\sideset{}{<sup>\*}\\sum\_{x\\bmod{q}}e<sub>q</sub></sup>(mx+n\\overline{x})”

**Sources:**

- [V. Vinay Kumaraswamy, Counting solutions to quadratic polynomials (2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.04328v1)

### Farey mediants expose Kloosterman sums

**Remember:** The Farey neighbor's denominator is minus the inverse of the numerator.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11P55 (Applications of the Hardy-Littlewood method), 11L05. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** The Farey fractions of order Q are the reduced fractions in \[0,1\] with denominator at most Q, in increasing order. The arc of a/p ends at the mediant (a+b)/(p+r) with its right neighbor b/r, which lies 1/(p(p+r)) beyond a/p (our own). Since bp − ar = 1, the neighbor denominator r is the residue −a⁻¹ modulo p in the range Q−p &lt; r ≤ Q.

**Problem.** Fix a prime p ≤ Q, integers m,n with p not dividing m, and β &gt; 0. The sum of exp(2πi(ma+na⁻¹)/p) over 1 ≤ a &lt; p whose arc ends at or beyond a/p+β is O(√p log p), with an absolute constant and inverses modulo p.

**How the definition helps.** The endpoint test is an upper bound on r, so it keeps the a whose residue −a⁻¹ lies in an interval (our own). Completing this interval modulo p costs a factor O(log p). Weil’s bound gives at most 2√p for each complete Kloosterman sum since p does not divide m.

**Wikipedia:** [Kloosterman sum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kloosterman_sum). It says: “the symbol n\* denotes the congruence class, inverse to n modulo m”

**Sources:**

- [H. D. Kloosterman, On the representation of numbers in the form ax² + by² + cz² + dt² (1926)](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF02564120)
- [A. Weil, On Some Exponential Sums (1948)](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.34.5.204)

### Numerator-free weights separate Poisson factors

**Remember:** The weight ignores the numerator, so numerators form one complete sum.

*True by definition.* MSC 11P55 (Applications of the Hardy-Littlewood method), 11D45. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Heath-Brown’s delta identity detects n = 0 by summing exp(2πian/q)h(q/Q,n/Q²) over q ≥ 1 and units a modulo q, times C/Q², with a weight h that does not depend on a (our own). Here Q &gt; 2, ω is smooth, supported on \[½,1\] and positive inside, C = Q/∑ⱼ≥₁ ω(j/Q), and h(x,y) = ∑ⱼ≥₁ \[ω(xj)−ω(\|y\|/(xj))\]/(xj). For an integer polynomial F in s variables, S(q,c) sums exp(2πi(aF(b)+c·b)/q) over vectors b modulo q and units a modulo q.

**Problem.** For smooth compactly supported W on ℝˢ, set I(q,c) = ∫ W(x)h(q/Q,F(x)/Q²)exp(−2πic·x/q) dx over ℝˢ. The sum of W(x) over integer zeros of F equals (C/Q²)∑ S(q,c)I(q,c)/qˢ over integers q ≥ 1 and vectors c ∈ ℤˢ.

**How the definition helps.** Because h does not see a, Poisson summation on each class b modulo q gives the same integral I(q,c) for every a (our own). The leftover phases exp(2πi(aF(b)+c·b)/q)/qˢ then sum over a and b to S(q,c).

**nLab:** [Poisson summation formula](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Poisson+summation+formula). It says: “equating a sum or integral of a function over a domain (e.g., a lattice) with a corresponding sum or integral of its Fourier dual over a dual domain”

**Sources:**

- [D. R. Heath-Brown, A New Form of the Circle Method, and its Application to Quadratic Forms (1996)](https://ora.ox.ac.uk/objects/uuid%3Abbd3c62f-f010-44b5-8be5-87e903fb0084/files/m7ec02df6e1b8303a66e7a6015ecb6044)

### Power densities give Waring’s Gamma factor

**Remember:** Powers convolve into powers, with a beta integral as constant.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11P55 (Applications of the Hardy-Littlewood method), 11P05. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For integers k,s ≥ 2, the real factor at N is the s-fold convolution at N of the power density f(t) = t<sup>(1/k−1)</sup>/k for t &gt; 0, with f(t) = 0 for t ≤ 0. This f is the density of t = xᵏ for x &gt; 0, and the convolution of two powers of t is a power of t times a beta integral (our own).

**Problem.** For N &gt; 0 and integers k,s ≥ 2, the real factor equals Γ(1 + 1/k)ˢ N<sup>(s/k − 1)</sup>/Γ(s/k). For sufficiently large s, this is the real factor in the classical Waring asymptotic.

**How the definition helps.** Euler’s beta formula B(x,y) = Γ(x)Γ(y)/Γ(x+y) evaluates each convolution, and the gamma denominators cancel step by step (our own). The circle method must still show that this density appears in the count of integer representations.

**nLab:** [Euler beta function](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Euler+beta+function). It says: “B(x,y) = \\int<sub>0</sub><sup>1</sup> t<sup>x-1</sup> (1-t)<sup>y-1</sup> d t = \\frac{\\Gamma(x)\\Gamma(y)}{\\Gamma(x+y)},\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,\\,Re x\\gt 0, \\,\\,\\,\\,Re y \\gt 0,”

**Wikipedia:** [Hardy–Ramanujan–Littlewood circle method](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hardy%E2%80%93Ramanujan%E2%80%93Littlewood_circle_method). It says: “the singularities, organised into the so-called singular series, predominate”

**Sources:**

- [G. H. Hardy and J. E. Littlewood, Some problems of Partitio Numerorum IV (1922)](https://gdz.sub.uni-goettingen.de/download/pdf/PPN266833020_0012/PPN266833020_0012.pdf)

### Power moments count integer solutions

**Remember:** One frequency per degree enforces one equality per degree.

*True by definition.* MSC 11P55 (Applications of the Hardy-Littlewood method). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** The Vinogradov mean value is the integral, over the unit cube of coefficients α₁,…,αₖ, of \|∑ exp(2πi(α₁n+…+αₖnᵏ))\|<sup>(2s)</sup>, with n from 1 to N. Each coefficient αⱼ tests one power sum, because the integral of exp(2πiαⱼm) over \[0,1\] is 1 if m = 0 and 0 otherwise.

**Problem.** The mean value counts the pairs of s-tuples from 1 to N whose jth power sums agree for every j from 1 to k. This system of equalities is unchanged when the same integer is added to every entry.

**How the definition helps.** Expanding the 2sth power gives one term per pair of tuples, and the integral keeps exactly the pairs with all power sums equal (our own). Translation invariance follows from the binomial theorem, because each shifted power sum is a combination of the lower ones and both tuples have length s.

**Wikipedia:** [Vinogradov's mean-value theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vinogradov%27s_mean-value_theorem). It says: “An alternative analytic expression for Jₛ,ₖ(X) is”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Primitive phases factor singular series

**Remember:** Primitive numerators make the phase sums multiplicative over coprime moduli.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11P55 (Applications of the Hardy-Littlewood method), 11D45. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For r integer polynomials F in s variables, A(q) is q<sup>(−s)</sup> times the sum of exp(2πia·F(x)/q) over x modulo q and primitive numerator vectors a, the r-tuples of residues with gcd(a₁,…,aᵣ,q) = 1. Using only primitive a makes A multiplicative, A(uv) = A(u)A(v) for coprime u and v (our own). The singular series is the sum of A(q) over q ≥ 1.

**Problem.** Assume the series of \|A(q)\| converges. Then the singular series equals the product over primes p of the sum of A(pʲ) over j ≥ 0.
