**How the definition helps.** The Chinese remainder theorem splits x and the primitive vectors a modulo uv into pairs modulo u and v, which gives A(uv) = A(u)A(v) (our own). Absolute convergence then lets the series factor into the product over primes.

**Paper or page:** [Integral solutions to systems of diagonal equations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.09256v2). It says: “In fact, \\\[ \\mathfrak{S}=\\prod\_{p\\textnormal{ prime}}\\chi(p), \\\] where \\\[ \\chi(p)=1+\\sum<sub>k=1</sub><sup>\\infty</sup>A(p<sup>k</sup>). \\\]”

**Sources:**

- [N. Rome and S. Yamagishi, Integral solutions to systems of diagonal equations (2026)](https://doi.org/10.2140/pjm.2026.340.179)

### Primitive phases telescope local densities

**Remember:** Grouping phases by their true denominator gives each density increment.

*True by definition.* MSC 11P55 (Applications of the Hardy-Littlewood method), 11D45. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For an integer polynomial F in s variables, A(q) is q<sup>(−s)</sup>∑ exp(2πiaF(x)/q) over vectors x modulo q and units a modulo q, with A(1) = 1, so it collects the phases of exact denominator q. The density at q is q times the fraction of vectors x modulo q with F(x) ≡ 0 modulo q.

**Problem.** For each prime p and integer j ≥ 0, the density at pʲ equals the sum of A(pⁱ) over integers 0 ≤ i ≤ j. If the series converges, its sum equals the limiting density.

**How the definition helps.** Averaging the sum of exp(2πiaF(x)/pʲ) over all residues a modulo pʲ and all x gives the density, by orthogonality (our own). Grouping a by the reduced denominator pⁱ of a/pʲ gives the terms A(pⁱ), because each vector modulo pⁱ has equally many lifts.

**Paper or page:** [Solving quadratic forms in restricted variables with the circle method](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.17949v1). It says: “The weighted p-adic density equals χ̃ₚ(𝒜), i.e. χ̃ₚ(𝒜) = lim \[m → ∞\] pᵐM(pᵐ).”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Residue averages separate major arcs

**Remember:** The residue average carries the fraction; the integral carries the offset.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11P55 (Applications of the Hardy-Littlewood method), 11P05, 11L07. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Let S(α) = ∑ e(αnᵈ) over 1 ≤ n ≤ X, with e(t) = exp(2πit) and d ≥ 2. For α = a/q + β, the rational phase e(anᵈ/q) depends only on n modulo q (our own). Its average over residues is C(q,a), and V(β), the integral of e(βtᵈ) from 0 to X, integrates the offset phase.

**Problem.** For α = a/q + β with a and q coprime, S(α) = C(q,a)V(β) + O(q(1+Xᵈ\|β\|)). The bound is uniform for X ≥ 1, real β and positive integers q at fixed d.

**How the definition helps.** On each class modulo q the rational phase is constant, so only the offset phase varies (our own). Partial summation compares its sum on the class with V(β)/q, with error O(1+Xᵈ\|β\|), and the q classes give the stated formula.

**Paper or page:** [Integral solutions to systems of diagonal equations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.09256v2). It says: “\\sum<sub>1\\le x\\le X</sub> e(\\alpha x<sup>d</sup>) = X q<sup>-1</sup> S(q,a) I(X<sup>d\\beta</sup>) + O\\left(\\frac{q}{\\gcd(q,a)}(1+X<sup>d\|\\beta\|</sup>)\\right).”

**Sources:**

- [N. Rome and S. Yamagishi, Integral solutions to systems of diagonal equations (2026)](https://doi.org/10.2140/pjm.2026.340.179)

### Smooth divisor differences detect zero

**Remember:** Subtract the same smooth weight at paired divisors.

*True by definition.* MSC 11P55 (Applications of the Hardy-Littlewood method), 11D45. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Fix Q &gt; 2 and smooth ω supported on \[½,1\] and positive inside, and set C = Q/∑ⱼ≥₁ ω(j/Q). The weight h(x,y) = ∑ⱼ≥₁ \[ω(xj)−ω(\|y\|/(xj))\]/(xj) at x = q/Q and y = n/Q² subtracts, at each divisor d = qj, the same weight at the complementary divisor \|n\|/d (our own). The Ramanujan sum c(q,n) sums exp(2πian/q) over units a modulo q.

**Problem.** For any integer n, C/Q² times ∑ over q ≥ 1 of c(q,n)h(q/Q,n/Q²) is 1 at zero and 0 elsewhere.

**How the definition helps.** The sum of c(q,n) over q dividing d is d when d divides n and 0 otherwise, which turns the sum into a sum over divisors d of n (our own). For n ≠ 0 the swap d ↦ \|n\|/d makes the two terms cancel. At n = 0 only the first term remains, and C normalizes it to one.

**Wikipedia:** [Hardy–Ramanujan–Littlewood circle method](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hardy%E2%80%93Ramanujan%E2%80%93Littlewood_circle_method). It says: “The integral Iₙ is divided up into integrals each on some arc of the circle”

**Sources:**

- [D. R. Heath-Brown, A New Form of the Circle Method, and its Application to Quadratic Forms (1996)](https://ora.ox.ac.uk/objects/uuid%3Abbd3c62f-f010-44b5-8be5-87e903fb0084/files/m7ec02df6e1b8303a66e7a6015ecb6044)

### The dual cone marks large sums

**Remember:** Off the dual cone the inverse phase is nonconstant.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11P55 (Applications of the Hardy-Littlewood method), 11L05. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Let Q(x) = xᵀMx have even dimension s ≥ 2, with M symmetric and invertible modulo an odd prime p. A frequency c is on the dual cone if cᵀM⁻¹c ≡ 0 modulo p, and off it otherwise. Completing the square leaves a Gauss sum, free of a since s is even, times the phase of −cᵀM⁻¹c/(4a) (our own).

**Problem.** Sum exp(2πi(aQ(x)+c·x)/p) over all vectors x and nonzero residues a modulo p. Its absolute value is pˢ⁄² off the dual cone and (p−1)pˢ⁄² on it.

**How the definition helps.** Off the dual cone the phases exp(−2πiD/(4ap)), with D = cᵀM⁻¹c, run once over the nonzero residues and sum to −1; on it they all equal 1 and sum to p−1. The Gauss factor has modulus pˢ⁄² and does not depend on a because s is even (our own). For example, Q(x,y) = x²−y² has D = 0 at c = (1,1).

**Paper or page:** [Counting solutions to quadratic polynomials](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.04328v1). It says: “S(m,n;q) = \\sideset{}{<sup>\*}\\sum\_{x\\bmod{q}}e<sub>q</sub></sup>(mx+n\\overline{x})”

**Sources:**

- [V. Vinay Kumaraswamy, Counting solutions to quadratic polynomials (2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.04328v1)

### Freiman models prevent false collisions

**Remember:** A usable model preserves both equal sums and unequal sums.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11P70 (Inverse problems of additive number theory, including sumsets), 11B30. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A Freiman isomorphism of order 8 is a bijection between subsets of abelian groups under which two sums of eight elements, repeats allowed, are equal exactly when their images are equal. 8A−8A is the set of differences of two such sums from A.

**Problem.** Let A be a finite nonempty set of integers, and let q be prime with q &gt; \|8A − 8A\|. Some subset of A of size at least \|A\|/8 is Freiman isomorphic of order 8 to a subset of ℤ/qℤ.

**How the definition helps.** The map must keep equal sums equal and unequal sums unequal, so no false collision appears in the model (our own). For example, reducing {0,1,3} modulo 5 sends 0+1 and 3+3 to the same residue, and six added zeros make it an eight-term collision (our own). The hard work is the Ruzsa modeling lemma, which picks the large subset and the map.

**Wikipedia:** [Freiman's theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freiman%27s_theorem). It says: “By the Ruzsa modeling lemma, there exists a subset A′ of A of cardinality at least \|A\|/8”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Eta shifts give partition inversion

**Remember:** The shifted partition series is the reciprocal of eta.

*True by definition.* MSC 11P82 (Analytic theory of partitions). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Let P(q) = ∑ p(n)qⁿ be the partition generating function, with q = exp(2πiτ) and τ in the upper half-plane. Multiplying by exp(−πiτ/12) = q<sup>(−1/24)</sup> gives 1/η(τ), the reciprocal of the Dedekind eta function, which satisfies η(−1/τ) = √(−iτ)η(τ).

**Problem.** For t &gt; 0, P(exp(−2πt)) equals √t exp(π(1/t − t)/12) times P(exp(−2π/t)).

**How the definition helps.** Put τ = it, so −1/τ = i/t and η(i/t) = √t η(it) (our own). Writing each η as q<sup>(1/24)</sup>/P(q) gives the stated factor, so the real work is the eta inversion law.

**nLab:** [Dedekind eta function](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Dedekind+eta+function). It says: “η(τ) = q¹⁄²⁴”

**Wikipedia:** [Dedekind eta function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dedekind_eta_function). It says: “η(−1/τ) = √(−iτ) η(τ).”

**Sources:**

- [G. H. Hardy and S. Ramanujan, Asymptotic Formulaae in Combinatory Analysis](https://doi.org/10.1112/plms/s2-17.1.75)

### Crank classes explain partition congruences

**Remember:** No ones: largest part. Ones: parts beyond their count, minus their count.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11P83 (Partitions; congruences and congruential restrictions), 05A17. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For a nonempty partition without ones, its crank is its largest part. For a partition containing ones, its crank is the number of parts larger than the number of ones, minus the number of ones.

**Problem.** For each integer n ≥ 0, the crank splits the partitions of 5n + 4 equally into five residue classes modulo 5. It does the same for 7n + 5 modulo 7 and 11n + 6 modulo 11. Each partition count is therefore divisible by its modulus.

**How the definition helps.** The crank turns each congruence into the claim that the five, seven or eleven residue classes have equal size. Andrews and Garvan’s crank generating function proves these equalities, and adding the equal sizes gives divisibility (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Crank of a partition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Crank_of_a_partition). It says: “M(9, 11, 11n + 6) = M(10, 11, 11n + 6) = p(11n + 6) / 11”

**Sources:**

- [George E. Andrews and F. G. Garvan, Dyson’s crank of a partition](https://doi.org/10.1090/S0273-0979-1988-15637-6)

### Defining ideal norms by prime factorizations makes them multiply

**Remember:** Raise each residue field size to its prime exponent, then multiply.

*True by definition.* MSC 11R04 (Algebraic numbers; rings of algebraic integers), 11R27. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For a nonzero integral ideal I = ∏ 𝔭ᵉ in the ring of integers O of a number field, define N(I) = ∏ \|O/𝔭\|ᵉ, using its unique prime factorization (our own).

**Problem.** The norm of a product of nonzero integral ideals equals the product of their norms.

**How the definition helps.** Exponents add when ideals multiply, so this norm multiplies (our own). The work moves to unique factorization into prime ideals and to \|O/𝔭ᵉ\| = \|O/𝔭\|ᵉ, which with the Chinese remainder theorem matches the usual index definition (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Lemma 8.4. (Properties of the absolute norm)](https://venhance.github.io/napkin/Napkin.pdf). It says: “For any other nonzero ideal 𝔟, Norm(𝔞𝔟) = Norm(𝔞)Norm(𝔟).”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Determinant field norms of algebraic integers are integers

**Remember:** The field norm takes the determinant of multiplication.

*True by definition.* MSC 11R04 (Algebraic numbers; rings of algebraic integers). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For a number field K and α ∈ K, the field norm N(α) is the determinant of multiplication by α on the ℚ-vector space K.

**Problem.** If α satisfies a monic polynomial with integer coefficients, then N(α) is an integer. Such an α is called an algebraic integer.

**How the definition helps.** Multiplication by an algebraic integer α preserves the ring of integers of K (our own). An integral basis therefore gives this map an integer matrix, whose determinant is an integer (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Field norm](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Field_norm). It says: “is defined as the determinant of this linear transformation.”

**Paper or page:** [An Infinitely Large Napkin: Alg Nt: Norm Trace](https://venhance.github.io/napkin/Napkin.pdf), [An Infinitely Large Napkin: Alg Nt: Norm Trace](https://venhance.github.io/napkin/Napkin.pdf). It says: “If α is an algebraic integer, its norm and trace are rational integers.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Index checks prevent false ramification

**Remember:** Check the index before reading ramification from polynomial factors.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11R04 (Algebraic numbers; rings of algebraic integers). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Let θ be an algebraic integer that generates a number field K. Call ℤ\[θ\] maximal at a prime p if p does not divide its index in the ring of integers of K, so that the two rings agree after reduction modulo p (our own).

**Problem.** Suppose ℤ\[θ\] is maximal at p. Each distinct irreducible factor of the minimal polynomial modulo p gives one prime ideal above p. Its multiplicity gives that prime’s exponent in the factorization of (p).

**How the definition helps.** Because the rings agree modulo p, the Dedekind–Kummer theorem reads the primes above p and their exponents from the factors of the minimal polynomial modulo p. For θ = √5 the index is two, and x²−5 has a double root modulo two (our own). Yet two stays prime, since (1+√5)/2 generates the full ring and x²−x−1 is irreducible modulo two (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Theorem 6.3. (Factoring algorithm / Dedekind-Kummer theorem)](https://venhance.github.io/napkin/Napkin.pdf). It says: “In particular, if K is monogenic with 𝒪ₖ = ℤ\[θ\] then j=1 and the theorem applies for all primes p.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Lattice-index ideal norms make principal ideal norms absolute field norms

**Remember:** Multiplication scales the lattice by the absolute value of its determinant.

*True by definition. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11R04 (Algebraic numbers; rings of algebraic integers), 11R27. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For a nonzero ideal I in the ring of integers O of a number field, its norm is the additive index \[O:I\] (our own).

**Problem.** The norm of a nonzero principal ideal equals the absolute value of the field norm of its generator.

**How the definition helps.** Multiplication by a nonzero generator a maps the lattice O onto (a) (our own). By Smith normal form, the image has index equal to the absolute determinant (our own). That determinant before taking absolute value is the field norm of a (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Lemma 8.4. (Properties of the absolute norm)](https://venhance.github.io/napkin/Napkin.pdf). It says: “If 𝔞 = (a) is principal, then Norm(𝔞) = \|Normₖ/ℚ(a)\|.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Requiring monic polynomials gives the right ring of algebraic integers

**Remember:** Algebraic integers are roots of integer polynomials with leading coefficient 1.

*Rules out counterexamples. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11R04 (Algebraic numbers; rings of algebraic integers), 13F05. arXiv math.NT, math.AC. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** An algebraic integer is a complex number that is a root of a monic integer polynomial, one with leading coefficient 1. In a number field the algebraic integers form the integral closure of ℤ, so the ring of integers is integrally closed (our own).

**Problem.** The ring of integers of a number field is a Dedekind domain. Every nonzero proper ideal therefore factors uniquely into nonzero prime ideals.

**How the definition helps.** A Dedekind domain is an integrally closed Noetherian domain of dimension one, and the ring of integers has all three properties (our own). The monic condition supplies integral closure: ℤ\[√−3\] omits the root (1+√−3)/2 of X²−X+1 and is not a Dedekind domain (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Algebraic integer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Algebraic_integer), [Quadratic integer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quadratic_integer). It says: “In contrast, Z\[√−3\] is not even a Dedekind domain.”

### Torus quotients preserve Mahler measure

**Remember:** A surjective torus map carries uniform probability to uniform probability.

*True by definition.* MSC 11R06 (PV-numbers and generalizations; other special algebraic numbers; Mahler measure). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** The logarithmic Mahler measure m(P) of a nonzero Laurent polynomial P, one that may have negative exponents, is the average of log\|P\| over a product of unit circles with uniform probability.

**Problem.** Let q map one product of unit circles onto another by monomials, replacing each variable by a product of integer powers of the new variables. Then m(P ∘ q) = m(P) for every nonzero Laurent polynomial P.

**How the definition helps.** Since m is an average, invariance is a change of variables: a surjective monomial map carries uniform probability to uniform probability (our own). This holds because every rotation of the target lifts through q, and uniform probability is the only rotation-invariant one (our own). The one analytic input is that log\|P\| is integrable near the zeros of P.

**Paper or page:** [General Boyd-Lawton Theorems with Multivariable Limits](https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.05910). It says: “In other words, suppose that\~ $q<sub>A</sub> \\colon {\\mathbb {T}}<sup>m</sup> \\to {\\mathbb {T}}<sup>n$</sup> is surjective. Then\\\[  \\int \_{{\\mathbb {T}}<sup>n</sup>} g \\,  d \\tau <sub>n</sub> \\;  = \\;  \\int \_{{\\mathbb {T}}<sup>m}</sup> g \\circ q<sub>A</sub> \\,  d \\tau \_m \\, .  \\\]”

### Regular primes are the primes where Kummer's proof of Fermat works

**Remember:** For regular p, an ideal with principal pth power is principal already.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11R18 (Cyclotomic extensions), 11R29, 11D41. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** An odd prime p is regular if p does not divide the class number of ℚ(ζₚ), where ζₚ is a primitive pth root of unity. Then an ideal of ℤ\[ζₚ\] whose pth power is principal is already principal (our own).

**Problem.** If p is a regular prime, then xᵖ + yᵖ = zᵖ has no solution in positive integers.

**How the definition helps.** Kummer’s proof factors xᵖ + yᵖ into the ideals (x + ζₚⁱy) (our own). When p does not divide xyz, these ideals are coprime, so each is a pth power of an ideal (our own). Regularity makes them principal, so the proof continues with elements; the case where p divides xyz needs a longer descent (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Regular prime](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Regular_prime). It says: “In 1850, Kummer proved that Fermat's Last Theorem is true for a prime exponent p if p is regular.”

**Sources:**

- [E. E. Kummer, Allgemeiner Beweis des Fermatschen Satzes, daß die Gleichung xλ+yλ=zλ durch ganze Zahlen unlösbar ist, für alle diejenigen Potenz-Exponenten λ welche ungerade Primzahlen sind und in den Zählern der ersten 1/2(λ) Bernoullischen zahlen als Factoren nicht vorkommen, J. reine angew. Math. 40 (1850), 130–138](https://doi.org/10.1515/crll.1850.40.130)

### Ignoring finite modules gives a structure theorem for Iwasawa modules

**Remember:** Up to finite error, Iwasawa modules are sums of cyclic pieces.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11R23 (Iwasawa theory), 13J05. arXiv math.NT, math.AC. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A quasi-isomorphism of modules over the Iwasawa algebra Λ = ℤₚ\[\[T\]\] is a homomorphism with finite kernel and finite cokernel, so it ignores finite modules.

**Problem.** Every finitely generated torsion Λ-module is quasi-isomorphic to a finite direct sum of Λ/(fⁿ), with f prime and n positive. Its characteristic series is unique up to a unit, and its μ and λ invariants are well defined.

**How the definition helps.** Ignoring finite modules lets the structure theorem describe each module by cyclic pieces Λ/(fⁿ) (our own). For instance, the finite module Λ/(p,T) is quasi-isomorphic to zero (our own). The prime powers fⁿ are unique, so their product, the characteristic series, is unique up to a unit, and μ and λ are well defined (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Iwasawa algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iwasawa_algebra). It says: “A quasi-isomorphism of modules is a homomorphism whose kernel and cokernel are both finite groups”

### Counting infinite places makes the unit rank places minus one

**Remember:** Count each real embedding once and each conjugate pair of nonreal embeddings once.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11R27 (Units and factorization). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** An infinite place of a number field is a real embedding into ℂ or a pair of complex conjugate nonreal embeddings, so each place gives one absolute value (our own). There are r₁ real places and r₂ complex places.

**Problem.** The unit group of the ring of integers is finitely generated with rank r₁ + r₂ − 1. So the rank is the number of infinite places minus one.

**How the definition helps.** The logarithmic embedding sends a unit to one coordinate per infinite place, with weight two at a complex place (our own). The coordinates sum to zero because the norm of a unit is ±1 (our own). Dirichlet’s unit theorem says that the image is a full lattice in this hyperplane of dimension r₁ + r₂ − 1, with finite kernel (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Dirichlet's unit theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dirichlet%27s_unit_theorem). It says: “There will be r + 1 Archimedean places of K, either real or complex.”

### Prime valuations count S-unit rank

**Remember:** Only primes in S may have nonzero exponents.

*True by definition.* MSC 11R27 (Units and factorization). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Fix a finite set S of nonzero prime ideals of the ring of integers of a number field K. An S-unit is an element x ∈ K× whose principal ideal has exponent zero at every prime outside S.

**Problem.** The rank of the S-unit group is the ordinary unit rank plus the number of primes in S.

**How the definition helps.** The exponents in S give a homomorphism to the integer lattice indexed by S, with kernel the ordinary units (our own). Finiteness of the ideal class group gives each prime a principal positive power (our own). Their exponent vectors span a subgroup of full rank, giving \|S\| additional directions (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [S-unit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/S-unit). It says: “An element x of K is an S-unit if the principal fractional ideal (x) is a product of primes in S (to positive or negative powers).”

### Unit regulators scale by index

**Remember:** The regulator is a cell volume, so index m multiplies it.

*True by definition.* MSC 11R27 (Units and factorization). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Send each unit to its log absolute values at the real embeddings and doubled log absolute values at one embedding from each nonreal pair, giving n coordinates (our own). The units modulo roots of unity form a lattice in the hyperplane of coordinate sum zero, and the regulator is its cell volume divided by √n (our own).

**Problem.** For a subgroup of the units modulo roots of unity of finite index m, the subgroup regulator is m times the full regulator.

**How the definition helps.** A sublattice of index m has a cell made of m cells of the full lattice, so its volume is m times larger (our own). The factor √n is the same for both and cancels (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Dirichlet's unit theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dirichlet%27s_unit_theorem). It says: “The volume of a fundamental domain of this lattice is R√(r + 1).”

### Determinants detect relative integral bases

**Remember:** Split off free summands and take the ideal class of the remaining summand.

*True by definition.* MSC 11R29 (Class numbers, class groups, discriminants). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Let B and A be the rings of integers in a number field and a subfield. As an A-module, B is a direct sum of free summands and one nonzero ideal I of A, and its Steinitz class is the class of I in the ideal class group of A.

**Problem.** Consider the ring of integers of a finite number field extension. It has a basis over the base ring of integers exactly when its Steinitz class is trivial.

**How the definition helps.** The decomposition leaves one ideal summand that could stop B from having a basis (our own). If its class is trivial, this ideal is principal and completes the basis (our own). Conversely, if B is free, its top exterior power is free and isomorphic to I (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Dedekind domain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dedekind_domain). It says: “The Steinitz class for P over R is the class \[I\] of I in Cl(R): it is uniquely determined.”

### Differentials give the monogenic different

**Remember:** Differentiate the defining relation to get the different.

*True by definition.* MSC 11R29 (Class numbers, class groups, discriminants). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** If B = A\[x\]/(f) for one monic polynomial f, differentiating the relation f(x) = 0 gives f′(x)dx = 0, with elements of A treated as constants. The Kähler different is the ideal generated by f′(x), the coefficient of dx in this relation.

**Problem.** Let L/K be an extension of number fields. Suppose α generates the integers of L over the integers of K and has minimal polynomial f. Then f′(α) generates the different.

**How the definition helps.** With one relation the Jacobian matrix has the single entry f′(α), so the Kähler different is generated by f′(α) (our own). The work lies in showing that the Kähler different equals the usual different, the inverse of the trace dual of the integers (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Lemma 49.7.4.](https://stacks.math.columbia.edu/tag/0BVZ). It says: “The Kähler different of B over A is the ideal of B generated by det(∂fᵢ/∂xⱼ).”

### Discriminant classes are squared Steinitz classes

**Remember:** The trace pairs two copies of the same line.

*True by definition.* MSC 11R29 (Class numbers, class groups, discriminants). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For number fields L/K, the Steinitz class of the integers of L over the integers of K is the ideal class of their top exterior power, a rank-one module. The trace determinant pairs this line with itself, and its image is the discriminant ideal (our own).

**Problem.** The relative discriminant of a number field extension represents the square of the Steinitz class of its ring of integers.

**How the definition helps.** The trace pairing is nondegenerate, so the tensor square of the line maps injectively onto the discriminant ideal (our own). So the discriminant represents the class of the tensor square, which is the square of the Steinitz class (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Different ideal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Different_ideal). It says: “indeed, it is the square of the Steinitz class for O<sub>L</sub> as a O<sub>K</sub>-module.”

### Norms give the discriminant tower law

**Remember:** Take norms of the different tower law.

*True by definition.* MSC 11R29 (Class numbers, class groups, discriminants). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For number fields L/K the relative discriminant is the ideal norm of the different (our own). The ideal norm acts multiplicatively, sending each prime to the prime below raised to the residue degree (our own).

**Problem.** For a tower of number fields L/K/S, write d(E/F) for the relative discriminant. Then d(L/S) = d(K/S)^\[L:K\] · Nₖ/ₛ(d(L/K)).

**How the definition helps.** Taking norms of the different tower law δ(L/S) = δ(L/K)δ(K/S) gives the discriminant tower law, because norms compose and the norm of an ideal extended from K is its \[L:K\]th power (our own). The work lies in the different tower law and in matching the norm with the trace-determinant discriminant (our own).

### Relative class numbers keep odd characters

**Remember:** Divide by the real class number to keep only odd characters.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11R29 (Class numbers, class groups, discriminants), 11M20. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For an odd prime p, let K = ℚ(ζₚ), with ζₚ a primitive pth root of unity, and let K⁺ be its real subfield, fixed by complex conjugation. The relative class number is h⁻ = h(K)/h(K⁺), and the zeta function of K is that of K⁺ times the L-functions of the odd characters modulo p (our own).

**Problem.** Put n = (p−1)/2, and let R and R⁺ be the regulators of K and K⁺. Then h⁻ = p(√p/π)ⁿ(R⁺/R) times the product of L(1,χ) over the characters χ modulo p with χ(−1) = −1.

**How the definition helps.** Dividing the class number formulas for K and K⁺ leaves only the odd L-values at 1 (our own). The rest of the factor comes from the ratios of roots of unity, 2p to 2, and of absolute discriminants, pⁿ (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Class number formula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Class_number_formula). It says: “there is a further formulation possible, as shown by Kummer.”

### Root discriminants ignore unramified extensions

**Remember:** The root cancels the extension degree.

*True by definition.* MSC 11R29 (Class numbers, class groups, discriminants). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** The root discriminant of a number field of degree n is the nth root of the absolute value of its discriminant, the determinant of the trace matrix of an integral basis. It measures the discriminant per unit of degree (our own).

**Problem.** The root discriminant stays constant in extensions unramified at every finite prime. This means that no prime ideal acquires a repeated factor in the larger ring of integers.

**How the definition helps.** The tower law gives \|d(L)\| = \|d(K)\|^\[L:K\] times the norm of the relative discriminant (our own). In an extension unramified at every finite prime the relative discriminant is the unit ideal, so the root of degree \[L:ℚ\] is unchanged (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Discriminant of an algebraic number field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discriminant_of_an_algebraic_number_field). It says: “The relation between relative discriminants in a tower of fields shows that the root discriminant does not change in an unramified extension.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Tameness gives different exponent e − 1

**Remember:** Tame ramification contributes exactly its index minus one.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11R29 (Class numbers, class groups, discriminants). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** In an extension of number fields, a prime is tamely ramified when the residue characteristic does not divide its ramification index e, its exponent in the prime below. The different is the inverse of the trace dual of the integers, and locally it is generated by f′(π) for a generator π of the local integers with minimal polynomial f (our own).

**Problem.** At a tame prime of ramification index e, the different has exponent e − 1.

**How the definition helps.** After completing and removing the unramified part, a uniformizer π has an Eisenstein minimal polynomial f of degree e (our own). In f′(π) the term eπ<sup>(e−1)</sup> has valuation e − 1, and tameness makes e a unit, so this term has strictly smaller valuation than the others (our own). In the wild extension ℚ₂(√2), the derivative 2√2 has valuation 3, not e − 1 = 1 (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Different ideal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Different_ideal). It says: “The precise exponent to which a ramified prime P divides δ is termed the differential exponent of P and is equal to e − 1 if P is tamely ramified”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### The different ideal shows exactly which primes ramify

**Remember:** Take the trace dual of the integers, then invert that ideal.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11R29 (Class numbers, class groups, discriminants), 11R32. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Let O be the integers of a number field L. Its inverse different consists of x ∈ L with Trₗ/ℚ(xy) ∈ ℤ for every y ∈ O. The different is the inverse of this fractional ideal (our own).

**Problem.** A prime ideal of L is ramified when it appears to a power above 1 in the factorization of the prime below. This happens exactly when it divides the different.

**How the definition helps.** The different is an ideal of L, so divisibility tests each prime above p separately (our own). Its exponent at a prime is at least e − 1 and is zero when e = 1, which gives the criterion (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Different ideal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Different_ideal). It says: “Pi divides the relative different δL / K if and only if Pi is ramified, that is, if and only if the ramification index e(i) is greater than 1.”

**Sources:**

- [Richard Dedekind, Über die Discriminanten endlicher Körper, Abhandlungen der Königlichen Gesellschaft der Wissenschaften zu Göttingen 29 (1882)](http://gdz.sub.uni-goettingen.de/en/dms/load/img/?IDDOC=39145)

### The narrow class group decides which primes a norm form represents

**Remember:** Signs matter for norm forms, so count ideals with positive generators.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11R29 (Class numbers, class groups, discriminants), 11R11, 11E16. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** The narrow class group is the group of fractional ideals modulo the principal ideals that have a totally positive generator, one that is positive under every real embedding.

**Problem.** Let K = ℚ(√d) have trivial narrow class group and discriminant D, and let q be the norm form of an integral basis. A prime p equals q(x,y) for some integers exactly in three cases. Either p divides D, or p = 2 and D ≡ 1 mod 8, or p is odd and (D/p) = 1.

**How the definition helps.** If the narrow class group is trivial, every prime ideal of norm p has a totally positive generator, whose norm is +p, so its coordinates give q(x,y) = p (our own). Conversely, an element of norm p generates a prime ideal of norm p, and the splitting criterion for quadratic fields lists exactly the primes with such an ideal (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Narrow class group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Narrow_class_group). It says: “However, this statement is false if we focus only on p and not −p (and is in fact even false for p = 2), because the narrow class group is nontrivial.”

**Sources:**

- [A. Fröhlich and M. J. Taylor, Algebraic Number Theory, Cambridge University Press, 1991](https://doi.org/10.1017/CBO9781139172165)

### Trace determinants square lattice indices

**Remember:** A basis change enters a trace determinant twice.

*True by definition.* MSC 11R29 (Class numbers, class groups, discriminants). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** An order in a number field is a subring of the integers that contains 1 and has full rank. Its discriminant is det T for the matrix T of traces Tr(bᵢbⱼ) of a ℤ-basis, and a change of basis by a matrix C replaces T by CᵀTC (our own).

**Problem.** If one order has index m in another order of the same field, its discriminant is m² times the larger order’s discriminant.

**How the definition helps.** If C writes the basis of the smaller order in the basis of the larger, the discriminant changes by (det C)² (our own). The absolute value of det C is the index m (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Discriminant of an algebraic number field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Discriminant_of_an_algebraic_number_field). It says: “The discriminant of an order in K with integral basis b₁,…,bₙ is defined in the same way.”

### Trace duals multiply in towers

**Remember:** Trace maps compose, so trace duals multiply.

*True by definition.* MSC 11R29 (Class numbers, class groups, discriminants). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For number fields L/K with rings of integers Oₗ and Oₖ, the trace dual of Oₗ is the set of x ∈ L with Trₗ/ₖ(xy) ∈ Oₖ for every y ∈ Oₗ. The different is the inverse of this fractional ideal (our own).

**Problem.** In a tower L/K/F, the different of L/F is the product of the different of L/K and the extended different of K/F.

**How the definition helps.** Since Trₗ/F is Trₖ/F after Trₗ/ₖ, x lies in the L/F dual exactly when every Trₗ/ₖ(xy) lies in the K/F dual (our own). Locally that dual has one generator, which factors out and leaves the L/K dual, so the duals multiply (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Different ideal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Different_ideal). It says: “In a tower of fields L/K/F the relative differents are related by δL/F = δL/K δK/F.”

### Unit signs explain narrow classes

**Remember:** The only signs that disappear come from units.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11R29 (Class numbers, class groups, discriminants). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** The narrow class group is the group of fractional ideals modulo principal ideals with a totally positive generator, one positive under every real embedding. The ordinary class group allows any nonzero generator.

**Problem.** Forgetting positivity maps narrow classes onto ordinary classes. Its kernel is the group of sign patterns at the real embeddings modulo the signs of units.

**How the definition helps.** A principal ideal is trivial in the narrow group exactly when some generator has only positive signs, and generators differ by units, so what remains is the sign pattern modulo unit signs (our own). Weak approximation, which lets one prescribe signs at all real embeddings, shows that every sign pattern occurs (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Narrow class group](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Narrow_class_group). It says: “where now Pₖ⁺ is the group of totally positive principal fractional ideals”

### Decomposition groups turn counting prime factors into orbit counting

**Remember:** Primes above p form one orbit; the stabilizer is the decomposition group.

*True by definition.* MSC 11R32 (Galois theory). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For a Galois extension L/K with group G and a prime P of L above p, the decomposition group of P is its stabilizer, the elements of G that send P to itself.

**Problem.** In a finite Galois extension of number fields, all primes above a nonzero prime p have the same ramification index e and residue degree f. Their number g equals \|G\|/\|D\| for the decomposition group D of any one of them, and the extension degree equals efg.

**How the definition helps.** The Galois group acts transitively on primes above p, so orbit-stabilizer gives g = \|G\|/\|D\| (our own). Conjugation preserves e and f, and the fundamental degree identity sums ef over those g primes (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Splitting of prime ideals in Galois extensions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Splitting_of_prime_ideals_in_Galois_extensions). It says: “the decomposition group of Pj, is the subgroup of elements of G sending a given Pj to itself.”

### Frobenius as a conjugacy class makes Chebotarev's theorem statable

**Remember:** Each prime picks a conjugacy class; classes are hit in proportion to size.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11R32 (Galois theory), 11R45. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Fix an unramified rational prime p in a finite Galois extension L/ℚ and a prime P above p. Its Frobenius is the unique automorphism preserving P that induces x ↦ xᵖ on the residue field (our own). The Frobenius class of p is its conjugacy class.

**Problem.** Let L/ℚ be a finite Galois extension with group G, and let C be a conjugacy class of G. The unramified primes whose Frobenius class is C have density \|C\|/\|G\|.

**How the definition helps.** Changing P conjugates its Frobenius, so the conjugacy class depends only on p. Chebotarev’s density theorem gives the density of primes with that class (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Chebotarev density theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chebotarev_density_theorem). It says: “The statement of the more general Chebotarev density theorem is in terms of the Frobenius element of a prime (ideal), which is in fact an associated conjugacy class C of elements of the Galois group G.”

- [Nikolai Tschebotareff, Die Bestimmung der Dichtigkeit einer Menge von Primzahlen, welche zu einer gegebenen Substitutionsklasse gehören, Mathematische Annalen 95 (1926)](https://doi.org/10.1007/bf01206606)

### Frobenius defined by a pth-power congruence restricts to Frobenius below

**Remember:** Restrict the same power map to the smaller residue field.

*True by definition.* MSC 11R32 (Galois theory). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Let L/ℚ be finite Galois and let 𝔓 lie above an unramified rational prime p. Its Frobenius is the unique σ ∈ Gal(L/ℚ) satisfying σ(x) ≡ xᵖ modulo 𝔓 for every x ∈ Oₗ (our own).

**Problem.** Let L ⊃ K be number fields, both Galois over ℚ, and let 𝔓 in L lie over 𝔭 in K, both unramified. The Frobenius of 𝔓 restricts on K to the Frobenius of 𝔭.

**How the definition helps.** The restriction to K satisfies the defining congruence there (our own). For x ∈ Oₖ the difference σ(x) − xᵖ lies in both 𝔓 and Oₖ, hence in 𝔭 (our own). Uniqueness at the unramified prime 𝔭 identifies the restriction (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Theorem 6.1. (Restrictions of Frobenius elements)](https://venhance.github.io/napkin/Napkin.pdf). It says: “Assume L/ℚ and K/ℚ are both Galois. Let 𝔓 and 𝔭 be unramified as above.”

### Restricted products put Poitou–Tate duality in one sequence

**Remember:** Unramified almost everywhere makes the infinite product locally compact.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11R34 (Galois cohomology), 11S25. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For a finite Galois module M over a number field k, the restricted product of the local groups H¹(kᵥ,M) holds the families whose entries are unramified, meaning trivial on inertia, at all but finitely many finite places (our own). Its topology makes the product of the unramified subgroups open, so the whole group is locally compact (our own).

**Problem.** For M and its twisted dual M′ = Hom(M, μ), with μ the roots of unity, Poitou–Tate duality gives a nine-term exact sequence through restricted products of local cohomology, with modified cohomology at archimedean places (our own). Summing local pairings gives a perfect pairing of the degree-one restricted products.

**How the definition helps.** Local compactness lets Pontryagin duality apply, and global classes land in the restricted product because they are unramified almost everywhere (our own). The work went into the global duality theorems of Poitou and Tate.

**Wikipedia:** [Tate duality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tate_duality). It says: “where ∏′ denotes a restricted product with respect to the unramified cohomology groups.”

**Sources:**

- [Jürgen Neukirch, Alexander Schmidt and Kay Wingberg, Cohomology of Number Fields, Springer (2008)](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-540-37889-1)

### Artin and Hecke factors agree

**Remember:** Both factors read χ at Frobenius, or equal one if ramified.

*True by definition.* MSC 11R37 (Class field theory), 11S40. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For a finite-order one-dimensional Galois character χ of a number field, its Hecke character is χ composed with the global reciprocity map on idele classes. Reciprocity is normalized so that a local uniformizer maps to arithmetic Frobenius modulo inertia (our own).

**Problem.** At every finite place of a number field, the Artin and Hecke Euler factors of these characters agree. An Euler factor is the local term in the product defining an L-function.

**How the definition helps.** Compatibility of local and global reciprocity gives the same local character on both sides at each place (our own). If it is nontrivial on local units, which map onto inertia, both Euler factors equal one; otherwise both use χ at arithmetic Frobenius (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Artin reciprocity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artin_reciprocity). It says: “connects Artin L-functions associated to abelian extensions of a number field with Hecke L-functions”

### Artin kernels turn composita into intersections

**Remember:** The compositum keeps only the classes that fix both fields.

*True by definition. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11R37 (Class field theory). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For a finite abelian extension L of a number field K, its Artin kernel is the set of idele classes of K that act trivially on L under global reciprocity (our own). Reciprocity identifies this kernel with the norm group from L (our own).

**Problem.** Take two finite abelian extensions of the same number field inside one algebraic closure. The norms on idele classes from their compositum form the intersection of their two norm subgroups.

**How the definition helps.** A class fixes the compositum exactly when it fixes both fields, so the kernel for the compositum is the intersection of the two kernels (our own). Global reciprocity does the hard step, identifying each kernel with the norm group (our own).

**nLab:** [class field theory](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/class+field+theory). It says: “by relating them to the idele class group.”

**Wikipedia:** [Class field theory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Class_field_theory). It says: “\\theta<sub>L/F</sub>: C<sub>F</sub>/{N<sub>L/F</sub>(C<sub>L</sub>)} \\to \\operatorname{Gal}(L/F),”

### Brauer reciprocity forces even ramification

**Remember:** Each nonsplit place contributes one half to a zero sum.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11R37 (Class field theory), 11S45. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** At each completion of ℚ, a quaternion algebra is split if it becomes a matrix algebra and ramified if it stays a division algebra. The local Brauer invariant is 0 at split places and ½ at ramified places, modulo ℤ.

**Problem.** A quaternion algebra over ℚ ramifies at an even number of places, counting the real place when it is nonsplit.

**How the definition helps.** Global Brauer reciprocity says that the local invariants, only finitely many nonzero, sum to zero modulo ℤ (our own). Each ramified place adds ½, so their number is even (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Quaternion algebra](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quaternion_algebra). It says: “The number of places where a quaternion algebra over the rationals ramifies is always even”

### Cyclicity repairs the norm principle

**Remember:** One generator turns the norm question into a cyclic algebra test.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11R37 (Class field theory). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A finite Galois extension L/K is cyclic if some σ ∈ Gal(L/K) generates Gal(L/K). The norm of x ∈ L× is the product of τ(x) over all τ ∈ Gal(L/K) (our own).

**Problem.** An element of a number field that is a local norm everywhere from a finite cyclic extension is a global norm.

**How the definition helps.** For a cyclic extension, x is a norm exactly when the cyclic algebra built from x and a generator σ is a matrix algebra (our own). The local–global theorem for central simple algebras then turns local norms into a global norm (our own). Hasse found that 3 is a local norm everywhere from the noncyclic ℚ(√−3, √13) but is not a global norm.

**Wikipedia:** [Hasse norm theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hasse_norm_theorem). It says: “Hasse gave the counterexample that 3 is a local norm everywhere for the extension ℚ(√−3, √13)/ℚ but is not a global norm.”

**Paper or page:** [A Projective Twist on the Hasse Norm Theorem](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.11159v1). It says: “\\mathrm {HNP}<sub>K</sub>(L) holds whenever L/K is cyclic.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Herbrand quotients make the first inequality computable

**Remember:** Divide the size in Tate degree zero by the size in degree one.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11R37 (Class field theory), 20J06. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For a finite cyclic group G acting on a module A with finite Tate cohomology in degrees zero and one, the Herbrand quotient is h(A) = \|Ĥ⁰(G,A)\|/\|Ĥ¹(G,A)\| (our own). It is multiplicative on short exact sequences and equals 1 for finite modules (our own).

**Problem.** For a cyclic extension L/K of number fields of degree n, the idele class group of L has Herbrand quotient n. So the index of the norm group in the idele class group of K is at least n.

**How the definition helps.** Because h multiplies and ignores finite modules, one can cut the idele class group into S-units and local unit groups, and the S-unit quotient follows from Dirichlet’s unit theorem (our own). The degree-zero group is the norm index, so the index is n times \|Ĥ¹\|, which is at least n.

**Wikipedia:** [Class formation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Class_formation), [Herbrand quotient](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herbrand_quotient). It says: “It is fairly straightforward to prove, because the Herbrand quotient is easy to work out, as it is multiplicative on short exact sequences, and is 1 for finite modules.”

### Moduli with real places let conductors tell real abelian fields apart

**Remember:** Put the real place in the modulus to record whether signs matter.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11R37 (Class field theory), 11R20. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A modulus assigns a nonnegative exponent to each finite prime, zero almost everywhere, and selects a set of real places. At a selected real place, two nonzero elements are congruent only if their ratio is positive there, so the modulus can record ramification at infinity (our own).

**Problem.** Every finite abelian extension of a number field has a conductor, the smallest modulus whose ray class field contains it. Over ℚ, let n be the least positive integer with K inside the nth cyclotomic field. The conductor of K is n if K is real and n times ∞ otherwise.

**How the definition helps.** A real place in the modulus is a sign condition, which is how ramification at infinity shows in the conductor. For example, ℚ(ζ₅) has conductor 5∞ and its real subfield ℚ(√5) has conductor 5, while without real places every ray class field over ℚ would be real (our own). The existence theorem of class field theory still does the hard work.

**Wikipedia:** [Modulus (algebraic number theory)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modulus_%28algebraic_number_theory%29), [Conductor (class field theory)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conductor_%28class_field_theory%29). It says: “the conductor of K is then n if K is fixed by complex conjugation and n ∞ otherwise.”

### Outside the special case, local powers are global

**Remember:** Only 2-adic cyclotomic accidents stop local n-th powers from being global.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11R37 (Class field theory). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For s ≥ 2 let ηₛ be 2cos(2π/2ˢ). A field is s-special if it contains ηₛ but none of i, ηₛ₊₁ and iηₛ₊₁. The special case occurs when K is s-special with 2ˢ⁺¹ dividing n, and S contains the 2-adic primes p where Kₚ is s-special.

**Problem.** Let S be a finite set of primes of a number field K. Outside the special case, an element that is an n-th power at every prime outside S is an n-th power in K.

**How the definition helps.** The special case lists exactly the 2-adic cyclotomic situations where the local–global principle for n-th powers fails, and even then the failure is a group of order 2. For example, ℚ is 2-special, and 16 is an 8th power at every odd prime but not in ℚ. Wang’s corrected proof uses class field theory (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Grunwald–Wang theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grunwald%E2%80%93Wang_theorem). It says: “In the special case the failure of the Hasse principle is finite of order 2”

### Ray moduli bound composita

**Remember:** The stricter modulus maps onto both weaker ray class groups.

*True by definition.* MSC 11R37 (Class field theory). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For a modulus m of a number field K, the ray class group is the idele class group of K modulo the image of local subgroups chosen by m, so a stricter modulus gives a smaller subgroup. These are units congruent to 1 modulo the given prime power at finite primes (all units at exponent zero), positive elements at selected real places, and all nonzero elements at other infinite places (our own).

**Problem.** The compositum of two ray class fields lies in the ray class field for the least common multiple of their moduli.

**How the definition helps.** The least common multiple imposes both sets of conditions, so its subgroup lies inside each of the two subgroups (our own). Class field theory reverses inclusions, so both ray class fields lie in the field for the least common multiple (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Ray class field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ray_class_field). It says: “They are sometimes easier to handle theoretically because they are all quotients of a single group, and thus easier to compare.”

### The transfer reduces the principal ideal theorem

**Remember:** Permute coset representatives and multiply the leftover subgroup factors.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11R37 (Class field theory), 20J06, 11R29. arXiv math.NT, math.GR. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** The transfer from a group G to a subgroup H of finite index multiplies the H-parts left over when g permutes coset representatives. Choose representatives T of the cosets tH, write gt = t′hₜ with t′ ∈ T and hₜ ∈ H, and send the class of g in G/\[G,G\] to ∏ₜ hₜ in H/\[H,H\] (our own).

**Problem.** Every ideal of a number field K becomes principal in the Hilbert class field of K.

**How the definition helps.** Artin reciprocity turns extending ideal classes from K to its Hilbert class field into the transfer from G to its derived subgroup, where G is the Galois group of the second Hilbert class field over K (our own). So the theorem says that this transfer is trivial, which Furtwängler proved by group theory in 1929.

**Wikipedia:** [Principal ideal theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Principal_ideal_theorem). It says: “he showed that it would follow if the transfer from a finite group to its derived subgroup is trivial.”

**Sources:**

- [Emil Artin, Idealklassen in Oberkörpern und allgemeines Reziprozitätsgesetz, Abhandlungen aus dem Mathematischen Seminar der Universität Hamburg 7 (1929)](https://doi.org/10.1007/bf02941159)

### Unramified at real places, the Hilbert class field matches the class group

**Remember:** Unramified everywhere, including at infinity, gives exactly the class group.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11R37 (Class field theory), 11R29. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** The Hilbert class field of a number field K is its largest abelian extension that is unramified at every place. Unramified at a real place means that the real embedding stays real in the larger field.

**Problem.** The Galois group of the Hilbert class field over K is isomorphic to the ideal class group of K. Its degree is the class number.

**How the definition helps.** The real-place condition excludes extensions that only the narrow class group sees (our own). For K = ℚ(√3), with class number one, K(i) is unramified at every finite prime but makes the real places complex, so allowing it would give the wrong degree (our own). Artin reciprocity for modulus one then identifies the Galois group with the ordinary class group (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Hilbert class field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilbert_class_field). It says: “That is, every real embedding of K extends to a real embedding of E, rather than to a complex embedding of E.”

### Centering pairs Hadamard factors

**Remember:** Center the reflection at zero and paired zeros cancel exponentials.

*True by definition.* MSC 11R42 (Zeta functions and L-functions of number fields). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Center the completed Dedekind zeta function Λ, with its discriminant and gamma factors, on the critical line and clear its poles at s = 0 and s = 1: F(z) = (z² + ¼)Λ(½ + iz) (our own). Then F is entire of order one, and Λ(s) = Λ(1 − s) becomes F(z) = F(−z) (our own).

**Problem.** F is even and F(z) = c·zᵐ ∏(1 − z²/w²), where c ≠ 0 and m is the vanishing order at zero. The product counts each opposite pair of nonzero zeros once with multiplicity.

**How the definition helps.** F is even, so its zeros come in opposite pairs ±w and its zero at the origin has even order (our own). In the Hadamard product of this order-one function, the exponential factors of w and −w cancel (our own). The remaining factor exp(a + bz) must also be even, so b = 0 (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Dedekind zeta function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dedekind_zeta_function). It says: “producing an entire function, and moves the critical line to the real line.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Equal zeta functions fix class number times regulator

**Remember:** Same zeta function, same residue at one.

*True by definition.* MSC 11R42 (Zeta functions and L-functions of number fields), 11R29. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Two number fields are arithmetically equivalent if their Dedekind zeta functions agree, so in particular they have the same residue at s = 1 (our own).

**Problem.** Arithmetically equivalent number fields have the same class number times regulator. The class number counts ideal classes, and the regulator measures the volume of the lattice formed from logarithms of units.

**How the definition helps.** The analytic class number formula writes the residue at s = 1 as class number times regulator times factors from the discriminant, signature and roots of unity (our own). Perlis’s theorem says arithmetically equivalent fields share those last three invariants (our own). So the products of class number and regulator agree (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Notes on Explicit Constructions of Arithmetically Equivalent Global Function Fields via Torsion Points On Drinfeld Modules](https://arxiv.org/abs/2107.08250v1), [Stronger arithmetic equivalence](https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.01956v4). It says: “product of regulator and class-number reg(𝒪ₖ)hₖ = reg(𝒪ₗ)hₗ”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Finite-place logarithms absorb missing zeta factors

**Remember:** Finite places enter the regulator with weight log N(v).

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11R42 (Zeta functions and L-functions of number fields). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** The S-regulator R(S) is the covolume, after dropping one coordinate, of the S-units under the log map with one coordinate per place v in S, using log\|x\|ᵥ (doubled at complex places), which at a finite prime is −ordᵥ(x) log N(v) (our own). Concretely, it is the absolute value of any maximal minor of this matrix for a basis of S-units modulo torsion (our own).

**Problem.** The S-zeta function omits prime factors at S. Its first nonzero Taylor coefficient at zero equals −h(S)R(S)/w. Here w counts roots of unity and h(S) counts ideal classes after allowing denominators at the finite primes in S.

**How the definition helps.** Each deleted Euler factor 1 − N(v)⁻ˢ vanishes at zero with derivative log N(v), and these logarithms reappear in R(S) (our own). The finite-prime rows contribute that product times an index, and h(S) is h divided by the same index (our own). So the ordinary leading term −hR/w becomes −h(S)R(S)/w (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Special values of L-functions on regular arithmetic schemes of dimension 1](https://arxiv.org/abs/2108.00811). It says: “We obtain from the analytic class number formula for the S-zeta function of K (the arithmetic zeta function of U)”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Gamma factors cancel trivial zeta zeros

**Remember:** One gamma factor per infinite place makes zeta symmetric.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11R42 (Zeta functions and L-functions of number fields). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** The completed Dedekind zeta function Λ(s) multiplies \|D\|ˢᐟ²ζꜰ(s), for a field of discriminant D, by one gamma factor per infinite place: π⁻ˢᐟ²Γ(s/2) for each real embedding and (2π)⁻ˢΓ(s) for each pair of complex embeddings (our own).

**Problem.** The completed function satisfies Λ(s) = Λ(1−s). In particular it is finite and nonzero at every negative integer, although the Riemann zeta function vanishes at −2.

**How the definition helps.** The reflection Λ(s) = Λ(1 − s) sends each negative integer −n to 1 + n &gt; 1 (our own). There the Euler product and every gamma factor are finite and nonzero, so Λ(−n) is too (our own). Proving the functional equation is the analytic work, done by Hecke.

**Wikipedia:** [Dedekind zeta function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dedekind_zeta_function). It says: “The functional equation for the Dedekind zeta function implies a set of trivial zeroes which cancel poles of the gamma factors in the equation”

### Integrating over ideles proves Hecke's functional equation by Poisson summation

**Remember:** Integrate test function, character and norm power over all ideles.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11R42 (Zeta functions and L-functions of number fields), 11R56. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Tate’s zeta integral of a Schwartz–Bruhat function φ on the adeles and a unitary idele class character χ is ∫ φ(x)χ(x)\|x\|ˢ d×x over the ideles, for Re s &gt; 1 (our own). For a product test function it splits into local integrals that give the Euler and gamma factors of the Hecke L-function (our own).

**Problem.** Every Hecke L-function of a number field extends to a meromorphic function on the whole complex plane. It satisfies a functional equation that relates s and 1 − s. It has poles only when the character is a power of the idele norm (our own).

**How the definition helps.** Poisson summation over the field inside the adeles relates the integral for φ and χ at s to the integral for the Fourier transform of φ and χ̄ at 1 − s (our own). This gives continuation and the functional equation at once (our own). The boundary terms give poles only when χ is a power of the norm (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Tate's thesis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tate%27s_thesis). It says: “Using harmonic analysis, more precisely the Poisson summation formula, he proved the functional equation and meromorphic continuation of the zeta integral and the Hecke L-function.”

### Nontrivial monomial characters give entire L-functions

**Remember:** Induce nontrivial characters and no zeta pole appears.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11R42 (Zeta functions and L-functions of number fields). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Here a monomial representation of a finite Galois group G is a direct sum of induced representations Indᴳₕ χ, where each χ: H → ℂ× is a nontrivial homomorphism on a subgroup H.

**Problem.** The Artin L-function of this direct sum is entire, meaning holomorphic on the whole complex plane.

**How the definition helps.** Artin’s induction formula turns the L-function of each summand into the Hecke L-function of χ over the field fixed by H. Hecke’s theorem makes the L-function of each nontrivial character entire. A trivial χ would give that field’s zeta function, with its pole at s = 1 (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Equivariant algebraic K-theory and Artin L-functions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.03578). It says: “this meromorphic continuation is entire if ρ is a direct sum of inductions of non-trivial abelian characters on subgroups.”

### Norm-one classes exclude shifted poles

**Remember:** Nontrivial on norm one means not a norm power.

*Rules out counterexamples. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11R42 (Zeta functions and L-functions of number fields). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A unitary Hecke character χ, a continuous homomorphism from the idele class group to the unit circle, is nontrivial on norm one if χ(x) ≠ 1 for some class x with \|x\| = 1 (our own). The characters that fail are exactly the norm powers x ↦ \|x\|ⁱᵗ with t real (our own).

**Problem.** If the character is nontrivial on the subgroup of norm one, its completed Hecke L-function is holomorphic everywhere.

**How the definition helps.** Tate’s continuation theorem shows that the completed L-function is entire unless χ is a norm power. For example, the ideal character N(𝔞)ⁱᵗ with real t ≠ 0 gives ζ(s − it), which has a pole at s = 1 + it (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Hecke character](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hecke_character). It says: “Hecke proved these L-functions have a meromorphic continuation to the whole complex plane, being analytic except for a simple pole of order 1”

**Remember:** G permutes the cosets of the subgroup that fixes E.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11R42 (Zeta functions and L-functions of number fields). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For L/K finite Galois with group G and a subgroup H with fixed field E, the coset representation lets G permute a basis indexed by the cosets G/H by left multiplication (our own). It is the representation of G induced from the trivial representation of H.

**Problem.** The Dedekind zeta function of E equals the Artin L-function of this representation over K. Decomposing the representation into irreducible pieces factors the zeta function, with one factor per piece.

**How the definition helps.** Artin’s induction formula says the L-function over K of an induced representation equals the L-function over E of the original one. The trivial representation over E has L-function ζ<sub>E</sub>, and a direct sum has the product of the L-functions of its pieces.

### Prime-power traces give Artin log derivatives

**Remember:** Weight prime powers by log norm times Frobenius trace.

*True by definition.* MSC 11R42 (Zeta functions and L-functions of number fields). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For a finite-dimensional complex representation ρ on V of a finite Galois group of number fields, give each prime power 𝔭ᵐ the weight log N𝔭 · Tr(Fᵐ on Vᴵ), where F is arithmetic Frobenius acting on the inertia-fixed vectors Vᴵ (our own). Other ideals get weight zero (our own).

**Problem.** For Re s &gt; 1, sum each weight times exp(−s log N𝔞) over nonzero integral ideals 𝔞, where N𝔞 counts residue classes. The sum equals −L′(s,ρ)/L(s,ρ) for the Artin L-function of ρ.

**How the definition helps.** These are the coefficients of −L′/L, because the Artin Euler factor at 𝔭 is det(1 − F N𝔭⁻ˢ on Vᴵ)⁻¹ (our own). Its logarithm is ∑ Tr(Fᵐ on Vᴵ) N𝔭⁻ᵐˢ/m, and differentiating cancels m and brings down log N𝔭 (our own). Absolute convergence for Re s &gt; 1 allows summing over all primes (our own).

### Primitive completion restores reflection

**Remember:** The smallest modulus keeps every factor needed for reflection.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11R42 (Zeta functions and L-functions of number fields). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Write a finite-order Hecke character χ at its conductor 𝔣, the smallest modulus through which it factors, so its L-function keeps the Euler factor at every prime outside 𝔣 (our own). Its completion Λ(s,χ) adds the archimedean gamma factors and the factor (D·N𝔣)ˢᐟ², with D the absolute discriminant (our own).

**Problem.** For a finite-order character, the completed function satisfies Λ(s,χ) = ε(χ)Λ(1−s,χ̄), with \|ε(χ)\| = 1. The same completion need not work if one drops factors at extra primes.

**How the definition helps.** Hecke’s functional equation needs every local factor that the smallest modulus keeps. For example, deleting one prime of norm q from the zeta function multiplies its completion by 1 − q⁻ˢ (our own). That multiplier has different absolute values at s = 2 and s = −1, so no constant of absolute value one can repair the reflection (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Hecke character](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hecke_character). It says: “Hecke showed these L-functions satisfy a functional equation relating the values of the L-function of a character and the L-function of its complex conjugate character.”

### Summing over ideals gives the Dedekind zeta function an Euler product

**Remember:** Sum over ideals, factor over prime ideals.

*True by definition. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11R42 (Zeta functions and L-functions of number fields). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Problem.** For Re s &gt; 1, the Dedekind zeta function is the product over all nonzero prime ideals P of 1/(1 − N(P)⁻ˢ).

**How the definition helps.** Unique factorization into prime ideals and multiplicativity of N split each term N(a)⁻ˢ into a product over the primes dividing a. Expanding each factor 1/(1 − N(P)⁻ˢ) as a geometric series then gives every ideal exactly once (our own). Absolute convergence for Re s &gt; 1 permits this (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Dedekind zeta function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dedekind_zeta_function). It says: “The norm function is multiplicative with respect to multiplication of ideals, which implies that the Dedekind zeta function has an Euler product over all non-zero prime ideals”

### Using inertia-fixed vectors makes the Artin local factor independent of Frobenius lift

**Remember:** Lifts differ by inertia, and inertia does nothing on fixed vectors.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11R42 (Zeta functions and L-functions of number fields), 11F80. arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** For a representation ρ on V with finite image, the local Artin factor at a prime p is 1/det(1 − N(p)⁻ˢρ(F)), taken on the vectors fixed by the inertia group I (our own). Here F is any lift of the Frobenius x ↦ x<sup>N(p)</sup>, and two lifts differ by an element of I (our own).

**Problem.** The local Artin factor does not depend on the chosen lift of Frobenius, even at a ramified prime.

**How the definition helps.** Elements of I act as the identity on the I-fixed vectors, so all lifts give the same operator there (our own). Inertia is normal in the decomposition group, so F preserves those vectors (our own). On all of V the choice matters: for a ramified quadratic character, inertia acts by −1, so two lifts give opposite values (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Artin L-function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artin_L-function). It says: “determinant is taken on a linear map restricted to”

**Sources:**

- [Jürgen Neukirch, Algebraic Number Theory, Chapter VII, §10 (1999)](https://doi.org/10.1007/978-3-662-03983-0)

### Virtual characters give meromorphic continuation

**Remember:** Allow negative multiplicities, so L-functions may divide.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11R42 (Zeta functions and L-functions of number fields). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** A virtual character of the group G of a finite Galois extension is an integer combination of characters of finite-dimensional complex representations. Its Artin L-function is the matching product of Artin L-functions, with negative exponents for negative coefficients (our own).

**Problem.** The Artin L-function of every virtual character extends meromorphically to the whole plane, so its only possible singularities are poles.

**How the definition helps.** Brauer’s induction theorem writes every virtual character as an integer combination of characters induced from one-dimensional characters of subgroups (our own). Artin induction and reciprocity turn each such L-function into a Hecke L-function, which is meromorphic (our own). Integer powers and products of meromorphic functions are meromorphic (our own).

**nLab:** [Artin L-function](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Artin+L-function). It says: “Then the corresponding Artin L-functions are equal:”

**Paper or page:** [Equivariant algebraic K-theory and Artin L-functions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.03578). It says: “The Artin L-function L(𝒪Ｆ,ρ,s) of any complex Galois representation ρ of G extends to a meromorphic function on the complex plane.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Characters isolate ray classes

**Remember:** Average characters to keep one class and kill the rest.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11R44 (Distribution of prime ideals). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** The projector onto a class a of a ray class group A sends b ∈ A to the average of χ(b)χ̄(a) over all complex characters χ of A, which is 1 when b = a and 0 otherwise (our own).

**Problem.** For a fixed number field and modulus, each of the h ray classes contains a proportion tending to 1/h of all prime ideals. Count prime ideals by the size of their residue fields.

**How the definition helps.** Weighting the prime ideal count by this projector splits it into one sum per character (our own). Kai’s weighted prime ideal theorem gives a main term only for the trivial character, with coefficient 1/h (our own). Partial summation removes the logarithmic weights (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Notes on Mitsui's Prime Number Theorem with Siegel zeros](https://arxiv.org/abs/2209.11816v2). It says: “where β is the potential Siegel zero mod 𝔮.”

**Sources:**

- [Wataru Kai, Notes on Mitsui's Prime Number Theorem with Siegel zeros](https://arxiv.org/abs/2209.11816v2)

### Fixed cosets count degree-one primes

**Remember:** Fixed cosets are the cycles of length one.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11R44 (Distribution of prime ideals). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** Put a number field K inside a finite Galois extension L of ℚ with group G, so G permutes the cosets of the subgroup H fixing K. At an unramified prime p, the cycles of Frobenius on these cosets match the primes of K above p, and each cycle length is the residue degree.

**Problem.** The number of primes of K above p with residue field of size p equals the number of cosets fixed by Frobenius. The density of rational primes with such a factor equals the fraction of group elements fixing a coset.

**How the definition helps.** A prime of residue degree one is a Frobenius cycle of length one, which is a fixed coset. Chebotarev’s theorem then turns the fraction of group elements fixing some coset into a density of primes (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Density questions on arithmetic equivalence](https://arxiv.org/abs/2106.01166v1). It says: “{\\rm Trace}(\\rho <sub>K</sub>({\\rm Frob}<sub>\\ell </sub>)) =a<sub>\\ell </sub>(K).”

**Sources:**

- [Guillermo Mantilla-Soler, Density questions on arithmetic equivalence (2021)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2106.01166v1)
- [N. Tschebotareff, Die Bestimmung der Dichtigkeit einer Menge von Primzahlen, welche zu einer gegebenen Substitutionsklasse gehören (1926)](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF01206606)

### Ideal norms isolate first-degree primes

**Remember:** An inert quadratic prime enters at its square.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11R44 (Distribution of prime ideals). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** The norm of a nonzero prime ideal 𝔭 above p is the size of its residue field, pᶠ with f the residue degree, so a prime of degree above one has norm at least p² (our own).

**Problem.** In a number field of degree n, at most n√x prime ideals of norm ≤ x have degree greater than one. Hence the count of degree-one prime ideals is asymptotic to x/log x.

**How the definition helps.** A prime of degree above one with norm ≤ x lies over some p ≤ √x, and each p has at most n primes above it (our own). This gives at most n√x such primes (our own). Landau’s prime ideal theorem counts all prime ideals of norm ≤ x as about x/log x, so n√x is negligible (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Landau prime ideal theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Landau_prime_ideal_theorem). It says: “the prime ideal theorem is dominated by the ideals of norm a prime number.”

**Sources:**

- [Edmund Landau, Neuer Beweis des Primzahlsatzes und Beweis des Primidealsatzes (1903)](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF01444310)

### Principal primes have reciprocal class-number density

**Remember:** Principal means identity in the Hilbert class field.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11R44 (Distribution of prime ideals). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** The Hilbert class field H of a number field K is its largest abelian extension unramified at every place, with no repeated prime factors and real embeddings staying real. A prime ideal of K is principal exactly when it splits completely in H.

**Problem.** Among prime ideals of K, the proportion that are principal tends to 1/h. Count primes by residue field size, and let h count ideal classes, which identify ideals differing by a field scalar.

**How the definition helps.** Class field theory identifies Gal(H/K) with the class group, of size h, and sends a prime to its class. Chebotarev’s theorem gives the identity element density 1/h (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Hilbert class field](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilbert_class_field). It says: “Its degree over K equals the class number of K”

**Sources:**

- [N. Tschebotareff, Die Bestimmung der Dichtigkeit einer Menge von Primzahlen, welche zu einer gegebenen Substitutionsklasse gehören (1926)](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF01206606)

### Quarter turns let prime angles equidistribute

**Remember:** Take angles modulo the rotations made by units.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11R44 (Distribution of prime ideals). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** The angle of a prime ideal of ℤ\[i\] is the argument of any generator, taken modulo π/2, because the four generators differ by powers of i, which are quarter turns (our own).

**Problem.** Order these prime ideals by norm, the size of their residue field. The fraction with angle in any fixed subinterval of \[0,π/2) tends to the interval length divided by π/2.

**How the definition helps.** Taking angles modulo π/2 makes exp(4in·arg a) a well-defined character on ideals for each integer n. For n ≠ 0, Hecke’s prime ideal theorem makes its average over primes tend to zero (our own). Weyl’s criterion then gives the stated proportions (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Hecke character](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hecke_character). It says: “The only units are powers of i, so the factor of 4 in the exponent ensures that the character is well defined on ideals.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Real places preserve principal-prime density

**Remember:** The ordinary class field keeps real places real.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11R44 (Distribution of prime ideals). arXiv math.NT. Level 3: graduate.

**Definition.** The ordinary Hilbert class field is the largest abelian extension in which no finite prime ramifies and every real embedding stays real. The narrow class field drops the condition on real embeddings.

**Problem.** For K = ℚ(√3), all prime ideals split completely in its ordinary Hilbert class field. In its narrow class field, the proportion tends to one half when primes are ordered by residue field size.

**How the definition helps.** ℚ(√3) has class number one, so its ordinary Hilbert class field is K itself and every prime splits trivially.
