### Zeta roots bound Kloosterman sums

**Remember:** The first coefficient is the negative sum of the two reciprocal roots.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11L05 (Gauss and Kloosterman sums; generalizations). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** For a prime p and a, b ∈ 𝔽ₚˣ, let S(r) sum exp(2πi Tr(ax + b/x)/p) over x ≠ 0 in the field with pʳ elements, with Tr the trace to 𝔽ₚ. The L-function L(t) = exp(∑<sub>r≥1</sub> S(r)tʳ/r) packs all these sums into one series whose linear coefficient is S(1).

**Problem.** There are complex numbers α and β of absolute value √p such that L(t) = (1−αt)(1−βt). Consequently \|S(1)\| ≤ 2√p.

**How the definition helps.** Weil’s work on the curve yᵖ − y = ax + b/x gives L(t) = (1 − αt)(1 − βt) with \|α\| = \|β\| = √p. Comparing linear coefficients gives S(1) = −α − β (our own), and the triangle inequality gives \|S(1)\| ≤ 2√p.

**Wikipedia:** [Kloosterman sum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kloosterman_sum). It says: “A fundamental technique of Weil reduces the estimate \|K(a,b;p)\| ≤ 2√p, when ab ≠ 0 to his results on local zeta-functions.”

**Sources:**

- [André Weil, On Some Exponential Sums (1948)](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.34.5.204)

### Cube-free moduli ensure square-root bounds

**Remember:** A prime cube can support a sum larger than the square-root bound.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11L07 (Estimates on exponential sums). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** For a fixed k ≥ 3, call q cube-free if no prime cube divides it, so q is a product of distinct primes and prime squares. Take integer polynomials f of degree at most k whose nonconstant coefficients have no common factor with q.

**Problem.** For cube-free q, the complete sum of exp(2πif(x)/q) over x modulo q is O(q to the power ½+ε) for every ε &gt; 0. The constant depends on k and ε. At q = p³ with prime p &gt; 3, the phase x³ instead gives the sum p².

**How the definition helps.** Complete sums split over the prime power factors of q, and at primes and prime squares the standard estimates give square-root bounds (our own). Modulo p³, the units cancel class by class modulo p² by character orthogonality. Each of the p² multiples of p contributes one, giving p².

**Paper or page:** [Lᵖ maximal estimates for Weyl sums with k ≥ 3 on 𝕋](https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.15527v1). It says: “q₂ ≥ 1 is cube free,”

**Sources:**

- [Xuezhi Chen, Changxing Miao, Jiye Yuan, Tengfei Zhao, Lᵖ maximal estimates for Weyl sums with k ≥ 3 on 𝕋](https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.15527v1)

### One critical moment controls all

**Remember:** Below the critical moment use Hölder, and above it use the maximum.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11L07 (Estimates on exponential sums). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** For k, N ≥ 1, the moment M(p) is the integral over \[0,1\]ᵏ of \|F(α)\|ᵖ, with F(α) = ∑<sub>n≤N</sub> exp(2πi ∑ⱼ αⱼnʲ). At the critical order 2K, with K = k(k + 1)/2, the two predicted sizes Nˢ and N²ˢ⁻ᴷ of M(2s) coincide.

**Problem.** Suppose M(2K) ≤ Cε Nᴷ⁺ᵋ for every ε &gt; 0. Then M(2s) ≤ C Nᵐ⁺ᵋ for every fixed s &gt; 0 and ε &gt; 0, where m = max(s,2s−K). Constants may depend on k, ε and the chosen order.

**How the definition helps.** Below 2K, Hölder’s inequality on the unit cube bounds M(2s) by M(2K) raised to s/K (our own reduction). Above 2K, the bound \|F\| ≤ N gives M(2s) ≤ N²ˢ⁻²ᴷ M(2K). The deep mean value theorem supplies the critical estimate.

**Paper or page:** [Decoupling estimates in Fourier analysis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2207.00652v1). It says: “N<sup>1/2</sup> + N<sup>{1</sup> - \\frac{k(k+1)}{2p}}”

**Sources:**

- [Jean Bourgain, Ciprian Demeter and Larry Guth, Proof of the main conjecture in Vinogradov’s Mean Value Theorem for degrees higher than three (2016)](https://doi.org/10.4007/annals.2016.184.2.7)

### Reduced phases exclude constant counterexamples

**Remember:** Over the prime field, remove powers of p before using the degree.

*Rules out counterexamples. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11L07 (Estimates on exponential sums). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Over 𝔽ₚ, reduce a polynomial phase by replacing each positive degree divisible by p with that degree divided by p, repeating and combining equal powers. Since xᵖ = x on 𝔽ₚ, the values do not change, and every positive degree left is coprime to p.

**Problem.** If the reduced phase has degree d ≥ 1, the complete sum of exp(2πif(x)/p) has absolute value at most (d−1)√p. A nonconstant original phase need not qualify, since xᵖ−x gives sum p.

**How the definition helps.** Reduction keeps the values, so xᵖ − x reduces to zero and is excluded, although its sum is p (our own). Every nonconstant reduced phase has degree coprime to p, so Weil’s bound applies.

**Wikipedia:** [Fermat's little theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fermat%27s_little_theorem). It says: “aᵖ ≡ a (mod p).”

**Sources:**

- [André Weil, On Some Exponential Sums (1948)](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.34.5.204)

### Exceptional weights isolate prime obstructions

**Remember:** Characters can follow the primes, and everything else must cancel.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11L20 (Sums over primes), 11T23. arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Take a pure weight-zero middle-extension sheaf on the affine line over 𝔽ₚ whose geometric representation is a sum of copies of one irreducible. It is exceptional when that irreducible is geometrically a Kummer character sheaf times a linear Artin–Schreier sheaf, either possibly trivial, so its trace is a character product.

**Problem.** Let K be the trace function of a nonexceptional system and V a fixed smooth function supported in \[1/2, 2\]. For 0 &lt; η &lt; 1/24, the sum of K(l)V(l/p) over primes l is O(p raised to 1 − η), with constant depending on η, V and the conductor, which measures rank and ramification.

**How the definition helps.** The excluded functions are character products, which can correlate with primes: for the constant one and nonnegative nonzero V, the prime number theorem gives a sum of order p/log p (our own example). For the other systems, Fouvry, Kowalski and Michel prove the saving using estimates for sums in two variables.

**Wikipedia:** [Prime number theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prime_number_theorem). It says: “The first such distribution found is π(N) \~ N/log(N)”

**Sources:**

- [Fouvry, Kowalski and Michel, Algebraic trace functions over the primes](https://people.math.ethz.ch/~kowalski/weights-over-primes.pdf)

### Root power sums give multiplicative weights

**Remember:** Root power sums add when monic polynomials multiply.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11L20 (Sums over primes), 11T23. arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** For k ≥ 1 and a nontrivial additive character ψ of 𝔽𝓆, set χ(f) = ψ(∑ rᵏ) for monic f over 𝔽𝓆, summing the kth powers of all its roots with multiplicity. The sum lies in 𝔽𝓆 because Frobenius permutes the roots, and it adds when polynomials multiply, so χ is multiplicative.

**Problem.** Set Λ(Pʲ) = deg P for monic irreducible P and j ≥ 1, and set Λ(f) = 0 otherwise. For n ≥ 1, the sum of Λ(f)χ(f) over degree-n monic polynomials has modulus at most √(qⁿ) gcd(k,qⁿ − 1).

**How the definition helps.** The Λ-weighted sum over degree-n monic polynomials equals the sum of ψ(Tr(yᵏ)) over all y in the field with qⁿ elements (our own). Each y with minimal polynomial P of degree e contributes to Pⁿᐟᵉ, and the e conjugates of y match the weight Λ = e. Counting kth powers with multiplicative characters and the Gauss sum bound give the estimate.

**Paper or page:** [Equidistribution of high traces of random matrices over finite fields and cancellation in character sums of high conductor](https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.01344). It says: “\|∑ (f ∈ ℳₙ,𝓆) Λ(f)χₖ,ψ(f)\| ≤ qⁿᐟ² gcd(k, qⁿ − 1).”

**Sources:**

- [Equidistribution of high traces of random matrices over finite fields and cancellation in character sums of high conductor](https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.01344)

### Complex shifts generate derivative moments

**Remember:** Differentiate independent shifts to get both derivative factors.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11M06 (ζ (s) and L(s, χ)). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Fix a Dirichlet polynomial A, a nonnegative integrable weight w of compact support, B(t) = \|A(½ + it)\|²w(t), and 0 &lt; r &lt; ¼. The shifted moment J(z₁,z₂) = ∫ ζ(½ + it + z₁)ζ(½ − it + z₂)B(t) dt over ℝ gives each zeta factor its own shift.

**Problem.** The integral of \|ζ′(½+it)\|²B(t) over the real line equals the mixed derivative of J at (0,0), taken once in each shift. So it is at most r⁻² times the maximum of \|J\| on \|z₁\| = \|z₂\| = r.

**How the definition helps.** The mixed derivative differentiates each zeta factor once, and at zero the two derivatives are conjugate, giving \|ζ′\|² (our own). Compact support and distance from the pole justify differentiating under the integral. Cauchy’s formula on the circles \|z₁\| = \|z₂\| = r gives the bound.

**Paper or page:** [Upper bounds for fractional joint moments of the Riemann zeta function](https://arxiv.org/abs/2106.00165). It says: “F(z<sub>1</sub>,z<sub>2</sub>) = \\sum <sub>h,k \\leq T<sup>\\theta</sup> </sub> \\frac {a<sub>h</sub> \\overline {a<sub>k</sub>}}{\[h,k\]} \\frac {(h,k)<sup>z<sub>1</sub> + z<sub>2</sub></sup>}{h<sup>z<sub>1</sub></sup> k<sup>z<sub>2</sub></sup>},”

**Sources:**

- [Michael J. Curran, Upper bounds for fractional joint moments of the Riemann zeta function](https://arxiv.org/abs/2106.00165)

### Factoring poles regularizes reciprocal moments

**Remember:** Divide by a zeta power to cancel each prime term.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11M06 (ζ (s) and L(s, χ)). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** For k &gt; 0, let μₖ(n) be the Dirichlet coefficients of ζ(s)⁻ᵏ on Re s &gt; 1, using the branch positive for real s &gt; 1. The normalized square sum is ζ(s) raised to −k² times ∑ μₖ(n)²n⁻ˢ, for real s &gt; 1, which cancels the prime term k²p⁻ˢ of every Euler factor.

**Problem.** The resulting quotient tends to a positive finite limit as s decreases to 1. The original square sum is asymptotic to that limit times (s−1) to power −k².

**How the definition helps.** The series for (1 − z)ᵏ gives μₖ(p) = −k, so each normalized Euler factor is positive and equals 1 + O(p⁻²) uniformly for real s ≥ 1 (our own proof). The product therefore converges to a positive limit. The simple pole of ζ at 1 then gives the growth (s − 1) raised to −k².

**Paper or page:** [Negative moments of the Riemann zeta-function](https://arxiv.org/abs/2302.07226). It says: “where μₖ(n) denotes the nth Dirichlet coefficient of ζ(s)⁻ᵏ.”

**Sources:**

- [Hung M. Bui, Alexandra Florea, Negative moments of the Riemann zeta-function](https://arxiv.org/abs/2302.07226)

### Inverse log shifts cap kernels

**Remember:** Keep the height cutoff when two shifts nearly coincide.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11M06 (ζ (s) and L(s, χ)). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** For T ≥ 3 and real d, set K(T,d) = \|ζ(1 + 1/log T + id)\|. The shift 1/log T caps the pole of ζ at 1, so K stays of size about log T even when d is near zero (our own).

**Problem.** Fix θ &gt; −1 and 0 ≤ β ≤ 1, let \|h₁\|, \|h₂\| ≤ (log T) raised to θ, and set Y(t) = \|ζ(½ + i(t + h₁))ζ(½ + i(t + h₂))\|. The mean of Y raised to 2β over \[T, 2T\] lies between constant multiples of (K(T, h₁ − h₂) log T) raised to 2β².

**How the definition helps.** The displacement 1/log T gives one formula for all shifts, including equal ones, where ζ(1 + id) itself would have a pole (our own check). The cited theorem proves both bounds for large T, uniformly over the allowed shifts.

**Paper or page:** [Freezing transition and moments of moments of the Riemann zeta function](https://arxiv.org/abs/2301.10634). It says: “\\frac {1}{T}\\int \_T<sup>2T</sup> \|\\zeta (\\tfrac {1}{2} + i t + ih<sub>1</sub>)\\zeta (\\tfrac {1}{2} + i t + ih<sub>2</sub>)\|<sup>2\\b </sup> \~dt \\ll (\\log T)<sup>2\\b ^2</sup> \|\\zeta (1 + i (h<sub>1</sub> - h<sub>2</sub>) + 1/\\log T)\|<sup>2\\b ^2</sup>.”

**Sources:**

- [Michael J. Curran, Freezing transition and moments of moments of the Riemann zeta function](https://arxiv.org/abs/2301.10634)

### Matching parity folds central moments

**Remember:** Match the weight to the character’s gamma factor.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11M06 (ζ (s) and L(s, χ)). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** For a primitive nonprincipal Dirichlet character χ modulo q, take h = ¼ for even χ and h = ¾ for odd χ, so Γ(h + u/2) is the gamma factor of L(½ + u, χ). For x &gt; 0, W(x) is 1/(2πi) times the integral along Re u = 2 of Γ(h + u/2)² exp(−u log x)/(uΓ(h)²).

**Problem.** Let L(s,χ) be the continuation of ∑ χ(n) exp(−s log n) from Re s &gt; 1, and let χ̄ be the conjugate character. Then \|L(½,χ)\|² equals twice the sum of χ(a)χ̄(b)W(πab/q)/√(ab) over positive integers a, b.

**How the definition helps.** With matching gamma factors, the completed product is invariant under u ↦ −u by the functional equation (our own). Moving the contour past u = 0 picks up the residue \|L(½,χ)\|², and reflection shows the two remaining contributions are equal. Expanding the Dirichlet series gives the stated double sum.

**Paper or page:** [Bounds for moments of Dirichlet L-functions to a fixed modulus](https://arxiv.org/abs/2103.00149). It says: “\|L(\\tfrac {1}{2}, \\chi )\|<sup>2</sup> = 2 \\sum <sup>\\infty </sup><sub>a, b=1</sub> \\frac{\\chi (a) \\overline{\\chi }(b)}{\\sqrt{ab}} \\mathcal{W}\_{\\mathfrak {a}} \\left(\\frac{\\pi ab}{q}\\right),”

**Sources:**

- [Peng Gao, Bounds for moments of Dirichlet L-functions to a fixed modulus](https://arxiv.org/abs/2103.00149)

### Mellin weights turn logarithms into poles

**Remember:** A logarithmic power becomes a higher pole.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11M06 (ζ (s) and L(s, χ)), 44A15. arXiv math.NT, math.CA. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** For Re s &gt; 1, let Z(s) be the integral of \|ζ(½ + it)\|⁴ exp(−s log t) over 1 ≤ t &lt; ∞, the Mellin transform of the fourth moment. It turns each logarithmic power (log t)ʲ into a pole j!/(s − 1)ʲ⁺¹ at s = 1 (our own).

**Problem.** The function Z extends meromorphically to Re s &gt; 7/8, meaning it is holomorphic there except for poles. Its only pole there has order five at s = 1. The coefficient of (s−1)⁻⁵ is 12/π².

**How the definition helps.** Heath-Brown’s integrated fourth moment is T times a quartic in log T with leading coefficient 1/(2π²), plus an error O(T raised to 7/8 + ε). Integrating by parts, the leading term gives 4!/(2π²) = 12/π² times (s − 1)⁻⁵, while the error part is holomorphic for Re s &gt; 7/8.

**nLab:** [Mellin transform](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Mellin+transform). It says: “its Mellin transform is the function given by the integral expression”

**Sources:**

- [D. R. Heath-Brown, The Fourth Power Moment of the Riemann Zeta Function, Proc. London Math. Soc. 38 (1979), 385–422](https://doi.org/10.1112/plms/s3-38.3.385)

### One prime blocks exceptional conductors

**Remember:** Remove one prime to remove every multiple of the bad conductor.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11M06 (ζ (s) and L(s, χ)), 11N13. arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Fix Q ≥ 100 and a small absolute c &gt; 0. Call a Dirichlet character exceptional if its conductor is at most Q and its L-function has a real zero above 1 − c/log Q. Let B be the largest prime factor of the exceptional character's conductor, or B = 1 if there is none, so a modulus coprime to B is never a multiple of that conductor.

**Problem.** Take any q ≤ Q coprime to B. Every zero σ+it of every Dirichlet L-function modulo q satisfies 1−σ ≥ c′/log(Q(1+\|t\|)) for an absolute c′ &gt; 0.

**How the definition helps.** Landau–Page and the standard zero-free region leave at most one exceptional primitive character (our own). A modulus q coprime to B is not a multiple of its conductor, so no character modulo q is induced by it. Every other character keeps the standard region, since passing to an imprimitive character adds zeros only on Re s = 0.

**Paper or page:** [Recent results on large gaps between primes](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.07176v2). It says: “whenever L(σ + it, χ) = 0 and χ is a character of modulus at most Q”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Vandermonde contours handle colliding shifts

**Remember:** Keep the shifts inside the contour rather than in separate denominators.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11M06 (ζ (s) and L(s, χ)). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Integrate G(z)Δ(z)²/∏ᵣP(zᵣ) over j copies of a positively oriented circle Γ that encloses all k shifts αₘ, and divide by (2πi)ʲ. Here P(w) = ∏ₘ(w−αₘ), Δ(z) = ∏<sub>r&lt;s</sub>(zₛ−zᵣ) is the Vandermonde product, and G is holomorphic near the j-fold product of the closed disk. The denominator never vanishes on Γ, so the integral stays holomorphic when shifts collide inside.

**Problem.** For distinct shifts, the Vandermonde contour integral equals the sum of G(u)Δ(u)²/∏ᵣP′(uᵣ) over ordered j-tuples u of different shifts. So this sum extends holomorphically to shifts that meet inside Γ.

**How the definition helps.** On Γ the denominators stay nonzero, so the integral is holomorphic in the shifts even when they meet inside Γ. For distinct shifts, residues pick one root of P in each variable, and Δ² kills every tuple with a repeated root. So the integral equals the residue sum, and that sum extends.

**Paper or page:** [Averages of quadratic twists of long Dirichlet polynomials](https://arxiv.org/abs/2208.01783). It says: “\\frac{1}{(2\\pi i)<sup>j}</sup> \\int \_\\Gamma \\cdots \\int \_\\Gamma \\frac{G(z) \\Delta (z)<sup>2}{\\Delta</sup> (z;A)}\\,  d<sup>j</sup> z = \\sum \_{u<sub>1</sub>,...,u<sub>j</sub> \\in A \\atop \\textrm{distinct}} \\frac{G(u<sub>1</sub>,...,u<sub>j</sub>)}{\\Delta (u; A-u)},”

**Sources:**

- [Brian Conrey, Brad Rodgers, Averages of quadratic twists of long Dirichlet polynomials](https://arxiv.org/abs/2208.01783)

### Exponential weights quantify zero repulsion

**Remember:** A zero near one leaves less weight for the other zeros.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11M20 (Real zeros of L(s, χ); results on L(1, χ)). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Weight each zero β+iγ by exp(−323905(1−β)log Q), so a zero near one weighs almost one and a far zero almost nothing. The zeros are those of all primitive Dirichlet L-functions of conductor at most Q ≥ 10, with β ≥ ½ and \|γ\| ≤ Q, counted with multiplicity.

**Problem.** For some absolute λ₁ &gt; 0, at most one such zero satisfies (1−β)log Q &lt; λ₁. If present, this zero β₁ is real. The other weights then sum to at most C(1−β₁)log Q for an absolute C.

**How the definition helps.** The weights turn repulsion from an exceptional zero into one bound on the total weight of all other zeros. Proposition 6.5 bounds that total by a constant times one minus the exceptional zero's weight. Since 1−exp(−u) ≤ u for u ≥ 0, this is at most C(1−β₁)log Q (our own).

**Paper or page:** [An explicit version of Bombieri's log-free density estimate and Sárközy's theorem for shifted primes](https://arxiv.org/abs/2208.11123). It says: “If there is an exceptional zero ρ∗ at scale Q, then”

**Sources:**

- [Jesse Thorner, Asif Zaman, An explicit version of Bombieri's log-free density estimate and Sárközy's theorem for shifted primes](https://arxiv.org/abs/2208.11123)

### Random Euler products factor moments

**Remember:** Independent local signs turn each moment into a product over primes.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11M20 (Real zeros of L(s, χ); results on L(1, χ)). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Z is the random Euler product ∏ₚ 1/(1−X(p)/p), taken as a limit over primes in increasing order. The X(p) are independent and mimic a quadratic character at p: each sign ±1 has probability p/(2(p+1)), and zero has probability 1/(p+1).

**Problem.** Average L(1,χᴰ)ᵗ over fundamental discriminants D of one fixed sign with \|D\| ≤ Y, where χᴰ is the quadratic character of D. For each positive integer t, this average tends to the expectation of Zᵗ as Y grows.

**How the definition helps.** Independence turns the expectation of Zᵗ into a product over primes of local averages. Expanding each local factor, the odd powers of the sign cancel, which matches the prime factors in Corollary 6.13 (our own). The corollary gives the arithmetic average, and bounded moments of order 2t justify passing to the limit.

**Paper or page:** [Counting quadratic points on Fano varieties](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.17940). It says: “the set of positive, and ℱ₋ the set of negative fundamental discriminants.”

**Sources:**

- [Francesca Balestrieri, Kevin Destagnol, Julian Lyczak, Jennifer Park, Nick Rome, Counting quadratic points on Fano varieties](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.17940)

### Short Euler products approximate L-values

**Remember:** For most conductors, only small primes are needed at one.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11M20 (Real zeros of L(s, χ); results on L(1, χ)). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** The short Euler product P(y,χ) is the product of 1/(1−χ(p)/p) over primes p ≤ y, so it uses only the values of the quadratic character χ at small primes. For Q ≥ 3 and fixed α &gt; 2, take the cutoff y = exp(8α² log log Q), a power of log Q.

**Problem.** Consider the nonprincipal quadratic characters χ of conductor at most Q, each taken modulo its conductor. For all of them except those of at most exp((2/α) log Q) conductors, \|L(1,χ)/P(y,χ)−1\| ≤ C(α) exp(−α log log Q).

**How the definition helps.** Proposition 2.1 shows that L(1,χ) is close to its product over small primes for all but a few conductors. It bounds both the error and the number of exceptional conductors. In our own reading, the exceptions are conductors whose L-functions have zeros near one.

**Paper or page:** [Amicable pairs and aliquot cycles on average](https://arxiv.org/abs/1403.5810). It says: “not in ℰα(Q), then”

**Sources:**

- [A. Granville and K. Soundararajan, The distribution of values of L(1,χᴰ) (2003)](https://doi.org/10.1007/s00039-003-0438-3)

### Fourier cutoffs shorten prime sums

**Remember:** Compact frequency support cuts the prime sum off exactly.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11M26 (Nonreal zeros of ζ (s) and L(s, χ); Riemann and other hypotheses), 11N05. arXiv math.NT, math.CV. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Choose a real even smooth function φ, rapidly decreasing with all its derivatives, whose Fourier transform φ̂(u) = ∫ φ(v)exp(−2πiuv) dv vanishes for \|u\| &gt; A. This compact support makes the prime side of the explicit formula stop at prime powers n ≤ exp(A log T).

**Problem.** Assume the Riemann hypothesis, write the zeros as ½ + iγ with multiplicity, and let T ≤ t ≤ 2T. Then ∑ φ((γ − t) log T/(2π)) = φ̂(0) − 2D(t)/log T + O(1/log T), where D(t) sums (log p)φ̂(log n/log T) cos(t log n)/√n over prime powers n = pᵏ ≤ exp(A log T).

**How the definition helps.** The explicit formula equates the zero sum with a prime-power sum weighted by φ̂(log n/log T). This weight vanishes once log n &gt; A log T, so the prime sum is finite (our own). A Gaussian would leave terms at arbitrarily large prime powers (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Selberg's Central Limit Theorem weighted by Linear Statistics of Zeta Zeros](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.04150). It says: “Nφ(t) = φ̂(0) + Sφ(t) + O(1/log T)”

**Sources:**

- [Selberg's Central Limit Theorem weighted by Linear Statistics of Zeta Zeros](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.04150)

### Gaussian weights permit interpolation

**Remember:** A Gaussian factor tames every vertical line without a cutoff.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11M26 (Nonreal zeros of ζ (s) and L(s, χ); Riemann and other hypotheses). arXiv math.NT, math.CV. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Set H(s) = ((s−1)/s)exp(α(s/T)²)ζ(s)M(s), where M(s) = ∑<sub>n≤X</sub> μ(n)n⁻ˢ uses the Möbius function μ, with α,T &gt; 0 and X &gt; 1. The factor s−1 removes the pole of ζ at one, and the Gaussian factor makes H decay along every vertical line (our own).

**Problem.** Let B(σ) be the integral of \|H(σ + it)\|² over all real t. Then log B is a convex function of σ on \[½, ∞).

**How the definition helps.** The Gaussian factor makes every B(σ) finite without cutting the integral off at height T (our own). Fourier transformation in t turns horizontal shifts into multiplication by real exponentials (our own). Plancherel's identity and Hölder's inequality then give convexity of log B (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Explicit zero density for the Riemann zeta function](https://arxiv.org/abs/2101.12263), [Explicit zero density for the Riemann zeta function](https://arxiv.org/abs/2101.12263). It says: “g(s) = ((s − 1)/s) exp(α(s/T)²).”

**Sources:**

- [H. Kadiri, A. Lumley, and N. Ng, Explicit zero density for the Riemann zeta function](https://arxiv.org/abs/2101.12263)

### Li’s variable circles critical zeros

**Remember:** The critical line becomes the unit circle; stray zeros fall inside.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11M26 (Nonreal zeros of ζ (s) and L(s, χ); Riemann and other hypotheses). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Li's variable z = 1 − 1/s sends the critical line Re s = ½ to the unit circle, and the half-plane Re s &gt; ½ into the open unit disk (our own). Set φ(z) = ξ(1/(1−z)), where ξ is the entire completed zeta function whose zeros are the nontrivial zeta zeros, and expand φ′/φ in a Taylor series at zero.

**Problem.** The Riemann hypothesis holds exactly when this Taylor series has radius of convergence at least 1.

**How the definition helps.** Each zero ρ gives a pole of φ′/φ at 1 − 1/ρ, which lies inside the unit disk exactly when Re ρ &gt; ½ (our own). The functional equation pairs ρ with 1 − ρ, so a zero off the line always has a partner with Re ρ &gt; ½ (our own). So the radius is below 1 exactly when the Riemann hypothesis fails (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Li's criterion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Li%27s_criterion). It says: “Hence, φ′(z)/φ(z) is holomorphic on the unit disk \|z\| &lt; 1”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Minimization gives the prime error scale

**Remember:** Minimize over height to find the scale of the error.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11M26 (Nonreal zeros of ζ (s) and L(s, χ); Riemann and other hypotheses), 11N05. arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Given a zero-free region σ &gt; 1 − η(\|t\|), with η continuous and decreasing from \[0,∞) into (0,½\], define ω(x) as the infimum over t ≥ 1 of η(t) log x + log t. It balances the saving from a zero's distance to the line σ = 1 against the loss from its height t (our own).

**Problem.** Suppose ζ has no zeros with σ &gt; 1 − η(\|t\|), and let ψ(x) sum log p over prime powers up to x. Then for every ε &gt; 0, ψ(x) − x = O(x exp(−(1 − ε)ω(x))), with the constant depending on ε and η.

**How the definition helps.** A zero near the boundary at height t contributes about x exp(−(η(t) log x + log t)) to ψ(x) − x, so the worst zero costs about x exp(−ω(x)) (our own). Pintz's theorem makes this rigorous at the cost of ε.

**Paper or page:** [On the connection between zero-free regions and the error term in the Prime Number Theorem](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.13780). It says: “Then for every ε &gt; 0, ψ(x) − x ≪ε x exp(−(1 − ε)ω(x)).”

**Sources:**

- [J. Pintz, On the remainder term of the prime number formula II. On a theorem of Ingham (1980)](https://doi.org/10.4064/aa-37-1-209-220)

### Squared sinc bounds multiplicities

**Remember:** Majorize coincidence with a weight whose frequencies are controlled.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11M26 (Nonreal zeros of ζ (s) and L(s, χ); Riemann and other hypotheses). arXiv math.NT, math.CV. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Weight each pair of zero heights by r(u) = (sin(πu)/(πu))², where u is their difference in units of 2π/log T, and r(0) = 1. This weight is at least one at equal heights, never negative, and its Fourier transform vanishes outside \[−1,1\] (our own), where Montgomery's pair correlation formula is known.

**Problem.** Assume the Riemann hypothesis, and let P(T) be the proportion of zeros with heights in (0,T\] that are simple, counting every zero with multiplicity. Then lim inf P(T) ≥ ⅔ as T tends to infinity.

**How the definition helps.** Montgomery's formula applied to this weight bounds the ordered pairs of equal heights by (4/3+o(1)) times the zero count. A zero of multiplicity m gives m² such pairs, and m² ≥ 2m for m ≥ 2. So repeated zeros account for at most a third asymptotically.

**Wikipedia:** [Montgomery's pair correlation conjecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montgomery%27s_pair_correlation_conjecture). It says: “proved under the Riemann hypothesis, that for \|α\| ≤ 1 this function converges uniformly”

**Sources:**

- [H. L. Montgomery, The Pair Correlation of Zeros of the Zeta Function (1973)](https://public.websites.umich.edu/~hlm/paircor1.pdf)

### Coproduct stabilizers give double shuffle groups

**Remember:** Symmetries of one coproduct compose and invert.

*True by definition.* MSC 11M32 (Multiple Dirichlet series and zeta functions and multizeta values). arXiv math.QA, math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** The stabilizer of the harmonic coproduct Δ is the set of g in 𝒢 with (g ⊗ g)Δ = Δg, for the corrected Ihara action on the harmonic module. These are the symmetries that preserve Δ, so they are closed under composition and inverses.

**Problem.** The normalized double shuffle solutions with parameter zero form a group under Ihara multiplication.

**How the definition helps.** The identification theorem shows that the normalized solutions with parameter zero are exactly 𝒢 intersected with this stabilizer. A stabilizer is closed under composition and inversion, and so is the subgroup 𝒢 (our own). Their intersection is therefore a group under Ihara multiplication.

**Paper or page:** [Double shuffle Lie algebra and special derivations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.02265v1). It says: “DMR₀(k) = Stab(Δ̂ᴹ,ᴰᴿ)(k) ∩ 𝒢”

**Sources:**

- [Double shuffle Lie algebra and special derivations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.02265v1)

### Counting threes lowers coaction level

**Remember:** Weight parity equals the parity of the number of threes.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11M32 (Multiple Dirichlet series and zeta functions and multizeta values). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Write motivic multiple zeta values with indices 2 and 3 as words, encoding 2 as 10 and 3 as 100, and let the level be the number of 3s. Fₗ is the ℚ-span of such values of level at most l, with F₋₁ = 0, and Dₘ is the infinitesimal coaction that cuts out m letters. Since the weight is twice the number of indices plus the number of 3s, the weight's parity is the parity of the number of 3s.

**Problem.** For odd m ≥ 3, Dₘ sends Fₗ into tensors whose second factors belong to Fₗ₋₁.

**How the definition helps.** An odd cut changes the parity of the weight, so it changes the parity of the number of 3s (our own). The cut formula shows that surviving words still use only the two blocks and have no more 3s than before. So the number of 3s drops by at least one.

**Paper or page:** [AGZT-Lectures on formal multiple zeta values](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.13630v1). It says: “For all ℓ,r ∈ ℕ we have D₂ᵣ₊₁(Fℓ ℬ₂,₃) ⊆ ℒ₂ᵣ₊₁ ⊗ Fℓ₋₁ ℬ₂,₃.”

**Sources:**

- [Francis Brown, Mixed Tate motives over ℤ, Annals of Mathematics 175 (2012), 949–976](https://annals.math.princeton.edu/2012/175-2/p10)
- [AGZT-Lectures on formal multiple zeta values](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.13630v1)

### Cyclotomic words give Fibonacci dimensions

**Remember:** One letter per weight from two, plus 2πi powers, gives Fibonacci.

*True by definition.* MSC 11M32 (Multiple Dirichlet series and zeta functions and multizeta values), 11G55. arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Deligne's word model for motivic iterated integrals on 0, 1 and a primitive sixth root of unity has a basis of pairs: a word and a power of the weight-one generator for 2πi. There is one letter of each integer weight ≥ 2, and weights add.

**Problem.** The dimension of these integrals in weight n is 1 for n = 0 and n = 1. Each later dimension is the sum of the previous two.

**How the definition helps.** Deligne's basis theorem makes each dimension a count of these pairs. The letters give t²/(1−t), so words give (1−t)/(1−t−t²), and the 2πi powers multiply this by 1/(1−t) (our own). The result 1/(1−t−t²) is the Fibonacci generating function.

**Paper or page:** [The Galois coaction on φ⁴ periods](https://arxiv.org/abs/1603.04289v2), [The Galois coaction on φ⁴ periods](https://arxiv.org/abs/1603.04289v2). It says: “If N ∈ {2, 6} then d₍N,n₎ is the Fibonacci sequence”

**Sources:**

- [Pierre Deligne, Le groupe fondamental unipotent motivique de 𝔾ₘ − μₙ, pour N = 2, 3, 4, 6 ou 8](https://doi.org/10.1007/s10240-010-0027-6)
- [Erik Panzer and Oliver Schnetz, The Galois coaction on φ⁴ periods](https://doi.org/10.4310/cntp.2017.v11.n3.a3)

### Depth quotients expose parity vanishing

**Remember:** Opposite weight and depth parity leaves only products and shallower terms.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11M32 (Multiple Dirichlet series and zeta functions and multizeta values). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Fix weight w and depth r ≥ 2, where depth is the number of exponents and weight is their sum. In the span of values of weight w and depth at most r, work modulo polynomials in multiple zeta values of depth below r. So a value is zero in this quotient exactly when it reduces to such a polynomial.

**Problem.** A convergent multiple zeta value of weight w and depth r ≥ 2 represents zero in this quotient whenever w + r is odd.

**How the definition helps.** Vanishing in the quotient says exactly that the value is a polynomial in shallower values. The parity theorem gives this reduction when w + r is odd, and each term it produces lies in the part divided out (our own).

**Paper or page:** [The Galois coaction on φ⁴ periods](https://arxiv.org/abs/1603.04289v2). It says: “if $n<sub>d</sub>+\\ldots+n<sub>1</sub>+d$ is odd.”

**Sources:**

- [Erik Panzer, The parity theorem for multiple polylogarithms](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.jnt.2016.08.004)

### Double shuffle coordinates are polynomial

**Remember:** Solutions form a line times a group, which is affine space.

*True by definition.* MSC 11M32 (Multiple Dirichlet series and zeta functions and multizeta values). arXiv math.NT, math.QA. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** The formal multiple zeta algebra is the rational shuffle algebra of words modulo normalization and the regularized double shuffle relations. It is the coordinate ring of the scheme of normalized double shuffle solutions, whose parameter λ is ζᶠ(2). So it is polynomial exactly when that scheme is an affine space.

**Problem.** The formal multiple zeta algebra over ℚ is a polynomial algebra, without assuming completeness of the relations for numerical values.

**How the definition helps.** Racinet's torsor theorem and one polynomial family of solutions identify the scheme with the parameter line times the parameter-zero group. The graded exponential identifies this prounipotent group with its Lie algebra, an affine space (our own). So the coordinate ring is polynomial.

**Paper or page:** [AGZT-Lectures on formal multiple zeta values](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.13630v1). It says: “The algebra 𝒵ᶠ of formal multiple zeta values is a free polynomial algebra.”

**Sources:**

- [Georges Racinet, Doubles mélanges des polylogarithmes multiples aux racines de l’unité](https://doi.org/10.1007/s102400200004)
- [AGZT-Lectures on formal multiple zeta values](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.13630v1)

### Endpoint labels prevent forest integral divergence

**Remember:** Start every total order with label one and end it with zero.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11M32 (Multiple Dirichlet series and zeta functions and multizeta values). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Order the vertices of a nonempty finite rooted forest with each root above its descendants, and label every minimal vertex 1, every maximal vertex 0, and the others 0 or 1. Integrate over times in (0,1) that increase along this order, using dt/(1−t) at a 1 and dt/t at a 0. Then every total order compatible with the forest starts with 1 and ends with 0, the convergence condition for words.

**Problem.** The resulting integral converges and is a finite sum of ordinary multiple zeta values, counted with multiplicity.

**How the definition helps.** Sorting the times splits the domain, up to measure zero, into regions indexed by the compatible total orders (our own). Each order starts with 1 and ends with 0, so its word integral is a convergent multiple zeta value. Without the labels, a chain ending in two 1s at the upper endpoint would diverge.

**Paper or page:** [Generalisations of multiple zeta values to rooted forests](https://arxiv.org/abs/2202.00611v4). It says: “The flattening map fl maps convergent forests to convergent words”

**Sources:**

- [Generalisations of multiple zeta values to rooted forests](https://arxiv.org/abs/2202.00611v4)

### First-letter deletion isolates the kernel

**Remember:** Only a word with no small first letter escapes every deletion.

*True by definition.* MSC 11M32 (Multiple Dirichlet series and zeta functions and multizeta values). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Brown's word model uses words in odd letters f₃, f₅, … (fᵣ has weight r) times powers of a commuting weight-two variable f₂. For odd r ≥ 3, deletion removes a first letter fᵣ, keeps the f₂ power, and gives zero for any other first letter. At weight N, only f<sub>N</sub> for odd N, or the pure power of f₂ for even N, has no first letter of weight below N.

**Problem.** At weight N ≥ 2, the operators for odd letters of weight below N have a one-dimensional common kernel. The single motivic zeta value ζᵐ(N) spans it.

**How the definition helps.** Deletion of fᵣ is injective on words starting with fᵣ, so coefficients cannot cancel and a kernel element uses only words that no deletion detects (our own). At weight N the only such word is the one named in the definition. Identifying the motivic coaction with this model sends ζᵐ(N) to a multiple of it.

**Paper or page:** [AGZT-Lectures on formal multiple zeta values](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.13630v1). It says: “\\ker(D<sub>&lt;N</sub>) \\cap \\mathcal{U}<sup>\\mathsf{f}<sub>N</sub></sup> = \\mathbb{Q} \\,s<sub>N</sub>.”

**Sources:**

- [Francis Brown, Mixed Tate motives over ℤ, Annals of Mathematics 175 (2012), 949–976](https://annals.math.princeton.edu/2012/175-2/p10)

### Formal zeta symbols parametrize solutions

**Remember:** An algebra with exactly the relations, so its maps are solutions.

*True by definition.* MSC 11M32 (Multiple Dirichlet series and zeta functions and multizeta values). arXiv math.NT, math.QA. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Take the rational shuffle algebra on two letters, whose product sums all order-preserving interleavings, and divide by the one-letter words and the regularized double shuffle relations. The formal zeta symbol ζᶠ(w) is the class of a word w, so the quotient satisfies exactly these relations and no others.

**Problem.** For every commutative ℚ-algebra R, maps of ℚ-algebras into R from this quotient correspond to normalized double shuffle solutions over R. Imposing ζᶠ(2) = λ selects the solutions with parameter λ.

**How the definition helps.** An algebra map from the quotient to R is a shuffle evaluation that kills the regularized relations, which is what a normalized solution is (our own). Racinet's comparison with the series conditions, including the corrected stuffle series, makes this precise. The numerical algebra is a further quotient, not known to equal this one.

**Paper or page:** [AGZT-Lectures on formal multiple zeta values](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.13630v1). It says: “the algebra 𝒵ᶠ of formal multiple zeta values.”

**Sources:**

- [Georges Racinet, Doubles mélanges des polylogarithmes multiples aux racines de l’unité](https://doi.org/10.1007/s102400200004)
- [AGZT-Lectures on formal multiple zeta values](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.13630v1)

### Missing barred ones kill weight-one cuts

**Remember:** Without a barred one, no nonzero weight-one cut survives.

*True by definition.* MSC 11M32 (Multiple Dirichlet series and zeta functions and multizeta values). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Write an Euler index as exponents mᵢ with signs εᵢ ∈ {−1,1}, in increasing summation order, and its integral word as blocks εᵢ⋯εᵣ each followed by mᵢ−1 zeros. A barred one is a position with mᵢ = 1 and εᵢ = −1. It is exactly a place where two adjacent sign letters, or the last sign and the endpoint 1, are opposite.

**Problem.** Let D₁ sum the one-letter cuts of the word, recording each cut separately from its remainder. For convergent motivic Euler sums without a barred 1, D₁ gives zero.

**How the definition helps.** A one-letter cut survives only between adjacent opposite nonzero letters, counting the final endpoint 1 (our own). Adjacent sign letters need mᵢ = 1, and their ratio is εᵢ. So a surviving cut needs a barred one.

**Paper or page:** [On Some Unramified Families of Motivic Euler Sums](https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.06925v3). It says: “If 1̅ does not appear in s then D₁ζₐᵐ(s) = 0”

**Sources:**

- [On Some Unramified Families of Motivic Euler Sums](https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.06925v3)

### Odd single zeta values have a two-term coaction

**Remember:** One letter 1 leaves no nontrivial proper coaction term.

*True by definition.* MSC 11M32 (Multiple Dirichlet series and zeta functions and multizeta values). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Write ζᶠ(k) as the word 1 followed by k−1 zeros, between endpoints 0 and 1. The coaction sums over the subwords kept on the right, putting each cut-out block on the left after the projection a that sets ζᶠ(2) to zero. Every nonempty proper cut-out block is either all zeros or starts at the 1 with both endpoints 0.

**Problem.** For odd k ≥ 3, Δζᶠ(k) = a(ζᶠ(k)) ⊗ 1 + 1 ⊗ ζᶠ(k).

**How the definition helps.** Each nonempty proper cut gives zero, so only the two extreme terms remain (our own). A block of only zeros vanishes by regularization, and a block that starts at the 1 has both endpoints 0, so its integral vanishes too.

**Paper or page:** [AGZT-Lectures on formal multiple zeta values](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.13630v1). It says: “ΔGon(ζᶠ(2n+1)) = a(ζᶠ(2n+1)) ⊗ 1 + 1 ⊗ ζᶠ(2n+1).”

**Sources:**

- [AGZT-Lectures on formal multiple zeta values](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.13630v1)

### Parity alphabets locate ordinary zeta values

**Remember:** With the parity basis, ordinary zeta values occupy the odd-letter words.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11M32 (Multiple Dirichlet series and zeta functions and multizeta values), 11G55. arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** At level N, the parity basis takes conjugation eigencomponents of Deligne's generators of cyclotomic motivic iterated integrals, real or purely imaginary as the weight prescribes. Its f-alphabet writes every motivic value in word coordinates, so membership in a subalgebra becomes a test on which letters appear.

**Problem.** For N equal to 2, 3, 4 or 6, the ordinary motivic multiple zeta values use only the letters of odd weight at least three. Their algebra is exactly the rational span of these words multiplied by even powers of 2πi.

**How the definition helps.** The parity basis makes membership in the ordinary algebra, generated by the letters 0 and 1, a test on words. Panzer and Schnetz prove that the parity coordinates respect conjugation and identify that algebra with the stated words. In our own reading, this comparison theorem excludes all the other letters.

**Paper or page:** [The Galois coaction on φ⁴ periods](https://arxiv.org/abs/1603.04289v2), [The Galois coaction on φ⁴ periods](https://arxiv.org/abs/1603.04289v2). It says: “be the sub-algebra of words in letters of odd weights ≥ 3 times even powers of 2πi.”

**Sources:**

- [Erik Panzer and Oliver Schnetz, The Galois coaction on φ⁴ periods](https://doi.org/10.4310/cntp.2017.v11.n3.a3)

### Path reversal gives zeta duality

**Remember:** Read the path backward and swap the two endpoints.

*True by definition.* MSC 11M32 (Multiple Dirichlet series and zeta functions and multizeta values). arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Encode a convergent iterated integral from 0 to 1 as a word, innermost form first, with 0 for dt/t and 1 for dt/(1−t); convergence means it starts with 1 and ends with 0. Its dual reverses the word and swaps 0 with 1, which is what the substitution t ↦ 1 − t does to the path.

**Problem.** A convergent word and its dual give the same motivic multiple zeta value.

**How the definition helps.** Substituting t ↦ 1 − t swaps the two forms and runs the path backward, so a word and its dual have the same integral (our own). Each step gives one minus sign per letter, and the signs cancel. Brown's motivic integral identities justify both steps before numerical evaluation.

**nLab:** [iterated integral](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/iterated+integral). It says: “Iterated integrals include nested integration of differential forms of the kind as it appears in the formulation of parallel transport”

**Sources:**

- [Francis Brown, Mixed Tate motives over ℤ (2012)](https://annals.math.princeton.edu/2012/175-2/p10)

### Projected coactions give derivations

**Remember:** Keep one positive-weight factor and discard products of two.

*True by definition.* MSC 11M32 (Multiple Dirichlet series and zeta functions and multizeta values). arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Take Brown's coaction Δ on motivic multiple zeta values and keep only the terms whose left factor has weight r &gt; 0. Then discard every left factor that is a product of two positive-weight elements.

**Problem.** The projected map satisfies the product rule D(uv) = (1 ⊗ u)D(v) + (1 ⊗ v)D(u).

**How the definition helps.** In Δ(u)Δ(v), every term whose left factor is a product of two positive-weight parts is discarded (our own). What survives pairs a weight-r part of one factor with the weight-zero part 1 ⊗ u or 1 ⊗ v of the other. Since Brown's coaction is multiplicative, this leaves exactly the two terms of the product rule.

**Paper or page:** [AGZT-Lectures on formal multiple zeta values](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.13630). It says: “is a derivation with respect to ∗”

**Sources:**

- [Francis Brown, Mixed Tate motives over ℤ (2012)](https://annals.math.princeton.edu/2012/175-2/p10)

### Projection removes single-valued period products

**Remember:** Project first and products drop out of the relation.

*True by definition.* MSC 11M32 (Multiple Dirichlet series and zeta functions and multizeta values), 33B30. arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** On weight n &gt; 0 of the graded de Rham Hopf algebra, the clean projector sends x to (1/n)∑ S(x₁)Y(x₂), where Δx = ∑ x₁ ⊗ x₂, S is the antipode and Y multiplies by weight. It kills every product of positive-weight elements, and clean single-valued evaluation applies it first (our own).

**Problem.** If a rational linear combination of motivic multiple polylogarithms equals a sum of products of positive weights, its clean single-valued combination vanishes.

**How the definition helps.** Clean evaluation projects before evaluating, so the product side of the identity contributes zero (our own). The projector kills products because Y satisfies the product rule and S cancels the coproduct in positive weight (our own). Ordinary single-valued evaluation can retain such products (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Clean Single-Valued Polylogarithms](https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.04344). It says: “for every linear combination of motivic MPL’s that can be reduced to products,”

**Sources:**

- [Steven Charlton, Claude Duhr and Herbert Gangl, Clean Single-Valued Polylogarithms (2021)](https://doi.org/10.3842/sigma.2021.107)

### Regularizing divergent Hurwitz-type multiple zeta values lets their two products be compared

**Remember:** Keep the divergent part as a variable, then compare the polynomials.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11M32 (Multiple Dirichlet series and zeta functions and multizeta values), 11M35. arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** A regularization extends convergent μ-multiple Hurwitz zeta values to all indices as polynomials in a variable T, sending the divergent weight-one index, normalized by a fixed base shift, to T. The stuffle version is an algebra map for the stuffle product, and the shuffle version respects the shuffle product of integral words.

**Problem.** An explicit linear map on polynomials in T converts stuffle regularization into shuffle regularization for each μ-multiple Hurwitz zeta index. With both base shifts equal to one, the comparison formula is independent of μ.

**How the definition helps.** Both regularizations take values in polynomials in T, so one linear map can compare them even for divergent indices (our own). Corollary 4.29 computes the map. With both base shifts equal to one, its shift corrections vanish.

**Paper or page:** [Regularized double shuffle relations of μ-multiple Hurwitz zeta values](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.11689v1). It says: “Our main goal is to prove the comparison theorem relating the two ways of regularization, which is an analog of Ihara, Kaneko, and Zagier's celebrated result concerning the regularization of multiple zeta values.”

**Sources:**

- [Jia Li, Jianqiang Zhao, Regularized double shuffle relations of μ-multiple Hurwitz zeta values, arXiv:2402.11689v1 (2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.11689v1)

### Separate regularizations avoid incompatible values

**Remember:** The two products need different values for the first divergent pair.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11M32 (Multiple Dirichlet series and zeta functions and multizeta values). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** A regularization is a ℚ-algebra map into real polynomials in T that extends convergent zeta evaluation and sends the divergent index (1) to T. Shuffle and stuffle each get their own: shuffle interleaves integral words, while stuffle interleaves index entries and may also merge pairs by addition.

**Problem.** Both extensions exist uniquely. They give T²/2 and (T² − ζ(2))/2 respectively for the index (1,1), so one extension cannot preserve both products.

**How the definition helps.** Separate extensions let the two products give different values to (1,1). Shuffling (1) with itself gives two copies of (1,1), while stuffling also adds the index (2), whose value ζ(2) is nonzero (our own). Existence and uniqueness use the polynomial description of each algebra over its convergent part.

**Paper or page:** [AGZT-Lectures on formal multiple zeta values](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.13630v1). It says: “Let T be a commutative variable and extend the stuffle product ∗ by ℚ\[T\]-linearity”

**Sources:**

- [K. Ihara, M. Kaneko and D. Zagier, Derivation and double shuffle relations for multiple zeta values](https://doi.org/10.1112/s0010437x0500182x)

### Stable ideals preserve the coaction

**Remember:** Impose only period relations that remain relations under the coaction.

*True by definition.* MSC 11M32 (Multiple Dirichlet series and zeta functions and multizeta values). arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Call a graded ideal I of the two-letter shuffle algebra stable if all its elements have numerical period zero, under tangentially regularized integration, and the motivic coaction sends I into A ⊗ I, where A is the coacting algebra. Divide by the sum of all stable ideals, so every imposed relation is true numerically and survives the coaction.

**Problem.** The quotient carries both the coaction and the map to numerical periods.

**How the definition helps.** Because Δ(I) ⊆ A ⊗ I, the coaction passes to the quotient, and because I lies in the kernel of the period map, so does evaluation (our own). A sum of stable ideals is stable, so a largest one exists. Brown constructs the coaction before imposing these relations.

**nLab:** [motivic multiple zeta values](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/motivic+multiple+zeta+values). It says: “The intricate combinatorics of these becomes often more tractable when re-expressing them as motivic multiple zeta values”

**Sources:**

- [Francis Brown, Mixed Tate motives over ℤ (2012)](https://annals.math.princeton.edu/2012/175-2/p10)
- [Pierre Deligne and Alexander Goncharov, Groupes fondamentaux motiviques de Tate mixte (2005)](https://numdam.org/articles/10.1016/j.ansens.2004.11.001/)

### Symmetric zeta sums lose their parameter

**Remember:** Reversal makes the common regularization shift cancel.

*True by definition. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11M32 (Multiple Dirichlet series and zeta functions and multizeta values). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Let Z(w;t) be the harmonic regularization of a descending multiple zeta index w, with Z((1);t) = t and Z(∅;t) = 1. Over every split w = uv, including empty parts, add up (−1) raised to the weight of u, times Z(reverse(u);T+πi/2), times Z(v;T−πi/2). The signed reversed prefix acts as an inverse, so a common shift of T cancels at the join.

**Problem.** This signed sum is independent of T.

**How the definition helps.** Shifting T by h multiplies the regularized word series on the left by exp(hy), where y stands for the index one. Signed reversal moves this factor to the right with the opposite sign in the exponent, so the two factors cancel (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Supercongruences of multiple harmonic q-sums and generalized finite/symmetric multiple zeta values](https://arxiv.org/abs/2012.07067v2). It says: “does not depend on T”

**Sources:**

- [Supercongruences of multiple harmonic q-sums and generalized finite/symmetric multiple zeta values](https://arxiv.org/abs/2012.07067v2)

### Top-depth stuffle becomes shuffle

**Remember:** At greatest depth, no letters have merged.

*True by definition.* MSC 11M32 (Multiple Dirichlet series and zeta functions and multizeta values). arXiv math.NT, math.QA. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Filter words in positive integers by length, and keep only the full-length terms of the stuffle product. Stuffle interleaves two words and may also merge paired letters by addition, and each merge shortens the result by one letter.

**Problem.** The associated graded algebra of the stuffle word algebra for this filtration is the shuffle algebra on the same alphabet.

**How the definition helps.** Only merge-free interleavings have length equal to the sum of the input lengths (our own). So the graded product is exactly the shuffle product. The cited theorem treats a larger alphabet whose positive-index letters give this product.

**Paper or page:** [An extension of the linearized double shuffle Lie algebra](https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.05024v1). It says: “grᴅ ∘ ∗ᵦ = ⧢”

**Sources:**

- [An extension of the linearized double shuffle Lie algebra](https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.05024v1)

### Word weights count motivic dimensions

**Remember:** Odd letters form arbitrary words, and the even variable contributes its own powers.

*True by definition.* MSC 11M32 (Multiple Dirichlet series and zeta functions and multizeta values). arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** In Brown's model, motivic multiple zeta values of weight n have a basis of words in letters of odd weight 3, 5, 7, …, times powers of an independent weight-two variable. Weight is the sum of the letter weights, and the empty word counts.

**Problem.** The series whose coefficient of tⁿ counts the dimension in weight n equals 1 ∕ (1 − t² − t³).

**How the definition helps.** The dimension is the number of basis elements in weight n (our own). One letter gives L = t³/(1−t²), so all words give 1/(1−L), and the weight-two powers give 1/(1−t²). The product is 1/(1−t²−t³).

**nLab:** [motivic multiple zeta values](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/motivic+multiple+zeta+values). It says: “The intricate combinatorics of these becomes often more tractable when re-expressing them as motivic multiple zeta values”

**Sources:**

- [Francis Brown, Mixed Tate motives over ℤ (2012)](https://annals.math.princeton.edu/2012/175-2/p10)

### Selberg factors telescope to Ruelle

**Remember:** A shift by one cancels every geodesic factor except the first.

*True by definition.* MSC 11M36 (Selberg zeta functions and regularized determinants; applications to spectral theory, Dirichlet series, Eisenstein series, etc. (explicit formulas)). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** On a closed oriented hyperbolic surface, Selberg's Z(s) is the product of 1−exp(−(s+n)ℓ) over integers n ≥ 0 and lengths ℓ of primitive oriented closed geodesics, each geodesic counted once. The Ruelle product R(s) keeps only the n = 0 factors, which are exactly what Z(s)/Z(s+1) leaves (our own).

**Problem.** The Ruelle product is Z(s)/Z(s+1) for Re s &gt; 1 and extends meromorphically by that quotient.

**How the definition helps.** Dividing Z(s) by Z(s+1) cancels every factor with n ≥ 1, and absolute convergence justifies this for Re s &gt; 1 (our own). Selberg's continuation of Z then continues R through the quotient (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Selberg zeta function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Selberg_zeta_function). It says: “where p runs over conjugacy classes of prime geodesics (equivalently, conjugacy classes of primitive hyperbolic elements of Γ)”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Finite-field cancellation truncates Goss values

**Remember:** Summing over each free coefficient kills high-degree terms at negative integers.

*True by definition. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11M38 (Zeta and L-functions in characteristic p). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** For polynomials over the field with q elements, the Goss zeta value at −k is a sum over degrees d. Its degree-d term sums the kth powers of all monic polynomials of degree d, which runs independently over d free coefficients in the field.

**Problem.** For k ≥ 1, only degrees at most k/(q−1) contribute to the Goss zeta value at −k.

**How the definition helps.** Over the field with q elements, the sum of cᵉ is zero unless e is a positive multiple of q−1 (our own). So each of the d free coefficients needs exponent at least q−1, and a surviving term needs d(q−1) ≤ k. Goss's continuation theorem identifies this finite sum with the zeta value.

**Wikipedia:** [Goss zeta function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Goss_zeta_function). It says: “is an analogue of the Riemann zeta function for function fields.”

**Sources:**

- [Jeffrey T. Sheats, The Riemann Hypothesis for the Goss Zeta Function for 𝔽q\[T\] (1998)](https://doi.org/10.1006/jnth.1998.2232)

### Conductor survives gamma regrouping

**Remember:** The conductor keeps the linear term of the gamma growth.

*True by definition.* MSC 11M41 (Other Dirichlet series and zeta functions). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** For F in the Selberg class with completing factor γ(s) = Qˢ∏Γ(λs+μ), where Q &gt; 0 and all slopes λ &gt; 0, put d = 2∑λ. The conductor is q = (2π)ᵈQ² times the product of exp(2λ log λ), which depends only on d and on log Q + ∑λ log λ, the two growth rates of log\|γ(x)\| (our own).

**Problem.** The conductor of F has the same value for every allowed completion. The exponential base Q alone can change when a gamma factor splits into several factors.

**How the definition helps.** Stirling's formula gives log\|γ(x)\| = (d/2)x log x + Bx + O(log x), with B = log Q + ∑λ log λ − d/2 (our own). Two completions differ by a constant factor, so they share d and B, which determine q.

**Wikipedia:** [Selberg class](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Selberg_class). It says: “the same gamma factor can be expressed in many different ways, involving different numbers of gamma functions with different constants.”

**Sources:**

- [Kaczorowski and Perelli, On the structure of the Selberg class, IV: basic invariants](https://doi.org/10.4064/aa104-2-1)

### In the Selberg class, degree below 2 means a Dirichlet L-function

**Remember:** Double the sum of gamma slopes to obtain the Selberg degree.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11M41 (Other Dirichlet series and zeta functions), 11M06. arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** The degree of F in the Selberg class is twice the sum of the slopes ωᵢ in the gamma factors Γ(ωᵢs + μᵢ) of its functional equation. Selberg showed it does not depend on how the gamma factors are written, so each F has one degree.

**Problem.** In the Selberg class, only F = 1 has degree below one. From degree one up to but excluding two, the functions are ζ(s) and L(s+iθ,χ) for real θ and nonprincipal primitive Dirichlet characters χ.

**How the definition helps.** Degree is an invariant, so the class can be sorted by it (our own). The degree-zero and degree-one classification theorems identify the listed functions. The Kaczorowski–Perelli degree-gap theorems exclude the intervening degrees.

**Wikipedia:** [Selberg class](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Selberg_class). It says: “showed that the only cases of dF &lt; 2 are the Dirichlet L-functions for primitive Dirichlet characters (including the Riemann zeta-function).”

**Sources:**

- [J. Kaczorowski and A. Perelli, On the structure of the Selberg class, VII: 1 &lt; d &lt; 2, Ann. of Math. 173 (2011) 1397–1441](https://doi.org/10.4007/annals.2011.173.3.4)

### The Euler axiom excludes nonconstant degree-zero polynomials

**Remember:** At degree zero, a nonconstant local polynomial violates the Euler bound.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11M41 (Other Dirichlet series and zeta functions). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** The Euler axiom requires log F to have coefficients only at prime powers pʳ, each bounded by a constant times p raised to rθ, for some θ &lt; ½. The degree is twice the sum of the positive slopes λ in the gamma factors Γ(λs+μ). The Euler bound keeps every local factor free of zeros for Re s &gt; θ, while the functional equation reflects any zero across ½.

**Problem.** Only 1 has degree zero in the Selberg class. Without the Euler axiom, F(s) = 1 + √p/pˢ gives a degree-zero example for each prime p.

**How the definition helps.** The degree-zero classification makes F a Dirichlet polynomial, which multiplicativity splits into local polynomials with zeros only at real part at most θ (our own). Reflection would place a partner zero to the right of ½, so each local factor is constant (our own). For the example, exp(s log(p)/2) completes F with no gamma factor.

**Paper or page:** [Beyond the extended Selberg class: 1 &lt; dꜰ &lt; 2](https://arxiv.org/abs/2011.07525v1). It says: “The set 𝔄♯₀ consists of Dirichlet polynomials of the form”

**Sources:**

- [Kaczorowski and Perelli, On the structure of the Selberg class, I: 0≤d≤1](https://doi.org/10.1007/bf02392574)

### Admissible tuples are the prime patterns that sieve theorems can reach

**Remember:** If a pattern covers every class mod p, one entry is always divisible by p.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11N05 (Distribution of primes), 11N36. arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** A k-tuple of distinct integers h₁,…,hₖ is admissible if, for every prime p, some residue class modulo p contains none of them. Otherwise one of n+h₁,…,n+hₖ is divisible by p for every n, and only primes p ≤ k need checking.

**Problem.** For every positive integer m, some k ensures that every admissible k-tuple has at least m prime entries n+hᵢ for infinitely many integers n.

**How the definition helps.** Admissibility removes exactly the local obstruction, as (0,2,4) shows by covering every class modulo three (our own). Maynard's sieve theorem then gives m primes infinitely often in every admissible tuple of large enough size.

**Wikipedia:** [Prime k-tuple](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prime_k-tuple). It says: “A k-tuple that includes every possible residue modulo p is said to be inadmissible modulo p.”

**Sources:**

- [G. H. Hardy and J. E. Littlewood, Some problems of 'Partitio numerorum' III: On the expression of a number as a sum of primes, Acta Math. 44 (1923) 1–70](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF02403921)
- [Y. Zhang, Bounded gaps between primes, Ann. of Math. 179 (2014) 1121–1174](https://doi.org/10.4007/annals.2014.179.3.7)
- [J. Maynard, Small gaps between primes, Ann. of Math. 181 (2015) 383–413](https://doi.org/10.4007/annals.2015.181.1.7)

### Empty windows recover gap tails

**Remember:** One extra step removes one empty window from each longer gap.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11N05 (Distribution of primes). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** For a prime X and integer h ≥ 0, Eₓ(h) counts starting points 2 ≤ n &lt; X whose window (n,n+h\] contains no prime. A gap of length g between consecutive primes holds max(g−h,0) such starting points.

**Problem.** Eₓ(h)−Eₓ(h+1) counts gaps between consecutive primes up to X that are longer than h. If Eₓ(⌊λ log X⌋)/X tends to exp(−λ) for every λ ≥ 0 along prime X, then the fraction of gaps longer than λ log X also tends to exp(−λ).

**How the definition helps.** Each gap of length g contributes max(g−h,0), so the first difference counts gaps longer than h (our own). These differences decrease in h, so averages over adjacent blocks of width ⌊ε log X⌋ bound each one, and the prime number theorem gives about X/log X gaps. Letting X grow and then ε shrink differentiates the tail exp(−λ).

**Wikipedia:** [Prime gap](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prime_gap). It says: “the ratio of the length of the gap to the natural logarithm is greater than or equal to a fixed positive number k”

**Sources:**

- [P. X. Gallagher, On the distribution of primes in short intervals, Mathematika 23 (1976), 4–9](https://doi.org/10.1112/s0025579300016442)

### Factorial moments remove repeated primes

**Remember:** Count ordered distinct primes to match the prime tuple formula.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11N05 (Distribution of primes). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Choose n uniformly from 1,…,X, and let N count primes in (n,n+H\] with H = ⌊λ log X⌋ for fixed λ &gt; 0. Its kth factorial moment, the mean of N(N−1)⋯(N−k+1), counts ordered lists of k distinct primes. For a set D of k shifts, the singular series is S(D) = ∏ₚ (1−νₚ(D)/p)/(1−1/p)ᵏ, where νₚ(D) counts the classes modulo p that D occupies.

**Problem.** Suppose that, for each fixed k ≥ 1, the probability that n+h is prime for all h in D is (S(D)+o(1))/(log X)ᵏ, uniformly over k-element subsets D of {1,…,H}. Then every kth factorial moment tends to λᵏ, and N converges in distribution to the Poisson law of mean λ.

**How the definition helps.** The kth factorial moment sums the assumed prime-tuple probabilities over ordered lists of k distinct shifts (our own). Gallagher's theorem says the mean singular series tends to one, and H/log X tends to λ, so the sum tends to λᵏ. These limiting factorial moments determine the Poisson law.

**Paper or page:** [Sums of singular series with large sets and the tail of the distribution of primes](https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.09775v2). It says: “Then there exists a β &gt; 0, dependent only on δ &gt; 0, with Tₖ(h) = hᵏ + O(hᵏ⁻ᵝ).”

**Sources:**

- [P. X. Gallagher, On the distribution of primes in short intervals, Mathematika 23 (1976), 4–9](https://doi.org/10.1112/s0025579300016442)

### Independent phases give Bessel factors

**Remember:** One shared phase per zero keeps the dependence between intervals.

*True by definition.* MSC 11N05 (Distribution of primes). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Give each chosen zero height γ one independent uniform point U on the unit circle, shared by all intervals. In interval j the zero contributes −2 Re(cⱼU), with a complex coefficient cⱼ for that zero and interval, and the model error Eⱼ sums these contributions over zeros.

**Problem.** For real ξⱼ, the mean of exp(i∑ξⱼEⱼ) is the product over zeros of J₀(2\|∑ξⱼcⱼ\|), where J₀(a) is the average of exp(ia cos t) over t in \[0,2π\]. This also holds for infinitely many zeros if each interval's coefficients have a finite sum of squared absolute values.

**How the definition helps.** Independence factors the mean over zeros, and the shared phase combines one zero's terms into −2 Re((∑ξⱼcⱼ)U) (our own). Rotation of U gives the Bessel average. Square summability gives mean-square convergence of the sums, hence convergence of their characteristic functions.

**Paper or page:** [Joint distribution of primes in multiple short intervals](https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.04000v3). It says: “is the Bessel function of order 0.”

**Sources:**

- [Sun-Kai Leung, Joint distribution of primes in multiple short intervals](https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.04000)

### Logarithmic sampling balances zero phases

**Remember:** Uniform log time gives each nonconstant Fourier mode a vanishing mean.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11N05 (Distribution of primes), 11M26. arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Logarithmic sampling picks x in \[2,X\] with density 1/(x log(X/2)), which makes log x uniform on an interval of growing length (our own). The phase of a zero height γⱼ at x is exp(iγⱼ log x).

**Problem.** Suppose γ₁,…,γᵣ are linearly independent over ℚ. Under logarithmic sampling their phases converge jointly in distribution to uniform measure on the product of r circles as X grows.

**How the definition helps.** By linear independence, each nonzero integer frequency vector gives a nonzero combination u of the heights. For uniform log x, the mean of exp(iu log x) tends to zero, so Weyl's criterion gives the uniform limit. Uniform sampling of x instead gives limiting mean magnitude 1/\|1+iu\|.

**Paper or page:** [Joint distribution of primes in multiple short intervals](https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.04000v3). It says: “is uniformly distributed over the torus 𝕋ᴺ.”

**Sources:**

- [Sun-Kai Leung, Joint distribution of primes in multiple short intervals](https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.04000)

### Normalization gives singular series mean one

**Remember:** Divide by independent survival to make each local average one.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11N05 (Distribution of primes). arXiv math.NT, math.CO. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** For k shifts, let νₚ count their classes modulo p, and divide the survival fraction 1 − νₚ/p by the independent survival probability (1 − 1/p)ᵏ. The truncated singular series multiplies these ratios over primes p ≤ z, and the full series for distinct shifts is the limit as z tends to infinity.

**Problem.** For any fixed z, the truncated series averages to 1 over all ordered tuples modulo the product of primes p ≤ z. For fixed k, the full series averages to 1 + o(1) over distinct ordered shifts in {1,…,H} as H tends to infinity.

**How the definition helps.** Both 1 − νₚ/p, averaged over shifts, and (1 − 1/p)ᵏ equal the chance that a random residue avoids k random shifts, so each local ratio averages to one (our own). The Chinese remainder theorem gives mean one for the product over p ≤ z. Gallagher's theorem controls the passage to the full product over distinct shifts.

**Paper or page:** [Sums of singular series with large sets and the tail of the distribution of primes](https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.09775v2). It says: “Tₖ(h) = hᵏ + O(hᵏ⁻ᵝ).”

**Sources:**

- [P. X. Gallagher, On the distribution of primes in short intervals, Mathematika 23 (1976), 4–9.](https://doi.org/10.1112/s0025579300016442)
- [Vivian Kuperberg, Sums of singular series with large sets and the tail of the distribution of primes, Theorem 1.1.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.09775v2)

### Relative windows fix zero weights

**Remember:** Scale the interval with x so the zero weights stop moving.

*True by definition.* MSC 11N05 (Distribution of primes). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Measure the prime error in a window of relative length δ, with 0 &lt; δ ≤ 1, as E(x) = (ψ((1+δ)x)−ψ(x)−δx)/√x. Here ψ(y) sums log p over prime powers up to y, and scaling the window with x makes each zero's coefficient independent of x.

**Problem.** Assume the Riemann hypothesis, write the zeros as ρ = ½+iγ, and take x,Z ≥ 2. Then E(x) = −∑ c(ρ)exp(iγ log x) + O(√x log²(xZ)/Z + log x/√x), summing over \|γ\| ≤ Z with multiplicity, where c(ρ) = (exp(ρ log(1+δ))−1)/ρ.

**How the definition helps.** The terms at the two endpoints share x raised to ρ, leaving the factor (1+δ) raised to ρ, minus one, which does not depend on x (our own). Division by √x turns the shared power into exp(iγ log x). The truncated von Mangoldt explicit formula gives the remainder.

**Paper or page:** [Joint distribution of primes in multiple short intervals](https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.04000v3). It says: “It follows immediately from the truncated von Mangoldt’s explicit formula”

**Sources:**

- [Sun-Kai Leung, Joint distribution of primes in multiple short intervals](https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.04000)
- [H. Iwaniec and E. Kowalski, Analytic Number Theory, AMS Colloquium Publications 53 (2004)](https://doi.org/10.1090/coll/053)

### Tent weights save a logarithm

**Remember:** Use a tent to soften both edges of the prime count.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11N05 (Distribution of primes). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Count primes near x with the tent weight max(0, h−\|n−x\|) instead of a sharp cutoff, times Λ(n), which is log p at powers of a prime p and zero elsewhere. The tent is a second difference of the integrated prime count, so each zero term in the explicit formula gains an extra denominator (our own).

**Problem.** Assume every zero of the Riemann zeta function with real part strictly between zero and one has real part ½. For some C&gt;0 and all sufficiently large x, there is a prime within C√x log x of x.

**How the definition helps.** Under the hypothesis, the extra denominator and a split at height x/h bound the zero terms by O(h√x log x), against a main term h² (our own). For large C the main term wins at h = C√x log x, and higher prime powers contribute only o(h²). So some prime near x has positive weight.

**Wikipedia:** [Riemann hypothesis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Riemann_hypothesis). It says: “Cramér proved that, assuming the Riemann hypothesis, every gap is O(√p log p).”

**Sources:**

- [H. Iwaniec and E. Kowalski, Analytic Number Theory, AMS Colloquium Publications 53 (2004)](https://doi.org/10.1090/coll/053)

### Truncated inverses give Heath-Brown’s identity

**Remember:** Raise the truncation error to the K to push it past X.

*True by definition.* MSC 11N05 (Distribution of primes). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Truncate the series for 1/ζ at Y = exp((log X)/K): M(s) = ∑ μ(m)m⁻ˢ over m ≤ Y, with μ the Möbius function, for fixed X ≥ 2 and integer K ≥ 1. Then 1 − ζM has no coefficients at n ≤ Y, so its Kth power has none at n ≤ X.

**Problem.** For positive integers n ≤ X, the von Mangoldt function Λ(n) equals the coefficient of n⁻ˢ in −ζ′(s)∑(−1)ʲ⁻¹ binom(K,j)ζ(s)ʲ⁻¹M(s)ʲ, summing from j=1 to K.

**How the definition helps.** Since (1−ζM)ᴷ has no terms up to X, multiplying 1−(1−ζM)ᴷ by −ζ′/ζ keeps the coefficients Λ(n) for n ≤ X (our own). Binomial expansion cancels the 1/ζ and gives the displayed sum.

**Wikipedia:** [Vaughan's identity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vaughan%27s_identity). It says: “Vaughan's identity was generalized by Heath-Brown”

**Sources:**

- [D. R. Heath-Brown, Prime Numbers in Short Intervals and a Generalized Vaughan Identity, Canadian Journal of Mathematics 34 (1982), 1365–1377](https://doi.org/10.4153/cjm-1982-095-9)

**Remember:** Prove the sieve for all allowed shapes, then choose the narrowest one.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11N05 (Distribution of primes). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** H(k) is the least width, largest entry minus smallest, of a set of k ≥ 2 integers that misses a residue class modulo every prime.

**Problem.** Suppose every such set has infinitely many integer translates with at least m primes, where 2 ≤ m ≤ k; then infinitely many blocks of m consecutive primes have width at most H(k). For m = 2 and k = 50, the Polymath sieve and H(50) ≤ 246 give infinitely many consecutive prime gaps at most 246.

**How the definition helps.** Apply the assumed sieve theorem to an admissible set of width H(k) (our own). Each successful translate puts at least m primes in an interval of width H(k), and the first m of them are consecutive.

**Remember:** A density exponent sets the interval length that the explicit formula can reach.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11N05 (Distribution of primes), 11M26. arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

Huxley's short-interval argument then gives the prime asymptotic.

### Corrected mass absorbs exceptional zeros

**Remember:** Put the exceptional zero in the main term, not the error.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11N13 (Primes in congruence classes), 11M06. arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Predict the prime count in a class a modulo q ≥ 2, with gcd(a,q) = 1, as λx/φ(q), where φ(q) counts invertible classes. If Thorner and Zaman's exceptional real zero β exists for a real character χ modulo q, set λ = 1−χ(a)exp((β−1)log x)/β, the main term corrected by that zero; otherwise set λ = 1.

**Problem.** For x ≥ 3 with λx/φ(q) ≥ x¹⁸⁄¹⁹, the sum of log p over primes p ≤ x congruent to a equals (λx/φ(q))(1 + O(exp(U) + exp(V))). Here U = −c log x/log q and V = −c(log x)³⁄⁵/(log log x)¹⁄⁵ for an effectively computable absolute c &gt; 0.

When χ(a) = 1 the correction can reduce the prediction substantially. The proof bounds the other zeros more sharply as β approaches 1.
