### Dilogarithms evaluate triangular Mahler measure

**Remember:** D is a primitive of the regulator form; integrals become endpoint values.

*True by definition.* MSC 11R06 (PV-numbers and generalizations; other special algebraic numbers; Mahler measure), 11G55. arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** For 0 &lt; \|z\| &lt; 1, the Bloch–Wigner dilogarithm is D(z) = Im Li₂(z) + arg(1−z) log\|z\|, where Li₂(z) = ∑ₙ≥₁ zⁿ/n² and arg is the principal argument; extend D continuously to zero and the unit circle. Its differential is the regulator form: dD(z) = log\|z\| d arg(1−z) − log\|1−z\| d arg z.

**Problem.** The uniform circle average of log\|1 + x + y\| over x and y equals D(exp(πi/3))/π. This average is the logarithmic Mahler measure.

**How the definition helps.** On the unit circle dD(−x) = −log\|1+x\| d arg x, so the integral left by Jensen’s formula is an endpoint difference of D (our own calculation). Jensen’s formula keeps the arc where \|1+x\| ≥ 1, from exp(−2πi/3) to exp(2πi/3). The endpoint values of D(−x) are D(exp(πi/3)) and its negative, giving the stated average.

**Wikipedia:** [Mahler measure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mahler_measure). It says: “m(1+x+y)=3√3/(4π) L(χ₋₃,2)”

**Paper or page:** [Generalized Mahler measures of Laurent polynomials](https://arxiv.org/abs/2308.04601). It says: “\\eta \\left(x, 1-x\\right) = d D\\left(x\\right).”

**Sources:**

- [Generalized Mahler measures of Laurent polynomials, Lemma 2.1](https://arxiv.org/abs/2308.04601)
- [Smyth, On measures of polynomials in several variables](https://doi.org/10.1017/S0004972700006894)

### Dominant coefficients exclude p-adic zeros

**Remember:** One strictly largest term cannot cancel on the p-adic unit torus.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11R06 (PV-numbers and generalizations; other special algebraic numbers; Mahler measure). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** A Laurent polynomial over ℂₚ has a dominant coefficient if one coefficient has strictly larger p-adic absolute value than every other. On the unit torus, where every coordinate has absolute value one, each term has the size of its coefficient, so the dominant term outweighs all the others.

**Problem.** A nonzero Laurent polynomial over ℂₚ has no zero on the unit torus exactly when it has a dominant coefficient.

**How the definition helps.** If one term dominates, the strict p-adic triangle inequality forbids cancellation, so there is no zero (our own explanation). The converse uses the lemma’s factorization into a monomial times one plus a polynomial with coefficients of absolute value below one. Our own example 1 − t has tied coefficients and vanishes at t = 1.

**Paper or page:** [A note on p-adic higher Mahler measures](https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.05724). It says: “Then $f$ does not vanish in any point of $T<sub>p</sub><sup>n$</sup> if and only if we have\\begin{align}  f(t<sub>1</sub>, \\cdots , t<sub>n</sub>)=at<sub>1</sub><sup>l<sub>1</sub></sup>\\cdots t<sub>n</sub><sup>l<sub>n</sub></sup>(1+g(t<sub>1</sub>, \\cdots , t<sub>n</sub>)) \\end{align}for some $a \\in \\mathbb {C}<sub>p</sub><sup>\\times </sup>, (l<sub>1</sub>, \\cdots , l<sub>n</sub>) \\in \\mathbb {Z}<sup>n$</sup> and $g \\in \\mathfrak {m}<sub>p</sub>\[t<sub>1</sub><sup>\\pm 1</sup>, \\dots ,t<sub>n</sub><sup>\\pm 1</sup>\]$.”

**Sources:**

- [A note on p-adic higher Mahler measures, Lemma 2.5](https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.05724)

### Exact symbols give boundary integrals

**Remember:** Each term supplies a primitive, so only the boundary remains to integrate.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11R06 (PV-numbers and generalizations; other special algebraic numbers; Mahler measure), 11G55. arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** On the smooth locus of an irreducible surface P(x,y,z) = 0, away from zeros and poles, require x∧y∧z to be a finite rational combination of terms f∧(1−f)∧g. Here ∧ is taken in the third exterior power, with rational coefficients, of the group of nonzero rational functions. Each such term has a known primitive for its regulator form, so the form log\|z\| dθ∧dφ gets a primitive β (our own explanation).

**Problem.** Let Γ be the chain of roots with \|z\| ≥ 1 above \|x\| = \|y\| = 1, counted with multiplicity and oriented by the angles θ, φ of x, y. If Γ is piecewise smooth in this open set, with its boundary, then m(P) minus the measure of the leading coefficient in z is an integral over the boundary of Γ.

**How the definition helps.** Jensen’s formula writes the difference of measures as the integral of log\|z\| dθ∧dφ over Γ divided by (2π)², and the decomposition makes this form exact. Trieu’s regulator identities give the primitive β as a weighted sum over the terms (our own explanation). Stokes’ theorem then replaces the integral over Γ by the integral of β over the oriented boundary.

**Paper or page:** [The Mahler measure of exact polynomials and special L-values of K3 surfaces](https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.00893). It says: “\\mathrm{m}(P) - \\mathrm{m}(\\tilde P) = \\dfrac {(-1)<sup>n-1</sup>}{(2\\pi i)<sup>n-1</sup>} \\int <sub>\\partial \\Gamma </sub> \\rho (\\xi ).”

**Sources:**

- [The Mahler measure of exact polynomials and special L-values of K3 surfaces, Theorem 1.11](https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.00893)

### Exterior roots give regulator integrals

**Remember:** Follow the big roots y as x circles; they carry the measure.

*True by definition.* MSC 11R06 (PV-numbers and generalizations; other special algebraic numbers; Mahler measure), 19F27. arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Let P(x,y) = 0 define an elliptic curve. As x runs counterclockwise once around the unit circle, γ is the oriented path traced on the curve by the roots y with \|y\| &gt; 1, counted with multiplicity. These are exactly the roots that Jensen’s formula keeps in the average of log\|P\| over y.

**Problem.** Assume γ is a finite union of smooth paths, and let P\* be the leading coefficient of P in y. Then m(P) − m(P\*), where m is the average of log\|·\| over the unit torus, equals −1/(2π) times the integral along γ of η = log\|x\| d arg y − log\|y\| d arg x.

**How the definition helps.** Jensen’s formula gives m(P) − m(P\*) as 1/(2π) times the integral of log\|y\| d arg x over the roots on γ (our own explanation). On γ, log\|x\| = 0, so η reduces to −log\|y\| d arg x. This gives the factor −1/(2π).

**Paper or page:** [Determinants of Mahler measures and special values of L-functions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.14714). It says: “m(P) − m(P\*) = −1/(2π) ∫γₚ η(x,y).”

**Sources:**

- [Determinants of Mahler measures and special values of L-functions, Theorem 2.1](https://arxiv.org/abs/2409.14714)

### Short relation bounds imply equidistribution

**Remember:** Large height means no short target monomial collapses to a constant.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11R06 (PV-numbers and generalizations; other special algebraic numbers; Mahler measure). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** A monomial map between tori replaces each target variable by a product of integer powers of the source variables. Its Boyd height is the least largest-absolute-coordinate of a nonzero exponent vector whose target monomial becomes constant after composing with the map, or infinity if there is none. So with large height every target monomial with small exponents stays nonconstant, and its source average is zero.

**Problem.** Fix the target torus and let the Boyd heights tend to infinity. Then for every continuous g on the target, the source average of g composed with the map tends to the target average of g, and the same holds for g = log\|P\| with P a fixed nonzero Laurent polynomial.

**How the definition helps.** Each fixed nonconstant monomial eventually stays nonconstant on the source, so its source average equals its target average zero (our own argument). Trigonometric polynomials approximate every continuous function uniformly, which gives the first claim. For log\|P\| the Boyd–Lawton theorem controls the region near zeros, where uniform approximation fails.

**Paper or page:** [General Boyd-Lawton Theorems with Multivariable Limits](https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.05910). It says: “If $g\\colon {\\mathbb {T}}<sup>n\\to</sup> {\\mathbb {C}}$ is continuous, then\\\[  \\int \_{{\\mathbb {T}}<sup>n</sup>} g \\,  d \\tau <sub>n</sub> \\;  = \\;  \\lim <sub>\\mu \\left( q<sub>A</sub> \\right)\\to \\infty </sub>\\;  \\int \_{{\\mathbb {T}}<sup>m}</sup> g \\circ q<sub>A</sub> \\;  d \\tau \_m,  \\\]”

**Sources:**

- [General Boyd-Lawton Theorems with Multivariable Limits, Corollary 6.1](https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.05910)

### Tempered faces prevent tame obstructions

**Remember:** Cyclotomic edge roots make every boundary tame symbol torsion.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11R06 (PV-numbers and generalizations; other special algebraic numbers; Mahler measure), 19D45. arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** A two-variable Laurent polynomial is tempered if, on every edge of its Newton polygon, the edge polynomial has only roots of unity as nonzero roots. The edge polynomial takes the coefficients at successive lattice points of the edge, zeros included, as the coefficients of a one-variable polynomial. Every boundary tame symbol of x and y is ± a power of an edge root, so temperedness makes them all torsion (our own).

**Problem.** Take an irreducible tempered polynomial over ℚ whose Newton polygon has positive area. On its smooth complete curve every tame symbol of x and y is a root of unity, so their symbol has no boundary obstruction with rational coefficients.

**How the definition helps.** At a point with uniformizer t, write x = tᵐa and y = tⁿb with units a, b, so the tame symbol is (−1)ᵐⁿaⁿ/bᵐ (our own calculation). For (m,n) ≠ (0,0) the lowest-order terms cancel along one edge, so the leading unit in its primitive direction is an edge root. Our own example x + y + 2 is not tempered, and its symbol at x = 0 is −1/2.

**Paper or page:** [A shifted Mahler measure identity for Boyd's family](https://arxiv.org/abs/2202.09974). It says: “Qₖ(x,y) and Qₖ(x−1,y) are tempered polynomials.”

**Sources:**

- [A shifted Mahler measure identity for Boyd's family, Lemma 3.1](https://arxiv.org/abs/2202.09974)
- [Yang, Liu and Tang, A Mahler Measure Identity Involving a Genus 2 Family, Section 1](https://ccj.pku.edu.cn/Article/DownLoad?id=364490499&type=ArticleFile)

### Monic polynomials are Hermite equivalent exactly when their rings ℤ\[X\]∕(f) are isomorphic

**Remember:** For monic polynomials, compare the rings, not the norm forms.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11R09 (Polynomials (irreducibility, etc.)), 11R54. arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** The norm form of a monic integer polynomial f of degree n sends integer coordinates (a₀,…,aₙ₋₁) to the norm of a₀ + a₁X + … + aₙ₋₁Xⁿ⁻¹ in ℤ\[X\]/(f), the determinant of multiplication by that element (our own description). Two monic polynomials are Hermite equivalent when an invertible integer change of coordinates turns one norm form into the other.

**Problem.** Let f and g be monic integer polynomials with nonzero discriminant. They are Hermite equivalent exactly when the rings ℤ\[X\]∕(f) and ℤ\[X\]∕(g) are isomorphic.

**How the definition helps.** A ring isomorphism carries an integer basis to an integer basis and keeps norms, so it identifies the norm forms (our own explanation). The hard direction recovers the ring from its norm form, which the paper proves for general orders.

**Paper or page:** [Hermite equivalence of polynomials](https://arxiv.org/abs/2109.02932v3). It says: “We show that the Hermite equivalence class of a polynomial has a very natural interpretation in terms of the invariant ring and invariant ideal associated with the polynomial.”

**Sources:**

- [Manjul Bhargava, Jan-Hendrik Evertse, Kálmán Győry, László Remete, Ashvin A. Swaminathan, Hermite equivalence of polynomials, arXiv:2109.02932v3 (2022). Acta Arithmetica, on-line first, 2023](https://arxiv.org/abs/2109.02932v3)

### Euclidean ideal classes force cyclic class groups

**Remember:** Let the Euclidean algorithm run on ideals, and the class group becomes cyclic.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11R29 (Class numbers, class groups, discriminants), 13F07, 11R27. arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** A nonzero integral ideal C of the ring of integers R of K is Euclidean if some map ψ, from the fractional ideals containing R to a well-ordered set, allows division with remainder. That is, for every such I and every x in IC outside C, some y in C gives ψ((x−y)⁻¹IC) &lt; ψ(I) (our own formulation). Each step multiplies the class of I by the class \[C\], so descent reaches every class as a power of \[C\] (our own).

**Problem.** A number field with a Euclidean ideal class has cyclic class group. Suppose K is Galois over ℚ, its Hilbert class field is abelian over ℚ, and its unit rank is at least four. Then a class is Euclidean exactly when it generates the class group.

**How the definition helps.** Descent along decreasing ψ makes every class a power of \[C\], so the class group is cyclic, as Lenstra proved. Murty and Graves prove the converse under the stated Galois, class field and unit-rank hypotheses.

**Paper or page:** [On the existence of a non-principal Euclidean ideal class in biquadratic fields with class number two](https://arxiv.org/abs/2009.06464), [Low degree extensions with Cyclic class group](https://arxiv.org/abs/2110.00225). It says: “Lenstra introduced the notion of a Euclidean ideal class, which is a generalization of the Euclidean domain. Lenstra also proved that the Euclidean ideal in a number field K implies that the class group of K is cyclic.”

**Sources:**

- [Srilakshmi Krishnamoorthy, Sunil Kumar Pasupulati, On the existence of a non-principal Euclidean ideal class in biquadratic fields with class number two, arXiv:2009.06464 (2022)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2009.06464)
- [Srilakshmi Krishnamoorthy, Sunil Kumar Pasupulati, Low degree extensions with Cyclic class group, arXiv:2110.00225 (2025)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2110.00225)
- [Hester Graves, M. Ram Murty, A family of number fields with unit rank at least 4 that has Euclidean ideals, Proceedings of the American Mathematical Society (2013)](https://doi.org/10.1090/s0002-9939-2013-11602-3)

### Pólya groups equal strongly ambiguous classes, giving short proofs

**Remember:** Galois-fixed ideals are products over whole fibres, so the groups agree.

*True by definition. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11R29 (Class numbers, class groups, discriminants), 11R32, 11R34. arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** For a Galois extension L/K of number fields with group G, the relative Pólya group Po(L/K) is generated by the classes of the products of all primes of L above one prime of K. A strongly ambiguous class is an ideal class that contains a fractional ideal fixed by G.

**Problem.** Po(L/K) equals the group of strongly ambiguous classes. Its order is h(K)∏ᵥ eᵥ/\|H¹(G,U(L))\| over the finite primes v of K, with eᵥ the ramification index, h(K) the class number and U(L) the unit group of L.

**How the definition helps.** G permutes the primes above each prime of K transitively, so a fixed ideal has constant exponents on each such set and is a product of powers of Pólya generators (our own argument). Each generator is itself fixed, which gives equality. Corollary 2.3 obtains the order from the Brumer–Rosen and Zantema exact sequence.

**Paper or page:** [Ostrowski quotients for finite extensions of number fields](https://arxiv.org/abs/2111.00442). It says: “For L/K a finite Galois extension of number fields, the relative Pólya group Po(L/K) coincides with the group of strongly ambiguous ideal classes in L/K.”

**Sources:**

- [Ehsan Shahoseini, Ali Rajaei, Abbas Maarefparvar, Ostrowski quotients for finite extensions of number fields, Pacific J. Math. 321 (2022) 415-429, arXiv:2111.00442](https://arxiv.org/abs/2111.00442)

### Galois sets identify completions

**Remember:** Restrict the coset action to D to read the completions.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11R32 (Galois theory). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** For a finite Galois extension L/ℚ with group G and an intermediate field K fixed by H, the embeddings of K into L correspond to the cosets H∖G. The decomposition group D of a prime of L above p, the automorphisms preserving that prime, acts on these cosets, and each D-orbit gives one completion of K above p (our own).

**Problem.** For two intermediate fields, the products of their completions above p are isomorphic as ℚₚ-algebras exactly when their coset sets are isomorphic as sets with D-action.

**How the definition helps.** The product of completions is the finite étale ℚₚ-algebra whose Galois set is H∖G with its D-action (our own). The correspondence between finite étale algebras and finite Galois sets gives both directions (our own).

**Paper or page:** [Stronger arithmetic equivalence](https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.01956v4). It says: “if and only if \[H₁∖G\] and \[H₂∖G\] are isomorphic as D𝔭-sets.”

**Sources:**

- [Andrew V. Sutherland, Stronger arithmetic equivalence (Proposition 2.19)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.01956v4)

### Locally integrally equivalent number fields have isomorphic class groups

**Remember:** Keep integer information at every prime, and the class group survives.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11R33 (Integral representations related to algebraic numbers; Galois module structure of rings of integers), 11R29, 11R42. arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Number fields K₁ and K₂ with common Galois closure L are locally integrally equivalent when the permutation modules ℤ\_ℓ\[G/H₁\] and ℤ\_ℓ\[G/H₂\] are isomorphic for every prime ℓ. Here G = Gal(L/ℚ) permutes the cosets of Hᵢ = Gal(L/Kᵢ).

**Problem.** Locally integrally equivalent number fields have isomorphic ideal class groups. They also have the same zeta function and the same regulator.

**How the definition helps.** The paper’s class-group theorem turns each ℓ-adic isomorphism into an isomorphism of ℓ-primary class groups (our own explanation). The modules are then rationally isomorphic too, which gives the same zeta function, and the class number formula gives equal regulators. Equal zeta functions alone permit different class numbers (our own comparison).

**Paper or page:** [Stronger arithmetic equivalence](https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.01956v4). It says: “In addition to having the same Dedekind zeta function (the usual notion of arithmetic equivalence), number fields that are equivalent in any of these stronger senses must have the same class number”

**Sources:**

- [Andrew V. Sutherland, Stronger arithmetic equivalence, arXiv:2104.01956v4 (2021). Discrete Anal. 2021, Paper No. 23, 23 pp](https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.01956v4)

### Cartesian conditions preserve Selmer torsion

**Remember:** Pull back the local tests to get the same test on torsion.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11R34 (Galois cohomology), 11F80. arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Let π generate the maximal ideal of a discrete valuation ring R, and let T be finite free over R/(πᵐ) with continuous Galois action. A Selmer group on T is the set of global classes whose restriction at each place lies in a chosen subgroup of H¹(Kᵥ,T). The conditions are Cartesian when those on T\[πⁱ\], and on T/πⁱT identified with T\[πⁱ\] by multiplication by πᵐ⁻ⁱ, are the pullbacks under inclusion.

**Problem.** Suppose the Galois group of the number field fixes no nonzero element of T modulo π. For 1 ≤ i ≤ m, both smaller Selmer groups identify with the subgroup killed by πⁱ in the Selmer group on T.

**How the definition helps.** With pulled-back conditions, a class on the smaller module is Selmer exactly when its image on T is Selmer (our own). With no fixed vectors modulo π, the exact sequences of Galois cohomology make that image map injective, with image the classes killed by πⁱ (our own). The cited theorem verifies the Cartesian property for one family of conditions.

**Paper or page:** [Bipartite Euler Systems for certain Galois Representations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2302.05181v1). It says: “The Selmer structure ℱ(𝔫) is cartesian for any 𝔫 ∈ 𝒩.”

**Sources:**

- [Bipartite Euler Systems for certain Galois Representations](https://arxiv.org/abs/2302.05181v1)

### Ext into units extends Artin–Verdier duality

**Remember:** Pair against the units, and every constructible sheaf gets a dual.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11R34 (Galois cohomology), 11R37, 14F20. arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Let X be the spectrum of the ring of integers of a totally imaginary number field. Artin–Verdier duality pairs étale cohomology of a sheaf F with Extʲ(F,𝔾ₘ), the maps into the sheaf of units, which are defined with no torsion condition on F. Here F is ℤ-constructible: locally constant with finitely generated stalks on each piece of a finite stratification.

**Problem.** For a constructible sheaf F on X, Deninger's theorem identifies the dual of Hʳ(X, F) with Ext³⁻ʳ(F, 𝔾ₘ) for r = 0, 1. For r = 2, 3 it identifies Hʳ(X, F) with the dual of that Ext group.

**How the definition helps.** Since Ext into 𝔾ₘ is defined for every sheaf, the duality extends past torsion sheaves. For F = ℤ and r = 2, H²(X,ℤ) is dual to the Galois group of the Hilbert class field, and Ext¹(ℤ,𝔾ₘ) is the class group (our own). So this case is unramified class field theory (our own).

**Wikipedia:** [Artin–Verdier duality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artin%E2%80%93Verdier_duality). It says: “proved Artin–Verdier duality for constructible, but not necessarily torsion sheaves. For such a sheaf F, the above pairing induces isomorphisms”

**Sources:**

- [Christopher Deninger, An extension of Artin–Verdier duality to non-torsion sheaves, Journal für die reine und angewandte Mathematik 366 (1986)](https://doi.org/10.1515/crll.1986.366.18)

### Tate-modified compact supports make Artin–Verdier duality hold

**Remember:** Tate cohomology at real places removes the 2-torsion that never stops.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11R34 (Galois cohomology), 14F20. arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** For a nonempty open U in the spectrum of the integers of a number field K, modified compactly supported cohomology is the mapping cone, shifted by −1, of restriction from étale cochains on U to local cochains at all omitted places, infinite ones included. At the archimedean places the local complex is the complete Tate complex, which cancels the high-degree cohomology that real places contribute (our own).

**Problem.** Let F be a constructible sheaf on U, one that is locally constant with finite stalks on the pieces of a finite partition. Then the Tate-modified compactly supported cohomology Ĥⁱc(U, F) is finite, is dual to Ext³⁻ⁱ(F, 𝔾ₘ) for every i, and vanishes for i ≥ 4.

**How the definition helps.** Ordinary cohomology of the integer spectrum of ℚ with ℤ/2 coefficients is nonzero in all high degrees because of the real place (our own example). The Tate complex at real places cancels this part (our own explanation). Modified Artin–Verdier duality then gives finiteness and the pairing, and vanishing for i ≥ 4 follows because negative Ext groups vanish.

**Wikipedia:** [Artin–Verdier duality](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Artin%E2%80%93Verdier_duality). It says: “The sum is taken over all places of K, which are not in U, including the archimedean ones.”

**Paper or page:** [Special values of L-functions on regular arithmetic schemes of dimension 1](https://arxiv.org/abs/2108.00811). It says: “If F is constructible, all groups are finite and the Artin-Verdier arrow is an isomorphism.”

**Sources:**

- [Barry Mazur, Notes on étale cohomology of number fields, Annales scientifiques de l'École Normale Supérieure 6 (1973)](https://doi.org/10.24033/asens.1257)
- [Adrien Morin, Special values of L-functions on regular arithmetic schemes of dimension 1, arXiv:2108.00811](https://arxiv.org/abs/2108.00811)

### Unit cohomology detects capitulation

**Remember:** A generator upstairs records the lost class through its conjugates.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11R34 (Galois cohomology), 11R29. arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** For a finite Galois extension K/F with group G, fix a finite set S of places of F containing the infinite places and the ramified primes, and use the places above S in K. The S-class group is the group of ideals made of primes outside S, modulo the prime-to-S parts of principal ideals, and an S-unit has no prime factors outside S. A class of F capitulates when it becomes principal in K, and a generator a in K gives the S-unit cocycle g ↦ g(a)/a.

**Problem.** The kernel of the map on S-class groups from F to K is the first cohomology of G acting on the S-units of K.

**How the definition helps.** Changing the generator a by an S-unit changes the cocycle g(a)/a by a coboundary, so each capitulated class gives one class in H¹ (our own argument). Hilbert’s Theorem 90 writes every S-unit cocycle in this form. The ideal of a then descends to F because its exponents are G-invariant and all ramification lies in S.

**Paper or page:** [The S-relative Pólya groups and S-Ostrowski quotients of number fields](https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.09362v1). It says: “0 → Ker(ε<sub>K/F,S</sub>) → H¹(G,U<sub>K,S</sub>)”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### A torus detects common scales

**Remember:** One cohomology class records whether all norms share a scale.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11R37 (Class field theory), 11S25. arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Given finite separable extensions L₁,…,Lₙ of a number field K, send (x₁,…,xₙ,c), with xᵢ in Lᵢ× and c in K×, to the tuple of norms N(xᵢ) each multiplied by c. The kernel T is an algebraic torus over K, one that becomes a product of multiplicative groups over a separable closure. A tuple in (K×)ⁿ is a commonly scaled norm tuple exactly when it lies in the image, and the connecting map gives it a class in H¹(K,T) that vanishes exactly then (our own).

**Problem.** The projective Hasse norm principle says that a tuple in (K×)ⁿ that becomes a tuple of norms after one common rescaling at each completion needs only one rescaling in K. It holds exactly when the map from first Galois cohomology of T to the product of its local counterparts is injective.

**How the definition helps.** Hilbert’s Theorem 90 shows that every class in first cohomology of T arises from a tuple, both globally and locally (our own). So injectivity says exactly that local vanishing at every completion forces global vanishing (our own).

**Paper or page:** [A Projective Twist on the Hasse Norm Theorem](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.11159v1). It says: “{PHNP} \_K(L<sub>1</sub>, L<sub>2</sub>, \\ldots , L<sub>n</sub>) is true if and only if H<sup>1</sup>(L/K, \\mathbf {T}(L)) \\to \\prod <sub>w\\mid v</sub> H<sup>1</sup>(L<sub>w</sub>/K<sub>v</sub>, \\mathbf {T}(L<sub>w</sub>)) is injective.”

**Sources:**

- [Thomas Rüd, Alan Bu, A Projective Twist on the Hasse Norm Theorem](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.11159v1)

### Local unit intersections join ring class fields

**Remember:** Join the fields by intersecting their idele subgroups.

*True by definition.* MSC 11R37 (Class field theory). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Let K be an imaginary quadratic field with ring of integers O and units ±1. The ring class field of conductor f is the class field of the subgroup of finite ideles generated by K× and the local units of the order ℤ + fO. A higher power of a prime in f gives a smaller local unit group at that prime.

**Problem.** The smallest field containing the ring class fields of conductors f and g is the ring class field of their least common multiple.

**How the definition helps.** Class field theory sends the compositum to the intersection of the two subgroups (our own calculation). For an idele in both, the two global factors differ by ±1, which lies in both orders, so one global factor serves for both. At each prime the intersection of local unit groups is the one for the larger exponent, which gives the least common multiple.

**Paper or page:** [CM Elliptic Curves: Volcanoes, Reality and Applications](https://arxiv.org/abs/2212.13316v1). It says: “The compositum of finitely many ring class fields of K is a ring class field of K.”

**Sources:**

- [CM Elliptic Curves: Volcanoes, Reality and Applications (Corollary 4.4)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2212.13316v1)

### Degree-one counts determine zeta functions

**Remember:** Degree-one counts give the whole permutation character.

*True by definition.* MSC 11R42 (Zeta functions and L-functions of number fields). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Embed both fields in one finite Galois extension L of ℚ with group G. The permutation character of K counts, for each g in G, the embeddings of K into L that g fixes. At the Frobenius of an unramified prime p, it counts the primes of K of norm p.

**Problem.** Suppose that, outside finitely many rational primes p, both fields have the same number of prime ideals of norm p. Then their Dedekind zeta functions, which sum over nonzero integral ideals by norm, are equal.

**How the definition helps.** Equal prime counts make the two characters agree at almost all Frobenius elements, and Chebotarev makes every conjugacy class such an element, so the characters are equal (our own deduction). Artin’s induction formula identifies their L-functions with the two zeta functions, ramified factors included.

**Paper or page:** [Density questions on arithmetic equivalence](https://arxiv.org/abs/2106.01166v1), [Stronger arithmetic equivalence](https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.01956v4). It says: “{\\rm Trace}(\\rho <sub>K</sub>({\\rm Frob}<sub>\\ell </sub>)) =a<sub>\\ell </sub>(K).”

**Sources:**

- [Guillermo Mantilla-Soler, Density questions on arithmetic equivalence (2021)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2106.01166v1)
- [Andrew V. Sutherland, Stronger arithmetic equivalence (2021)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.01956v4)

### Degree-zero divisors read Stark ranks

**Remember:** Taking degree zero subtracts one trivial character.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11R42 (Zeta functions and L-functions of number fields). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Let H/F be a finite abelian extension with group G, and S a finite set of places of F containing the infinite and ramified ones. Let Y have one basis vector per place of H above S, permuted by G, and let X be the vectors in Y whose coefficients sum to zero. So X is Y minus one trivial character, and Y contains χ once for each place in S whose decomposition group lies in the kernel of χ (our own count).

**Problem.** For a complex character χ of G, omit the finite prime factors at S from its Artin L-function. Its order of vanishing at zero equals the number of copies of χ in X.

**How the definition helps.** The order of vanishing at zero is the number of places in S whose decomposition group lies in the kernel of χ, minus one when χ is trivial, which is the multiplicity of χ in X. For infinite places this follows from the functional equation and nonvanishing at one. Each omitted finite Euler factor vanishes simply at zero exactly when χ is trivial on that decomposition group.

**Paper or page:** [Borel's rank theorem for Artin L-functions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2209.10044). It says: “Consider the Artin L-function L(s,ρ) attached to a Galois representation”

**Sources:**

- [Karl Rubin, A Stark conjecture over ℤ for abelian L-functions with multiple zeros (1996)](https://aif.centre-mersenne.org/articles/10.5802/aif.1505/)

### Mixed parities exclude critical integers

**Remember:** Mixed signs put a gamma pole at every integer.

*True by definition.* MSC 11R42 (Zeta functions and L-functions of number fields). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** For a finite-order Hecke character of a totally real field, the L-function has one gamma factor Γ((s+ε)/2) per real place, times a nonvanishing factor, with ε = 0 or 1 by the character’s sign there. An integer m is critical when no gamma factor has a pole at m and no dual gamma factor has a pole at 1−m. The factor Γ((s+ε)/2) has a pole exactly where s+ε is an even integer at most zero.

**Problem.** A finite-order Hecke character of a totally real field has no critical integers if both real signs occur.

**How the definition helps.** For m ≤ 0, the place whose ε makes m+ε even gives a pole at m (our own calculation). For m ≥ 1, the same test applies at 1−m ≤ 0, since the dual character has the same signs. So no integer is critical.

**Paper or page:** [Notes on the arithmetic of Hecke L-functions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2207.03399v1). It says: “If there exists $v<sub>1</sub>, v<sub>2</sub> \\in S<sub>r</sub>$, such that $\\epsilon <sub>v<sub>1</sub></sub> \\neq \\epsilon <sub>v<sub>2</sub></sub>$ then ${\\rm Crit}(L(s,\\chi )) = \\emptyset .$”

**Sources:**

- [A. Raghuram, Notes on the arithmetic of Hecke L-functions (2022)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2207.03399v1)

### Prime norms extend Brauer–Siegel

**Remember:** Count primes and places per unit of log discriminant.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11R42 (Zeta functions and L-functions of number fields). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** In a tower of number fields, measure counts against g = log√D, where D is the absolute discriminant. For each prime power q, φ(q) is the limit of the number of prime ideals with residue field of size q, divided by g. Likewise φ(ℝ) and φ(ℂ) are the limits of the numbers of real embeddings and of conjugate pairs of nonreal embeddings, divided by g.

**Problem.** For a strictly increasing tower of finite Galois extensions of ℚ with these limits, log(hR)/g tends to 1 + ∑ φ(q)log(q/(q−1)) − φ(ℝ)log 2 − φ(ℂ)log(2π), summed over prime powers. Here h is the class number and R is the regulator.

**How the definition helps.** The class number formula writes log(hR) as the logarithm of the zeta residue plus terms in D, r₁ and r₂, and the per-g counts give the limit of each term (our own comparison). Tsfasman and Vlăduţ prove the required limit for the zeta residues. All correction terms vanish when the degree divided by g tends to zero.

**Wikipedia:** [Brauer–Siegel theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brauer%E2%80%93Siegel_theorem). It says: “\[Kᵢ : ℚ\]/log\|Dᵢ\| → 0 as i → ∞.”

**Sources:**

- [M. A. Tsfasman and S. G. Vlăduţ, Infinite global fields and the generalized Brauer–Siegel theorem (2002)](https://doi.org/10.17323/1609-4514-2002-2-2-329-402)
- [A. I. Zykin, Asymptotic properties of the Dedekind zeta-function in families of number fields (2009), Theorem 1](https://doi.org/10.1070/RM2009v064n06ABEH004657)

### Primitive characters isolate a zeta quotient

**Remember:** Exclude each prime-order subgroup from the character kernel.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11R42 (Zeta functions and L-functions of number fields). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** For a cyclic extension E/F of degree m, a character of its Galois group is primitive if it is injective, that is, trivial on no subgroup of prime order. For each divisor d of m, let E(d) be the field fixed by the subgroup of order d, so the characters trivial on that subgroup are the characters of Gal(E(d)/F).

**Problem.** Multiply the Artin L-functions of all primitive characters. The result is the product over d dividing m of ζ<sub>E(d)</sub>(s) to the power μ(d), where μ is the Möbius function.

**How the definition helps.** Inclusion-exclusion over the subgroups of prime order, with Möbius signs, isolates the injective characters (our own explanation). By Artin’s factorization theorem, the L-functions of the characters trivial on the subgroup of order d multiply to ζ<sub>E(d)</sub>.

**Paper or page:** [Equivariant algebraic K-theory and Artin L-functions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.03578). It says: “Let χ : Gal(F′/F) ↪︎ ℂ× be a primitive (injective) character.”

**Sources:**

- [Elden Elmanto and Ningchuan Zhang, Equivariant algebraic K-theory and Artin L-functions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.03578)

### Reflection bounds fields by zeta values

**Remember:** Reflect past zero to expose a positive discriminant power.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11R42 (Zeta functions and L-functions of number fields). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Complete the Dedekind zeta function ζ<sub>K</sub>(s) by multiplying by exp((s/2)log D), by A(s) = π⁻ˢ⁄²Γ(s/2) to the power r₁, and by B(s) = 2(2π)⁻ˢΓ(s) to the power r₂. Here D is the absolute discriminant and r₁, r₂ count real and complex places. The functional equation then gives ζ<sub>K</sub>(s) as ζ<sub>K</sub>(1−s) times exp((½−s)log D) times a gamma ratio.

**Problem.** Fix a positive integer n, a negative real noninteger s and B &gt; 0; then only finitely many degree-n number fields, up to isomorphism, satisfy \|ζ<sub>K</sub>(s)\| ≤ B. For real s &gt; 1, infinitely many quadratic fields satisfy this inequality for one common B.

**How the definition helps.** For negative s the factor exp((½−s)log D) grows with D (our own calculation). For fixed degree the gamma ratio takes finitely many nonzero values and ζ<sub>K</sub>(1−s) ≥ 1, so the bound forces bounded D, and Hermite’s theorem gives finiteness. For s &gt; 1 each quadratic Euler product is at most ζ(s)².

**Paper or page:** [On the Northcott property of Dedekind zeta functions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2209.13854v1), [On the Northcott property of Dedekind zeta functions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2209.13854v1). It says: “The Northcott property does not hold”

**Sources:**

- [Xavier Généreux, Matilde Lalín, On the Northcott property of Dedekind zeta functions (2022)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2209.13854v1)

### Smoothing clears Stickelberger denominators

**Remember:** Smoothing multiplies by factors that clear denominators.

*Rules out counterexamples. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11R42 (Zeta functions and L-functions of number fields). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Let H/F be finite abelian with F totally real and H a CM field, and let S contain the infinite and ramified places. The Stickelberger element is the group-ring element whose χ-component is L(S,χ⁻¹,0), the L-value with Euler factors at S removed. Smoothing at a finite prime set T disjoint from S multiplies it by the factors 1 − Nv·σᵥ⁻¹ for v in T, with σᵥ the arithmetic Frobenius.

**Problem.** Suppose the only root of unity in H that is congruent to one modulo every prime above T is 1. Then the smoothed Stickelberger element has integer coefficients in the basis of Galois automorphisms.

**How the definition helps.** The smoothing factors cancel the denominators that roots of unity in H create, and the condition on T is what makes this work; Deligne–Ribet and Cassou-Noguès prove this integrality (our own summary). Without smoothing, denominators occur even for ℚ(i)/ℚ with S = {∞, 2}. There the trivial character gives zero and the other gives one half, so the element is (1−c)/4, with c complex conjugation (our own example).

**Paper or page:** [Two encounters with the p-adic Stark conjecture](https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.03299). It says: “The Brumer–Stark conjecture holds over ℤ\[1/2\].”

**Sources:**

- [Samit Dasgupta and Mahesh Kakde, On the Brumer–Stark conjecture (2023)](https://annals.math.princeton.edu/2023/197-1/p05)
- [Karl Rubin, A Stark conjecture over ℤ for abelian L-functions with multiple zeros (1996)](https://aif.centre-mersenne.org/articles/10.5802/aif.1505/)

### Cyclic induction reduces Chebotarev

**Remember:** Induce one cyclic point to its whole conjugacy class.

*True by definition.* MSC 11R44 (Distribution of prime ideals). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Let G be the Galois group of a finite extension of number fields, c an element with conjugacy class C, and H the cyclic subgroup generated by c. The indicator of c induced from H to G takes, at g, the number of x in G with x⁻¹gx = c, divided by \|H\|.

**Problem.** The induced function equals \|G\|/(\|C\|·\|H\|) on C and zero elsewhere. Consequently, prime counts weighted by the class indicator can be studied through abelian L-functions.

**How the definition helps.** The number of such x is \|G\|/\|C\| on C and zero elsewhere, by the orbit–stabilizer count, so dividing by \|H\| gives the formula (our own calculation). On cyclic H the indicator of c is a combination of one-dimensional characters. Artin induction and class field reciprocity identify the induced L-functions with Hecke L-functions over the fixed field of H.

**Paper or page:** [A new bound on the relative error in the Chebotarev density theorem](https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.01802v2). It says: “If $H$ be a subgroup of $G$ and $\\chi $ is a representation of $H$, then $L(s,\\operatorname{Ind} \_H<sup>G\\chi</sup> ,L/K)=L(s,\\chi ,L/L<sup>H</sup>)$.”

**Sources:**

- [Jesse Thorner and Zhuo Zhang, A new bound on the relative error in the Chebotarev density theorem](https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.01802v2)
- [Henryk Iwaniec and Emmanuel Kowalski, Analytic Number Theory (2004)](https://doi.org/10.1090/coll/053)

### Liouville weights reduce Landau’s theorem

**Remember:** Balanced factor parity is enough for Landau’s theorem.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11R44 (Distribution of prime ideals). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** The Liouville function of a number field K gives each nonzero integral ideal the weight 1 if it has an even number of prime ideal factors, counted with repetition, and −1 if odd.

**Problem.** Sum these weights over ideals of norm at most x. If the sum divided by x tends to zero, the number of prime ideals of norm at most x is asymptotic to x/log x.

**How the definition helps.** The weight turns balance between even and odd factor counts into cancellation in one sum (our own formulation). Burgin proves that this cancellation implies the prime ideal theorem, and that the cancellation holds.

**Paper or page:** [A New Elementary Proof of Landau's Prime Ideal Theorem, and Associated Results](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.08565v4). It says: “i.e., that Ω is equidistributed modulo 2.”

**Sources:**

- [Alex Burgin, A New Elementary Proof of Landau's Prime Ideal Theorem, and Associated Results](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.08565v4)

### Null boundaries permit infinite Chebotarev

**Remember:** A null boundary lets finite-level sets squeeze X from both sides.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11R44 (Distribution of prime ideals). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Give the profinite Galois group G of an infinite Galois extension its Haar probability measure, the translation-invariant one. Take a set X stable under conjugation whose boundary has measure zero. Then X lies between two finite unions of cosets of open normal subgroups whose measures differ by as little as one likes.

**Problem.** Let L be a possibly infinite Galois extension of a number field K, ramified at only finitely many primes. The proportion of primes with Frobenius in X tends to its Haar measure as the residue field size bound grows.

**How the definition helps.** Finite Chebotarev applies to both squeezing sets, so the upper and lower densities of X lie within any ε of its measure (our own argument). The boundary condition is needed: in the cyclotomic ℤ₃-extension of ℚ, the countable set of Frobenius elements has measure zero but contains the Frobenius of every unramified prime (our own counterexample).

**Wikipedia:** [Chebotarev density theorem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chebotarev_density_theorem). It says: “Let X be a subset of G that is stable under conjugation and whose boundary has Haar measure zero.”

**Sources:**

- [N. Tschebotareff, Die Bestimmung der Dichtigkeit einer Menge von Primzahlen, welche zu einer gegebenen Substitutionsklasse gehören (1926)](https://doi.org/10.1007/BF01206606)

### Odd torsion removes norm obstructions

**Remember:** Odd torsion cannot see an obstruction of order two.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11R70 (K-theory of global fields), 19D50. arXiv math.KT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** For a finite extension L/F of number fields, the norm on K-groups comes from viewing L-vector spaces as F-vector spaces, and its p-primary part acts on the elements killed by a power of p. Real places of F can stop it from being onto, through classes of order two (our own explanation).

**Problem.** For i ≥ 1 and odd p, the norm in degree 2i maps onto the p-primary torsion of F from that of L. For ℚ(i) over ℚ, surjectivity fails on the 2-primary torsion in degree two.

**How the definition helps.** An obstruction of order two is invisible to odd-primary torsion, and Lim proves the surjectivity for odd p. In our own example, the symbol {−1,−1} in K₂(ℚ) has order two and stays nonzero over ℝ. Norms from ℂ vanish under the real sign symbol, so this class does not come from ℚ(i).

**Paper or page:** [Norm principle for even K-groups of number fields](https://arxiv.org/abs/2109.06482). It says: “is surjective for every odd prime p.”

**Sources:**

- [Meng Fai Lim, Norm Principle for Even K-groups of Number Fields](https://doi.org/10.1007/s40840-022-01413-x)

### Exceptional local field extensions give the ramification bound for exceptional covers

**Remember:** An exceptional cover gives a bijection over infinitely many finite extensions.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove. Confidence: medium.* MSC 11S15 (Ramification and extension theory), 11G20. arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Let X→Y be a finite separable cover of smooth geometrically integral curves over 𝔽q. It is exceptional if the induced map on 𝔽qᵏ-points is bijective for infinitely many positive integers k.

**Problem.** For an exceptional cover X→Y over 𝔽q, the ramification index at each 𝔽q-rational point of X is coprime to q−1.

**How the definition helps.** Completing at a rational point produces an exceptional local extension by Theorem 3.3. Its degree is the ramification index because the residue fields agree (our own explanation). Theorem 2.1 makes that degree coprime to q−1.

**Paper or page:** [Exceptional extensions of local fields and the Carlitz--Wan conjecture](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.12877v1). It says: “As a consequence, we obtain three new proofs, using quite different tools, of a theorem of Guralnick and Müller about ramification indices in exceptional maps between curves over 𝔽q.”

**Sources:**

- [Zhiguo Ding, Wei Xiong, Qifan Zhang, Exceptional extensions of local fields and the Carlitz--Wan conjecture, arXiv:2505.12877v1 (2025)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.12877v1)

### Logarithmic coordinates diagonalize graded differentiation

**Remember:** In the basis dt/t, differentiating a pole multiplies its coefficient by minus its order.

*True by definition.* MSC 11S15 (Ramification and extension theory). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Over the Laurent series field k((t)), with k perfect of characteristic p, write differentials as multiples of dt/t, and filter functions and differentials by pole order at most n. In this basis d(t⁻ⁿ) = −n t⁻ⁿ dt/t, so differentiation keeps the pole order.

**Problem.** On the quotient that retains only the coefficient of pole order n, differentiation acts by multiplication by −n in the basis dt/t.

**How the definition helps.** So on the pole-order-n quotient, differentiation multiplies the coefficient by −n, and it vanishes when p divides n (our own calculation). In the basis dt the order would shift by one. The cited lemma also proves that the identification is independent of the parameter.

**Paper or page:** [Ramification groups of some finite Galois extensions of maximal nilpotency class over local fields of positive characteristic](https://arxiv.org/abs/2102.07928v4). It says: “The derivation d induces a morphism ∂ : Grₙ K → Grₙ Ω¹ₖ. We have ∂ = −n ⋅ μ.”

**Sources:**

- [Ramification groups of some finite Galois extensions of maximal nilpotency class over local fields of positive characteristic](https://arxiv.org/abs/2102.07928v4)

### Drinfeld division points detect norms

**Remember:** The symbol is zero when β’s automorphism fixes the division point.

*True by definition.* MSC 11S31 (Class field theory; p-adic formal groups). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Over a local field L of positive characteristic, take a formal Drinfeld module, whose scalar multiplications are additive power series, with stable reduction of height one as in the cited proposition, and assume L contains all points killed by the chosen division map. For α in the maximal ideal, choose a division point ξ mapping to α. For nonzero β in L, the symbol is σ(ξ) − ξ, where σ is the automorphism that local reciprocity attaches to β.

**Problem.** The formal Drinfeld norm residue symbol is zero exactly when β is a norm from the field obtained by adjoining ξ.

**How the definition helps.** The symbol is zero exactly when σ fixes ξ, that is, acts trivially on L(ξ) (our own). Conjugates of ξ differ from ξ by division torsion, which lies in L, so L(ξ)/L is abelian (our own). Local reciprocity says the elements acting trivially on an abelian extension are exactly its norms (our own).

**Paper or page:** [The norm residue symbol for formal Drinfeld modules](https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.10368v1). It says: “β is a norm from L(ξ)”

**Sources:**

- [Marwa Ala Eddine, The norm residue symbol for formal Drinfeld modules](https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.10368v1)

### Drinfeld symbols commute with norms

**Remember:** An Artin action upstairs restricts to the action of the norm downstairs.

*True by definition.* MSC 11S31 (Class field theory; p-adic formal groups). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Over a local field L of positive characteristic, take a formal Drinfeld module, whose scalar multiplications are additive power series, with stable reduction of height one as in the cited proposition, and assume L contains all points killed by the chosen division map. For α in the maximal ideal, choose a division point ξ mapping to α. For nonzero β in L, the symbol is σ(ξ) − ξ, where σ is the automorphism that local reciprocity attaches to β.

**Problem.** Let M/L be finite separable, let α belong to the maximal ideal of L, and let β be nonzero in M. The symbol over M equals the symbol over L evaluated at α and the norm of β.

**How the definition helps.** The same ξ serves over M and over L, so the comparison is a restriction of automorphisms (our own). Local reciprocity says the automorphism attached to β over M restricts to the one attached to its norm over L (our own). So both move ξ by the same amount (our own).

**Paper or page:** [The norm residue symbol for formal Drinfeld modules](https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.10368v1). It says: “Then (\\alpha ,\\beta )<sub>M,n</sub> =(\\alpha ,\\operatorname {N}<sub>M\|L</sub>(\\beta ))<sub>L,n</sub>.”

**Sources:**

- [Marwa Ala Eddine, The norm residue symbol for formal Drinfeld modules](https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.10368v1)

### Deleting one factor restores continuity

**Remember:** Drop the Euler factor at p; its power of p jumps.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11S40 (Zeta functions and L-functions), 11M41. arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Fix an odd prime p, and for each positive multiple n of p−1 set A(n) = (1−pⁿ⁻¹)ζ(1−n), the zeta value with its Euler factor at p removed. The removed factor is the problem: along integers that tend p-adically to n, the power pⁿ⁻¹ tends to zero, not to its value at n.

**Problem.** These corrected values extend continuously in the p-adic variable n away from n=0, where the extension has a pole. For p=5, the original values have no continuous extension at n=4.

**How the definition helps.** Kubota–Leopoldt interpolation extends A continuously away from the pole at n = 0 (our own explanation). For p = 5, the integers n = 4+4·5ᵏ tend 5-adically to 4 and 5ⁿ⁻¹ tends to zero, so ζ(1−n) tends to A(4) = (1−5³)ζ(−3). Since ζ(−3) ≠ 0, this differs from ζ(−3) (our own calculation).

**Wikipedia:** [P-adic L-function](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/P-adic_L-function). It says: “except that the Euler factor at p is removed, otherwise it would not be p-adically continuous.”

**Sources:** none listed. No primary source with a working link was found.

### Regularization bounds Bernoulli weights

**Remember:** Subtract the rescaled Bernoulli weight to cancel the denominator N.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11S80 (Other analytic theory (analogues of beta and gamma functions, p-adic integration, etc.)). arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Fix an odd prime p and positive integers d and c, with c ≥ 2 coprime to dp. At level N = dpⁿ, the Bernoulli weight of a residue a, taken with 0 ≤ a &lt; N, is a/N − 1/2, which can be p-adically large because pⁿ divides N. The regularized weight subtracts c times the weight of b, the representative of c⁻¹a modulo N, which gives (a−cb)/N + (c−1)/2.

**Problem.** For odd p the regularized distribution is a bounded p-adic measure, even though the original Bernoulli distribution is not.

**How the definition helps.** Both terms are p-adic integers, since cb ≡ a modulo N and p is odd, so the regularized weights are bounded (our own calculation). They still add under subdivision, because Bernoulli weights do and multiplication by c permutes the subdivisions. For d = a = 1 the original weights have unbounded p-adic size (our own example).

**Paper or page:** [Dirichlet Series Expansions of p-adic L-Functions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2102.02851v3). It says: “Let p be a prime, c, d ∈ ℕ, and c ≥ 2 such that (c, dp) = 1.”

**Sources:**

- [Dirichlet Series Expansions of p-adic L-Functions](https://arxiv.org/abs/2102.02851v3)

### Convolution lifts Gaussian periods

**Remember:** Fourier transformation turns the lift of periods into a power of Gauss sums.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11T22 (Cyclotomy), 11T24. arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Let e ≥ 2 divide q−1, and label the cosets of the eth powers in 𝔽q× by ℤ/eℤ. The Gaussian period function sends each label to the sum of a fixed nontrivial additive character ψ over that coset; over the degree-n extension, label elements by the coset of their norm and use ψ composed with the trace. Its Fourier transform over ℤ/eℤ consists of Gauss sums (our own explanation).

**Problem.** Over the degree n extension, the Gaussian period function equals the n-fold cyclic convolution of the base function times the sign (−1)ⁿ⁻¹.

**How the definition helps.** Davenport–Hasse lifts each Gauss sum to (−1)ⁿ⁻¹ times its nth power. Fourier transformation turns cyclic convolution into multiplication, so inversion gives the stated convolution power.

**Paper or page:** [Davenport and Hasse's theorems and lifts of multiplication matrices of Gaussian periods](https://arxiv.org/abs/2105.14872). It says: “is the n-fold product of ηᵣ with respect to the convolution product.”

**Sources:**

- [Akinari Hoshi and Kazuki Kanai, Davenport and Hasse's theorems and lifts of multiplication matrices of Gaussian periods](https://arxiv.org/abs/2105.14872)

### Conductor bounds complete trace errors

**Remember:** One conductor controls both the size and the number of error terms.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11T23 (Exponential sums), 14F20. arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Let F be a middle-extension ℓ-adic sheaf on the affine line over 𝔽q, with ℓ prime to q, so that at each singular point its stalk is the local inertia invariants. Its conductor c is its generic rank plus the sum of 1 + Swanₓ(F) over the singular points on the projective line, where Swan measures wild ramification. So c bounds both the number of singular points and, through the Euler characteristic formula, the size of first compactly supported cohomology (our own).

**Problem.** Assume all Frobenius eigenvalues at closed points of the largest locally constant open set U have complex modulus one. Sum the Frobenius traces of F over the whole affine line over 𝔽q. This differs from the Frobenius trace on second compactly supported geometric cohomology of U with coefficients F by O(c²√q), with an absolute constant.

**How the definition helps.** The trace formula writes the sum as the trace on second cohomology plus a trace on first cohomology, corrected at the singular points (our own explanation). The Euler characteristic formula bounds the first cohomology by O(c²), and Deligne bounds each of its eigenvalues by √q. Each of the at most c omitted points contributes at most the rank.

**Wikipedia:** [Grothendieck trace formula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grothendieck_trace_formula). It says: “Taking logarithmic derivatives of both formal power series produces a statement on sums of traces for each finite field extension E of the base field k:”

**Sources:**

- [Deligne, La conjecture de Weil II](https://www.numdam.org/item/PMIHES_1980__52__137_0/)
- [Fouvry, Kowalski, Michel and Sawin, Lectures on applied ℓ-adic cohomology](https://people.math.ethz.ch/~kowalski/applied-ell-adic.pdf)

### Disjoint characters preserve hypergeometric purity

**Remember:** Disjoint lists prevent a character from canceling a parameter.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11T23 (Exponential sums), 14F20. arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Two length-n lists of multiplicative characters of 𝔽q, with n ≥ 1, are disjoint when no character occurs in both. The hypergeometric sum at t runs over nonzero tuples x and y with ∏xᵢ = t∏yᵢ, multiplying the first characters at the xᵢ, the inverse second characters at the yᵢ, and ψ(Σxᵢ − Σyᵢ), with ψ a nontrivial additive character. Disjointness stops a character in one list from cancelling the same character in the other.

**Problem.** For disjoint lists and t different from zero and one, the sum is a signed trace of n eigenvalues. Each eigenvalue has modulus q raised to (2n − 1)/2, so the sum has modulus at most n times that number.

**How the definition helps.** For disjoint lists, Katz’s hypergeometric sheaf theorem gives n eigenvalues, all of the stated modulus. Without disjointness the size can drop. Our own example takes n = 1 and the trivial character in both lists, so the sum is the sum of ψ((t−1)y) over nonzero y, which is −1.

**Paper or page:** [Traces of Hecke Operators via Hypergeometric Character Sums](https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.02918). It says: “are algebraic numbers and have the same absolute value”

**Sources:**

- [Katz, Exponential Sums and Differential Equations, Chapter 8](https://web.math.princeton.edu/~nmk/wholebookcorrms.pdf)

### Fourier sheaves exclude completion spikes

**Remember:** Exclude additive characters to keep Fourier mass spread out.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11T23 (Exponential sums), 11L26. arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Take a middle-extension sheaf on the affine line over 𝔽ₚ, extended across missing points by local invariants, whose Frobenius eigenvalues on the regular part have absolute value one. It is a Fourier sheaf if no irreducible piece over the algebraic closure comes from an additive character x ↦ ψ(ax), with a = 0 included. Those pieces are exactly the ones whose Fourier transform concentrates at a single frequency.

**Problem.** Let K be its Frobenius trace function, and let its conductor c be the rank plus the sum of 1 + Swan over all singularities, infinity included. On each integer interval of length at most p, the sum of K has modulus O(c²√p log p), with an absolute constant.

**How the definition helps.** Completing the sum pairs the Fourier coefficients of K with those of the interval, and for a Fourier sheaf the applied cohomology lectures bound every coefficient of K, so no single frequency carries the sum. The interval’s coefficients give the log p factor (our own explanation). Our own counterexample is the constant function, whose sum over a full interval is p.

**Wikipedia:** [Quadratic residue](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Quadratic_residue). It says: “for any nonprincipal Dirichlet character χ(n) modulo q and any integers M and N,”

**Sources:**

- [Fouvry, Kowalski, Michel and Sawin, Lectures on applied ℓ-adic cohomology](https://people.math.ethz.ch/~kowalski/applied-ell-adic.pdf)

### Frobenius traces give Kloosterman recurrences

**Remember:** Each Kloosterman sum is minus a trace of a 2×2 Frobenius power.

*True by definition.* MSC 11T23 (Exponential sums), 14F20. arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Fix a nonzero a in 𝔽q and a nontrivial additive character ψ, and let S(n) be the sum of ψ(Tr(ax+1/x)) over nonzero x in the degree-n extension. By the trace formula, S(n) = −tr(Fⁿ), where F is Frobenius on the two-dimensional first compactly supported cohomology of the punctured line with the Artin–Schreier sheaf of ax+1/x (our own description).

**Problem.** Write S(n) for the sum in degree n. For n ≥ 1, it satisfies S(n+2) = −S(1)S(n+1) − bS(n), where b = (S(1)² + S(2))/2.

**How the definition helps.** A sequence −tr(Fⁿ) for a 2×2 matrix F obeys the recurrence of its characteristic polynomial, with b = det F (our own deduction). The cited calculation gives dimension two in degree one and zero elsewhere. Since S(1) = −tr F and S(2) = −tr F², det F = (S(1)² + S(2))/2.

**Paper or page:** [Matrix Kloosterman sums](https://arxiv.org/abs/2109.00762). It says: “\\\[\\dim H<sup>i<sub>c</sub></sup>(\\mathbb {A}<sup>1\\setminus</sup> \\mathbb {A}<sup>0</sup>,f\_\\alpha )=\\left \\{\\begin {array}{ll}2, &amp; \\mathrm {if\~} i=1,\\\\ 0, &amp; \\mathrm {if\~} i\\neq 1\\end {array}\\right .\\\]”

**Sources:**

- [Márton Erdélyi and Árpád Tóth, Matrix Kloosterman sums](https://arxiv.org/abs/2109.00762)

### Geometric nonisomorphism forces small correlations

**Remember:** Over the algebraic closure, no common piece means no main term.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11T23 (Exponential sums), 14F20. arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Take two locally constant systems F and G of ℓ-adic vector spaces on an open U of the affine line over 𝔽q, with ℓ different from the characteristic, both irreducible over the algebraic closure. They are geometrically distinct if they are not isomorphic over the algebraic closure. By Schur’s lemma there is then no nonzero invariant map between them, so their correlation has no main term (our own explanation).

**Problem.** Assume both systems have weight zero, meaning all pointwise Frobenius eigenvalues have complex absolute value one. For geometrically distinct systems, sum the trace of F times the conjugate trace of G over U(𝔽𝓆). The modulus is O(√q), with constant depending on the ranks, omitted points and local ramification.

**How the definition helps.** With no invariant maps, the top cohomology term of the trace formula vanishes, and Deligne’s bound controls the rest (our own). For example, constant rank-one systems with Frobenius scalars 1 and −1 give a correlation of modulus q on the affine line. They become isomorphic over the algebraic closure.

**Wikipedia:** [Grothendieck trace formula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grothendieck_trace_formula). It says: “where the cohomology groups are replaced by cohomology with coefficients in the sheaf.”

**Sources:**

- [Fouvry, Kowalski, Michel and Sawin, Lectures on applied ℓ-adic cohomology](https://people.math.ethz.ch/~kowalski/applied-ell-adic.pdf)

### Good twists erase boundary terms

**Remember:** A good twist leaves no cohomology at zero or infinity.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11T23 (Exponential sums), 14F20. arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Let F be a locally constant system of r-dimensional ℓ-adic spaces on the line with zero removed over 𝔽q, with ℓ prime to q, and twist it by the one-dimensional system of a multiplicative character χ. Call χ good if, for the twist, extension by zero to the projective line agrees with derived direct image. The two differ only through local cohomology at zero and infinity.

**Problem.** Over any finite extension field, at most 2r multiplicative characters fail this test. For every good character, ordinary cohomology of the twist agrees with its cohomology with compact supports.

**How the definition helps.** Agreement of the two extensions gives the same cohomology with and without compact supports (our own explanation). A bad twist must cancel a local tame character on the subspace fixed by wild inertia at zero or at infinity. Each such subspace has dimension at most r, so at most 2r characters fail.

**Paper or page:** [Wasserstein metrics and quantitative equidistribution of exponential sums over finite fields](https://arxiv.org/abs/2505.22059). It says: “let 𝒳ᵢ be the set of characters χ : kᵢ× → ℂ× which are “good” for ℱᵢ(1/2)\[1\]”

**Sources:**

- [Katz, Convolution and Equidistribution](https://web.math.princeton.edu/~nmk/mellin398.pdf)

### Newton polytopes bound torus sums

**Remember:** No face missing zero may have a critical point on the torus.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11T23 (Exponential sums), 14F20. arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** For a Laurent polynomial f in m variables, let Δ be the convex hull of zero and its exponent vectors. Then f is nondegenerate if, for every face of Δ missing zero, the part h of f on that face has no point with all coordinates nonzero, over the algebraic closure, where all xᵢ∂h/∂xᵢ vanish.

**Problem.** Assume Δ has dimension m and f is nondegenerate. For any nontrivial additive character ψ of 𝔽𝓆, sum ψ(f(x)) over tuples of nonzero field elements. The modulus is at most √(qᵐ) times the volume of Δ measured in units of 1/m! of a lattice cube.

**How the definition helps.** Nondegeneracy lets the Adolphson–Sperber theorem put all cohomology in one degree, with dimension the normalized volume (our own explanation). Deligne bounds each eigenvalue by √(qᵐ). In odd characteristic (x+y)² fails the test along y = −x, and its sum over nonzero x, y has size about q√q (our own example).

**Paper or page:** [Robba's method on exponential sums](https://arxiv.org/abs/2109.02825). It says: “Suppose that f is nondegenerate. Then H(i)=aᵢ for all integer i≥0. Moreover, we have H(k)=0 for k&gt;nM, ∑ₖ₌₀ⁿᴹ H(k)=n! Vol(Δ(f)).”

**Sources:**

- [Robba's method on exponential sums](https://arxiv.org/abs/2109.02825)

### Odd multiplicities force symplectic cancellation

**Remember:** An odd number of standard symplectic factors cannot contain a fixed vector.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11T23 (Exponential sums), 14F20. arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Take a list of fractional linear maps x ↦ (ax+b)/(cx+d) over 𝔽ₚ, and call it normal if some map occurs an odd number of times. With symplectic monodromy, the central element −I then acts by −1 on that map’s tensor factor, so the product has no invariant vectors (our own explanation).

**Problem.** Let F be a weight-zero middle-extension sheaf over 𝔽ₚ with full symplectic geometric monodromy in its standard representation. Assume only the identity fractional linear map over the algebraic closure preserves F up to a rank-one twist. For a normal list, the product of transformed traces sums to O(√p) over finite inputs away from poles.

**How the definition helps.** No invariants means no main term, and Deligne’s bound gives O(√p), with a constant depending on list length, rank and ramification. The hypothesis on F makes distinct transforms independent. Repeating one map twice instead lets the symplectic pairing contribute an invariant.

**Wikipedia:** [Grothendieck trace formula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grothendieck_trace_formula). It says: “where the cohomology groups are replaced by cohomology with coefficients in the sheaf.”

**Sources:**

- [Fouvry, Kowalski and Michel, A study in sums of products](https://people.math.ethz.ch/~kowalski/sums-of-products.pdf)

### Signed multiplicities force special linear cancellation

**Remember:** Count ordinary factors positively and conjugate factors negatively, modulo the rank.

*Rules out counterexamples.* MSC 11T23 (Exponential sums), 14F20. arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Give each occurrence of a fractional linear map x ↦ (ax+b)/(cx+d), with ad−bc ≠ 0, a sign: plus for its trace and minus for its conjugate trace. The list is r-normal if some map has signed multiplicity, plus count minus minus count, not divisible by r. A central scalar of SL(r) then acts on that map’s factor by a nontrivial power, so there are no invariants (our own explanation).

**Problem.** Let F be a weight-zero middle extension over 𝔽ₚ, with p &gt; r ≥ 3 and geometric monodromy SL(r) in its standard representation. Geometrically, only the identity fractional linear map preserves F up to twist, and none carries F to its dual up to twist. For an r-normal list, the sum over 𝔽ₚ away from poles of the product of transformed traces, conjugated at negative signs, is O(√p).

**How the definition helps.** No invariants means no main term, and Deligne’s bound gives O(√p), with a constant depending on list length, rank and ramification. The hypotheses on F make the distinct transforms independent. A trace paired with its own conjugate has signed multiplicity zero, and the identity map is then an invariant.

**Wikipedia:** [Grothendieck trace formula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grothendieck_trace_formula). It says: “where the cohomology groups are replaced by cohomology with coefficients in the sheaf.”

**Sources:**

- [Fouvry, Kowalski and Michel, A study in sums of products](https://people.math.ethz.ch/~kowalski/sums-of-products.pdf)

### Character spaces isolate Jacobi factors

**Remember:** Each character pair labels its own Frobenius eigenvalue.

*Makes the theorem clean to state or prove.* MSC 11T24 (Other character sums and Gauss sums), 14G10. arXiv math.NT, math.AG. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** On the smooth projective Fermat curve xᵐ+yᵐ = 1 over 𝔽q, with m a prime power dividing q−1, pairs of mth roots of unity act by scaling x and y. Split first ℓ-adic étale cohomology over the algebraic closure, ℓ prime to q, into eigenspaces for this action, and label each by a pair of characters of 𝔽q× through x ↦ x raised to (q−1)/m (our own convention). Frobenius commutes with the scalings, which are defined over 𝔽q, so it acts on each eigenspace.

**Problem.** Each pair χ, ψ of nontrivial multiplicative characters of 𝔽q with orders dividing m and nontrivial product labels a one-dimensional space. Frobenius acts there by −∑χ(x)ψ(1 − x), summing over 𝔽q and extending the characters by zero at zero.

**How the definition helps.** Splitting by characters attaches each Frobenius eigenvalue to one character pair (our own explanation). The dimensions, and the identification of the eigenvalues with Jacobi sums, still need the cohomological point-count formula.

**Paper or page:** [On the variation of the Frobenius in a non abelian Iwasawa tower](https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.16774). It says: “The eigenvalues of $\\sigma \_q$ on the eigenspace $M<sub>n</sub>(\\eta )$ are given by the Jacobi sum 

\\\[ -J<sub>q</sub>(\\chi \_1,\\chi \_2) = -\\sum <sub>x \\in \\mathbb F<sub>q</sub></sub>\\chi \_1(x)\\chi \_2(1-x). \\\]”

**Sources:**

- [Asvin G, On the variation of the Frobenius in a non abelian Iwasawa tower](https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.16774)

### Frobenius preserves strict Waring numbers

**Remember:** Strip off Frobenius before counting the needed powers.

*True by definition.* MSC 11T55 (Arithmetic theory of polynomial rings over finite fields), 11P05, 11P55. arXiv math.NT. Level 4: research.

**Definition.** Over a polynomial ring in t over a finite field of characteristic p, let J(k) be the set of finite sums of kth powers. G(k) is the least s such that every m in J(k) of large degree is a sum of s kth powers with bases of degree at most ⌈deg(m)/k⌉, plus one if k divides deg(m) and the leading coefficient of m is not a sum of kth powers in the field. When p divides k, each kth power is the Frobenius image uᵖ of a (k/p)th power (our own).

**Problem.** For a positive integer k divisible by p, G(k) = G(k/p), with G(1) = 1.

**How the definition helps.** Frobenius is injective, sends sums of (k/p)th powers to sums of kth powers with the same bases, and every sum of kth powers arises this way (our own calculation). It multiplies degrees by p, which keeps the degree bound, and maps the field’s power-sum sets onto each other. So both sides need the same number of summands, and G(1) = 1 since m is itself a first power.

**nLab:** [Frobenius morphism](https://ncatlab.org/nlab/show/Frobenius+morphism). It says: “the characteristic of the field is used to show (a + b)ᵖ = aᵖ + bᵖ.”

**Sources:**

- [Y.-R. Liu and T. D. Wooley, Waring’s problem in function fields, §1](https://www.math.purdue.edu/~twooley/publ/wpfqt110809.pdf)
